title: Multi-scale haplotype signatures distinguish among evolutionary processes
authors: Khan, M., DeGiorgio, M., Arnab, S. P., Santander, C., Amin, M. R.
abstract: Natural selection embeds distinct genomic signatures as populations adapt to environmental pressures. Machine learning approaches, particularly deep neural networks, have emerged as powerful tools to detect adaptive signatures from genomic data. While machine learning has dramatically improved our ability to extract these signals from sequence variation, distinguishing among multiple evolutionary processes remains challenging. We introduce SHADES, a deep learning framework that employs information about sequence differences and their frequencies at various spatial resolutions to capture evolutionary signatures at different genomic scales. We found that SHADES has the capacity to distinguish among neutrality, selective sweeps, balancing selection, and adaptive introgression and outperformed several contemporary methods evaluated for both classification accuracy and power. In addition, SHADES remained robust to a number of confounding factors, with only modest changes in classification performance. Furthermore, application of SHADES to empirical haplotypic variation from European humans recovered previously reported signals for selective sweeps, balancing selection, and adaptive introgression, while also identifying novel genes broadly involved in immune defense, inflammatory regulation, and epithelial barrier biology.

title: Dynamic evolution of diaphorin biosynthetic genes against a background of genome conservation in Profftella
authors: Yasuda, Y., Piel, J., Malenovsky, I., Gjonov, I., Hirose, Y., Nakabachi, A.
abstract: The Asian citrus psyllid Diaphorina citri (Insecta: Hemiptera), a major agricultural pest, harbors the unusual obligate bacterial symbiont "Candidatus Profftella armatura" (Profftella), which is intimately integrated with its host yet devotes a remarkably large proportion of its highly reduced genome to the production of diaphorin, a bioactive polyketide. To gain insight into the evolution of this distinctive symbiont, we determined the genomes of Profftella and the co-resident nutritional symbiont "Candidatus Carsonella ruddii" (Carsonella) from Diaphorina lycii and compared them with previously characterized counterparts from D. citri and D. cf. continua. The Profftella and Carsonella chromosomes from D. lycii were 471 and 174 kb, respectively, and Profftella harbored an 8-kb plasmid. Genome organization and gene content were highly conserved across the three lineages. The diaphorin biosynthetic system likewise retained its overall organization, consistent with an important role for diaphorin in the Diaphorina symbiotic system. Remarkably, however, pronounced lineage-specific structural variation was observed in diaphorin synthases DipP and DipT, encoded by two of the 20 diaphorin biosynthetic genes. These synthases contained three extensively amplified tandem arrays of acyl carrier protein (ACP) domains that carry growing polyketide intermediates, with up to seven copies compared with one or two at corresponding positions in the related pederin synthases. All three regions of tandem ACP repeats showed copy-number variation among the Profftella lineages. This variation indicates that ACP amplification remains evolutionarily dynamic despite the otherwise highly constrained symbiotic genome. Together, our findings show that even highly integrated obligate symbionts retain evolutionary flexibility in specialized functional systems.

title: In silico codon optimization and phylogenetic analysis of various strains of Sapovirus
abstract: Introduction: Sapovirus (SaV) is an emerging enteric pathogen of rising public health importance, responsible for acute gastroenteritis in people of all ages and most often in children under five. Its genome is approximately 7.1-7.7 kb long, positive-sense, single-stranded RNA, comprising two principal open reading frames; processing of the ORF1 product yields seven non-structural proteins and the major capsid protein VP1, while ORF2 encodes the minor structural protein VP2. Given the absence of therapies or an approved vaccine and the low yields of recombinant capsid protein, improving expression remains a priority. Methods: VP1 and VP2 sequences from twelve selected human SaV strains were aligned, phylogenetic trees were reconstructed by maximum likelihood method under the Tamura-Nei model with 1,000 bootstrap replicates, and both genes were optimized in silico for Escherichia coli using the OPTIMIZER. Results: The trees resolved three genogroups, GI, GII and GV, each strain placed alike by both genes. Every optimized sequence reached the ceiling value of 1.000 for the codon adaptation index (CAI). Mean CAI and GC% increased by 3.07 (207.0%) and 1.11 (11.1%) fold for VP1, and 3.11 (210.9%) and 1.14 (14.1%) fold for VP2, while AT% decreased. All changes were statistically significant (p < 0.001) and the encoded amino acid sequences were unaltered. Conclusion: Our findings indicate that Optmization raised host-matched codon usage in both capsid genes with no truncated proteins produced. The redesigned VP1 and VP2 sequences warrant further investigation as potential candidates for biotherapeutic and vaccine development. KEYWORDS: Sapovirus,CAI, codon optimization, VP1 capsid protein, GC content, DNA, phylogenetic analysis, vaccines

title: Single-base mapping of m6A in lncRNAs reveals a distinct landscape linked to transposable elements and RNA processing
authors: Kwon, E., Li, Z., Zhou, C.
abstract: N6-methyladenosine (m6A) is the most abundant internal RNA modification with established roles in mRNA metabolism. Although m6A has been characterized in several well-known long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs), its transcriptome-wide landscape and roles remain poorly understood. Here, we characterized the m6A landscape of lncRNAs at single-base resolution, identified m6A deposition-associated features, and investigated potential roles of m6A in lncRNA processing. Unlike in mRNAs, m6A sites are broadly distributed along lncRNAs. We further found that these differences in m6A patterns between lncRNAs and mRNAs may reflect contributions from transposable element-derived sequence to motif availability and local RNA structure, together with splicing-related constraints on m6A deposition near exon junctions. Additionally, m6A may be relevant to the regulation of lncRNA polyadenylation. Together, these findings define the single-base-resolution m6A landscape in lncRNAs, and connect lncRNA methylation to transposable elements, RNA structure, splicing, and polyadenylation. This study broadens our understanding of m6A in the lncRNA epitranscriptome.

title: Genomic expansion in the dark: A repeat-rich genome of a cave-dwelling remipede sheds light on the evolution of the hexapod sister group.
authors: Borda, E., Sharma, P. P., Santibanez-Lopez, C. E., Ballesteros, J. A., Garcia-Bernal, A., Calderon-Gutierrez, F., Simoes, N., Yanez-Rivera, B., Llera-Herrera, R.
abstract: Remipedes are enigmatic blind, venomous crustaceans endemic to anchialine cave ecosystems (aphotic, hypoxic subterranean environments) and occupy a pivotal phylogenomic position within Pancrustacea as the sister group to Hexapoda. A high-quality genome assembly has long proven elusive for this taxon, due to accessibility challenges and the fragility of remipedes when removed from their habitat. Here we present a highly contiguous, chromosome-level genome assembly for the remipede Xibalbanus tulumensis (Xibalbanidae) spanning 8.05 Gb on 30 chromosome-scale scaffolds, placing it among the largest arthropod genomes reported to date. The protein-coding gene repertoire was highly conserved, with over 97% of arthropod orthologs recovered, and microRNA surveys showed a high level of completeness (94%) relative to pancrustacean genomes. Genome expansion appears to be driven primarily by proliferation of intronic and repetitive elements, which comprise ~71% of the genome. Comparative genomic analyses reveal extensive gene family turnover, with relatively few families showing lineage-specific expansions and contractions. Venom-associated gene families included the remipede-specific Xibalbins, while significant expansion and episodic positive selection affected other venom-associated gene families. Comparative analysis of macrosynteny revealed that the remipede genome retains the signature of ancient fusion-with-mixing events that unite Pancrustacea and Allotriocarida, with considerable similarity in the chromosome architecture of remipedes and basally branching insect orders. Our findings provide the first genomic framework for Remipedia and reveal a highly expanded, repeat-rich genome that retains deep phylogenetic signals in its architecture, despite being adapted to a highly unusual environment.

title: ChAI-Net learns a regulatory code for chromatin co-accessibility
authors: Lee, J., Zhang, K., Shurberg, E., Ramani, V. S., Pollard, K. S.
abstract: The regulation of chromatin accessibility is critical for cell function and identity. Advances in single-molecule long-read footprinting have enabled near-nucleotide-resolution readout of chromatin fiber organization, capturing both coordination of transcription factor (TF) binding and variation in nucleosome positioning previously obscured by bulk methods. Here we combine this technique with deep learning to study how protein-DNA interactions are coordinated within different types of cis-regulatory elements in mouse embryonic stem cells. First, we quantify the frequency with which pairs of positions are simultaneously accessible on individual molecules. Then, we train ChAI-Net, a neural network that predicts these locus-specific chromatin co-accessibility maps from the underlying DNA sequence. Through model interpretation and in silico experiments, we show that ChAI-Net learns unique combinations of sequence motifs underlying co-accessibility within enhancers, promoters, and CTCF-bound sites. Many of these motifs are missed when modeling average accessibility, suggesting a specific role in coordinated binding. ChAI-Net's regulatory grammar also highlights the importance of TF motif orientation, spacing, positioning, and co-occurrence in driving co-accessibility. Thus, our framework for extracting regulatory rules from footprinting data expands understanding of TF cooperativity, while laying the groundwork to elucidate how these rules vary across cellular contexts as single-molecule genomics is deployed at scale.

title: FiberBrowser: a unified framework for single-molecule genomics
authors: Tullius, T. W., Catalano, C., Ranchalis, J., Hu, J., Vollger, M. R., Stergachis, A. B., Levine, M. S.
abstract: Single-molecule footprinting methods are rapidly transforming chromatin biology. They resolve nucleosome positioning, regulatory-factor occupancy, and accessibility on individual DNA fibers, revealing combinatorial heterogeneity that bulk measurements average away. Emerging footprinting methods leverage diverse enzyme systems and sequencing platforms, necessitating tools that can accommodate these systems. We present FiberBrowser, a unified platform that converts these diverse datasets into a common per-molecule representation of nucleosomes, accessible DNA, and subnucleosomal footprints for interactive and scripted analyses. Its inference engine, FiberHMM, weighs each observation against the assay's informative sites and sequence-specific modification probabilities, separating missing information from protection in four assays. FiberBrowser clusters, sorts and compares these calls across thousands of molecules in seconds, linking chromatin architecture to haplotype, CpG methylation and non-reference structural variants on the same molecules. Because the representation is independent of chemistry, models also transfer between assays. A classifier trained on Fiber-seq footprints identifies 12 scDAF-seq cells as lymphoblastoid without retraining, whereas models trained on raw modification patterns fail to transfer. FiberBrowser thus provides a unified, expandable analytical framework for single-molecule chromatin footprinting.

title: Organisms associated with siphonophores revealed by short-read whole-genome sequencing
authors: Dunn, C. W., Ahuja, N., Destanovic, D., Manko, M. K., Dal Bello, M., Church, S. H.
abstract: Siphonophores are associated with prey, parasites, microbes, and other organisms in the open ocean, but little is known about these siphonophore cobionts. To learn more about them, we investigated molecular bycatch: their DNA captured during siphonophore genome sequencing. We reanalysed 213 specimens of Physalia, Nanomia, Bargmannia and other siphonophores sequenced in four previously published studies. We recovered 104 bacterial genomes forming 32 genome clusters, including recurrent Metamycoplasmataceae and diverse proteobacteria, groups also found with other cnidarians. Bacterial communities differed among Physalia species sampled in the southwestern Pacific. We identified non-siphonophore eukaryotes from ribosomal markers in 38 specimens, including fish and copepods consistent with prey, parasitic flatworms, and Perkinsela-like relatives of amoeba endosymbionts. Alfonsino (Beryx) sequences in one Hawaiian P. utriculus specimen are consistent with capture of pelagic young of deepwater fishes. Molecular bycatch reveals the diversity of siphonophore associates from specimens already collected for genome research.

title: Small molecule structure elucidation from NMR spectra with generative and reasoning models
authors: Xiong, Z., Ying, V. Y., Huang, J. Z., Koch, Z., Clark, J. D., Heeter, R. C., An, J. S., Matanachai, K., Rodriques, S. G., White, A. D., Seyedsayamdost, M. R., Zhong, E.
abstract: Elucidating the structures of unknown small molecules remains a major challenge in chemistry, pharmacology, and drug discovery. While nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is the gold standard for structure elucidation, interpreting spectra remains labor-intensive and requires expert knowledge to navigate the vast space of possible structures. Here, we present an AI system for rapid, automated de novo structure elucidation that combines a molecular generative model with a scientific reasoning agent. Its generative component, ChefNMR2, is an atomic flow-matching model that predicts small-molecule structures from molecular formulae and one-dimensional 1H and 13C NMR spectra. ChefNMR2-Agent augments our generative model with large language models (LLMs) to reason over and refine candidate structures. Across diverse benchmarks, ChefNMR2 substantially outperforms existing tools, offering calibrated confidence estimates and two to three orders of magnitude faster inference than frontier LLMs. We use ChefNMR2-Agent to elucidate the structures of four novel natural products, matching human-chemist accuracy in a fraction of the time. Our work demonstrates how specialized generative models and general-purpose reasoning agents can unite to solve challenging scientific inverse problems and accelerate NMR structure elucidation, thus opening new possibilities for AI-driven small-molecule discovery across diverse disciplines.

title: Silent travelers: the potential of migratory birds and their ticks to introduce emerging viruses into Switzerland
authors: Gerber, C. M., Zezza, G., Guidi, V., Wyler, M., Bachofen, C., Kubacki, J.
abstract: Switzerland hosts over 400 bird species, many of which are migratory. Through diverse movement patterns, ranging from short distances to almost global migrations, these birds can introduce zoonotic viruses, such as West Nile virus (WNV) or avian influenza virus (AIV), as well as unknown and potentially emerging viruses. Furthermore, they facilitate the global dispersal of infected ectoparasites, particularly ticks, risking the introduction of novel tick-borne diseases. To assess this risk, we sampled 42 bird species (39 migratory, 3 resident) over seven months in 2023 at the Bolle di Magadino nature reserve and the Piano di Magadino area in the canton Ticino (Switzerland). This region, because of its transitional climate, serves as an important resting and breeding ground for migratory birds. In total, 496 oropharyngeal-cloacal swabs, 164 sera, and 22 associated ticks were collected. While RT-qPCR of the swabs detected no active WNV or AIV infections, ELISA testing identified Orthoflavivirus antibodies in 15 of 164 sera, indicating prior exposure. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing revealed a viral landscape spanning 33 families (29 of which were identified in birds). Within this virome, DNA viruses, predominantly Circoviridae, Genomoviridae, and Parvoviridae, dominated in abundance but exhibited low diversity. In contrast, the highly diverse RNA virome primarily reflected the birds dietary habits and the local habitat at the nature reserve. Notably, we report the first detection of Bole tick virus 4 (BoTV4) in Switzerland, identified in several ticks (Rhipicephalus turanicus) associated with long-distance migrants. This member of the newly established Pestiviridae family is already established in parts of Asia, Africa, and Europe. This study provides the first active surveillance of the wild bird virome in Switzerland. Our findings establish a framework for the early detection of emerging viruses and underscore the role of migratory birds as dispersal vectors for ticks and novel tick-borne viruses.

title: EMBER: Contextualized gene representations enable compositional prediction across cellular perturbations
authors: Ho, N., Xing, E. P., Ma, J.
abstract: Predicting the effects of individual and combined perturbations is central to identifying context-specific vulnerabilities and designing targeted interventions. Yet learning gene representations that integrate functional relationships with cellular state and transfer across perturbation tasks remains challenging. Here, we present EMBER, a gene-centric foundation model that learns context-dependent functional representations of genes. EMBER combines interaction-guided contrastive learning with masked expression reconstruction during pretraining on a single-cell corpus curated for diversity and balanced sampling across cell types and experimental batches. EMBER decouples gene representation learning from task-specific prediction through a composable embedding framework: the pretrained encoder remains frozen, while lightweight probes combine contextualized gene embeddings to predict individual and combined perturbation effects. The same pretrained representations support single-gene perturbation-response prediction, digenic interaction prediction, and multi-target drug-response prediction. EMBER improves cross-context perturbation-response prediction and genetic-interaction ranking relative to evaluated baselines. EMBER also prioritized SCFD1, a mediator of autophagosome-lysosome fusion, as a candidate dependency during mTOR inhibition. Together, these results establish contextualized gene embeddings as reusable building blocks for modeling genetic and pharmacological perturbations, supporting the prioritization of genetic interactions and context-specific interventions for experimental testing.

title: Single-cell foundation models transfer across deep evolutionary distances
authors: Trnovec, L., Katoh-Kurasawa, M., Arey, R. N., Shaulsky, G., Zupan, B.
abstract: Single-cell foundation models are trained mostly on human and other vertebrate cells, yet are proposed as general-purpose models. Whether they transfer far beyond their training species is unknown. We evaluated zero-shot embeddings from Geneformer, scGPT and UCE against PCA and scVI in developmental atlases of Dictyostelium discoideum and Caenorhabditis elegans, separated from humans by 1.2 billion and 600 million years. Without retraining, the models recovered developmental order and preserved organism-specific cell identities. UCE encodes genes by protein sequence and could use 97% of measured genes, whereas Geneformer and scGPT, after ortholog mapping, used under one-fifth. UCE performed most consistently, often exceeding species-native baselines. Restricted to ortholog-mappable genes, it still scored above vocabulary-based models on five of six annotation tasks, some narrowly. Foundation models can thus yield informative cell embeddings across more than a billion years of evolution, and protein-sequence gene representations make these embeddings more complete and often more accurate.

title: tWhEEL: a transcript-aware workflow for quantifying CRISPR knockout feasibility using transcriptome assembly
abstract: Gene redundancy can complicate loss-of-function experiments (knockout), and its extent varies among organisms and biological functions. Relating variation in gene redundancy to the availability of genome-editing targets can help researchers select tractable biological functions and experimental organisms. Here, we present the transcript-aware Whole-genomic Evaluation for Editing Locus (tWhEEL), a pipeline that infers redundancy in silico from transcript information and cross-references it with specific guide RNA designs. tWhEEL integrates CRISPR-Cas9 guide design with Gene Ontology (GO) and pathway annotations to compute a knockout feasibility index (KFI) for individual genes and functional categories. Interactive HTML reports link GO-associated KFI and pathway-associated KFI summaries to the contributing groups, genes, and guide candidates with links to QuickGO or WikiPathways. By linking sequence-level guide candidates to functional-level targetability, tWhEEL can support the selection of biological functions and organisms for reverse-genetic experiments. Applications to model and nonmodel datasets revealed distinct targetability profiles, including high full targetability in yeast and query-protein-set dependence in zebrafish. A zebrafish Fanconi anemia case study recovered 14 of 19 published target-site designs. By connecting sequence-level guide candidates with function-level experimental planning, tWhEEL provides a framework for comparing reverse genetic tractability and prioritizing biological functions and organisms for further study.

title: Genomic Correlates of APOBEC-Associated Mutagenesis in Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma
authors: Ansah, E. O., Yentumi, J. A., Kodom, E. Y., Mensah, P. O., Fosu, K., Adu, I. K., Boahen, E. A.
abstract: Background and Aims: APOBEC-associated mutagenesis is prominent in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), but genomic features associated with its intertumoral variability remain incompletely characterized. We investigated genomic correlates of APOBEC-associated mutagenesis while accounting for the compositional structure of mutational signature data. Methods: Mutational signatures were analyzed in 552 ESCC tumors from eight countries. APOBEC-associated mutagenesis was quantified as SBS2 plus SBS13 using absolute mutation counts and proportional contributions. Associations with co-occurring mutational signatures, total SBS burden, recurrent driver-gene alterations, and country were evaluated using correlation, sensitivity, and multivariable analyses. Principal component and regression-model robustness were additionally assessed. Results: APOBEC burden varied markedly across tumors (median, 2,002 mutations; IQR, 987-4,346). Several associations observed using signature proportions were not maintained in absolute-count analyses: SBS1, SBS3, and SBS5 changed direction, indicating sensitivity to compositional representation. In contrast, SBS18 remained inversely associated with APOBEC-associated mutagenesis in all variable pairings examined: proportion versus proportion (Spearman rho = -0.527), APOBEC proportion versus SBS18 absolute count (r = -0.435), and absolute count versus absolute count (Pearson r = -0.319, P = 1.59 x 10^-14; Spearman rho = -0.317). These are distinct comparisons rather than discrepant estimates. Notably, this cohort-wide relationship was primarily characterized by higher APOBEC burden in SBS18-negative than SBS18-positive tumors rather than a continuous inverse relationship among SBS18-positive tumors. The multivariable model had an in-sample R^2 of 0.400 but lower and variable 10-fold cross-validated performance (mean R^2 = 0.273). Country added little explanatory information to this model (delta R^2 = 0.008; global P = 0.402). ZNF750-mutant tumors had higher APOBEC burden than wild-type tumors (BH-FDR q = 0.0032), although only 12 tumors carried ZNF750 alterations. Conclusion: Genomic correlates of APOBEC-associated mutagenesis in ESCC are sensitive to the representation of mutational signature activity. SBS18 showed the most consistent inverse association, whereas the ZNF750 association warrants independent validation.

title: Dissecting functional elements in giant genomes using the first generation of high quality salamander assemblies
authors: Timoshevskaya, N., Timoshevskiy, V. A., Eskut, K. I., Jarvis, E. D., Voss, S. R., Smith, J. J.
abstract: Salamanders are an enduring and historically significant group that helped originate multiple scientific fields of study, including regeneration, cytogenetics, experimental embryology, cloning, evolutionary developmental biology and evolution of extreme genome size. We generated a high-quality, single haplotype assembly for the 32 Gb axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) genome using an F1 hybrid between axolotl and a divergent relative the tiger salamander (A. tigrinum). Using multi-genome alignments to other salamanders that meet VGP metrics, we leveraged strong conservation of karyotypic structure to identify >523,000 highly conserved non-coding elements within massively expanded intronic and intergenic regions, the vast majority of which are unique to the salamander lineage. Orthogonal measures of chromatin state and enhancer activity confirmed that many conserved elements correspond to cis-regulatory sequences and identified several thousand that are utilized during regeneration. The conserved elements identified here will enable robust functional genomic analyses of tissue regeneration and other traits that uniquely empower salamander models in biological research.

title: Bioactivity foundation model for hit identification and hit-to-lead optimization from sequence data
authors: Koh, H. Y., Koh, H. J. W., Zheng, Y., Naranbhai, V., Schmidt, D. F., Barthelemy, J., Chen, Y.-J., Nguyen, A. T. N., Pan, S., May, L. T., Webb, G. I.
abstract: Learning from large-scale bioactivity archives is complicated by heterogeneous assay readouts and differences in data reliability. Here we show that a model that predicts probability distributions over binding affinities from sequence data opens model training to vast and diverse troves of heterogeneous bioactivity data. We develop PSICHIC+, a bioactivity foundation model trained on approximately 82 million protein-ligand records using a distributional objective that preserves quantitative resolution while incorporating variation in data reliability. Given a protein sequence and ligand SMILES, PSICHIC+ predicts binding affinity in milliseconds. In zero-shot virtual-screening benchmarks without target-specific training data, it improves enrichment over regression- and classification-based approaches and performs competitively with leading structure-based methods. In lab-in-the-loop campaigns, distribution-guided acquisition improves recovery of high-activity compounds under fixed screening budgets. Combining PSICHIC+ with Boltz-2 improves hit-to-lead affinity prediction over Boltz-2 alone, with mean correlation approaching that of FEP+ on the evaluated benchmarks, without requiring high-resolution protein structures. These results support distributional learning as a scalable approach to using heterogeneous bioactivity data for hit identification and hit-to-lead optimization.

title: EpiRank: partner-agnostic surface-patch retrieval for epitope prediction of protein binding interfaces
abstract: Structure-based interface predictors are normally reported as a single pooled ROC AUC over a residue test set. For a protein designer the operative question is different and much harder: given one target chain, will the top-ranked surface patch be a real binding site? We built EpiRank, a partner-agnostic epitope predictor, on HumanPPI 29,246 predicted human dimers, 12,296 target chains, 4.18 M residues using only single-chain geometry and physicochemistry (170 features, no partner, no sequence search, no structural alphabet), and evaluated it as a retrieval problem with homology- and partner-graph-controlled splits, on the 3,529 chains that survive an explicit partner-contamination filter. The model places a real epitope in its top-ranked patch 64 % of the time. That number is far less informative than it looks. Compact patches placed at random hit a real epitope 41 % of the time under the same rule, so the model's lift is 1.57 x, not 64 %; 54 % of all predicted patches land on nothing; and when the same chains are scored by models trained on a 2,000-chain and an 11,669-chain superset, a substantial fraction change answer while the aggregate barely moves. We document four specific ways this task invites overstatement partner-graph percolation across splits, single-linkage homology percolation at the conventional 30 % identity threshold, a count-only hit rule that rewards spatial smoothing rather than signal, and hotspot precision conditioned on success, which ranks a random baseline above the trained model. Each was hit during development and each inverted a conclusion we had already drawn. We argue that interface-prediction papers should report lift over a geometry-matched random baseline, patch precision, and per-target stability alongside AUC, and we release the evaluation harness that computes them.

title: Structure-resolved fold annotation of the medicinal-leech salivary-EV cargo: a Ly-6/uPAR three-finger scaffold and a structurally dark fraction
authors: Cen, H., Zhao, F., Zhao, J., Tong, X., Liu, Z., Zhao, F.
abstract: Many proteins that medicinal leeches package into salivary extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry no interpretable sequence annotation, so the least-characterised part of a pharmacologically important secretome lacks even a fold assignment. A companion Astral-DIA study of Hirudinaria manillensis nominated 17 ultra-enriched candidate EV cargo proteins. Here we ask whether structure prediction and structural search can assign folds where sequence methods fail, and which candidates remain unresolved under prespecified criteria. With an offline pipeline (ESMFold, TM-align, Foldseek against AFDB-SwissProt and PDB100, UniRef90 search, protein-to-genome alignment), the candidates separate into intracellular/membrane machinery and a secreted, cysteine-dense fraction of three proteins with no Pfam domain. The predicted structure of the leech Protein-sleepless homolog g21166 supports its assignment to the Ly-6/uPAR three-finger fold (TM 0.58 vs CD59; best significant PDB match Lynx1); no function is inferred. g436 and g20791 returned no match meeting the criterion (alnTM [≥] 0.5, E [≤] 0.05) in either database, g436 even after homolog-informed modelling. Gene structure and splice junctions support a conserved locus for the two-Trypsin-segment model g8114 (catalytic unit not established). A Boltz-2 thrombin pilot did not support target engagement, and a pre-registered nicotinic test was terminated as undecidable. The results yield a structure-informed shortlist for experimental follow-up.

title: The Braarudosphaera bigelowii genome reveals cellular remodeling around a nitrogen-fixing organelle
authors: Zehr, J., Coale, T., Mak, W. K. E., Turk-Kubo, K. A., Hagino, K., Cornejo-Castillo, F. M., Fussy, Z.
abstract: Braarudosphaera bigelowii hosts the nitrogen-fixing cyanobacterial organelle UCYN-A, or the nitroplast, but the absence of a reference genome has limited investigation of the genomic features accompanying this association. Here, we present nuclear and organellar genome resources for the cultured B. bigelowii strain FR-21. The assembly comprises a 472.1-Mb nuclear genome together with representative nitroplast, chloroplast, and mitochondrial genomes of 1.49 Mb, 107 kb, and 44 kb, respectively. The four genomic compartments have strongly differentiated GC compositions, consistent with their distinct evolutionary origins. The large nuclear genome does not appear to reflect a corresponding expansion of protein-coding capacity. Repeat annotation indicates that approximately 77% of the nuclear assembly is repetitive, leaving approximately 108 Mb of nonrepetitive sequence containing roughly 16,000 predicted protein-coding genes. Phylogenomic analysis places B. bigelowii within the expected diversity of haptophytes, indicating that its unusual diazotrophic lifestyle is not associated with an anomalous phylogenetic position. Comparative analysis of nitrogen metabolism genes reveals extensive remodeling of host nitrogen acquisition and assimilation. B. bigelowii lacks major components required for nitrate and nitrite assimilation and has reduced capacity to use urea, cyanate, and several internally recycled nitrogen sources. In contrast, ammonium transport and the glutamine synthetase-glutamate synthase pathway are retained. This combination suggests reduced flexibility in nitrogen use and a host metabolism increasingly centered on ammonium supplied by the nitroplast. B. bigelowii also encodes an expanded set of flavodoxin and cryptochrome genes. Eleven of 14 flavodoxin candidates and 21 of 39 cryptochrome candidates contained motifs linked to nitroplast targeting. Together with previous evidence that some of these proteins are abundantly imported into the nitroplast, these expansions point to host-encoded roles in nitroplast redox metabolism and diel regulation. These genome resources establish a foundation for investigating nitroplast protein import, host-organelle metabolic integration, and the genomic consequences of acquiring an intracellular nitrogen-fixing compartment. They further show that the evolution of the B. bigelowii-UCYN-A relationship involved substantial remodeling of genome architecture and nitrogen metabolism in both partners.

title: Transcript quantification using context-aware MAPQ modeling
abstract: Long-read RNA-sequencing enables accurate transcript-level quantification, but prior static filtering of MAPping Quality (MAPQ) can ignore transcriptome-intrinsic ambiguity, and discarding reads on this basis distorts abundance estimates. We present CALMeR (Context-Aware Long-read MAPQ-based Rescuer), which conditions MAPQ filtering on transcript properties rather than a fixed cutoff. CALMeR fits a zero-one inflated beta regression on various transcript and read-level features to model the expected MAPQ distribution for each alignment. Reads whose MAPQ fits this context, such as low-MAPQ reads from multi-isoform genes and paralog families are retained; reads with anomalously low MAPQ are removed as likely artifacts. Retained reads can be summed per transcript or passed to any downstream quantifier. Compared with a MAPQ [≥] 1 filter and expectation-maximization-based transcript quantification methods, CALMeR recovers more spike-in transcripts and better matches known spike-in concentrations. CALMeR is available at https://github.com/sparthib/CALMeR.

title: Comprehensive evaluation of antibody language models across multiple antibody design tasks
abstract:
Background
                      Antibody language models (ALMs) have emerged as powerful tools for computational antibody design, but their performance across a variety of tasks remains underexplored. 
                  
                     Results
                      We establish a comprehensive benchmark to evaluate eight ALMs, namely AntiBERTy, AntiBERTa, AntiBERTa2, AbLang, AbLang2, ReprogBert, BERT2DAb, and BALM, across five distinct downstream tasks relevant to antibody design. These tasks include sequence-level tasks, such as HER2-binding prediction, SARS-CoV-2-binding prediction, and binding-affinity regression, and token-level tasks, such as paratope and complementarity-determining region (CDR) prediction. We assess the influence of several factors on ALM performance, including pretraining dataset size, fine-tuning strategies, and training data volume. Our results show that AbLang, AntiBERTa2, and AbLang2 are the best models overall, with distinct task-specific strengths, whereas BALM demonstrates superior performance in binding-affinity regression. For binary tasks, such as HER2-binding and paratope prediction, performance differences among the models are minimal. Furthermore, reducing the pretraining dataset to 576,000 antibody sequences has a negligible effect on model performance, with some models even showing improvements. We also explore the necessity and effectiveness of various fine-tuning methods and investigate the influence of fine-tuning dataset size. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      This study provides valuable insights into the strengths and limitations of ALMs and offers guidance for improving pretraining methods, fine-tuning strategies, and model architectures to enhance their application in antibody design.

title: Guard cell size and initial conductance influence stomatal closure kinetics
authors:
Christopher D. Muir, 
Wei Shen Lim
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         In fluctuating environments, the kinetics of stomatal opening and closing influence the balance between carbon gain and water loss. Smaller guard cells may respond faster to fluctuating environmental conditions because of their greater surface area for osmolyte flux relative to cell volume. A related hypothesis is that operational stomatal conductance () is often well below its theoretical maximum () because at this stomatal aperture, guard cell volume is poised to change rapidly with small changes in turgor pressure. 
                       
                       
                         
                          We analyzed 2125 estimates of stomatal closure kinetics in response to an abrupt increase in vapor pressure deficit (VPD) among 29 diverse wild tomato populations in the genus
                           Solanum 
                          .
                         
                       
                       
                         Leaves with small guard cells and a lower initial stomatal conductance () closed faster, but each explained variation in kinetic parameters at different levels of biological organization. Guard cell size had high phylogenetic heritability and varied relatively little within populations, whereas  varied mostly among individuals and between light‐intensity treatments. 
                       
                       
                         Smaller stomata can be speedier, but the current physiological state of the leaf also affects the responsiveness of stomatal conductance to fluctuations. Selection on stomatal speed may influence not only anatomical traits like guard cell size but also physiological controls on .

title:
JrTTG2 confers drought tolerance in walnut via the
                     JrGSTU8 
                    -mediated antioxidant pathway and interaction with JrEPSIN1
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Drought significantly limits the productivity and quality of Juglans regia, yet the regulatory mechanisms governing drought tolerance in this economically vital nut tree remain largely elusive. Here, we report that the WRKY transcription factor JrTTG2 acts as a central hub in the walnut drought response by integrating transcriptional and protein-interaction networks. We identified JrTTG2 as a hypersensitive early-response gene, exhibiting a robust 333-fold induction in walnut roots under drought stress. Ectopic expression of JrTTG2 in Arabidopsis and poplar significantly enhanced drought tolerance, primarily by maintaining root architecture, increasing biomass, and reducing oxidative damage. Conversely, RNAi-mediated silencing of PagTTG2 in poplar led to stunted root systems and compromised antioxidant defense under water deficit. Transcriptomic and molecular analyses revealed that JrTTG2 directly binds to the W-box in the promoter of the JrGSTU8 gene to activate its transcription, thereby facilitating ROS scavenging. Furthermore, yeast two-hybrid and BiFC assays demonstrated that JrTTG2 physically interacts with the vesicle trafficking protein JrEPSIN1. Both JrGSTU8 and JrEPSIN1 showed highly synchronized induction with JrTTG2 in walnut roots during drought. Taken together, this study provides a novel dimension to the molecular mechanisms of woody plant adaptation and offers a promising candidate gene for breeding drought-tolerant walnut varieties.

title: The E3 ligase PpMBR2 targets PpABI5 for degradation and negatively regulates cold tolerance in peach fruit
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Abscisic acid (ABA) is known to alleviate chilling injury (CI) of peach fruit, but the molecular mechanisms is poorly understood. Here, a regulatory module that mediates peach fruit CI response at both transcriptional and post-translational levels was identified. ABA induced the gene expression and protein accumulation of abscisic acid-insensitive 5 (PpABI5). In turn, PpABI5 stimulated the expression of genes involved in proline and flavonoid biosynthesis, antioxidant defense, and fatty acid desaturation. Transient and ectopic overexpression of PpABI5 enhanced cold tolerance in peach and tomato fruit, accompanied by elevated proline and flavonoid biosynthesis, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and fatty acid desaturation. PpABI5 interacted with an E3 ligase MED25-binding RING-H2 protein2 (PpMBR2), which ubiquitinated PpABI5 at the specific site of K140, thereby modulated its degradation and attenuated PpABI5-mediated transactivation of target genes. PpMBR2-overexpression aggravated fruit CI, whereas PpMBR2-silencing produced the opposite effect. Furthermore, PpABI5 interacted with an ethylene response factor CRF3 (PpERF-CRF3), and this interaction enhanced their transcriptional regulation of target genes. Collectively, the results reveal a dynamic regulatory module PpMBR2-PpABI5-PpERF-CRF3 that governs cold tolerance in peach fruit by regulating proline and flavonoid biosynthesis, antioxidant defense and fatty acid desaturation. These findings advance our understanding of phytohormone crosstalk and site-specific ubiquitination modification in fruit CI.

title: A brake for pathogen-induced reactive oxygen species burst

Loss of splicing factor SR45 reshapes tissue-dependent alternative polyadenylation landscapes and transcriptome responses to salt in
                     Arabidopsis
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Serine/arginine-rich 45 (SR45) is a plant-specific SR-like splicing factor and an RNA-binding protein involved in Arabidopsis development and stress responses. Although SR45 has been primarily studied for its role in pre-mRNA alternative splicing (AS), whether it also regulates alternative polyadenylation (APA) remains unclear. Here, we combined poly(A) tag sequencing (PAT-seq) and RNA-seq to examine APA, AS, and gene expression in wild-type (WT) and sr45-1 plants across inflorescence, leaf, and root under normal conditions, and in leaf and root under prolonged mild salinity. Under normal conditions, SR45 loss caused widespread changes in poly(A) site usage, with distal site shifts occurring more frequently than proximal shifts across tissues. APA, AS, and differential gene expression showed only partial overlap, with significant enrichment between APA and AS but not with gene expression changes, indicating that APA represents a distinct layer of SR45-mediated transcriptome regulation. Under prolonged mild salinity conditions, pairwise analyses showed preference of distal poly(A) site usage in WT and proximal site usage in sr45-1, particularly in leaf. Replicate-aware genotype-by-treatment interaction analyses further identified genotype-dependent differences in APA and gene expression, where more genotype-treatment interacting genes detected in leaf than in root. Genes encoding polyadenylation and splicing factors also showed changes in APA, AS, or transcript abundance. Together, these results expand the known role of SR45 from splicing regulation to APA-associated transcriptome remodeling and reveal that SR45 is required for proper salt-responsive changes in transcript abundance in Arabidopsis.

title: The art of multi-tasking: plant responses to their environment
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Plant growth, development and survival are a continuous balancing act, integrating numerous environmental signals with core developmental programs. Nevertheless, in plant physiological research we usually study responses to the environment one factor at the time. It was the advent of microarray-based transcriptomics, and specifically the demonstration that combined treatments produce unique transcriptional signatures, that transformed stress combination into a defined molecular research program. We highlight how the field has evolved from the first seminal reports that combined severe abiotic stress treatments to a more comprehensive understanding of plant response to a range of conditions, including temperature, water availability, nutrients and light. We propose to broaden the conceptual framework from “combined stress” to a more inclusive consideration of context-dependent integration of environmental signals into responses. Integration of dose-, time- and location-dependent responses to the key plant hormones auxin, abscisic acid, ethylene and jasmonate are discussed. To further this research domain, we recommend accurate recording of environmental conditions and routine incorporation of treatment gradations, from mild to severe, in our research. Realizing this integrative view will require combining data-rich omics and machine-learning approaches with focused, hypothesis-driven experiments.

title: SlJRE4-SlTPP1 confers carbon starvation tolerance by inhibiting starch degradation in tomato leaves at night
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Under carbon starvation, plants have evolved a precise regulatory network governing starch degradation rates to avert excessive depletion of starch reserves, thereby sustaining carbon homeostasis and prolonging survival. We previously found that overexpression of the trehalose-6-phosphate phosphatase gene SlTPP1 slows nocturnal starch degradation in tomato leaves under neutral-day conditions; however, its function and regulatory mechanism underlying leaf starch degradation under low light (LL)-induced carbon starvation remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate that SlTPP1 slows nocturnal starch degradation in tomato leaves under carbon starvation. SlTPP1 overexpression suppresses nocturnal starch degradation and inhibits β-amylase activity in tomato leaves under neutral-day, short-day, and LL conditions. LL induces the expression of starch-degrading enzyme genes while concurrently upregulating SlTPP1 transcription in leaves. Furthermore, the jasmonic acid (JA)-responsive ERF transcription factor SlJRE4 directly binds to the GCC-box cis-element in the SlTPP1 promoter and activates its expression. SlJRE4 transcription is also induced by LL. SlJRE4 overexpression similarly slows nocturnal starch degradation and represses β-amylase activity in leaves under neutral-day, short-day, and LL conditions. Additionally, exogenous methyl jasmonate under LL inhibits leaf starch degradation and upregulates the expression of SlJRE4 and SlTPP1. LL upregulates the expression of JA biosynthesis genes and elevates JA levels in tomato leaves. Moreover, SlTPP1 overexpression indirectly enhances SlJRE4 expression in leaves. Collectively, our findings uncover that the SlJRE4–SlTPP1 module acts as a braking mechanism to attenuate the rapid starch degradation in leaves triggered by LL-induced carbon starvation, representing a critical adaptive strategy for plants to improve survival under carbon starvation stress.

title:
Revisiting ethylene metabolism: Identification of an ethylene glycol-glucose conjugate reveals active ethylene metabolism in
                     Populus
abstract:
Abstract 
                   In many plant species, the role of ethylene as a phytohormone signal has been well-studied, yet its direct metabolism in planta has received less attention. Consequently, this gap constrains our understanding of the full impact ethylene has on plant systems. During multiple evaluations of resilience in Populus spp., we detected an unidentified metabolite with plausible links to ethylene. In this study, we structurally characterize and identify this molecule as an ethylene glycol glucose conjugate (EGGC). Ethylene-perturbation experiments revealed EGGC abundance is positively correlated with endogenous ethylene production, supporting EGGC as an ethylene-derived metabolite. Stable-isotope labeled EGGC supplied to the media was detected in stem/leaf tissue, indicating long-distance translocation of the compound. These studies also revealed enzymatic conversion in stem/leaf tissue of EGGC to ethylene glycol (EG), with EG levels maintained and accompanied by shifts in downstream metabolites (i.e., glycolic acid and oxalic acid). These results suggest that EGGC participates in active metabolism rather than serves as a waste product. Collectively, the findings reported in this study demonstrate that EGGC is a biomarker of whole-plant ethylene production and position it as a tool for monitoring ethylene-associated stress responses.

title: Embodied artificial intelligence: from understanding the world to changing it
abstract: Corresponding author . E-mail:  dinghan@hust.edu.cn

title: A Unified Systematic Framework for Human-AI Collaboration: Technologies, Evaluation Metrics, and a Tiered Taxonomy
abstract:
Abstract 
                   The rapid development of artificial intelligence has positioned Human-AI Collaboration (HAIC) as a promising paradigm for integrating the complementary strengths of humans and AI systems. However, due to its interdisciplinary nature, existing studies often focus on isolated aspects within specific topics or applications, lacking a unified system-level abstraction. In this paper, we propose a unified HAIC framework grounded in a multi-agent system, encompassing five core technological pillars: situation assessment, social understanding, shared decision and control, human-AI interaction, and collaborative learning. Within this framework, we conduct a literature synthesis to consolidate recent advances across these dimensions. Building on these insights, we introduce a system-level evaluation methodology that integrates multi-dimensional metrics to assess HAIC effectiveness. Finally, we propose a tiered HAIC taxonomy characterizing capability evolution from basic assistance to symbiotic HAIC. Together, these contributions establish a structured, extensible foundation for designing and evaluating next-generation HAIC systems.

title: Efficient white electroluminescence based on a single multi-resonance TADF emitter with dual emission feature
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Pure organic white organic light-emitting diodes (WOLEDs) based on a single dopant offer distinct advantages over traditional WOLEDs with RGB emitters, especially in terms of simple fabrication process and low cost. However, the maximum external quantum efficiency (EQEmax) of the reported pure organic single-dopant WOLED devices remains below 15%, which could be attributed to insufficient exciton utilization. Herein, a multi-resonance thermally activated delayed fluorescence (MR-TADF) molecule (Th-DBN) with extended π-conjugation is reported, along with highly efficient excimer emission and dual TADF features. The single-dopant WOLEDs based on Th-DBN deliver outstanding performance, achieving a record EQEmax of 27.1%, Commission Internationale de l’Eclairage (CIE) coordinates of (0.35, 0.50), and a significant operational lifetime (LT80) of 398 h at 1000 cd m−2, which are among the best reported results of pure organic single-dopant WOLEDs. This work not only provides the first example of a single-dopant WOLED based on an MR-TADF molecule, but also paves the way to designing pure organic WOLEDs with a single dopant and efficient exciton utilization.

title: Decoction-inspired thermo-mechanical coupling creates hierarchical nanohelix from herbal medicine for lipophagy therapy
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Oral supramolecular nanomedicines often suffer from kinetic trapping, forming metastable aggregates with poor gastrointestinal stability and premature drug release. Conventional assembly methods rarely overcome these barriers. Inspired by the traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) decoction process, which intrinsically combines heating with mechanical stirring, we applied a thermo-mechanical coupling strategy to baicalin and berberine assemblies. Coupled thermal energy and fluid shear drove a transition from kinetically trapped metastable aggregate to thermodynamically stable left-handed nanohelix with an ordered crystalline lattice. This higher degree of structural order conferred improved gastrointestinal tolerance and extended the in vivo mean residence time to 23.06 ± 0.47 h. Sustained systemic exposure activated the AMPK–FoxO1–TFEB–lysosome axis, promoted hepatic lipophagy, and alleviated metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease in mice. These findings provide a physical chemistry framework for overcoming kinetic traps in supramolecular assembly, elucidate the nanoscale organization underlying traditional decoction, and offer a design strategy for long-acting oral nanotherapeutics.

title: Concentric brick-and-mortar architecture: beyond planar nacre-mimics
abstract:
Abstract 
                   The brick‑and‑mortar (BM) architecture of natural nacre is a classic paradigm for biomimetic materials combining strength and toughness. However, conventional planar BM (PBM) architectures exhibit pronounced anisotropy; their direction-dependent weakness compromises structural reliability under complex multi-directional stresses. Here, we introduce a concentric BM (CBM) architecture, with microplatelets circumferentially aligned in a polymer matrix. This design spatially redistributes the weak interlamellar direction axisymmetrically, leaving no globally aligned weak plane and enhancing strength and toughness across multiple loading modes. These gains arise from improved stress homogenization, suppressed interfacial slip and delamination, and energy-dissipative multi-directional crack propagation. Notably, fatigue life under cyclic flexure exceeds that of the PBM counterpart by over three orders of magnitude (>10³-fold) at equal stress. By reconfiguring the PBM motif into a CBM architecture while preserving its strength–toughness synergy, this work provides a biomimetic design strategy for rod-shaped structural components subjected to multi-directional loading.

title: A domesticated totivirus-like tandem array undergoes interspecific transfer and asymmetric evolution
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Functional genes derived from nonretroviral RNA viruses are generally expected to evolve more slowly following integration into host genomes. Here, we characterize STORM (Scheffersomyces Totivirus-like ORF Repeat Module), a tandem array of four totivirus-derived ORFs (TLC1-TLC4) maintained in wood- and insect-associated yeasts for at least 15 million years. STORM has nevertheless accumulated greater amino-acid divergence than sampled exogenous totiviruses. Host calibrated rate analyses estimated that STORM evolved approximately seven-fold faster than related exogenous viral lineages. Evolution within the array was asymmetric. RELAX identified strong gene-wide relaxation in TLC4 (K = 0.29), whereas BUSTED detected no episodic positive selection. Despite this relaxation, TLC4 retained predicted decapping-associated residues, with evidence of purifying selection at several positions. Structural predictions indicated that STORM proteins retain a totivirus-like architecture, and RNA-seq comparisons revealed paralog-specific expression. Among 3,527 complete nuclear gene trees, none recovered all relationships defining any of the three STORM discordances with strong support, indicating that these patterns are exceptional relative to the nuclear genomic background. Local synteny and preservation of the four-copy array further support three interspecific transfers. In the best-supported transfer, STORM was flanked by an ATP10 pseudogene and a transposase pseudogene from YEET, a newly identified Tc1/mariner-like transposon family. Both pseudogenes grouped phylogenetically with the inferred donor clade, and YEET1a-like terminal inverted repeats at the locus were characteristic of that clade. STORM therefore illustrates the selective maintenance, rapid asymmetric evolution, and horizontal mobility of a nonretroviral paleoviral array.

title: More than just a centromere: evolution of a structural supergene causing female meiotic drive in monkeyflowers
abstract: Abstract Meiotic drivers capitalize on vulnerabilities in eukaryotic meiosis and gametogenesis to gain greater-than-equal transmission to the next generation. In most plants and animals, asymmetric female meiosis presents an arena for meiotic drive, as centromeric variants may bias their segregation to the one egg cell. Although centromeric drive is predicted to be pervasive, its mechanisms and consequences remain obscure. Here, we build on representative chromosome-scale assemblies of yellow monkeyflowers  (Mimulus guttatus  species complex )  to compare three functionally distinct haplotypes at Meiotic Drive Locus on Chromosome 11 (MDL11). The driving  D  allele at MDL11 was previously shown to be centromere-containing, costly, and maintained as a balanced polymorphism in wild  M. guttatus  populations.  D  has diverged from nondrivers via at least two major rearrangements (including a hemicentric inversion creating linked arrays of centromeric satellite  Cent728  separated by > 200 trapped genes), massive expansions of a novel MDL11-specific subfamily of satellite repeats ( Cent728D ) that increase the length of the driver chromosome by >50% over homologues, and the build-up of a 2Mb  D -exclusive pericentromeric region containing ∼37 extra  D -associated genes duplicated and translocated from diverse genomic sources. Differences in centromeric satellite arrays, particularly the recent expansion of  Cent728D  are primary candidates for generating female meiotic drive. However, substantial divergence in gene content and sequence among the three haplotypes also points to candidate genic modifiers that may enhance  D  drive and contribute to differences in drive-susceptibility among non-drivers. Overall, our findings support the sequential buildup of this model centromeric driver, reveal intriguing parallels with other selfish supergenes, and provide a strong platform for understanding the mechanisms of its dramatic violation of Mendelian rules.

title: EHD‐LIFT: Electrohydrodynamic Laser Induced Forward Transfer
authors:
Ankit Das, 
Jordi Torres‐Durall, 
J. Marcos Fernández‐Pradas, 
Chien‐Fang Ding, 
Martí Duocastella, 
Craig B. Arnold
abstract:
Electrohydrodynamic laser‐induced forward transfer (EHD‐LIFT) introduces electric field‐assisted control to LIFT. Through laser‐patterning a conductive absorber layer, local curvatures are induced in the donor film, enabling flow‐focusing for transfer of smaller droplets at lower laser energies. Through this additional degree of process control, EHD‐LIFT expands the tunability of LIFT and enables higher‐resolution printing across a broad range of functional materials.








ABSTRACT
Adding new degrees of control to established manufacturing techniques can significantly expand their functionality and unlock new application spaces. In laser‐induced forward transfer (LIFT) of liquids, jetting characteristics dictate the transfer features, essential for micro and sub‐microscale patterning. However, a simple strategy for dynamic tunability of the jet beyond conventional laser parameters is still lacking. Here, we introduce an electrohydrodynamic method to control the donor interfacial curvature, enabling precise tuning of the jetting dynamics through the flow focusing effect. As a result, narrower jets could be achieved at energies 66% lower than in conventional LIFT, leading to a 97% reduction in the minimal printed droplet radius. By introducing an additional degree of control independent of laser parameters, this method expands the operational capabilities of LIFT and provides a promising pathway for high‐resolution printing of functional materials, with potential applications in microelectronics, biomedical systems, and advanced engineering technologies.

title: MAGI3 Acts as an Intestinal Epithelial Gatekeeper in Inflammation‐Associated Colorectal Cancer by Suppressing the STAT3‐CCL2 Axis and TAM‐Mediated Immunosuppression
authors:
Yumeng Yang, 
Zhigang Bai, 
Haibo Wang, 
Yu Guo, 
Yan Zhang, 
Meihan Hu, 
Shuaikang Fan, 
Ran Song, 
Tongmei Zhang, 
Mengqi Deng, 
Xiaomei Yang, 
Zhongtao Zhang, 
Junqi He
abstract:
Our study identifies MAGI3 as an intestinal epithelial gatekeeper that restrains inflammation‐associated colorectal tumorigenesis but is itself suppressed under highly inflammatory conditions. MAGI3 deficiency activates the STAT3‐CCL2 signaling, thereby promoting TAM‐mediated immunosuppression and inflammation‐associated colorectal tumor progression. Targeting the MAGI3–STAT3 axis may provide a therapeutic strategy to interrupt the inflammation‐to‐cancer transition.








ABSTRACT
Chronic intestinal inflammation is a major driver of colorectal cancer (CRC). As the mucosal barrier's frontline sentinel, the intestinal epithelium initiates the inflammation‐to‐cancer transition. However, the early cell‐intrinsic events that convert inflammatory responses into a sustained pro‐tumorigenic program remain unclear. In this study, we identify MAGI3 as an intestinal epithelial guardian progressively lost during inflammation‐associated colorectal tumorigenesis. Low MAGI3 correlates with heightened inflammatory activity and poor prognosis. Inflammation‐induced epithelial MAGI3 downregulation drives STAT3 hyperactivation, CCL2 upregulation, and recruitment of M2‐like tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs), thereby promoting an immunosuppressive microenvironment and tumor progression. By contrast, single‐cell RNA sequencing (scRNA‐seq) demonstrated that MAGI3 overexpression reshapes the composition of TAMs and limits M2‐like TAM infiltration. Mechanistically, the PDZ1 domain of MAGI3 binds directly to the C‐terminus of STAT3, blocking the SH2 pocket, impairing the interaction between STAT3 and IL‐6R/JAK2, and ultimately inhibiting STAT3 phosphorylation at Tyr705. Clinically, the MAGI3‐STAT3 axis offers a new therapeutic strategy for chemotherapy‐resistant CRC, with low MAGI3 expression predicting enhanced sensitivity to STAT3 inhibitors. Collectively, these findings establish MAGI3 as a gatekeeper of the intestinal epithelium in inflammation‐associated CRC, with the MAGI3‐STAT3 axis regulating TAM recruitment. Targeting the MAGI3‐STAT3 axis could offer an early intervention to reverse inflammation‐to‐cancer transition.

title: Single‐Cell Insights Into Pathogenic Profile of Orchitis and SREBP2‐Associated Cholesterol Dysregulation in Spermatogenic Failure
authors:
Yanlin Tang, 
Qiaoling Jiang, 
Yuwen Liu, 
Wenxiu Zhang, 
Lina Cui, 
Xiaojian Lu, 
Ziyan Zhuang, 
Jianxing Cheng, 
Songzhan Gao, 
Yangyi Fang, 
Kai Hong, 
Jie Qiao, 
Xiaoyan Wang, 
Hui Jiang, 
Zhe Zhang, 
Jingtao Guo, 
Qiang Liu
abstract:
A first single-cell atlas of human orchitis reveals coordinated germ-cell loss, somatic niche dysfunction, and immune-metabolic remodeling. Aberrant SREBP2 activation in testicular somatic cells emerges as a central pathogenic node, while Fatostatin-mediated inhibition of the SREBP pathway improves spermatogenesis, fibrosis, and lipid accumulation in a mouse orchitis model.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Orchitis, a testicular inflammation often triggered by infection, is a major cause of male infertility due to disruption of the testicular immune microenvironment and progressive loss of germ cells. Currently, no effective or targeted therapies are available. Here, we profile 66,147 single-cell transcriptomes from testes of orchitis patients and healthy controls, complemented by histological validation. We observe profound remodeling of testicular cell composition, with marked infiltration of CD8 +  effector T cells and inflammatory macrophages, accompanied by germ cell loss. Undifferentiated spermatogonia exhibit cell-cycle arrest, while somatic cell populations display fibrosis, apoptosis, and loss of homeostatic functions. Notably, interstitial cells show SREBP2- associated reprogramming of cholesterol metabolism, characterized by increased synthesis. Inhibition of SREBP2 in a mouse orchitis model improves spermatogenesis, reduces lipid accumulation, and alleviates fibrosis. These findings demonstrate that immune activation–induced SREBP2 upregulation drives cholesterol metabolic imbalance and spermatogenic failure in orchitis, offering potential therapeutic options for inflammation-associated male infertility.

title: Loss of Lepr in Fibroblasts Drives Tumor Development by Promoting Macrophage Infiltration
authors:
Manyu Song, 
Wuqi Yang, 
Bangran Qi, 
Liyuan Hou, 
Xu Yang, 
Jiuzhi Xu, 
Shengyuan Tian, 
Shuiling Jin, 
Lu Yu, 
Zhengquan Yu, 
Min Deng, 
Jiaqiang Huang, 
Suoqin Jin, 
Cong Lv
abstract:
TNFα and TGFβ signaling reprograms Lepr +  fibroblasts toward a Lepr neg Mmp high  inflammatory CAF (iCAF) state, with downregulation of the Tcf21-Lepr axis contributing to this transition. Lepr loss induces Csf3, which contributes to the enhanced macrophage-recruiting capacity of these iCAFs, thereby promoting tumor development. Thus, inflammatory signaling reshapes fibroblast states to establish a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment in colorectal cancer.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are critical regulators of colorectal cancer (CRC) progression, yet the mechanisms governing their functional plasticity and state transitions remain incompletely understood. Here, we uncover a tumor-driven fibroblast state transition in CRC characterized by loss of leptin receptor (Lepr) expression and acquisition of pro-inflammatory features. We show that cooperative TNFα and TGFβ signaling drives this reprogramming, accompanied by repression of the Tcf21-Lepr regulatory axis. Fibroblasts undergoing this transition acquire the capacity to promote macrophage recruitment and accelerate tumor development. Loss of Lepr or Tcf21 in fibroblasts upregulates Csf3, which contributes to the enhanced macrophage-recruiting capacity of the reprogrammed fibroblasts. Consistently, blockade of TNFα and TGFβ signaling disrupts fibroblast reprogramming and attenuates macrophage infiltration. Together, our findings uncover how inflammatory signaling reshapes stromal cell states to promote macrophage accumulation, ultimately fostering a pro-tumorigenic niche that accelerates CRC progression.

title: Nanocatalytic Immunotherapy Targeting Tumor‐Resident Intracellular Bacteria for Triple‐Negative Breast Cancer Treatment and Metastasis Suppression
authors:
Xiaojing Leng, 
Tao Jiang, 
Zhao Guo, 
Zhimin Zhang, 
Yihan Chen, 
Pan Li, 
Min Ge, 
Han Lin, 
Liang Zhang
abstract:
Bacteria residing within tumor cells contribute to breast cancer progression, but few therapies target their elimination. FeSe 2  nanosheets coated with cancer cell membranes accumulate in tumors and generate reactive oxygen species under ultrasound, killing tumor cells and their harbored bacteria at the same time. This dual effect stimulates antitumor immunity and markedly inhibits tumor growth and lung metastasis.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Tumor-resident intracellular bacteria (TRIB) are prevalent within triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). As integral components of the tumor pathological microenvironment, TRIB accelerate TNBC development by regulating cell proliferation, metabolism and immunosuppression. They also enhance the resistance of circulating tumor cells to mechanical stress through cytoskeletal rearrangement, boosting tumor metastasis and hindering clinical therapy. This work develops an advanced TRIB-targeted therapeutic strategy to block TNBC progression by eliminating tumor cells and intracellular bacteria, remodeling tumor immunity and suppressing metastatic colonization. We fabricate cancer cell membrane-modified narrow-bandgap FeSe 2  nanosheets for enhanced ultrasound-triggered reactive oxygen species production and image-guided precise treatment. Such nanoplatforms utilize endogenous H 2 O 2  and GSH to amplify chemodynamic effects, induce severe oxidative stress and ferroptosis in tumor cells. Combined damage-associated and pathogen-associated molecular patterns efficiently activate dendritic cells and initiate robust antigen-specific T-cell immune responses. This study provides an alternative and promising strategy for the treatment of clinically metastatic breast cancer through intratumoral microbiota intervention.

title: Intelligent Polymer Electrolytes for Next‐Generation Zinc‐Based Energy Storage Devices
authors:
Sanath Kumar, 
Jhansirani Kesavan, 
Muhammad Asim, 
Atul Verma, 
Yen‐Pei Fu
abstract:
Intelligent polymer electrolytes are organized into a three-level hierarchy that advances zinc-based energy storage from passive ion conduction toward active, adaptive, and intelligent operation. Molecular regulation of Zn +  coordination, water activity, desolvation, ion flux, and interfaces underpins adaptive self-healing, anti-freezing, adhesion, and mechanical responses, while feedback and AI/ML enable future self-adaptive ZIBs, ZABs, and ZIHCs.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Intelligent polymer electrolytes for zinc-based energy-storage devices have attracted considerable attention as multifunctional platforms capable of simultaneously regulating ion transport, water activity, interfacial chemistry, and mechanical stability. This review presents a comprehensive overview of intelligent polymer electrolytes for zinc-ion batteries (ZIBs), zinc–air batteries (ZABs), and zinc-ion hybrid capacitors (ZIHCs), encompassing hydrogels, organo-hydrogels, composite polymer electrolytes, and solid-state polymer systems. Particular attention is given to the molecular and structural strategies underlying ion-solvation regulation, selective ion transport, dendrite suppression, corrosion inhibition, antifreezing behavior, self-healing, adhesion, and mechanical adaptability. Emerging functionalities, including self-healing, antifreezing, self-adhesive, stretchable, and temperature-responsive behavior, are highlighted in the context of improving operational durability under mechanical deformation and extreme temperatures. Bio-derived polymer electrolytes and the growing use of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and computational simulations for electrolyte discovery and optimization are also discussed. Finally, key challenges associated with scalability, reproducibility, manufacturing, cost, sustainability, and practical full-cell validation are critically assessed. Future research should prioritize multifunctional, adaptive, sustainable, and scalable polymer architectures that concurrently regulate ion transport, interfacial reactions, mechanical integrity, and environmental stability. Collectively, this review provides a framework for the rational design of intelligent polymer electrolytes toward safer, more durable, flexible, and commercially viable zinc-based energy-storage technologies.

title: RUNX1‐Mediated Hypoxic Signaling Impairs Myogenesis and Promotes Fibrosis in Myopathies
authors:
Liang Zhao, 
Taijiang Hou, 
Lin Zhang, 
Feng Gao, 
Tong Xing
abstract:
Myofiber overgrowth was associated with reduced blood flow and a potential hypoxic state in broiler breast muscle, accompanied by increased RUNX1 expression. Elevated RUNX1 impaired myogenic regeneration, promoted fibrosis, and disrupted the signaling niche required for efficient muscle repair, contributing to pathological degeneration in Wooden Breast (WB) myopathy. Comparative analyses further suggest that the HIF1A/RUNX1 regulatory axis may be relevant to muscle diseases in humans and mice, highlighting RUNX1 as a potential therapeutic target. The TOC figure was created with  BioGDP.com  and Adobe Illustrator.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Compromised myogenic repair with enhanced fibrosis is common in myopathies, including Wooden Breast (WB) myopathy in broilers, but the underlying mechanism of their co-occurrence remains elusive. Using WB myopathy as a model, we investigated the common pathological origins of these co-occurring features. Our single-nucleus RNA sequencing results showed enhanced oxidative stress and profibrotic remodeling of myofibers, increased proliferation but decreased differentiation of satellite cells (SCs), and aggravated differentiation of fibroblasts (FBs) in WB samples. Differential gene expression and pseudotime trajectory analysis further identified RUNX1 as a key regulator for both SCs and FBs, which was further supported by gene functional studies in respective cell culture models. Moreover, reduced blood flow and oxygen supply may indicate a hypoxic state in WB muscle, which was associated with enhanced RUNX1 expression. Consistently, coordinately enhanced  HIF1A  and  RUNX1  expressions were found in differentiated FBs of human muscles and in muscles with diseases. Collectively, our study found that hypoxia-associated upregulation of  RUNX1  disrupted the myogenic progression of SCs and exacerbated fibrotic differentiation of FBs, contributing to pathological degeneration in myopathies. Targeting RUNX1 may therefore represent a potential therapeutic strategy for prevention and treatment, which warrants future in vivo investigations.

title: MRSA‐Triggered Disassembly of an Immune‐Recruiting NIR Probe for Bacterial Imaging and Clearance
authors:
Jiacheng Du, 
Yongyi Chen, 
Ling Lei, 
Yunzhe Tao, 
Yu Peng, 
Qingyang Zhang, 
Qinghua Wang, 
Hai‐Yu Hu
abstract:
A bacteria–immune cell-bridging supramolecular amphiphile,  Dman-C11 , undergoes MRSA membrane-triggered disassembly to activate NIR fluorescence and photodynamic killing, inducing ferroptosis-like bacterial death and immune-assisted clearance in wound infection and keratitis models.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Methicillin-resistant  Staphylococcus aureus  (MRSA) infections remain a major clinical challenge due to increasing antimicrobial resistance and limited strategies for precise bacterial recognition and clearance. Here, we report an immune-recruiting supramolecular amphiphile,  Dman-C11 , that undergoes MRSA-triggered structural reorganization for activatable bacterial theranostics.  Dman-C11  consists of a hemicyanine near-infrared (NIR) fluorophore, a D-mannosamine immune-recruiting motif, and a hydrophobic C11 chain that promotes bacterial membrane association. The amphiphilic architecture drives spontaneous nanoparticle formation with suppressed fluorescence through aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ). Upon interaction with the MRSA membrane, nanoparticle disassembly redistributes the probe within the lipid bilayer, producing a 20-fold fluorescence turn-on response while simultaneously restoring efficient singlet oxygen generation under 655 nm irradiation. The activated photodynamic process induces ferroptosis-like bacterial death characterized by extensive lipid peroxidation and oxidative membrane damage. Meanwhile, the D-mannosamine motif promotes immune-cell recruitment toward bacterial pathogens, thereby facilitating host-assisted bacterial clearance. In murine wound infection and bacterial keratitis models,  Dman-C11  achieves approximately 20-fold reductions in bacterial burden without detectable systemic toxicity. This membrane-triggered supramolecular disassembly strategy establishes a single-molecule theranostic approach that links bacterial recognition, activatable imaging, photodynamic antibacterial activity, and immune-assisted clearance for precise treatment of MRSA infections.

title:
3′‐UTR Hypermethylation and ABA Signaling Coordinate Transcriptional Activation of
                     SWEET14 
                    for High Sugar Accumulation in Citrus
authors:
Yike Zeng, 
Yue Wang, 
Yilei Wang, 
Haowei Chen, 
Qiyu Chen, 
Wei Xiao, 
Aoqing Zhang, 
Xin Jiang, 
Xiangming Shang, 
Zhicheng Yang, 
Xi Zeng, 
Wenqiang Hu, 
Chunlong Li, 
Ji‐Hong Liu
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   
                    Sugar accumulation is pivotal for fruit quality, yet the molecular regulation of this process remains elusive. By comparing transcriptomes of sweet lemon (
                     Citrus limon 
                    , SL, high sugar level) and Eureka (EL, trace amount of sugar), we identified the sucrose transporter CliSWEET14 as a key driver of sugar accumulation. Methylome atlas showed that the 26‐bp sequence within 3′‐untranslated region (UTR) of
                     CliSWEET14‐SL 
                    was substantially hypermethylated relative to
                     CliSWEET14‐EL 
                    . Notably, the 3′‐UTRs of both genes formed chromatin loops with their native promoters. ClibHLH105 bound to unmethylated CACGAT sequence in the loop and repressed
                     CliSWEET14‐EL 
                    . In contrast, hypermethylation of the CACGAT motif disrupted ClibHLH105 interaction and repression on
                     CliSWEET14‐SL 
                    . Additionally,
                     CliSWEET14‐SL 
                    was positively regulated by CliNAC56, which was further activated by CliABF3. Both CliNAC56 and CliABF3 regulated sucrose accumulation in a
                     CliSWEET14‐ 
                    dependent manner. Moreover, the regulatory cascade CliABF3‐CliNAC56‐
                     CliSWEET14 
                    in SL was activated by ABA (abscisic acid) to a greater degree due to higher ABA level. Taken together, 3′‐UTR hypermethylation‐mediated relief of transcriptional repression and stronger activation by ABA signaling robustly boost
                     CliSWEET14 
                    expression and sucrose accumulation. These findings substantially advance our understanding of sugar accumulation in fruit and provide novel epigenetic and transcriptional targets for improving fruit quality in citrus and beyond.

title: NUB1 Regulates Muscle Atrophy in Lung Cancer Cachexia via NF‐κB Signaling Pathway
authors:
Yuqi Han, 
Yaru Xia, 
Weiquan Li, 
Jiaming Wu, 
Tiexi Yu, 
Diaoyi Tan, 
Daojia Miao, 
Wen Li, 
Xuejiao Dong, 
Jiemin Li, 
Yu Jiao, 
Guixiao Huang, 
Xiaoping Zhang, 
Hongmei Yang
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   
                    Cancer‐associated cachexia (CAC) is a devastating multifactorial syndrome characterized by progressive skeletal muscle atrophy. Its mechanisms remain incompletely clarified, with limited effective therapeutic targets. NUB1, a negative regulator of ubiquitin‐like proteins mediating protein degradation, has not been fully elucidated in CAC‐induced muscle atrophy. Here, NUB1 was significantly upregulated in skeletal muscles of Lewis lung carcinoma (LLC) cachexia mice and C2C12 myotube atrophy models stimulated with LLC tumor‐conditioned medium (LCM).
