Combined with an Earth-system model, our data reveal notable decreases in global continental weatherability following the end-Permian mass extinction, inferred to associations with widespread deforestation (extinction of deep-rooted plants) and the collapse of terrestrial ecosystem. This diminished weathering response to volcanic carbon emissions likely contributed to prolonged high atmospheric CO
                     2 
                    and global temperature during the Early Triassic. The sustained greenhouse conditions, in turn, inhibited contemporaneous marine and terrestrial ecosystem recoveries. Our findings highlight the importance of terrestrial ecosystem in modulating global carbon cycle stability, and its effects on Earth’s habitability.

title: Induced-fit anti-GFRAL antibody ameliorates cancer cachexia and attenuates sympathetic outflow in tumor-bearing mice
abstract: The GDF15–GFRAL–RET neuroendocrine axis is a key regulator of body-weight homeostasis and metabolic control. GFRAL, a hindbrain-restricted receptor for the stress-responsive cytokine GDF15, signals by assembling a ternary complex with GDF15 and the tyrosine kinase RET. Pathological hyperactivation of this axis drives disease-associated weight loss, including cancer-associated cachexia. Here, we report a GFRAL-binding and GDF15–GFRAL pathway-blocking antibody (GB2Ab) and its humanized lead with potent preclinical efficacy. The GB2Ab Fab–GFRAL D3 crystal structure reveals an induced-fit mechanism in which GB2Ab sterically occludes the GFRAL–RET interface and remodels the primary RET CLD1–CLD2 binding site, providing a structural basis for high-affinity binding, slow dissociation, and potent antagonism. Structure-guided humanization preserves high-affinity and cross-reactivity. The humanized antibody reaches the area postrema, attenuates GDF15-evoked neural activation, ameliorates cachectic phenotypes, and suppresses sympathetic preganglionic activity in an orthotopic cancer cachexia model, establishing receptor-centric GDF15–GFRAL–RET antagonism as a promising strategy for cancer-associated cachexia and other GDF15-driven diseases.

title: Monsoon zonal seesaw: Development of the South Asian monsoon aridified North Africa in the Cenozoic
abstract: North Africa experienced a pronounced transition from humid to arid conditions during the early Cenozoic. Meanwhile, the South Asian monsoon underwent substantial intensification, largely driven by the uplift of the Himalayan-Tibetan Plateau. Here, we demonstrate that the two events, which greatly shaped the paleoenvironment and modern regional climate, are not independent responses to paleogeography changes; rather, the former is primarily driven by the latter through the monsoon-desert mechanism, in which South Asian monsoon diabatic heating produces large-scale subsidence and aridity over North Africa. Using multiple ensembles of paleoclimate simulations and a model for the atmospheric response to imposed diabatic heating, we show that the intensification and poleward shift of Asian monsoon rainfall each make comparable contributions to the aridification of North Africa. Our findings identify a persistent dynamical pathway linking the South Asian and North African monsoons and suggest that it played a major role in early Cenozoic North African aridification, while its climatic expression at other times depended on the relative strengths of competing forcings.

title: An oxidized ribonucleotide 8-oxoGTP drives neuroinflammation and accelerates cognitive decline
abstract: Oxidative stress is a hallmark of aging and a key driver of neurodegenerative diseases. While much attention has been given to oxidative damage of macromolecules, the functional consequences of oxidizing the abundant nucleotide triphosphate (NTP) pool remain largely unknown. Here, we identify oxidized GTP (8-oxoGTP)—a major product of NTP oxidation—not as a mere marker of damage, but as an endogenous signaling molecule that drives microglial activation and neuroinflammation. 8-oxoGTP accumulated in the aging mouse brain, and its elevation was sufficient to induce synaptic dysfunction, tau hyperphosphorylation, neuronal loss, and cognitive decline. Mechanistically, 8-oxoGTP functioned as a potent activator of heterotrimeric G proteins, binding more strongly to Gα subunits than GTP itself, triggering Src kinase/MAPK/Akt/NF-κB signaling in microglia, leading to pro-inflammatory cytokine production, reactive oxygen species generation, and neurotoxicity. Pharmacological inhibition of Src family kinases rescued the neuroinflammatory and cognitive phenotypes induced by 8-oxoGTP. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism linking nucleotide oxidation to age-associated neurodegenerative processes.

title: RNA binding by ADARs prevents RNA interference from attacking self-produced dsRNA
abstract:
The ability of an organism to distinguish between self and foreign double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is central to eliciting an immune response when needed while preventing autoimmunity. Using
                     Caenorhabditis elegans 
                    , we investigated the interplay between two host pathways that regulate dsRNA expression and function, adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing by adenosine deaminases that act on RNA (ADARs), and RNA interference (RNAi). We found that the number of small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) targeting edited genes is significantly up-regulated in ADAR mutant animals. In addition, despite an almost complete depletion of primary siRNAs generated from editing sites in wild-type animals, secondary siRNAs are generated from edited transcripts, suggesting that ADARs antagonize only the first step of RNAi processing. We show that ADARs interfere with the efficacy of exogenous RNAi in vivo, likely to prevent trans-silencing, and provide evidence that ADR-2 binding to dsRNA is required for efficient RNAi suppression. This work sheds light on how RNA editing safeguards self-dsRNAs against immune recognition and by-product degradation.

title: Chirality-selective second-harmonic response with Floquet engineering
Robust pan-junctional reinforcement preserves the gut epithelial barrier under mechanical stress
abstract: Epithelia are specialized tissue barriers that safeguard the organism’s internal milieu from the external environment, a function critically dependent on intercellular junctions. In the colon, this barrier is repeatedly challenged by mechanical distension from feces, but it is unknown whether and how the colon adapts to this stress, which could otherwise compromise barrier integrity. Here, we show that feces-mediated mechanical distension triggers coordinated remodeling at cell and tissue scales, consistent with a mechanoadaptative response. This response includes recruitment of junctional proteins at all three types of adhesive cell-cell junctions (tight junctions, adherens junctions, and desmosomes). We identified protein-specific temporal profiles of junctional enrichment during distension, with ZO-1, E-cadherin, desmocollin 2, and plakoglobin exhibiting sustained junctional enrichment, whereas desmoplakin and keratin 8 showed progressive accumulation peaking at 15 min of distension. Distension was also accompanied by perijunctional recruitment and activation of nonmuscle myosin II (NMMII). Through genetic, pharmacological, and mechanical perturbations, we demonstrated that NMMII activation is required for epithelial mechanoadaptation. This process depends on extracellular calcium availability and mechanosensitive ion channel activity, supporting a role for calcium-dependent mechanosensitive signaling in NMMII-mediated junctional reinforcement. Loss of NMMII function impaired the junctional response to distension across all three junctional complexes, including desmosomes, resulting in disorganized junctions and barrier breach. Together, our findings uncover a robust physiological mechano-adaptive response of the adult colonic epithelium to an extrinsic mechanical stress, whereby coordinated reinforcement of all junctional complexes, requiring myosin II activity and calcium-dependent mechanosensitive signaling, preserves intestinal barrier integrity.

title: Oxygen-dependent constraint of glycolysis through the mitochondrial electron transport chain
abstract:
Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) are constitutively active in clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) cells. Here, we investigated whether these cells could still respond to hypoxia independently of canonical HIF activation. We found that hypoxia provokes a NADH reductive stress that attenuates lactate release when the supply of extracellular pyruvate becomes limited, a response that was restored by the ectopic expression of the cytosolic and mitochondria-targeted NADH oxidase (
                     Lb 
                    NOX). Suppression of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (mtETC) alone is sufficient to attenuate glycolytic flux when extracellular pyruvate is limited, a situation consistent with metabolomic data from human ccRCCs. Furthermore, this response can be mimicked by pharmacological or genetic inhibition of mitochondrial complex IV (CIV) activity and restored by the mitochondrial-targeted alternative oxidase (AOX). Therefore, our data suggest that cells can respond to low oxygen tension through a mitochondrial-dependent elevation of NADH/NAD
                     + 
                    , resulting in the suppression of glycolysis when pyruvate availability is compromised.

title: Machine psychology for language models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show increasingly advanced emergent capabilities and are being incorporated across various societal domains. Understanding their behavior and reasoning abilities is therefore important. We argue that a fruitful direction for research is engaging LLMs in experiments inspired by psychology that have traditionally been aimed at understanding human cognition and behavior. Here, we highlight and summarize theoretical perspectives, experimental paradigms, and computational analysis techniques that this approach brings to the table. It paves the way for a “machine psychology” for LLMs that goes beyond performance measurements and focuses instead on computational insights that move us toward a better understanding and discovery of emergent abilities and behavioral patterns in LLMs. We review existing work taking this approach, synthesize best practices, and highlight promising future directions. We also describe the important caveats of applying methodologies designed for understanding humans to machines. We posit that leveraging tools from experimental psychology to study LLMs will become increasingly valuable as models evolve to be more powerful, opaque, multimodal, and integrated into complex agentic real-world settings.

title: Trans-synaptic interaction of orphan GPCR GPR88 and adhesion GPCR BAI3 through C1ql1 maintains synapse integrity
abstract: GPR88 is an orphan GPCR with genetic variants associated with multiple neuropsychiatric conditions. GPR88 exhibits enriched expression in the striatum, olfactory tubercle, and inferior olive. Despite these functional associations, its endogenous ligand and its downstream molecular pathways remain unresolved. Here, we found that climbing fiber (CF)–localized GPR88 regulates CF-Purkinje cell synapses in the cerebellum and associative learning behaviors. The results support the CF-secreted protein C1ql1 as the ligand of GPR88 and further revealed that C1ql1 activates biased Gq signaling to enhance CF synapses. Last, we demonstrated that GPR88 anchors C1ql1 and, via C1ql1, forms a tripartite complex with the postsynaptic adhesion GPCR BAI3 in vitro. These findings resolve the orphan status of GPR88 and likely reveal a mechanism by which a secreted protein links two GPCRs to fine-tune synaptic signaling at pre- and postsynaptic sites.

title: Hyperlocal sensing and inverse modeling reveal community impacts of urban air pollutant emissions
abstract: Addressing urban air pollution requires identifying, quantifying, and mitigating emission sources, yet bottom-up inventories often lack fine spatiotemporal precision and rarely capture unpermitted or informally operated sources. We combine dense mobile and fixed-site measurements in a Bayesian inverse modeling framework to produce hourly, hyperlocal black carbon (BC) emission maps (150 meters by 150 meters) that reveal how and where key sources are underrepresented. In West Oakland, CA—an overburdened community near major freight infrastructure—our approach identifies underestimated and unaccounted emission sources, increasing estimated BC emissions by ∼33%. These corrections quadruple the contribution of neighborhood and port-related sources to population-weighted exposures (from 5 to 20%), disproportionately affecting low-income neighborhoods adjacent to freight corridors. Our results demonstrate that combining dense observational data with inverse modeling enables detection and quantification of overlooked emissions, supporting targeted intervention. Sensitivity analyses indicate similar performance with a substantially reduced fixed-site network (∼10 monitors; ∼1 site per square kilometer, compared with 6.7 sites per square kilometer in the full campaign), paired with time-averaged mobile maps, supporting applicability in data-limited urban settings.

title: A nematic framework for sprouting angiogenesis
abstract: Sprouting angiogenesis is critical for embryogenesis, wound healing, and tumor growth. Here, we show that the liquid crystal framework, which has recently been leveraged to study various morphogenetic events, provides unique insight into angiogenic sprouting. In response to vascular endothelial growth factor, a potent proangiogenic factor, endothelial cells cultured on the surfaces of soft collagen hydrogels form elongated cell streams that coexist with more polygonal cell regions. Angiogenic sprouting initiates preferentially at cell stream tips, where nematic order gradients are most pronounced. We demonstrate that cell streams are associated with large traction forces that lead to three-dimensional deformations of the underlying hydrogel and that stream formation results from a delicate balance between microtubule polymerization and actomyosin contractility. Last, we show that active control of nematic order allows modulation of sprout formation, highlighting the key role of endothelial cell orientation gradients in angiogenic sprouting and paving the way for new therapeutic avenues.

title: Graph-based pangenome analysis uncovers structural and functional impacts of allopolyploidization events
abstract:
The emergence of graph pangenomes has advanced the study of structural variants (SVs) across diverse species, yet the impact of complex ploidy on SV landscapes remains poorly explored.
                     Brettanomyces bruxellensis 
                    , a yeast shaped by multiple allopolyploidization events, offers a compelling model due to its well-characterized genomic and phenotypic diversity. Here, we integrated subgenome-resolved assemblies with population-scale genomic and transcriptomic datasets to characterize SV distribution and functional impact at the species level. Leveraging a reference graph pangenome, we detected 5972 unique SVs across 1060 isolates. Allopolyploid genomes harbored significantly more SVs (320 on average) than diploids (116), reflecting hybridization’s extensive impact on genome architecture. Functional association analysis revealed that 27.5% of SVs locally influence gene expression. Furthermore, a subset of SVs originating from ancestral divergence between subgenomes (hybridization-associated SVs) formed hotspots of structural diversity and disproportionately affect gene expression, with larger effect sizes than other SVs. These findings underscore allopolyploidization as a driver of structural and functional genomic diversification, highlighting the value of graph-based approaches in dissecting complex genome evolution.

title: Decoder-FFPE-seq enables sensitive, genome-wide spatial transcriptomics of archival tissues at single-cell resolution
abstract:
Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue–compatible spatial transcriptomics (ST) is transforming biology and histopathology, but achieving high sensitivity, genome-wide coverage, single-cell resolution, and researcher accessibility remains challenging. To address these challenges, we here present a dendrimeric DNA coordinate barcoding design for FFPE tissue–adapted spatial RNA sequencing (Decoder-FFPE-seq) by integrating RNA-to-DNA probe conversion with blotting-assisted barcoding. Decoder-FFPE-seq provides single-cell resolution with a >2.6-fold sensitivity increase in whole-transcriptome mouse brain and archived human sample profiling over existing platforms, resolving potential cellular identity of low-abundance genes, finer tissue architecture, and capturing an epithelial-mesenchymal transition–associated signature for prognostic value. With expanded probe libraries, Decoder-FFPE-seq captures long noncoding and viral RNAs, revealing their spatial coregulatory networks with messenger RNAs in oral squamous cell carcinomas (OSCCs). In an OSCC immunotherapy cohort, two CD8
                     + 
                    T cell subpopulations were respectively identified in pre- and postchemoimmunotherapy samples, potentially linked to treatment response. Decoder-FFPE-seq establishes a robust, high-resolution, and accessible framework for sensitive ST profiling of archival tissues in fundamental and translational studies.

title:
Natural variation in the evolutionarily conserved F‐box gene
                     SDEF 
                    promotes seed dormancy in rice
authors:
Yuliang Zhou, 
Yueping Wang, 
Guangmiao Zhao, 
Chunbao Liu, 
Ruizhen Zeng, 
Wenxuan Liang, 
Ru Han, 
Hui Kong, 
Xiaofan Cao, 
Minshi Li, 
Huhui Chen, 
Bin Tan, 
Hong Liu, 
Zhenjiang Xu
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   
                    Insufficient seed dormancy causes pre‐harvest sprouting (PHS) and severe yield losses in rice; however, genetic resources with practical breeding value remain limited. Here, we isolated a major dormancy gene,
                     SDEF 
                    , via map‐based cloning using chromosomal single segment substitution lines (SSSLs), identifying a functional SNP (Arg‐to‐Trp) as the causal mutation. CRISPR/Cas9‐mediated knockout of
                     SDEF 
                    led to PHS susceptibility, while overexpression significantly enhanced dormancy. Importantly,
                     SDEF 
                    enhanced seed dormancy without compromising grain yield in SSSLs, confirming it as a promising breeding target. Moreover,
                     SDEF 
                    encodes an angiosperm‐conserved, nuclear‐localized F‐box protein and is preferentially expressed in the embryo, with expression increasing during seed maturation and declining upon germination. Mechanistically, protein interaction assays confirmed that SDEF recruits OSK1, with the Trp‐type SDEF
                     K 
                    exhibiting a more stable interaction than the Arg‐type SDEF
                     H 
                    .
                     SDEF 
                    is induced by abscisic acid (ABA) and appears to promote seed dormancy through the ABA pathway by activating ABA signaling genes and repressing α‐amylase genes, as evidenced by the reduced ABA sensitivity of
                     sdef 
                    mutants. Additionally, haplotype analysis revealed that natural variation in
                     SDEF 
                    is associated with divergent dormancy levels, and reduced nucleotide diversity in cultivated rice indicates that
                     SDEF 
                    was selected during domestication. Collectively, our results provide insights into the molecular basis of
                     SDEF‐ 
                    mediated dormancy, providing an ideal target for breeding PHS‐resistant rice.

title:
OsYchF1 
                    suppresses
                     OsEF1Bγ 
                    ‐mediated
                     ER 
                    detoxification to co‐involve the growth‐maintenance trade‐off in rice
authors:
Liyang Gao, 
Lulu Yu, 
Dongyu Chen, 
Rongfang Li, 
Yuhe Wang, 
Yunchuan Liao, 
Yetao Meng, 
Qian Li, 
Ying Miao, 
Gefei Hao, 
Rui Miao
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   
                    Translation elongation is a fundamental biological process, yet its direct role in stress adaptation remains unclear. In this study, we uncover a novel regulatory axis in rice involving the unconventional G protein OsYchF1, which gates the detoxification activity of the elongation factor 1Bγ (OsEF1Bγ) in the endoplasmic reticulum. OsEF1Bγ is a subunit of the eEF1B complex and possesses an N‐terminal glutathione S‐transferase (GST) domain. We demonstrate that overexpression of OsEF1Bγ enhances rice tolerance to osmotic and saline stress by lowering malondialdehyde levels, suggesting its role as a positive regulator
                     via 
                    GST‐mediated detoxification. Conversely, we found that OsYchF1 interacts with OsEF1Bγ across multiple domains. This interaction competitively inhibits the binding of reduced glutathione to OsEF1Bγ by approximately 40‐fold, thereby suppressing its GST activity
                     in vitro 
                    . Consistently,
                     OsYchF1 
                    knockout mutants phenocopy OsEF1Bγ overexpressors, displaying enhanced stress tolerance, reduced reactive oxygen species accumulation, and increased antioxidant enzyme activities. Furthermore, we show that stress‐induced downregulation of OsYchF1 acts as a physiological trigger, releasing this molecular brake to enable rapid activation of OsEF1Bγ‐mediated detoxification in response to challenging environments. Collectively, our findings reveal a post‐translational mechanism where OsYchF1 serves as a molecular brake on the ER‐localized detoxification engine of OsEF1Bγ, fine‐tuning abiotic stress adaptation and establishing an unexpected link between the translation machinery and cellular redox homeostasis.

title: Water stable isotopes reveal the ecohydrological importance of stemflow infiltration for mature and juvenile European beech
authors:
Simon Haberstroh, 
Simon Keller, 
Laura Kinzinger, 
Judith Mach, 
Kathrin Kühnhammer, 
Markus Weiler, 
Natalie Orlowski, 
Christiane Werner
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         Stemflow of forest trees can contribute a significant fraction of water to forest's water fluxes; however, it is still unclear whether and to what extent trees and their neighbours use stemflow for water uptake and supply. 
                       
                       
                         
                          We applied deuterium‐enriched stemflow equivalent to a 23‐mm throughfall event to adult
                           Fagus sylvatica 
                          trees to trace stemflow through the soil and trees. We continuously measured
                           in situ 
                          water stable isotopes in soil and xylem water and destructively sampled xylem water in the crowns of adult labelled, nonlabelled
                           F. sylvatica 
                          and nonlabelled
                           Picea abies 
                          , complemented by destructive xylem water sampling of neighbouring juvenile
                           F. sylvatica 
                          .
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          Stemflow water supported up to 5.7 ± 2.1% of daily sap flux of adult
                           F. sylvatica 
                          trees labelled at the stem base and was detectable in xylem water for several weeks. In the soil, deuterium‐enriched stemflow was present at a maximum distance of 0.40 m from the labelled tree. Moreover, nonlabelled juvenile trees within a distance of 2 m showed uptake of labelled water, indicating rooting into soil compartments affected by stemflow.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          We demonstrate the importance of stemflow as a water source for both adult and neighbouring juvenile
                           F. sylvatica 
                          , even when soil water is not limiting.

title:
RCD1 
                    nuclear shuttling releases
                     WRKY47 
                    to trigger
                     bHLH105 
                    /
                     bHLH115 
                    ‐dependent iron acquisition
authors:
Xi Wu, 
Qian Ma, 
Mengfan Wu, 
Jiena Xu, 
Yong Yan, 
Hui Song, 
Shuqing Cao
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         Iron (Fe) deficiency limits plant growth, yet its upstream regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. 
                       
                       
                         
                          Here, we identify WRKY47 as a positive regulator of Fe‐deficiency responses in Arabidopsis. WRKY47 directly binds and activates
                           bHLH105 
                          and
                           bHLH115 
                          , key IVc bHLH factors that trigger the Fe uptake cascade.
                         
                       
                       
                         We further show that RCD1 interacts with WRKY47 and suppresses its DNA‐binding and transcriptional activity. Fe deficiency also promotes the redistribution of RCD1 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, suggesting a potential mechanism for modulating WRKY47 activity during the response. 
                       
                       
                         Our findings uncover a previously uncharacterized regulatory mechanism linking WRKY transcription factors and the bHLH cascade through RCD1‐mediated modulation, providing a conceptual framework for engineering crops with enhanced Fe acquisition and stress resilience.

title: A beneficial root endophyte buffers natural variation in pathogen susceptibility across Arabidopsis accessions
authors:
Natalie Peltz, 
Laura Armbruster, 
Christopher Stephens, 
Vivien Joisten‐Rosenthal, 
Tim Thomsen, 
Alex W. Yan, 
Nick Dunken, 
Renan Granado, 
Stanislav Kopriva, 
Juliette de Meaux, 
Gregor Langen, 
Anna Koprivova, 
Björn Usadel, 
Alga Zuccaro
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         
                          Host genetic diversity shapes pathogen susceptibility within plant populations, raising the question of whether beneficial root microbes can buffer these differences. The fungal root endophyte
                           Serendipita indica 
                          (
                           Si 
                          ) promotes plant growth and can mitigate disease caused by the pathogen
                           Bipolaris sorokiniana 
                          (
                           Bs 
                          ). Here, we assessed how natural host genetic variation influences
                           Si 
                          ‐mediated protection against
                           Bs 
                          in
                           Arabidopsis thaliana 
                          .
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          We screened 47
                           A. thaliana 
                          accessions for susceptibility to
                           Bs 
                          with and without
                           Si 
                          colonization and performed phenotypic, transcriptomic, and comparative genomic analyses of two genetically and geographically proximate Swedish accessions, T510 and T530, that differed strongly in
                           Bs 
                          colonization.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                           Si 
                          conferred consistent protection against
                           Bs 
                          across all accessions, despite variation in baseline susceptibility and immune‐gene content. T510 and T530 differed in
                           Bs 
                          colonization, disease symptoms, transcriptional responses, and immune‐gene repertoires, including presence–absence variation of the TIR‐NLR gene
                           ISI 
                          . T530 lacks
                           ISI 
                          , and mutation of
                           ISI 
                          in Col‐0 increased
                           Bs 
                          susceptibility, demonstrating that
                           ISI 
                          contributes to root immunity. However,
                           Si 
                          ‐mediated protection was retained in the absence of
                           ISI 
                          , demonstrating that
                           ISI 
                          is not required for this protective effect.
                         
                       
                       
                         Beneficial fungal endophytes can thus buffer phenotypic consequences of natural variation in pathogen susceptibility, stabilizing disease outcomes across genetically diverse plant populations.

title: Decomposition and mycorrhizal suppression of saprotrophs remain stable after wildfire and clearcut disturbance in boreal forests
authors:
Timon Callebaut, 
Michael J. Gundale, 
Vincent Buness, 
Isabella M. Garrioch, 
Sydney Nute, 
Maja K. Sundqvist, 
Ilse van Duuren, 
Daniel B. Metcalfe
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         Boreal forests store a large portion of global terrestrial carbon, primarily in soils, yet their sensitivity to environmental changes remains uncertain. Disturbance is one major agent of change, with dominance shifting from wildfire to forest management over the past century. Mycorrhizal suppression of saprotrophic decomposition may be an important control on boreal soil carbon storage, but its occurrence and magnitude remain uncertain. Additionally, the distinct impacts of wildfire and clearcutting on decomposition and soil microbial communities remain largely unexplored. 
                       
                       
                         We quantified mycorrhizal suppression of saprotrophs and decomposition in needle and humus litter through a root‐exclusion experiment in 31 sites across wildfire (4–375 yr since disturbance) and clearcut chronosequences (1–109 yr since disturbance) in northern Sweden. 
                       
                       
                         Mycorrhizas suppressed decomposition by 15.5 ± 5.9% overall, with no consistent change over time after disturbance. This pattern was linked to absolute fungal abundance but not to other microbial community shifts, soil temperature or soil moisture. Decomposition rates were stable across time since disturbance for all substrates and disturbance types. 
                       
                       
                         Our findings improve understanding of mycorrhizal‐decomposition interactions and highlight the need to further explore key fungal traits and compositional changes, especially at the soil surface, that regulate carbon storage dynamics in boreal soils.

title: NSP2 phosphorylation modulates HYL1 nuclear import via KETCH1 to promote miRNA biogenesis in Arabidopsis
authors:
Tingting Zhai, 
Mengjie Gu, 
Yanjiao Wang, 
Ke Qu, 
Ping Liu, 
Wei Yang, 
Shuxin Zhang
abstract:
Arabidopsis NITRILE-SPECIFIER PROTEIN 2 (NSP2) is a phosphorylation-regulated scaffold that coordinates HYL1 nuclear trafficking and microprocessor assembly. Dephosphorylation of NSP2 promotes the nuclear import of HYL1, thereby facilitating microRNA biogenesis.
  
 ABSTRACT 
 MicroRNA (miRNA) biogenesis in plants relies on the precise nuclear-cytoplasmic trafficking of the HYL1 protein. Here, we report that the NITRILE-SPECIFIER PROTEIN 2 (NSP2) is a previously unrecognized component of the Arabidopsis miRNA pathway. Through yeast two-hybrid, BiFC, Co-IP, and genetic analyses, we demonstrate that NSP2 physically interacts with HYL1 and genetically suppresses  hyl1-2 . NSP2 overexpression increases global miRNA abundance. Mechanistically, NSP2 acts as an adapter that bridges the importin-β family member KETCH1 to HYL1, thereby regulating HYL1 nuclear import and dicing-body (D-body) assembly. Dephosphorylation of NSP2 at a conserved threonine (T314) strengthens KETCH1–HYL1 association and further enhances pri-miRNA processing. Our study establishes NSP2 as a phosphorylation-regulated scaffold that coordinates HYL1 nuclear trafficking and microprocessor assembly, and reveals critical roles for NSP2 in miRNA biogenesis.

title:
Transcriptional coordination of the aromatic amino acid metabolic network in
                     Petunia 
                    and beyond
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Plants produce vast arrays of specialized metabolites mediating ecological interactions, notably including phenylalanine-derived metabolites. Biosynthesizing these metabolites requires not only defined structural pathways, but also tight coordination between the shikimate pathway, aromatic amino acid production, and downstream specialized metabolism, such as benzenoid metabolism. Regulation occurs at multiple levels, including post-translational control of enzymes through mechanisms such as allostery, wherein binding of a regulatory metabolite alters catalytic activity. However, transcriptional regulation is also a flux control mechanism in these pathways and has increasingly been studied. Here, we summarize recent developments in this field. Petunia emerged as a key model for understanding how transcriptional networks regulate this metabolic system, complemented by discoveries in other species. Central to this regulation are MYB transcription factors, including PhODO1, PhEOBI, and PhEOBII, which coordinate the expression of genes involved in both precursor supply and volatile formation. These regulators operate within broad networks that integrate environmental signals, including light, circadian rhythms, temperature, and hormonal cues, through additional transcription factors. Developmental regulators, particularly MADS-box transcription factors, link floral organ identity with metabolism, ensuring scent production occurs within appropriate developmental stages and tissues. Beyond transcriptional and enzymatic regulation, accumulation and utilization are also influenced by post-synthetic processes, including glycosylation, intracellular sequestration, transport, storage, and export. Together, these elements form multilayered frameworks that coordinates primary and specialized metabolism, ultimately determining composition, accumulation, and utilization of specialized metabolites. Expanding this framework across plant species will be essential for understanding metabolic regulation and enabling targeted manipulation of aroma and stress-related traits in crops.

title: Phenylboronic acid-induced defects in maize roots are independent of rhamnogalacturonan-II dimerization
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Soil boron deficiency is a global abiotic stress, negatively impacting on crop yield. In the dicot model species Arabidopsis thaliana, inhibition of root elongation is one of the earliest symptoms of boron deficiency. In the monocot model maize (Zea mays L.), boron deficiency-induced root defects are widely unexplored. In this study, we assessed boron deficiency-induced defects in the primary root system of maize and tested the suitability of phenylboronic acid (PBA) as boron deficiency mimic by performing phenotypic, histological, molecular, and biochemical analyses. Our analyses showed that boron deficiency and PBA resulted in similar defects in primary root elongation and lateral root density. The PBA-induced defects, however, were much stronger than those induced by boron deficiency, particularly regarding lateral root development. We provide evidence that the PBA-induced defects were caused by the boric acid moiety and show that both boron deficiency and PBA altered the levels of auxin and reactive oxygen species. Strikingly, PBA did not affect rhamnogalacturonan-II (RG-II) dimerization. Interference of boron-mediated RG-II crosslinking, however, was previously proposed to be the mode of action of PBA in planta. Our study shows that PBA is particularly suited for the molecular dissection of lateral root development in maize and suggests that PBA does not mimic known molecular boron deficiency responses.

title: CsVTT1, a PQ-loop vacuolar amino acid transporter, mediates vacuolar theanine storage in tea plant roots under nitrogen supply
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Theanine, a unique and major nitrogen storage amino acid in tea plants, is responsible for the tea umami taste and confers numerous health benefits. Despite its importance, the molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating its biosynthesis and accumulation remain poorly understood. In this study, we identified a PQ-loop amino acid transporter, CsVTT1 (Vacuolar Theanine Transporter 1), through integrative analyses including yeast mutant library screening, along with correlation analysis between gene expression and theanine accumulation, and homologous gene complementation. Our findings revealed that CsVTT1 expression is nitrogen-inducible and strongly correlates with theanine accumulation in tea plant roots under different nitrogen regimes. Functional characterization in both yeast and Xenopus laevis oocytes demonstrated that CsVTT1 facilitates cytoplasmic to vacuolar transport of theanine, glutamine, arginine and other amino acids. Genetic manipulation experiments showed that CsVTT1 overexpression significantly enhanced theanine accumulation in tea plant roots, whereas its knockdown reduced theanine levels. Notably, CsVTT1 overexpression in rice greatly increased arginine accumulation, the main nitrogen storage amino acid in non-tea plants, suggesting a conserved role for CsVTT1 in nitrogen metabolism and storage, consistent with its newly identified function in mediating theanine storage in the vacuole. Consequently, CsVTT1 emerges as a promising target for genetic strategies aimed at simultaneously enhancing tea quality and nitrogen use efficiency.

title:
Sorghum grain biofortification by
                     SbSTP20 
                    -mediated hexose influx and sub-aleurone thickening
abstract: Abstract Biofortification offers a sustainable solution to "hidden hunger, " yet the trade-off between grain yield and nutritional quality remains a persistent breeding bottleneck. Modern crop breeding emphasises the balance between high yield and nutritional values. Use of novel genes/alleles for grain quality lost during domestication and genetic improvement has been proven an efficient way to help achieve the dual goals. In sorghum, we report here the discovery of  SbSTP20 , encoding a sorghum monosaccharide transporter, as an essential component for biofortification by mediating the endosperm hexose influx and sub-aleurone (SA) thickness.  SbSTP20  was ectopically expressed in sorghum developing grains and its expression levels were negatively associated with SA thickness. CRISPR edited  Sbstp20  lines decreased the influx of hexoses, and exhibited thicker sub-aleurone layers and 6.6-7.5% higher grain protein and enriched micronutrients (Fe, Zn).  SbSTP20  thick  natural variant increased sub-aleurone layer thickness and improved grain nutritional quality without altering grain size or thousand-grain weight. The  SbSTP20  thick  allele was absent in 93% of modern improved lines, implying that the genomic region containing  SbSTP20  showed a moderate selection signature. The metabolizable energy of  SbSTP20  thick  containing sorghum lines was up to 6% higher than that of commercial corn standards in swine digestion and metabolism experiments. Reintroducing this haplotype via marker-assisted selection could provide a molecular strategy for nutritional enhancement.

title: Temperature-gated active salt secretion enables stable photothermal evaporation
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Photothermal evaporation offers a sustainable solution for brine and seawater desalination, yet its long-term operation is fundamentally limited by salt accumulation arising from diffusion-limited ion transport, especially under high evaporative flux. Here, inspired by the active salt secretion of the mangrove, we develop a temperature-responsive evaporator that actively regulates ion transport through temperature-gated channel dynamics for stable high-flux evaporation. By integrating thermoresponsive poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) within an ordered reduced graphene oxide-carbon nanotube architecture, the system achieves reversible contraction and swelling with a ratio of 87%, enabling continuous water replenishment during heating and efficient expulsion of concentrated brine upon cooling. This salt secretion process accelerates salt backflow by over 2 orders of magnitude compared with conventional diffusion-driven transport, effectively renewing the evaporation surface and sustaining stable high-flux water collection (∼3.40 kg m−2 h−1) under diverse saline conditions and solar intensities. By replacing passive structural optimization with active transport regulation, this work establishes a new strategy for salt management in photothermal desalination and adaptive interfacial transport systems.

title: High-order nanofluidic spiking encoding
abstract:
Abstract 
                   High-order memristor is needed in neuromorphic engineering for sophisticated neural encoding. Progress has been made in solid-state memristor with electronic dynamics, which, however, presents a significant disparity with the ionic-chemical signaling in the human brain. Herein, we realize high-order nanofluidic spiking encoding based on synergizing the high porosity for non-linear ion transport, light responsibility for optical sensing, and catalytic chemistry for biological perception of a multifunctional covalent organic framework under nanoconfinement. The unique multimodal responses make possible the co-encoded spiking by electricity, light and real neurotransmitter glutamate in the physiological media, leading to the significantly enriched synaptic plasticity towards high-order spiking encoding behaviors, i.e. the rate encoding, time-to-first-spike encoding, rate and temporal fusion encoding, and history-dependent spiking encoding. It is expected to be a starting point for high-order nanofluidic spiking encoding.

title: Ultrafast singlet–triplet intersystem crossing gated by nonrelativistic nuclear dynamics
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Transitions between electronic states of different spin multiplicities, known as intersystem crossing (ISC), are of fundamental importance in optoelectronics and materials chemistry. ISC has traditionally been viewed as directly driven by spin–orbit coupling (SOC), a relativistic interaction that enables spin-forbidden transitions. Recent studies suggest that vibronic interactions can modulate spin-orbit coupling and induce enhanced mixing between electronic spin states, enabling efficient ISC at specific nuclear configurations. Despite the recognized importance of vibration–spin-orbit coupling, direct manipulation of ISC dynamics through controlled nuclear motions remains challenging. Here, using ultrafast pulse-sequence spectroscopy, we accelerate ISC by nearly three orders of magnitude, reducing its timescale from 1.3 ns to 1.4 ± 0.2 ps. This dramatic enhancement is achieved by selectively tuning vibrational motions in the singlet excited state of the chalcone (E)-3-(4-(dimethylamino)phenyl)-1-(2-methoxyphenyl)prop-2-en-1-one (E-DMPO). Photoexcitation activates benzene-skeleton vibrations that drive the singlet excited state toward geometries near the singlet–triplet crossing region, resulting in rapid and efficient singlet-to-triplet population funneling. These results demonstrate that SOC, although an essential prerequisite for ISC, is not the sole determinant of ISC rates. Instead, nuclear dynamics—an intrinsic nonrelativistic factor—can critically regulate the accessibility of singlet–triplet crossing regions and thereby dominate the ISC kinetics. In other words, nuclear motion can effectively gate ISC. This insight suggests promising molecular- and vibrational-design strategies, beyond the conventional approach of enhancing SOC through heavy-atom incorporation.

title: Heterogeneous tandem catalysis for regioselective hydroaminomethylation of olefins to linear amines by a composite catalyst
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Hydroformylation of olefins followed by reductive amination is a key route to aliphatic amines, yet industrial processes suffer from energy-intensive aldehyde isolation and side reactions. Hydroaminomethylation offers a one-pot alternative, but heterogeneous catalysts have long struggled to combine high linear regioselectivity with chemoselectivity due to mismatched kinetics and unselective hydrogenation. Here we report a heterogeneous tandem catalytic system comprising Rh@MFI zeolite for selective hydroformylation of α-olefins to linear aldehydes and Pd1Cu1/SiO2 for subsequent imine hydrogenation. The confined Rh species within the MFI framework deliver exceptional linear regioselectivity. In the PdCu alloy, Cu disrupts Pd ensembles, weakens multi-coordinated CO adsorption, and increases Pd electron density, thereby accelerating imine hydrogenation while suppressing competitive hydrogenation of olefins and aldehydes. This kinetic coupling enables the direct conversion of α-olefins and amines into linear secondary and tertiary amines with >99% regioselectivity and high yields (typically 85–98%) across a broad substrate scope. In situ X-ray absorption fine structure, infrared spectroscopy, and density functional theory calculations elucidate the origins of the (regio)selectivity and efficient tandem catalysis. The ligand-free, easily separable composite catalyst offers a practical, atom-efficient, and sustainable platform for producing high-value linear amines from abundant olefins.

title: Genome compartmentalization in a fungal insect pathogen reveals a second mating-type locus on an accessory chromosome
abstract:
Abstract 
                   The genomes of many fungal pathogens include rapidly evolving regions with high transposable element densities. Such regions often contain genes important for pathogenicity and may be non-core genomic elements carried on accessory chromosomes that are variably present among isolates considered to be members of the same species. Here we present a pangenomic analysis of a fungal insect pathogen, Metarhizium acridum, using six chromosomal assemblies that include isolates from four different continents. We show that the pangenome of M. acridum exhibits a continuum of compartmentalization, with a core genome that contains most of the carbohydrate-active enzymes, while accessory genes are primarily located in gene-sparse regions which encode many small secreted proteins, termed effectors, that are active during host interaction. Furthermore, we identified the first accessory chromosome in M. acridum. In contrast to the accessory chromosomes of many other fungal species, this chromosome does not encode any known effectors or secondary metabolite proteins related to pathogen-host interactions. Instead, the accessory chromosome is enriched in functions related to sexual reproduction and carries genes from both the MAT1-1 and MAT1-2 mating-type idiomorphs, in addition to the canonical MAT locus found on the core chromosomes. Notable as, within the genus Metarhizium, M. acridum is one of few species considered to regularly reproduce sexually. Our findings suggest that the presence of this accessory chromosome further facilitates sexual reproduction, possibly even primary homothallism, in the otherwise heterothallic M. acridum. Overall, our study suggests a novel mechanism in which an accessory chromosome may enhance the capacity for a fungal pathogen to undergo recombination.

title: Polygenic adaptation signals reveal selection on key behavioral traits early in dog domestication history
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Dogs, the first domesticated animals, show behavioral and morphological changes shaped by artificial selection, but when and where these traits were selected remains unclear. Analyzing two independent canine genomic datasets comprising 1,987 and 722 individuals, we found that polygenic shifts in key behavioral traits associated with domestication were more consistently shared across dog lineages than those in morphological traits. Specifically, we first grouped breeds into three major genetic lineages—Asian Spitz, African–Middle Eastern, and European Modern—and integrated genomic variation with breed-level measures of 36 behavioral and four morphological traits. We then tested for polygenic adaptation using pairwise population comparisons and PolyGraph. Across both datasets, pro-social behavioral shifts, particularly reduced owner-directed aggression and non-social fear, showed the most consistent selection signals. PolyGraph detected shifts toward lower values for both traits on branches ancestral to the major dog lineages. Trainability showed an ancestral increase, whereas attachment/attention seeking increased in specific lineages, based on dog-only analyses designed to minimize rearing-related confounding in wolves. Hunting-related behaviors also showed lineage-specific shifts, while morphological traits varied substantially across datasets and lineages. Ancient genetic trait scores mirrored these patterns: prehistoric dogs already differed from wolves in shared pro-social behavioral traits and displayed lineage-specific shifts in hunting-related behaviors, whereas morphological scores remained heterogeneous. Together, these findings indicate that both shared behavioral changes and functional differentiation among dog lineages began early in domestication.

title: Repeatability of adaptation in interacting species
abstract: Abstract In many evolving systems, mutations have background-dependent fitness effects due to genetic interactions between loci within a genome (intragenomic epistasis). In coevolving species, genetic interactions can span across genomes, a phenomenon described as intergenomic epistasis. It is known that intragenomic epistasis can make adaptation more repeatable by constraining accessible mutational paths from a specific starting genotype, generating path repeatability. Here, we investigate how endpoint repeatability – how often adaptation from different starting genotypes reaches the same states in the genotype and fitness space – is influenced by the interplay of intra- and intergenomic epistasis. To this end, we model a two-species community in which the fitness of each genotype depends on the combination of present genotypes of both species. We implement this by constructing and simulating adaptation on coevolutionary fitness landscapes using an  NKC(S)  model, an extension of Kauffman's  NK  model of evolution that includes intergenomic epistasis. On these fitness landscapes, we simulate adaptive walks that alternate between mutations in a focal and a partner species. To quantify the repeatability of adaptation, we track the endpoints of adaptive walks and record the fitness of both species at the evolutionary endpoints. We find that individual fitness landscapes with intergenomic epistasis can maintain high endpoint repeatability. Yet, intergenomic epistasis causes highly variable fitness outcomes across different fitness landscapes. Thus, patterns of repeatability deviate from expectations based on single-species adaptation in the presence of intragenomic epistasis, due to varying fitness trade-offs between species, which can lead to cycling and large coevolutionary fitness loads.

title: Correction: Sperm entry without genome inheritance: incorporate or exclude—egg-intrinsic control of paternal genome fate in Cobitis fish
abstract: This is a correction to: Eleonora Pustovalova, Daniel Kulik, Anatol Marta, Grzegorz Skórzewski, Jan Kotusz, Karel Janko, Katerina Komrskova, Dmitrij Dedukh, Sperm entry without genome inheritance: incorporate or exclude—egg-intrinsic control of paternal genome fate in  Cobitis  fish,  Genetics , Volume 234, Issue 2, October 2026, iyag193,  https://doi.org/10.1093/genetics/iyag193

title: Assessment of LLMs on basic bioinformatics tasks requiring multi-step reasoning and code writing
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Large Language Models (LLMs), AI agents and co-scientists promise to accelerate scientific discovery across fields ranging from chemistry to biology. Bioinformatics—the analysis of DNA, RNA and protein sequences plays a crucial role in biological research and is especially amenable to AI-driven automation given its computational nature. Here, we assess the bioinformatics capabilities of popular general-purpose LLMs on a set of tasks covering basic analytical questions that include code writing and multi-step reasoning in the domain. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     Utilizing questions from Rosalind, a bioinformatics educational platform, we compare the performance of the LLMs on 104 questions relative to expert ground truth and 68 760 humans with varying levels of expertise. Among the frontier LLMs evaluated (GPT-5.2, GPT-4o, GPT-3.5, Llama-3-70B, Llama-4 and Claude Sonnet 4.6), GPT-5.2 exhibited top performance, providing correct answers for 80/104 (77%) questions followed by Claude Sonnet 4.6. LLM performance varied widely depending on the biological categories of questions. While the latest generation of frontier LLM models showed overall improvements in performance, their performance in specific categories of biological questions was lower than first generation models. Overall, LLMs performance mirrored that of humans with lower performance in tasks in which humans had low performance and vice versa. However, LLMs also failed in some instances where most humans were correct and, in a few cases, LLMs excelled where most humans failed. To the best of our knowledge, this presents the first assessment of general purpose LLMs on basic bioinformatics tasks in distinct areas relative to both expert and non-expert ground truths. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and Implementation 
                     The complete analysis was implemented in Python; all code is available at https://github.com/SiwoResearch/lllm-bioinformatics.

Mark A. Ratner (1942–2026): Founded molecular electronics while spearheading the growth of science at Northwestern University
abstract: Recently, we lost one of the original developers of the field of molecular electronics. Mark A. Ratner wrote a famous paper in 1974 that developed the theoretical framework for making a molecule act as a rectifier. This idea, and a host of further ideas that were stimulated by this and other papers, led to a huge amount of experimental and theoretical studies that continue to this day. But Mark’s career was much more than that, with leadership at Northwestern University and beyond that continues to shape the scientific enterprise.

title: Reply to Cirillo: Early-life exposure to the sugar-rationing regime, not a measured sugar dose, drives the cancer gradient
Reply to Yu and Yu: Clarifying the role of carnitine metabolism in the ALDH9A1-associated immunotherapy resistance program
Reassessing the causal interpretation of the UK sugar-rationing natural experiment
Evidence and gaps in the proposed ALDH9A1–carnitine–acetyl-CoA–IL-1β axis
D-termining factors influencing phenotypic evolution in prehistoric Europe
Deep mutational scanning of the GPCR rhodopsin reveals pleiotropic mutational effects and their roles in modulating receptor signaling
abstract: Biophysical pleiotropy, the phenomenon in which a mutation affects multiple protein properties, underlies many genetic diseases and shapes protein evolution, yet remains poorly understood, limiting synthetic biology and therapeutic development. Although extensively studied in soluble proteins, little is known about how pleiotropic effects shaped the evolution of receptor protein functions. Here, we developed a cell-based assay designed to assess pleiotropic effects in G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest receptor class in eukaryotes. Because our assay allows for multiple GPCR molecular phenotypes (basal activity, ligand-dependent signaling, and cellular receptor abundance) to be simultaneously assessed, we applied it to study rhodopsin, a visual GPCR that evolved for high phototransduction capabilities by maximizing light-driven responses while minimizing noise. To investigate this, we integrated our assay with deep mutational scanning to test the impacts of ~2,000 single-residue substitutions in rhodopsin across all three molecular phenotypes (~6,000 measurements). By analyzing these data in the context of rhodopsin’s protein structures, we found complex pleiotropic effects that act asymmetrically to impose joint constraints, restricting mutational tolerance in rhodopsin’s retinal binding pocket and G protein interaction interface. A dose–response analysis of rhodopsin signaling revealed that these pleiotropic constraints arise from the dual functions of its chromophore, which acts as an agonist upon light-driven isomerization but also an inverse agonist in darkness. Because these constraints reflect mechanistically driven limitations in the evolution of receptor signaling, these findings reveal a role for biophysical pleiotropy in shaping the signaling capabilities of receptor proteins.

title: Structural basis of glycoprotein recognition by the human folding sensor UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase
abstract: UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) plays a central role in quality control of glycoprotein folding within the early secretory pathway, yet the molecular basis of UGGT1 substrate recognition remains poorly understood. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human full-length multidomain UGGT1. Monomeric UGGT1 structures reveal two conformational states corresponding to “open” and “closed” architectures. Three-dimensional variability and molecular dynamics simulations suggest the existence of intermediate conformations, leading to a model in which a continuum of structural transitions underlies UGGT1 function. Notably, in the open state, the EM-maps reveal at the top of the U-shaped protein a density that bridges the sensory TRXL2 and the glucosyltransferase catalytic domains, consistent with substrate association. This observation supports a mode of binding that places the substrate near the catalytic domain. A dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. To better understand the spatial relationship between the site of misfolding and that of UGGT-mediated N-glycan reglucosylation, we identified N-glycosylation sites on endogenous glycoprotein substrates by glycoproteomics. No consensus sequence was found flanking modified sites, indicating that substrate recognition relies on mechanisms beyond primary sequence. Mutations in the UGGT1 gene cause a novel congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, and the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Together, our data provide insight into the relationship between UGGT1 structure and function, integrating enzyme conformational states with client glycoprotein interaction and processing.

title: In-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling
abstract: Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.

title: HAR1 receptor kinase links nodule autoregulation with repression of auxin signaling and lateral root development
abstract:
Nitrogen-fixing root nodules develop as lateral organs on legume roots and their formation is restricted by autoregulation of nodulation (AON), a systemic mechanism with unclear evolutionary origins. We identify
                     Lotus japonicus NUCLEAR FACTOR Y 
                    subunit
                     A4 
                    (
                     NF-YA4 
                    ) gene as a central target of the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinase HAR1, which controls both AON and root system architecture. Under nonsymbiotic conditions, HAR1 suppresses expression of
                     NF-YA4 
                    and its close paralog
                     NF-YA1 
                    , at least in part through a miR169-dependent mechanism, mirroring the
                     Arabidopsis 
                    CLAVATA1/2-miR169-
                     NF-YA 
                    module. Loss of
                     HAR1 
                    leads to
                     NF-YA4 
                    overexpression, broad transcriptional reprogramming, and induction of
                     LATERAL ORGAN BOUNDARIES DOMAIN 
                    ,
                     STYLISH 
                    , and
                     YUCCA 
                    auxin biosynthesis genes, enhancing auxin signaling and lateral root development. Grafting experiments show that
                     HAR1 
                    constrains
                     NF-YA4 
                    -mediated branching both locally in roots and systemically from shoots. Because
                     NF-YA4 
                    functions partly redundantly with
                     NF-YA1 
                    to mediate nodule emergence, our results suggest a model in which duplication and neofunctionalization of an ancestral NF-YA-dependent pathway controlling lateral root development facilitated its recruitment to the nodulation program. They also raise the possibility that AON could have evolved, at least in part, through the co-option of a LRR-RK/miR169/
                     NF-YA 
                    regulatory module that limited lateral root development.

title: Reply to Zhou and Tsao: Synergy rarely underlies the benefits of combination cancer therapy
Multiscale Brownian dynamics simulations reveal effects of macromolecular crowding on protein–ligand association
abstract: Macromolecular crowding is known to influence the diffusive, binding, kinetic, and equilibrium properties of proteins in a range of environments such as occur inside biological cells or in highly concentrated solutions of protein therapeutics. However a quantitative understanding of the effects of macromolecular crowding on the rates of protein-small molecule binding is lacking. Here, we present an adaptive model to simulate the association of two solutes in a macromolecularly crowded environment using Brownian dynamics and to compute the corresponding bimolecular association rate constant. The adaptive model represents interactions with atomistic detail for short-range crowder–noncrowder interactions, while using a coarse-grained approach for long-range crowder–noncrowder interactions and all crowder–crowder interactions. This multiscale approach is integrated in the Simulation of Diffusional Association (SDA) software for Brownian dynamics simulation of biomolecular diffusion. We applied this model to compute the rates of association for two contrasting protein-small molecule inhibitor complexes in environments varying in macromolecular crowder type and density, and we used Markov State modeling of the encounter trajectories to analyze the binding pathways. The results reveal competing effects: While the presence of the crowders can hinder ligand binding by reducing the translational diffusion rates of the solutes and obstructing the protein binding sites, crowders can also enhance the bimolecular association rate by other mechanisms, including channeling and the caging effect.

title: Origami state machine with time-varying magnetic fields
abstract: Achieving reliable, remote control over multiple stable states in modular systems remains a challenge due to the coupling between modules and history-dependent transitions. Here, we present magnetic origami state machines that enable deterministic navigation from any unknown initial state to any target state under magnetic actuation. By assuming mutually distinct energy barriers in modular Kresling origami assemblies, we realize fully accessible transition graphs with scalable state spaces. Guided by the graph associated to the state machine, a rotating magnetic field induces a universal reset that autonomously drives the system to a known equilibrium state from arbitrary states without sensing or feedback, while pulsed magnetic inputs further enable programmable transitions to any target state via prescribed actuation sequences. A reduced-order Lagrangian mechanics model predicts snap-through dynamics across reset, stepwise programming (between graph nodes), and shortcuts (by adapting pulse magnitude and orientation) where inertia triggers simultaneous multicell transitions with a single pulse. These results establish a general framework for programmable magneto-mechanical state machines with autonomous state reset and full state-space control.

title: AR signaling context and the apparent lack of synergy between AR-targeted therapy and PARP inhibition
Mechanism of catalytic regulation by an allosteric hot spot in dihydrofolate reductase
abstract: Allostery is central to catalysis and regulation, yet how distal perturbations control enzyme activity remains unresolved. Here we elucidate how a distal allosteric hot spot regulates catalysis in dihydrofolate reductase, a benchmark enzyme exhibiting latent allostery. We combine enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, and perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with evolutionary analysis and experimental kinetics to obtain a comprehensive molecular description of conformational landscapes, catalytic activity, and allosteric communication. We show that a mutational perturbation at the hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations with a subtle but critical structural difference that makes one catalytically competent and the other not. Nonequilibrium relaxation simulations further reveal that the transition between these two states in the mutant proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion. Guided by this mechanism, we rationally engineer a compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity. These results provide a unified thermodynamic and kinetic view of allostery and establish a general, mechanistically guided framework for engineering allosteric regulation in enzymes.

title: Where intention goes, responsibility flows: Grounding AI accountability in the machine learning paradigm
abstract: An opening salvo of lawsuits in US courts has begun holding AI companies accountable through independent doctrinal routes: Product liability and agency law cut as swords, while the shields of Section 230 immunity and First Amendment doctrine begin to crack. This Perspective points out that these converging paths share a unifying principle, built on the very engineering architecture of machine learning (ML) itself. Every ML system, across all variants, is constituted by a human-specified objective function before learning begins. Training data, deployment context, user interaction, and postdeployment oversight add further layers of deliberate human intention traceable to identifiable actors. AI output is therefore not the expression of a single speaker but a composite of layered human intents. It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care. This transforms AI accountability from a philosophical puzzle into a tractable legal inquiry: Trace the chain of intentional design decisions across the ML pipeline, grade each actor’s responsibility by their intent’s specificity and foreseeability, and apportion liability accordingly, following the standard three doctrine-neutral questions (attribution, causation, apportionment). Sufficient for most cases, four gaps remain: who owes what share when many hands build one system, proving fault inside an opaque model, harms that surface only after deployment, and remedies that match the technology’s pace. Targeted reforms drawing on environmental, vaccine, and financial regulatory precedents can close these gaps without requiring new legal categories, AI speech rights, AI legal personhood, or defining AI consciousness.
