title:
Light‐induced
                     phyB 
                    ‐
                     NPR1 
                    interaction activates systemic acquired resistance
authors:
Srayan Ghosh, 
Shraboni Ghosh, 
Xian Long, 
Mansi Mansi, 
Lisa Clark, 
Anjil Kumar Srivastava, 
Sumesh Kakkunnath, 
Beatriz Orosa, 
Prakash Kumar Bhagat, 
Mark Bailey, 
Catherine Gough, 
Cunjin Zhang, 
Miguel de Lucas, 
Ari Sadanandom
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         Light perception by phytochromes controls different aspects of plant–environment interactions including plant immunity; however, the underpinning molecular mechanisms are less well‐understood. Upon localized attack on leaves by avirulent pathogens, the systemic accumulation of salicylic acid (SA) is required for the establishment of systemic acquired resistance (SAR) throughout the plant to curtail pathogen spread. 
                       
                       
                         We demonstrate that light‐mediated Small Ubiquitin‐like Modifier 1 (SUMO) conjugation to phytochrome B (phyB) is critical for increasing cellular SA levels to orchestrate SAR upon avirulent bacterial infection. SA promotes SUMOylation of phyB, which enables it to interact with the SA receptor, Nonexpressor of Pathogenesis‐Related 1 (NPR1) via its SUMO1‐interacting motif. SUMOylation of phyB is enhanced by the accumulation of SUMO‐Conjugating Enzyme (E2) (SCE1) and the degradation of SUMO protease Overly Tolerant to Salt 1 (OTS1) in SAR‐induced systemic tissues. 
                       
                       
                         
                          Using confocal imaging, we show that SUMOylated phyB undergoes liquid–liquid phase separation together with NPR1 in nuclear bodies. We further validated through immunoprecipitation, ChIP and RNA‐seq analysis that SUMOylated phyB associates with NPR1 and TGA transcription factors in nuclear photobodies to induce the expression of
                           PR1 
                          gene.
                         
                       
                       
                         We reveal a post‐translational modification mechanism in which light‐induced SUMOylation of photoreceptors promotes SAR by regulating NPR1 function.

title: Tree and neighborhood damage have distinct effects on delayed mortality after a severe hurricane
authors:
Alyssa Joy Brown, 
David Bauman, 
Gabriel Arellano, 
Daniel Zuleta, 
Jess K. Zimmerman, 
María Uriarte
abstract:
Directed acyclic diagram (DAG) illustrating causal relationships between variables to estimate the effects of individual and neighborhood damage on delayed mortality.
 
 
 Summary 
 
Tropical forest resilience, biodiversity, and carbon sequestration depend on tree survival. Disturbance events, such as hurricanes, generate distinct forms of damage at the individual-tree and neighborhood scale, providing a unique setting to disentangle the causal contributions of mortality drivers.
Leveraging post-hurricane census data for nearly 4000 trees in the Luquillo Forest Dynamics Plot, Puerto Rico, we used a causal inference framework combined with Bayesian multilevel models to estimate the effect of individual- and neighborhood-scale damage on delayed tree mortality following Hurricane Maria (2017).
Individual damage effects depended on species identity and tree size. Stem break emerged as the most lethal form of damage across the community. Neighborhood damage was associated with elevated mortality following Hurricane Maria, independent of focal tree damage. This effect was strongest among large trees, consistent with disproportionately high physiological stress resulting from greater inherent metabolic demands, refoliation energy costs, and evapotranspiration following canopy recovery. Severe biomass loss (> 75% crown loss) buffered large trees from negative neighborhood effects, revealing a positive pruning effect on survival.
Our study advances mechanistic understanding of delayed tree mortality, while also suggesting how mortality patterns may shift with expected increases in disturbance severity under a warming climate.
 
 Resumen 
 
La resiliencia, la biodiversidad y el secuestro de carbono de los bosques tropicales dependen de la supervivencia de los árboles. Las perturbaciones, como los huracanes, generan distintos tipos de daño tanto a escala del árbol individual como de su vecindario, proporcionando un escenario único para desentrañar las contribuciones causales de los factores determinantes de la mortalidad.
Utilizando censos de aproximadamente 4000 árboles en la Parcela de Dinámica del Bosque de Luquillo, Puerto Rico, usamos un método de inferencia causal combinado con modelos multinivel bayesianos para estimar el efecto del daño a escala individual y de vecindario sobre la mortalidad diferida de los árboles tras el huracán María (2017).
Los efectos del daño individual dependieron de la identidad de la especie y del tamaño del árbol. La rotura del tronco resultó ser el tipo de daño más letal en toda la comunidad. El daño en el vecindario se asoció con un aumento de la mortalidad tras el huracán María, independientemente del daño sufrido por el árbol focal. Este efecto fue más fuerte entre los árboles grandes, lo cual concuerda con un estrés fisiológico desproporcionadamente alto debido a mayores demandas metabólicas inherentes, costos energéticos de refoliación y evapotranspiración tras la recuperación del dosel. La pérdida severa de biomasa (> 75 % de pérdida de copa) amortiguó los efectos negativos del vecindario sobre los árboles grandes, revelando un ‘efecto poda’ positivo sobre la supervivencia.
Nuestro estudio avanza en la comprensión mecanística de la mortalidad diferida de los árboles y, además, sugiere cómo los patrones de mortalidad pueden cambiar con los aumentos esperados en la severidad de las perturbaciones bajo un clima en calentamiento.

title: Glutamate promotes cold tolerance through CsGLR3.2- and Ca2+-associated CBF signaling in tea plants
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Low temperature limits the productivity and quality of tea plants, particularly when spring cold spells damage vulnerable young shoots. However, the metabolic signals that regulate C-repeat binding factor (CBF)-mediated cold responses remain unclear. Time-series metabolomic analysis revealed progressive glutamate accumulation in cold-treated tea shoots, accompanied by a marked decline in theanine content. Exogenous glutamate enhanced cold tolerance in tea shoots. By contrast, co-silencing of CsGGT2 and CsGGT4 attenuated cold-induced glutamate accumulation and compromised cold tolerance, indicating that CsGGT2/CsGGT4-associated theanine turnover contributes to cold-induced glutamate accumulation. Silencing CsGLR3.2 attenuated the protective effect of glutamate and reduced glutamate-enhanced CsCBF1–CsCBF4 expression. Pharmacological treatments provided complementary support for the involvement of GLR- and Ca2+-associated signaling in this response. Transcriptomic analysis further showed that glutamate altered the expression of genes associated with flavonoid biosynthesis and redox homeostasis. Collectively, these findings connect the characteristic theanine metabolism of tea plants with cold-responsive glutamate signaling and support a model in which glutamate enhances CsCBF expression through CsGLR3.2- and Ca2+-associated signaling. Glutamate metabolism and GLR-associated signaling therefore represent potential targets for improving cold tolerance in tea plants.

title: 4-hydroxyphenethyl alcohol, a phenolic metabolite synthesized by GhADH1, positively regulates cotton fiber elongation
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Cotton is the dominant natural fiber for global textiles, with fiber length being a critical determinant of quality and agronomic yield. While phytohormones and primary metabolism are known to affect fiber growth, secondary metabolism’s regulatory roles remain poorly characterized. Here, we identify two medium-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (MDR) homeolog genes, GhADH1-A and GhADH1-D, highly expressed during the fiber elongation stage in Gossypium hirsutum (G. hirsutum). Functional analyses showed that GhADH1 knockout plants produced significantly shorter fibers and smaller bolls, whereas GhADH1 overexpression enhanced both traits. Metabolomic profiling revealed reduced levels of the phenolic alcohol 4-hydroxyphenethyl alcohol (4-HPEA) in fibers of GhADH1 knockout lines while overexpression lines contained enhanced 4-HPEA levels. LC–MS and in vitro enzymatic assays showed that GhADH1 catalyzes the conversion of 4-hydroxyphenylacetaldehyde (4-HPAA) to 4-HPEA. In vitro ovule culture assays showed that both 4-HPAA and 4-HPEA promote fiber elongation in a concentration-dependent manner, with 4-HPAA effect requiring GhADH1 activity. Transcriptomic profiling showed that GhADH1 overexpression and 4-HPEA treatment trigger consistent responses, with auxin signaling as the dominant regulatory hub. GhADH1 and 4-HPEA increased endogenous auxin levels in fibers, while auxin inhibitor treatments abrogated their elongation-promoting effects, confirming the pathway’s dependence on auxin homeostasis. Together, these findings uncover a GhADH1–4-HPEA metabolic pathway positively regulating cotton fiber elongation by modulation of auxin homeostasis, revealing a new role for secondary metabolism in fiber development.

title:
A homolog of
                     Growth Regulating Factor 
                    Targets Protein Synthesis Genes to Regulate Seed Protein Accumulation in Soybean
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Growth Regulating Factor (GRF) genes encode a family of highly conserved plant transcription factors that control diverse developmental processes. However, no GRF5 orthologs have been directly linked to seed protein accumulation. Here we demonstrate that GmGRF5a, a soybean homolog of GRF5, functions as a key positive regulator of seed protein accumulation. GmGRF5a is preferentially expressed in reproductive tissues, with transcript levels gradually increasing throughout seed development. Overexpression of GmGRF5a driven by its native promoter or the CAB3 promoter increased seed protein content by approximately one percentage point—comparable to the effect of known protein QTLs in soybean—without yield penalty across three independent field seasons, whereas CRISPR/Cas9-generated mutants showed reduced protein and oil contents. Integrative analysis of genome-wide DAP-seq and transcriptome profiling identified hundreds of direct GmGRF5a target genes significantly enriched in pathways related to protein synthesis, ribosomal biogenesis, and energy metabolism. Multiple independent molecular assays, including ChIP-qPCR, EMSA, and dual-luciferase reporter assays, confirmed that GmGRF5a directly activates genes encoding seed storage proteins (e.g., GmCupin1-1) and translational components (e.g., GmRPS4 and GmGOGAT2). Furthermore, natural variation at amino acid position 124 near the WRC DNA-binding domain is associated with seed protein content and exhibits a latitude-dependent distribution pattern consistent with regional breeding priorities. Our findings demonstrate that GmGRF5a coordinates a transcriptional network governing seed protein synthesis and highlight its potential as a promising target for breeding high-protein soybean cultivars without compromising agronomic performance.

title:
PlMYB51 
                    and
                     PlMYB1R1 
                    switch
                     PlABI5 
                    -
                     PlCesA6 
                    function to regulate seed dormancy and germination in
                     Paeonia lactiflora
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Seed dormancy is a key strategy for plants to adapt to fluctuating environments and ensure population propagation. Paeonia lactiflora seeds exhibit typical double dormancy, characterized by a prolonged germination cycle and low emergence rate that severely restrict their large-scale propagation. Although ABI5, the core transcription factor (TF) in the abscisic acid (ABA) signaling pathway, acts as a critical hub in maintaining seed dormancy, its upstream dynamic regulatory mechanism and downstream cell-wall-related target genes remain largely unknown. In this study, two upstream regulators of PlABI5, PlMYB51 and PlMYB1R1, were identified via yeast one-hybrid screening, and their regulatory mechanism was characterized. The results showed that both PlMYB51 and PlMYB1R1 belonged to the R2R3-MYB family. When acting alone, they directly bound to and activated the PlABI5 promoter, inhibiting seed germination. Upon forming a protein complex in the nucleus, their regulatory function was reversed and they repressed PlABI5 transcription to promote germination, supporting a proposed monomer activation-complex inhibition switch model. Furthermore, PlABI5 specifically targeted the PlCesA6 promoter and inhibited its expression without affecting the homolog PlCesA3. PlCesA6 positively regulated seed germination by promoting hypocotyl cell elongation, and its overexpression rescued the inhibition caused by PlMYB51/PlMYB1R1 overexpression. Collectively, this study proposes a working model for the PlMYB51/PlMYB1R1-PlABI5–PlCesA6 cascade in controlling seed dormancy and germination, and identifies a putative functional switching mode of MYB TFs mediated by protein-protein interactions. These findings provide key gene resources and a theoretical basis for artificial dormancy breaking and molecular breeding in P. lactiflora.

title:
Allelic tuning of
                     PtoRLK609 
                    kinase activity shapes adaptive xylem remodeling in
                     Populus tomentosa
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Climate change poses unprecedented challenges to perennial trees. However, the molecular mechanisms by which trees achieve long-term adaptive xylem remodeling remain poorly understood. Here, using transcriptomics and population genomics in 302 Populus tomentosa accessions sampled from three climatically distinct subpopulations, we identified receptor-like kinases (RLKs) associated with climate-related variation in xylem lignification. Among 49 candidates, the wall-associated kinase PtoRLK609 showed among the strongest signatures of population differentiation, a pattern consistent with climate-associated selection. Two major PtoRLK609 haplotypes, defined by four linked missense variants, showed marked geographic differentiation, with PtoRLK609Hap2 reaching fixation or near-fixation in northern populations that experience drier and cooler climates, and was associated with elevated lignin content. PtoRLK609 phosphorylates the transcription factor PtoERF105 at Ser171, which promotes its nuclear accumulation and enhances activation of the lignin biosynthesis genes PtoLAC4 and PtoCCoAOMT1, as well as the vessel development regulator PtoVND7. The PtoRLK609Hap2 protein variant showed higher kinase activity and more efficient phosphorylation of PtoERF105 than PtoRLK609Hap1, linking natural protein variation to differential transcriptional output. Consistent with this mechanism, gain- and loss-of-function analyses showed that PtoRLK609 promotes secondary cell wall lignification, elevates the syringyl-to-guaiacyl (S/G) ratio, increases vessel density, and is associated with better maintenance of stem water status under controlled water deficit. These findings characterize a PtoRLK609–PtoERF105 phosphorylation module associated with xylem remodeling and identify an RLK locus that is a strong candidate for contributing to climate-associated divergence in perennial trees.

title: Verix: a toolkit for benchmarking and harmonization of complex structural variants
abstract: Abstract  Summary Complex structural variants (CSVs) represent a critical yet under-characterized class of large-scale genomic rearrangements. CSV discovery requires not only the accurate detection of individual breakpoints but also their assembly into a single, structurally resolved CSV event. However, CSV method development is currently limited by a diagnostic gap: existing SV evaluation frameworks are designed for single-interval or single-junction SVs and cannot quantify multi-breakpoint CSV reconstruction fidelity or systematically distinguish between different types of reconstruction errors, such as over-segmentation or collapse of independent breakpoints. Here we present Verix, a comprehensive toolkit designed for the fine-grained evaluation and integration of CSVs. Verixintroduces granular diagnostic metrics that enable researchers to thoroughly characterize CSV predictions and stratify performance based on breakpoint sensitivity, precision, and structural integrity. In addition to pairwise callset-to-truthset comparisons, Verixalso provides an intra- and inter-callset harmonization module for generating consensus calls for a single tool’s output or across disparate discovery pipelines. As such, Verixprovides the infrastructure needed to rigorously evaluate and reconcile CSV calls, accelerating the standardization of CSV discovery in both research and clinical settings. Availability and implementation Verixis available under the MIT license at  https://github.com/PopicLab/verix  and  https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22998063 . Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at  Bioinformatics  online.

title: PRIDA: Cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction based on biological language models and conditional domain-adversarial learning
abstract: Abstract  Motivation The interaction between RNA and proteins is a complex process that involves atom-level details and dynamic changes. Accurate prediction of protein-RNA interactions helps researchers to develop protein-targeted small nucleic acid drugs. However, the scarcity of protein-RNA complexes and experimental data limits the ability of existing data-driven supervised learning methods to learn latent patterns, leading to limited performance. Results In this study, we propose PRIDA ( P rotein- R NA  I nteraction prediction based on  D omain- A dversarial learning), a protein-RNA interaction framework that combines bilinear attention with conditional domain-adversarial learning. Powered by pretrained protein and RNA language models, PRIDA improves interaction prediction under protein-level distribution shifts and limited labeled data. By integrating PRIDA with Monte Carlo Tree Search, we apply it to a virtual screening pipeline to generate RNA aptamer candidates for specific target proteins. Experimental results show that PRIDA achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction and provides effective guidance for RNA aptamer virtual screening. Availability The data and source code of the proposed method are available at GitHub ( https://github.com/zhouyyang/PRIDA ) and Zenodo ( https://zenodo.org/records/23644677 ) Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at  Bioinformatics  online.

title: Correction for Bernabé-Rubio and Watt, Caspase-8-dependent autophagy regulates neutrophil infiltration in oral squamous cell carcinoma
Complexity functions of infinite sequences
abstract: We address the inverse problem for complexity functions of infinite words, which asks which functions can occur as complexity functions of infinite words. We survey our recent advances on this problem and several of its ramifications. We describe an asymptotic solution to the inverse problem, realizing every function satisfying two necessary conditions as the complexity function of an infinite word up to asymptotic equivalence. We then turn to phenomena beyond asymptotic equivalence, presenting constructions of infinite words with seemingly contradictory behavior of the discrete derivatives of their complexity functions. These lead to a solution of a 1995 problem of Cassaigne and to applications in symbolic dynamics, including the question of convergence of Rauzy graphs, as well as to the growth and asymptotic invariants of algebraic structures.

title: Hydration at the base of the mantle transition zone by ancient subductions in Asia
abstract: Whether and how the subduction processes result in water enrichment at the base of the mantle transition zone (MTZ) remain elusive. The major orogenic belts of the Asian continent, including the Central Asian, Tethyan, and Alpine–Himalayan belts, which record extensive subduction processes, offer an ideal target to address the hydration of the MTZ and its relationship with subduction. Here, we map water content at the MTZ base by combining mineral physics constraints on hydrous pyrolite and global seismic observations of velocity structure and 660-km discontinuity topography. Our results indicate an average global water content of approximately 0.14 wt%, with pronounced hydration anomalies in parts of Asia. Linking these anomalies with reconstructions of past subduction events since 410 Ma reveals extensive water delivery to the MTZ, particularly beneath parts of the Mongol–Okhotsk suture zone, the Central Asian Orogenic Belt, and the Tethyan orogenic domain, where water content exceeds 0.5 wt%. These results connect ancient subduction history to present-day mantle hydration, offering insights into Earth’s deep water cycle.

title: A symbiogenic merger enabled by oxygen initiated the evolution of eukaryotes
abstract: Recently, extensive genetic information about archaeal hosts at the basis of eukaryogenesis has come to light. Characterization of these first eukaryotic common ancestor (FECA) related organisms allows improved understanding of the enigmatic FECA to last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) transition. However, these gene-centered discoveries have the unfortunate side effect of entrenching erroneous ideas about early eukaryotic evolution. This is apparent in the two-Domain vision of life, with eukaryotes seen as specialized Asgard archaea, while underestimating the contribution of the endosymbiont to eukaryogenesis. Establishment of the alpha-proteobacterium as the future mitochondrion is treated as one of many such endosymbiotic occurrences, ignoring its unique evolutionary position. I will marshal evidence for symbiogenic mechanisms involved in the FECA to LECA transition, with a key role for the endosymbiont’s electron transport chain and its acceptor molecular oxygen, especially in the incarnation of reactive oxygen species occurring in the host cytoplasm. We should overcome overestimating gene determinism, while not sufficiently allowing for effects of biological hierarchies, emergent properties, and chance. Many eukaryotic properties are best understood by envisaging the crucial uptake of the future mitochondrion as a merger instead of an acquisition. This merger is characterized by a new kind of elaborate cellular entity emerging as a result of rapid coevolution, replacing a scenario in which already complex pre-eukaryotes acquired endosymbionts, accompanied by important, but limited, changes. Successful mergers are rare because they are intrinsically more difficult, but synergistically open up completely new areas of possibilities, as illustrated by incredible eukaryotic success.

title: Global bee bioregions mirror those of other taxa despite a uniquely bimodal latitudinal diversity gradient
abstract: Bioregionalization, the partitioning of the globe into areas of biotic similarity, is one of nature’s most striking patterns, and highly congruent boundaries have been identified across plants, tetrapods, ants, and butterflies. However, these taxa also share a unimodal latitudinal diversity gradient (LDG), raising the question of whether bioregionalization and the LDG are mechanistically coupled or instead arise from largely independent processes acting on different timescales. Bees (Hymenoptera: Anthophila) provide a natural test, their diversity peaking at mid-latitudes rather than in the tropics. Using range estimates for 3,370 species and a phylogenetic beta-diversity framework, we recover 21 bee bioregions nested within at least six major realms (Australasia, Indomalaya-Oceania, Nearctic, Neotropics, Palearctic, and Sub-Sahara) that closely align with those of other taxa despite bees’ atypical diversity gradient. We propose that bioregionalization and species richness are decoupled because they arise from distinct processes: the former reflects historical dispersal and evolutionary history, the latter local diversification, extinction, and environmental filtering. Our analysis provides a global biogeographic framework for future bee research and highlights the processes shaping the world‘s major biogeographic boundaries.

title: A chemomechanical bifurcation landscape unifies sustained growth, length homeostasis, and regenerative collapse in axons
abstract: Axonal growth machinery is largely shared across neurons, but axons exhibit strikingly different fates depending on developmental and environmental context: sustained elongation in peripheral neurons under permissive conditions, length homeostasis in cortical neurons after target innervation, and pathological collapse into dystrophic endbulbs in injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons. These divergent outcomes have resisted explanation by length-sensing and biomechanical models that treat long-range transport and local force generation as separate problems. We unify these phenomena through a mechanochemical model that couples bidirectional motor transport and intracellular signaling to growth-cone balance of axonal tension, actomyosin contraction, and adhesion within a single feedback loop: The lengthening axon uses its own growing transport delay to establish self-limiting mechanical feedback, as the accumulating delay reshapes signaling waveforms to progressively elevate myosin contractility against actin-driven protrusion. Two physical parameters, the transport delay and the signaling feedback strength, organize axon fate into a unified state-space landscape spanning sustained growth, length homeostasis, and pathological collapse. Reduced feedback strength weakens this self-limiting mechanical feedback by simultaneously enhancing protrusion and suppressing contractility, providing a mechanistic interpretation of axon lengthening under partial reduction of retrograde transport. Bistability in the inhibitory regime explains why mature CNS tracts persist where nascent sprouts collapse, recasting regenerative failure as a state-dependent gate rather than a capacity limit. The framework predicts that partial rather than complete inhibition of retrograde transport could shift collapsed axons across the bifurcation into a growth-permissive regime, identifying a class of interventions complementary to existing capacity-restoration strategies for nerve injury.

title: A sulfotyrosine motif in the human TrkB extracellular domain is required for activation by the agonist antibody ZEB85
abstract: The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) signaling axis is a key effector of synaptic plasticity and neuroprotection. While TrkB activation is a major target to prevent neural dysfunction, stimulation with exogenous BDNF administration has not proven tractable given the unfavorable physiochemical properties of BDNF. In addition, BDNF also activates a cell death pathway by binding to the neurotrophin receptor p75. The TrkB agonist antibody ZEB85 provides an alternative route to the selective activation of TrkB. To understand the ZEB85 mechanism of action, we mapped the binding site for ZEB85 to the TrkB extracellular juxtamembrane domain and found a sulfotyrosine modification at residue 400 crucial for ZEB85 interaction and activation of TrkB signaling. We determined the structures of ZEB85 and BDNF bound to their respective binding sites on human TrkB suggesting independent sites for each ligand, despite prior evidence of direct competition. Using structure-guided BDNF- and ZEB85-binding deficient TrkB mutants, we assessed their ability to sequester ligands from full-length TrkB in cultured human neurons. We found that the BDNF binding site extends into the juxtamembrane domain of TrkB but does not require the sulfotyrosine 400 to activate TrkB. Together with biophysical analysis and AlphaFold modeling, these results explain how BDNF can displace ZEB85 from TrkB through an overlapping epitope. Our findings reveal unique features of TrkB, not present in the related neurotrophin receptors TrkA and TrkC and suggest future directions to explore the role of sulfotyrosine in TrkB signaling.

title: Elucidating molecular regulatory rules of nanoparticle biological identity via standardized deep proteomics
abstract: The biological identity of nanoparticles is often redefined upon exposure to physiological fluids through the formation of a protein corona (PC), However, the molecular rules linking synthetic design to biological fate remain elusive owing to the fragmented and inconsistent proteomics data. Here, leveraging a standardized deep proteomic database of 42 diverse nanomaterials, we reveal the general molecular selection rules that govern the PC formation. We demonstrate that the PC is not a product of random adsorption but is shaped by strict property-dependent recruitment. First, surface charge regulates cellular uptake, with anionic nanoparticles specifically recruiting adhesion proteins to promote Itgav-mediated endocytosis, thus forming a causal charge-corona-receptor chain. Second, PEGylation engineers immune evasion by selectively depleting specific complement and coagulation factors, rather than merely preventing protein adsorption. Third, nanoparticle geometry imposes structural constraints and selects proteins based on specific physicochemical features such as lysine content. Beyond mechanistic insights, we show that material-specific PCs can rebalance the serum proteome and enable the detection of low-abundance disease biomarkers. This work shifts the paradigm from empirical description toward rule-based prediction and provides a foundational framework for rationally engineering nanomedicines with predictable and programmable biological identities.

title: Direct atomic-scale observation reveals rare earth element fractionation at mineral–water interfaces
abstract: Clay minerals, ubiquitous across diverse geological systems, exert fundamental controls on critical geochemical processes, particularly through their adsorptive interactions with economically vital elements such as heavy rare earth elements (HREEs). The adsorption of HREEs onto clay surfaces is not only the key process that enriches these critical resources but also a potential archive for dating significant weathering events. However, the atomic-scale mechanisms governing the preferential adsorption and fractionation of rare earth elements (REEs) at mineral–water interfaces have remained poorly constrained. Here, employing in situ atomic-scale imaging via high-resolution atomic force microscopy, we systematically investigate the adsorption behaviors of light and heavy REEs (La, Y, Yb) onto key crystallographic planes—Si-basal, Al-basal, and edge terminations—of representative clay minerals (kaolinite, illite, mica) under environmentally relevant conditions (pH 4.8 to 6.4). We directly visualize and quantitatively reveal that Si-basal planes selectively enrich HREEs with pH-enhanced adsorption capacity, whereas Al-basal planes exhibit negligible REE adsorption below pH 5.8 but preferential HREE adsorption at pH 6.4. Integrating synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we identify the adsorption mechanism of REE on Si-basal and Al-basal/edge planes as outer-sphere complexation and inner-sphere binding, respectively. Furthermore, we quantify the contributions of distinct planes via surface complexation modeling, revealing Si-dominated to Al- and edge-controlled adsorption with elevating pH. These atomic-scale findings not only resolve long-standing debates about clay mineral-mediated REE fractionation but also redefine fundamental paradigms of surface reactivity at silicate mineral–water interfaces, offering insights into the cycling and metallogeny of other critical metals in aqueous and sedimentary environments.

title: The efficiency of information gain by natural selection
abstract:
Natural selection enriches populations for genotypes that are well adapted to their environments, accumulating information about the selective conditions in the process. Therefore, selection can be viewed as a learning process through which populations acquire information about the environment. Motoo Kimura derived a relationship between the amount of information gained by selection and a measure of the inefficiency of the selective process, known as substitution load [M. Kimura,
                     Genet. Res. 
                    2, 127–140 (1961)]. Due to the gradual nature of selection and the ongoing mismatch of types to the environment, a lineage that is still acquiring information has lower mean fitness than a lineage that already has it. While this has been an influential insight, we find that Kimura’s model is inconsistent with selection experiments involving
                     Escherichia coli 
                    . To address limitations in this model and develop a more robust measure for the efficiency of selection, we turn to computational learning theory. We show that the learning-theoretic concept of regret quantifies the inefficiency of selection as a learning process in terms of relative lineage fitness. We establish bounds on the efficiency of information gain in general settings, including frequency-dependent selection and arbitrary environmental change. We experimentally validate these bounds and demonstrate that our extended theory recovers Kimura’s fundamental insight. Finally, we show that selection is an asymptotically optimal algorithm for the basic problem faced by evolving populations and that it acquires information more efficiently than comparable processes in complex environments.

title: Intrinsic function of leptin receptor–regulated endothelial PD-L1
abstract: Programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) is an immune checkpoint protein expressed in vascular endothelial cells (ECs). In contrast to cancer, our understanding of endothelial PD-L1 in relation to metabolic syndromes and its vascular complications is less studied. For example, its regulation and intrinsic function remain unclear. Here, we showed that endothelial PD-L1 is regulated by leptin receptor signaling in male mice. In particular, endothelial PD-L1 expression is affected by leptin resistance. A lack of leptin receptors leads to PD-L1 downregulation in vascular ECs via posttranslational degradation. To understand the fundamental roles of endothelial PD-L1, RNA interference and selective knockout are employed in human endothelium and animals, respectively. Silencing or deleting endothelial PD-L1 expression delays cell cycle progression and proliferation due to rat sarcoma (RAS)/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) inactivation. In obesity, endothelial PD-L1 deficiency impairs the EC turnover and worsens the vascular function. Overall, we provide an insight into how endothelial PD-L1 contributes to vascular homeostasis, suggesting its pathophysiological importance in maintaining cellular turnover.

title: Potential energy landscape networks of confined vortex matter
abstract:
Advances in nanoscale patterning of superconducting films [Y. L. Wang
                     et al 
                    .,
                     Nat. Nanotechnol. 
                     13 
                    , 560–565 (2018)] and the availability of submicron-sized superconducting single crystals with controlled geometry allow for the investigation of superconducting vortex matter under extreme confinement [A. K. Geim
                     et al 
                    .,
                     Nature 
                     390 
                    , 259–262 (1997)]. It has been observed in these systems that the interplay between sample geometry and vortex number results in the emergence of so-called “magic number” configurations which show unusually high stability against thermal fluctuations. However, a detailed, comprehensive theoretical study of the ground state and metastable states of confined vortex matter has not yet been developed. Here we show that the intricate properties of a system of vortices under extreme confinement can be characterized in detail by mapping the potential energy landscape of the system onto a network [J. P. K. Doye,
                     Phys. Rev. Lett. 
                     88 
                    , 238701 (2002)] with nodes corresponding to local potential energy minima and edges to transition states between local minima. We apply these techniques to systems featuring repelling particles/vortices confined in small containers of various geometric shapes. We demonstrate that the ground state almost always belongs to a subset of system states within the deepest network core. We find that the emergence of magic number configurations in the ground state results in a drastic decrease in the complexity of the entire network. We use large-scale molecular dynamics simulations to study the size dependence of melting in different configurations. We find that as confinement effects increase, magic number configurations transition to states with lower symmetry.

title: Crowding limits relative bacterial surface accumulation with density-induced effective heating
abstract: The accumulation of microswimmers near walls has been studied for decades. While hydrodynamics and single-cell kinematics are well-explored, the role of cell-cell interactions remains understudied. However, in realistic, crowded environments such as the human gut, these interactions can be just as crucial. Here, we demonstrate that they actively weaken bacterial surface accumulation. Analysis of entrapped cell tracks reveals that crowding enhances orientational fluctuations, which increase the effective rotational diffusion and facilitate wall escape. A minimal model shows that this collective effect is equivalent to raising the system’s effective temperature with density.

title:
Ddx3x 
                    deficiency in mice impairs corticofugal motor circuits and causes motor deficits that are attenuated by early-life exercise
abstract:
The X-linked RNA helicase
                     DDX3X 
                    is a high-risk gene for autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability primarily in females. Individuals with pathogenic variants in
                     DDX3X 
                    have pervasive and often severe motor manifestations. Using mouse models, we studied the circuits underlying the motor phenotypes associated with
                     Ddx3x 
                    deficiency and examined the feasibility of an early intervention to ameliorate motor trajectories. We show that
                     Ddx3x 
                    controls both the development and later plasticity of motor circuits connecting the motor cortex with the pontine nuclei.
                     Ddx3x 
                    haploinsufficiency during development affects the dendritic arborization of corticopontine neurons. Juvenile-onset
                     Ddx3x 
                    loss in corticopontine neurons is sufficient to induce adult motor impairments overlapping with those caused by chemogenetic disruption of corticopontine circuits. Further,
                     Ddx3x 
                    mutant mice engage corticopontine circuits in skilled motor tasks in a sex-dependent manner. Last,
                     Ddx3x 
                    haploinsufficient female mice undergoing a juvenile motor intervention show long-lasting specific benefits in their adult motor function. Together, these findings establish
                     Ddx3x 
                    as an essential regulator of corticopontine neuron development and function and provide an early motor intervention to ameliorate motor outcomes in a mouse model of
                     DDX3X 
                    haploinsufficiency.

title: Enhanced cfDNA methylation profiling by detection and correction of jagged ends
abstract: Nature Methods, Published online: 29 October 2026;  doi:10.1038/s41592-026-03278-5  The computational tool JEEPERS detects and corrects jagged-end-induced errors in cell-free DNA methylation analysis, demonstrating improved performance in multiple applications, such as cancer detection and monitoring.

title: Advancing morphological profiling with self-supervised learning through comparative insights into representation learning of cellular perturbations
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                    Self-supervised learning (SSL) enables scalable, label-free foundation models (FMs) that learn task-agnostic representations directly from images, bypassing cell segmentation and feature engineering inherent to classical morphological profiling. We present a large-scale evaluation of SSL FMs for image-based phenotypic profiling, covering contrastive (DINO), masked-based generative (MAE, iTPN) and hybrid (DINOv2) learning mechanisms, pretrained on all unannotated chemical perturbations from the Joint Undertaking for Morphological Profiling–Cell Painting (JUMP–CP) dataset (119,876 compounds, ~1.77 million images, 7 laboratories). Here we show that top-performing SSL models outperformed CellProfiler in compound-replicate retrieval on the held-out JUMP–Target2 set (302 annotated compounds,
                     P 
                     ≤ 0.001). DINO and DINOv2 generalized across diverse perturbations and cell types, outperforming CellProfiler with 31–37% gains in site-averaged mean average precision for mechanism-of-action retrieval on EU-OPENSCREEN Bioactives (2,464 compounds), and consistently surpassing masked-based models across all benchmarks. This study provides a systematic assessment of SSL approaches for advancing morphological profiling and offers pretrained FMs to accelerate drug discovery.

title: Directional water transport system resolves fertilization–dispersal conflicts in  Marchantia
abstract: Nature Plants, Published online: 29 October 2026;  doi:10.1038/s41477-026-02450-1  In the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha, the female reproductive structure evolved a directional water transport system to ensure fertilization success on land, showing how functional demand conflicts drive the assembly of an integrated trait complex.

title: The SCHENGEN pathway regulates lignin barrier formation via the receptor-like cytoplasmic kinase BIK1 in plant immunity
abstract: Nature Plants, Published online: 29 October 2026;  doi:10.1038/s41477-026-02446-x  This study reveals that the SCHENGEN pathway, known for forming a diffusion barrier in roots, also functions in plant immunity by linking pathogen recognition to protective lignin barrier formation and disease resistance.

abstract: Nature, Published online: 29 October 2026;  doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03386-4  The theoretical objects would have left a larger imprint on cosmic radiation if they were a source of the invisible force pulling together the galaxies.

title: Over a billion more dark-morning school commutes for K–12 children under the Sunshine Protection Act
abstract: Rodríguez Ferrante et al. show that permanent DST would push most US school start times before sunrise in winter, adding hundreds of millions of dark-morning commutes across 14 states and billions nationwide, while pedestrian-crash risk is higher before sunrise, especially for children.

title: The rise and diversification of spidroins in the deep-time evolution of spiders
abstract: Jiang et al. reveal a comprehensive picture of spidroin evolution in a dated phylogeny of spiders. Four new types of atypical spidroins are widespread in true spiders and may affect silk properties. The number of spidroin types, silk gland types, and total spidroin copies may influence diversification rates of spiders.

title: Microbial products trigger chemosensory dialogues through intestinal G protein-coupled receptors
abstract: Kadoki et al. developed GPCR-seq, a high-throughput platform to identify how the gut senses environmental chemicals. They discovered gut microbial products that activate intestinal receptors, triggering serotonin release or linking to inflammatory bowel disease. This work provides a scalable template for decoding how host-microbe communication influences human health.

title: Genetic coupling of floral rewards and signals underlies pollinator attraction
abstract: Floral rewards and signals must be coordinated to attract pollinators, but the underlying genetic mechanisms remain poorly understood. Using melon as a model system, this study reveals how the developmental regulator YAB5 coordinates nectar production, flower opening, and floral signals to promote bee visitation.

title: Innate sensor responses set a supra-unitary threshold for viral replication
abstract: Single-cell analysis reveals that viral replication requires a supra-unitary input of viral genomes, which varies with different viruses and cell types. We show that supra-unitary viral genome quantities, independently of viral protein synthesis, activate negative feedback regulators of RIG-I, MDA-5, and PKR, suppressing the innate immune response and allowing replication.

title: Guardians at the gate: cMAF keeps the brain’s vasculature in check
abstract: In this issue of Cell, Brioschi et al. identify cellular musculoaponeurotic fibrosarcoma (cMAF) as a key regulator of brain perivascular macrophages that supports cerebrovascular function through insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) production. This cMAF-IGF1 program is enhanced in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), potentially reflecting a protective response that is lost in APOE4 carriers.

title: Calorie restriction uncouples mutation rate from lifespan
abstract: In this issue of Cell, Grońska-Pęski et al. examine how calorie restriction (CR) affects DNA mutation rates. While CR lowers the accumulation of mutations, this effect does not scale with the degree of lifespan extension. Their work raises important new questions about how CR impacts the causal mechanisms of aging.

title: Toward planetary microbial systems biology
abstract: Planetary microbial systems biology, encompassing multi-omics, AI, and field-to-lab interaction, is proposed as a framework to study Earth’s interconnected microbiomes at a planetary scale.

title: Roads not taken: The mismatch between safety and regulation of plant breeding innovation
abstract: Meeting global food security goals while reducing agriculture’s environmental impact requires continued crop improvement and innovation. Advances in transgenesis, cisgenesis, and genome editing now enable increasingly precise genetic modification with risks comparable to those of conventional breeding, yet regulatory frameworks remain focused on the method used rather than the product. We highlight recent examples, including immune receptor transfer, cisgenesis-based disease resistance stacking, photosynthesis engineering, and AI-guided protein design, that illustrate innovations constrained by current regulatory approaches. A decisive shift toward science-based, proportionate, and product-focused regulation is needed so that improved crops are evaluated on the basis of their properties, not how they were made.

title:
Salivary Citrate Deficiency Defines an Endogenous Dentin Remineralization Failure State Through Glandular MT1/2‐Zn
                     2+ 
                    ‐ACO2 Dysregulation
authors:
Ran You, 
Wenhui Wang, 
Franklin R. Tay, 
Haotian Dong, 
Mutong Wei, 
Ruoyun Wu, 
Xin Song, 
Chen Chen, 
Haifeng Xie
abstract:
Salivary citrate deficiency in early-stage Sjögren's syndrome accompanies impaired dentin remineralization despite preserved salivary flow and mineral availability. Matched-ion experiments reveal disrupted mineral organization and reduced dentin recovery at disease-associated citrate levels. Glandular MT1/2–Zn 2 
 + –ACO2 dysregulation accompanies citrate depletion, while zinc repletion restores citrate and improves mineralization, highlighting citrate availability as a key factor in mineral utilization.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Rapid caries progression occurs even when salivary flow and calcium phosphate availability are preserved, suggesting a knowledge gap in how available minerals are used for repair. Early-stage Sjögren's syndrome was examined as a clinical model of this condition. Salivary citrate was markedly lower in the disease cohort and was inversely associated with caries burden, whereas salivary flow and the major mineral ions did not differ from healthy controls. In mineralization systems with matched calcium and phosphate concentrations, the disease-associated citrate concentration reduced intrafibrillar mineral deposition, disrupted hydroxyapatite organization, and limited structural and mechanical recovery of demineralized dentin. Human salivary gland tissue, an immunization-induced rat model, and primary salivary gland epithelial cells showed a similar metabolic pattern: increased metallothionein 1/2 (MT1/2), reduced labile Zn 2+ , increased aconitase 2 (ACO2) activity, and citrate depletion. ZnSO 4  repletion increased intracellular Zn 2+ , reduced ACO2 activity, restored citrate toward control levels, and improved the mineralization activity of epithelial-cell supernatants. The data indicate that citrate availability influences dentin mineral utilization and associate citrate depletion with glandular MT1/2-Zn 2+ -ACO2 dysregulation. These findings support an association between glandular zinc-citrate dysregulation and impaired remineralization, suggesting that this mechanism may account for impaired endogenous remineralization despite preserved availability of the major mineral ions.

title:
Overcoming the *H‐NO
                     
                       x 
                     
                    Coupling Bottleneck via Palladium‐Enabled Relay Catalysis on CuCo
                     2 
                    O
                     4 
                    Toward Ampere‐Level Nitrate‐to‐Ammonia
authors:
Yuhuan Cui, 
Yingying Xu, 
Jingyao Guo, 
Yao Liu, 
Yuxuan Li, 
Zixuan Feng, 
Yitong Zhou, 
Yongjun Gao, 
Zhili Wang
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   
                    Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO
                     3 
                    RR) represents a sustainable route for both ammonia (NH
                     3 
                    ) production and nitrate‐contaminated water remediation, yet its practical application is crippled by the kinetically sluggish multi‐electron/proton transfer and insufficient targeted active hydrogen (*H) supply. Herein, a Pd‐doped CuCo
                     2 
                    O
                     4 
                    (Pd‐CuCo
                     2 
                    O
                     4 
                    ) hollow spiny microsphere catalyst is designed to tackle this challenge via a synergistic relay catalysis mechanism coupled with rapid *H replenishment. Kinetics studies and theoretical calculations collectively demonstrate a clear tandem pathway for NH
                     3 
                    synthesis: NO
                     3 
                     − 
                    is preferentially reduced to NO
                     2 
                     − 
                    on Cu sites, and then migrates to neighboring Co sites for further conversion to NH
                     3 
                    . Crucially, the incorporated Pd dopants promote NO
                     3 
                     − 
                    adsorption on Cu sites and *H generation on Co sites precisely. The efficient *H supply and co‐adsorption for intermediates eliminates the intrinsic kinetic bottleneck of poor *H‐NO
                     
                       x 
                     
                    coupling, ensuring the tandem catalysis proceeds smoothly without interruption. Benefiting from the *H‐spillover boosted relay mechanism, an ultra‐high current density over −2.0 A cm
                     −2 
                    and a remarkable NH
                     3 
                    yield rate of 100.43 mg h
                     −1 
                    cm
                     −2 
                    are achieved. This study underscores the synergistic interplay among the three active sites and provides a blueprint for designing high‐rate, practical NO
                     3 
                    RR electrocatalysts.

title: DTX3 Suppresses the NPM3–RUVBL1 Axis to Inhibit Homologous Recombination Repair and Abrogate Tumor Radioresistance
authors:
Jia‐Hao Xiao, 
Chang‐Jun Xie, 
Yan‐Hua Chen, 
Hao Cheng, 
Shuang‐Hui Li, 
Wei Li, 
Ya‐Wen Bin, 
Rui‐Min He, 
Ying‐Qing Li, 
Ping Feng
abstract:
Deltex 3 (DTX3) catalyzes K27‐linked ubiquitination of nucleophosmin 3 to disrupt homologous recombination repair and reverse tumor radioresistance. Low DTX3 predicts poor survival and radiotherapy recurrence, serving as a radiosensitizing therapeutic target.








ABSTRACT
Aberrant remodeling of DNA damage repair pathways after radiotherapy constitutes a primary driver of tumor radioresistance and compromised therapeutic efficacy. Ubiquitination has been reported as a critical post‐translational modification governing the DNA damage response and repair cascade. However, the precise molecular mechanisms underlying ubiquitination‐mediated radioresistance remain poorly characterized. The E3 ubiquitin ligase Deltex 3 (DTX3) is validated as a negative regulator of tumor radioresistance that improves radiotherapy efficacy in vitro and in vivo models. Mechanistically, DTX3 physically interacts with nucleophosmin 3 (NPM3), catalyzes K27‐linked polyubiquitination of NPM3 at the Lys102 residue, and consequently triggers proteasomal degradation of NPM3. Loss of NPM3 further destabilizes the RUVBL1–TIP60 complex, diminishes H4K16 acetylation, and impairs homologous recombination repair. Consistently, elevated NPM3 expression counteracts DTX3‐mediated radiosensitization. Clinically, low DTX3 levels are correlated with inferior overall survival and elevated post‐radiotherapy recurrence across multiple human malignancies. The study reveals DTX3 as a potent suppressor of homologous recombination repair and a promising therapeutic candidate to overcome tumor radioresistance.

title: A Damage‐Gated Small‐Molecule Chimera Selectively Enhances Mitophagy by Coupling Dysfunctional Mitochondria to Autophagy
authors:
Ratislav M. Ozhiganov, 
Ekaterina А. Guseva, 
Alexander Yu. Rudenko, 
Konstantin G. Lyamzaev, 
Sofya Y. Sokolskaya, 
Julia A. Golubeva, 
Maria V. Belopolskaya, 
Nadezda V. Andrianova, 
Olga V. Fadeeva, 
Elena О. Morgun, 
Elena A. Tukhovskaya, 
Marina S. Kazakova, 
Vladimir M. Pavlov, 
Daria K. Yagoda, 
Elena I. Marusich, 
Rose‐Lys Zaranaina, 
Valeriya B. Vays, 
Irina M. Vangeli, 
Egor Y. Plotnikov, 
Maxim L. Lovat, 
Lora E. Bakeeva, 
Arkady N. Murashev, 
Vladimir I. Polshakov, 
Olga A. Dontsova, 
Peter V. Sergiev
abstract:
MG‐1 is a bifunctional small molecule that enhances the removal of damaged mitochondria through autophagy, the cell's recycling pathway. Its activity increases under mitochondrial stress, with minimal effects on basal autophagy. MG‐1 also improves movement in a zebrafish model of mitochondrial dysfunction, supporting further investigation of this approach to mitochondrial quality control.








ABSTRACT
Mitophagy is a central mitochondrial quality‐control pathway, and its pharmacological activation is considered to be geroprotective. However, its small‐molecule activators act indirectly by perturbing metabolism or mitochondrial function, limiting selectivity and increasing toxicity. Here, we describe a chemical biology strategy for activating damage‐responsive mitophagy using bifunctional small molecules that couple mitochondrial recognition to the recruitment of the autophagic machinery. We designed and synthesized a focused library of chimeric molecules and identified MG‐1 as a lead compound. It had minimal effects on basal autophagy but markedly enhanced autophagic flux and mitochondrial clearance under conditions of mitochondrial stress. Biochemical analyses, together with fluorescence and electron microscopy, showed that MG‐1 promotes lysosomal degradation of damaged mitochondria without acting as a direct mitochondrial uncoupler. MG‐1 was well tolerated across experimental systems and improved locomotor performance in a zebrafish model of MPTP‐induced mitochondrial dysfunction. These findings establish damage‐gated small‐molecule chimeras as a promising approach for selective control of mitochondrial quality.

title: Contact‐Free Human‐Machine Interfaces via Printed Thermopile Infrared Arrays
authors:
Zirui Wang, 
Nan Luo, 
Amrutha Bose, 
Muhammad Irfan Khan, 
Jiayi Liu, 
Leon Viktor Klinder, 
Leonard Franke, 
Mohamed Hussein, 
Uli Lemmer, 
Md Mofasser Mallick
abstract:
Can a printed sheet locate and sense a fingertip without being touched? Fully printed, flexible thermoelectric arrays convert the infrared from a hovering finger directly into voltage, with no external power. Aerosol-jet-printed silver mirrors partially shield each pixel, creating a local temperature gradient. With responsivities up to 0.9 V W − 
 1 , the arrays enable contact-free dialing and handwriting.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Human-machine interfaces (HMIs) are evolving as key components for advanced sensing in communication and control systems. In particular, contact-free HMIs can facilitate unique advantages in hygiene, durability, and non-destructive sensing. However, spatially resolved sensing platforms remain challenging using bulk approaches. Here, we report flexible infrared interface arrays (TIA1 and TIA2) with ≥10 pixels that exploit the photo-thermoelectric (PTE) infrared sensing properties of Bi-Te-based thermoelectric (TE) materials via a dual-stage energy conversion process: radiation-to-thermal, followed by thermal-to-electric. The p- and n-type TE materials and electrodes were printed on polyimide to fabricate TIAs. After encapsulation with a black absorber, radially patterned silver mirrors are printed on the outer part of the pixels using aerosol jet-printing to partially shield each thermocouple. This induces a localized temperature gradient, hence an output voltage via the Seebeck effect under infrared illumination. The pixels exhibit responsivities of 0.7 VW −1  (TIA1) and 0.9 VW −1  (TIA2), respectively, under CO 2  laser irradiation (10.6 µm), with pixel-to-pixel variation within ± 10%. The TIAs were demonstrated as non-contact handwriting and dialing interfaces, converting human gestures into digital signals. These results pave the way for a self-powered and contactless interface for future human–machine interaction technologies.

title: Injectable Peptide‐Based Functional Amyloid Hydrogels as Tunable Depots for Sustained Drug Delivery
authors:
Ranjit Shaw, 
Niyamat M. A. Chimthanawala, 
Shouvik Manna, 
Sadhana Sathaye, 
Samir K. Maji
abstract:
An injectable and tunable peptide‐based functional amyloid hydrogel provides sustained insulin release while preserving insulin stability and bioactivity. The hydrogel enables prolonged glycemic regulation in vivo, exhibits excellent biocompatibility, and shows no detectable IAPP and α‐Syn heterologous cross‐seeding, highlighting its potential as a safe platform for long‐acting therapeutic protein delivery.








ABSTRACT
Sustained delivery of therapeutic proteins remains a major challenge because rapid degradation and diffusion necessitate frequent dosing, compromising therapeutic efficacy. Here, we present an injectable peptide‐based functional amyloid hydrogel as a versatile drug depot that preserves protein stability while enabling sustained cargo release. As a representative therapeutic application, insulin delivery for diabetes was employed to validate the platform. It exhibited excellent biocompatibility and injectability, providing controlled insulin release over 90 h while preserving its structural stability. Following a single subcutaneous administration in diabetic rats, it restored normoglycemia within 30 min and maintained it for 60 h, followed by a rebound at 66 h, representing a much longer period of glucose maintenance than free insulin. Long‐term in vivo biosafety studies confirmed the absence of systemic toxicity following repeated administration. To demonstrate the tunability of this platform, it was further engineered with sodium alginate as a representative bioadditive, thereby enabling tunable release kinetics and extending sustained insulin release while maintaining injectability and biocompatibility. Collectively, these findings establish peptide‐based functional amyloid hydrogels, either alone or engineered with a bioadditive, as a safe, injectable, and tunable platform for sustained therapeutic delivery, with diabetes serving as a representative proof of concept for broad biomedical applications.

title: A UBE3A‐UTX Proteostasis‐Epigenetic Axis Governs Hypothalamic Energy Homeostasis
authors:
Junekyoung Lee, 
Jaeyoung Yoo, 
Young A. Kim, 
Zhuodu Wei, 
Yunseo Lee, 
Woo‐Jeong Shon, 
Je Kyung Seong, 
Seunghee Lee
abstract:
Ubiquitin protein ligase E3A (UBE3A) regulates hypothalamic energy homeostasis and promotes degradation of the histone demethylase UTX (KDM6A). Neuronal UBE3A loss increases susceptibility to diet-induced obesity and is accompanied by UTX accumulation, reduced histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation, and altered endoplasmic reticulum stress-responsive gene expression. These findings suggest a link between neuronal proteostasis, chromatin regulation, and systemic metabolism.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Energy homeostasis requires integration of metabolic and stress signals within hypothalamic circuits, yet the role of neuronal proteostasis remains unclear. Ubiquitin protein ligase E3A (UBE3A) regulates the stability of lysine demethylase 6A (KDM6A), also known as ubiquitously transcribed tetratricopeptide repeat containing, X chromosome (UTX). Hypothalamic neuronal deletion of  Ube3a  results in hyperphagia, obesity, hyperleptinemia, and impaired glucose homeostasis under high-fat diet conditions; selective deletion in agouti-related peptide (AgRP) neurons is sufficient to recapitulate these phenotypes. UBE3A promotes UTX degradation, whereas UBE3A loss stabilizes UTX and decreases repressive histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3). Integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic analyses implicate UTX and activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4) in altered endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress-responsive transcriptional programs, although their causal contribution to the metabolic phenotype remains to be established. Treatment with GSK-J4, an inhibitor of KDM6-family demethylases, increases hypothalamic H3K27me3 levels and improves metabolic outcomes in  Ube3a -deficient mice, although the specific contribution of hypothalamic UTX inhibition to these effects remains to be established. These findings support a link between neuronal proteostasis, chromatin regulation, and systemic metabolic homeostasis and warrant further investigation of the relevance of UTX-associated pathways to metabolic dysfunction in a subset of individuals with Angelman syndrome.

title: Topology‐Driven X‐Shaped DNA as a cGAS Stimulator to Promote Dendritic Cell Activation and Antitumor Vaccine Efficacy
authors:
Jiabei Li, 
Xuan Wang, 
Dali Wei, 
Zhejie Chen, 
Ziyi Wang, 
Qing Yu, 
Yu Yang, 
Shengpeng Wang
abstract:
X-shaped DNA promotes multivalent cGAS assembly and enhances cGAS-STING signaling. When conjugated with antigenic peptides, the resulting X-DNA-based peptide vaccine promotes dendritic cell activation, antigen presentation, and antitumor T-cell responses. These findings highlight the potential of programmable DNA structure design in the development of more effective and structurally defined antitumor peptide vaccines.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Vaccine adjuvants are essential for enhancing immune responses, yet the development of safe and potent adjuvants remains challenging. Here, we report a topology-guided nucleic acid adjuvant based on a four-way Holliday junction framework (X-DNA) designed to potentiate cGAS-STING signaling. In contrast to linear dsDNA, X-DNA presents a flexible, multibranched architecture that increases local DNA density and multivalent interaction potential, thereby favoring productive cGAS assembly. Molecular dynamics simulations demonstrate that X-DNA forms a more stable complex with cGAS and facilitates the establishment of the active 2:2 cGAS-DNA core assembly. Consistent with this mechanism, X-DNA markedly enhances cGAMP production and IFN-β secretion, promotes dendritic cell maturation and antigen presentation, and, when conjugated with antigenic peptides, strengthens antigen-specific CD8 +  T-cell responses in vivo. In murine tumor models, X-DNA significantly improves the therapeutic efficacy of peptide vaccination and suppresses tumor progression. These findings identify DNA topology as a programmable determinant of cGAS activation and establish X-DNA as a structurally defined nucleic acid adjuvant for enhancing antitumor subunit vaccine efficacy.

title:
The Interplay Between Molybdopterin Synthase and Metal Metabolism Contributes to Pathogenicity in
                     Acinetobacter baumannii
authors:
Min Jiao, 
Wenbo He, 
Zhenlin Ouyang, 
Ruochen Wang, 
Jiaxin Zhang, 
Xin Liu, 
Yiting Jing, 
Qinyue Yu, 
Xiaoyu He, 
Qian Qin, 
Litao Guo, 
Peter M. Hwang, 
Fang Zheng, 
Yurong Wen
abstract:
Pathogenic  Acinetobacter baumannii  scavenges metal ions as nutritional elements to survive within the host. This study demonstrates that molybdopterin synthase is essential for pathogenesis and full virulence during infection. Molybdopterin synthase subunit MoaE constitutes an intrinsically disordered C-terminal histidine rich tail, which mediates metal interaction and homeostasis, uncovering a functional link between molybdenum metabolism and broader metal-ion homeostasis during host infection.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Molybdoenzymes are required in a large amount of essential redox activity and ubiquitously existing in bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes. The molybdenum cofactor (Moco) is a pterin-based catalyst, whose synthesis is accomplished by molybdopterin synthase, heterotetrametric MoaE-MoaD enzyme. We demonstrate that molybdopterin synthase in  Acinetobacter baumannii  plays important roles in bacterial growth, morphology determination, ROS tolerance, biofilm formation, and interplay with the metabolism and homeostasis of other metal ions besides molybdenum. Further, the crystal structure of MoaDE complex was solved and revealed an intrinsically disordered histidine-rich C-terminal tail in MoaE that is active in metal chelation and modulating protein stability.  Acinetobacter baumannii  MPT synthase is associated with virulence, which was verified in both  Galleria mellonella  and murine pneumonia model. Our study sheds light on the structural and functional diversity of bacterial molybdopterin synthases and explores crosstalk between different metal homeostasis pathways, providing potential for antibacterial development.

title: An Epidermal Sweat Patch for Tracking Metabolite Levels and Correlation Analysis in Biofluids
authors:
Yao Chen, 
Xinhao Wan, 
Haoxin Fan, 
Hengwei Lou, 
Jialu Wang, 
Jie Gao, 
Dan Wen
abstract:
This work presents an epidermal sweat patch for continuous glucose monitoring that validates a strong correlation between sweat, interstitial fluid and blood, enabling a reliable and non-invasive platform for systemic health management.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Continuous, in situ monitoring of sweat biomarkers offers a promising approach for non-invasive metabolic assessment, but its practical implementation remains limited by sensing stability and the insufficiently defined physiological relationship between sweat and systemic biofluids. Here, we develop an epidermal sweat patch that integrates a non-enzymatic electrochemical interface based on Au–Ni(OH) 2  dual aerogels for glucose monitoring. The complementary roles of Ni(OH) 2 -mediated glucose adsorption and Au-assisted electrooxidation enable sensitive and stable sensing, with a calculated detection limit of 0.1 µM and >95% signal retention after 5 weeks. Combined with microfluidic sweat sampling, signal processing and wireless communication, the patch enables real-time on-body tracking of sweat glucose during daily activities. In human studies, sweat glucose shows positive associations with interstitial fluid and blood glucose, with Pearson correlation coefficients of up to 0.828, while subgroup analyses further reveal interindividual variability. These results support the physiological relevance of sweat glucose as a complementary signal for metabolic monitoring. Overall, this work integrates non-enzymatic sensing, wearable system design and cross-biofluid analysis within a single platform, providing a practical framework for physiologically interpretable sweat-based glucose monitoring.

title: Integrated Single‐Cell and Spatial Transcriptomics Reveal Convergence on a Senescence‐Associated B Cell–MIF Signaling Axis in Joint Aging and Osteoarthritis Progression
authors:
Weida Li, 
Yi Wang, 
Yongqing You, 
Yue Cui, 
Jiayun Liu, 
Xingbiao Ma, 
QiuYu Zhu, 
Qiang Wu, 
Zanjing Zhai, 
Zuyan Lu, 
Kerong Dai, 
Ye Sun
abstract:
Single‐cell and spatial transcriptomics implicate senescent B cells and macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) signaling in aging and osteoarthritic joints. An injectable hydrogel combining quercetin with siRNA targeting MIF attenuates cartilage degeneration in a mouse model of osteoarthritis. These findings support local targeting of B cell senescence and MIF signaling as a potential therapeutic strategy.








ABSTRACT
Osteoarthritis (OA) involves age‐associated structural and immune changes, yet whether senescence‐associated B‐cell states contribute to cartilage degeneration remains unclear. Integrated single‐cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics of healthy, aged, and OA mouse joints identify reduced B‐cell abundance but enrichment of a low‐proliferative, inflammatory state with heightened macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF) signaling. Cell–cell communication and spatial ligand–receptor analyses identify enhanced predicted MIF–CD74/CD44 interactions in B‐cell‐associated regions adjacent to cartilage. Constitutive MIF deficiency attenuates senescence‐associated B‐cell changes, MMP13 induction, and cartilage damage in vivo. Joint‐derived B cells from aged and OA mice induce chondrocyte senescence, reduce COL2A1 and HMGB1, and increase FN1 and MMP13 through MIF‐dependent paracrine signaling. These effects are suppressed by MIF neutralization and restored by recombinant MIF in MIF‐deficient co‐cultures. A composite hydrogel carrying quercetin and MIF‐siRNA‐loaded PLGA microspheres for local co‐delivery. The microspheres show gradual siRNA release over 96 h in vitro. In DMM‐induced OA, the formulation reduces MIF, P16, and MMP13 signals, restores HMGB1, and preserves cartilage. These findings support a senescence‐associated B cell–MIF signaling axis associated with joint aging and chondrocyte dysfunction and provide proof of concept for a local biomaterial‐based strategy that attenuates OA‐associated changes.

title: A Novel Bioactive Component, Efoba, From Aged Garlic Targets CTSC to Suppress NET‐Driven Neuroinflammation and Ameliorate Secondary Brain Injury After Intracerebral Hemorrhage
authors:
Junjun Meng, 
Jianhua Wang, 
Tao Zhang, 
Xiaofan Fan, 
Jinxiu Guo, 
Shiyuan Zhao, 
Wenxue Sun, 
Pei Jiang
abstract:
Efoba, a novel bioactive component derived from aged garlic, confers neuroprotection against intracerebral hemorrhage. It acts on microglia to suppress CTSC release, inhibits NET‐mediated neural injury, and blocks pathological microglia‐neutrophil crosstalk. This study provides a highly promising lead compound for hemorrhagic‐stroke therapy.








ABSTRACT
Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a devastating neurological disorder with high mortality and disability, where neuroinflammation‐driven secondary brain injury is a key pathological hallmark. Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) serve as critical pathogenic mediators that amplify neuroinflammation, disrupt blood‐brain barrier integrity, and exacerbate brain damage after ICH. This study identifies Efoba, a novel bioactive monomer from aged garlic, and establishes a scalable total‑synthesis route for hundred‑gram‑scale high‑purity production, overcoming low‑yield and supply‑limiting bottlenecks for natural product research. In vivo and in vitro experiments show Efoba markedly ameliorates ICH‑induced neurological impairments and inhibits NET formation. Integrative analyses (Lip‐MS, virtual screening, proteomics, transcriptomics) identified cathepsin C (CTSC) as the direct binding target of Efoba. Efoba stabilizes microglial lysosomal membranes, inhibits CTSC release, blocks NET generation, and exerts neuroprotection against NETs‐driven neuroinflammation. CTSC knockout and CTSC overexpression assays further confirm the indispensable role of CTSC in mediating Efoba's neuroprotective and anti‑inflammatory activities. Collectively, this work demonstrates for the first time that Efoba targets CTSC to suppress NET‐mediated neuroinflammation, highlighting its therapeutic potential and the translational value of natural active components.

title: Gel‐Free Capture of Microvolt‐Level Neural Signatures Via a 3D Monolithic Carbon Fiber Dry Electrode
authors:
Haoxuan Sun, 
Nikolay Novitskiy, 
Dongwook Jang, 
Yixiang Liu, 
Shaoqi Pan, 
Ting Huang, 
Yitong Li, 
Huisi Yang, 
Leonardo Nicholas Adi Wijaya, 
Md Masruck Alam, 
Patrick CM Wong, 
Zhaoli Gao
abstract:
A compressible carbon fiber/PEDOT:PSS electrode enables gel-free contact at hairy scalp sites. Its conductive porous framework supports low interfacial impedance and retains contact performance after repeated mechanical and sweat-related challenges. Beyond routine electrophysiological recording, the electrode captures microvolt-level speech-evoked frequency-following and long-latency responses, highlighting its potential for gel-free recording of weak neural signals.

 
 
 ABSTRACT 
 Gel-based wet electrodes remain the gold standard for electrophysiology, but gel dehydration limits recordings. Existing dry electrodes partially address this limitation but suffer from high interfacial impedance. Here, a carbon fiber-based porous electrode (CFPE) is reported, comprising a three-dimensional conductive network coated with poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrene sulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS). The CFPE establishes contact at hairy-scalp sites with an impedance of approximately 10 kΩ·cm 2 . On the forearm, its impedance at 10 Hz without skin preparation is 11.09 ± 1.03 kΩ·cm 2 , compared with 13.57 ± 2.07 kΩ·cm 2  for wet electrodes. After 6 h of wear, CFPE impedance reaches 1.3 times its initial value without skin preparation or gel, whereas wet-electrode impedance reaches 56 times its initial value when applied with skin preparation and conductive gel. High-fidelity electrocardiography, electromyography, and electroencephalography signals are captured with correlation coefficients exceeding 90% and signal-to-noise ratios comparable to wet electrodes. The CFPE further resolves microvolt-level speech-evoked frequency-following responses (FFR) and long-latency responses (LLR), with fidelity comparable to wet electrodes and significantly higher LLR SNR. These results demonstrate gel-free acquisition of weak neural biomarkers, opening a pathway toward prolonged, preparation-free neurophysiology.

title: Field‐Driven Proton Transport in Water Revealed by Machine Learning Molecular Dynamics
authors:
Alicia van Hees, 
Zhan‐Yun Zhang, 
Linnéa Andersson, 
Chao Zhang
abstract:
Using a reactive and polarizable machine‐learning molecular dynamics (MLMD) framework, the authors show that excess‐proton drift remains nearly linear with applied electric field up to 0.15 V/Å. It is also found that the protonic defect mitigates the field‐induced structural changes observed in neat water, revealing a distinct high‐field response of protonated water.








ABSTRACT
Excess‐proton transport in water arises from the coupling of proton transfer (PT), hydrogen‐bond rearrangement, and solvent polarization. While equilibrium Grotthuss diffusion has been widely studied, its response under strong electric fields remains difficult to resolve because simulations must capture both chemical reactivity and induced polarization over long time scales. Here, we have developed a reactive and polarizable machine‐learning interatomic potential for molecular dynamics simulations of the hydrated excess proton in water. A fine‐tuned PiNet2 model provides an accurate zero‐field reference for structure and diffusion, while an AD(OS)‐based finite‐field coupling enables non‐equilibrium simulations under an applied electric field. In the linear‐response regime, below 0.04 V/Å, the proton mobility obtained from drift velocity agrees closely with the equilibrium diffusion coefficient. The proton drift velocity remains nearly linear with field strength up to 0.15 V/Å, a field strength at which the ionic mobility of a constrained hydronium ion decreases. Our simulations revealed a distinct field‐response of protonated water, whose hydrogen‐bond network largely preserves its structural fluctuations and mobility without a comparable dielectric‐saturation signature. Furthermore, free‐energy analysis shows that strong fields stabilize the hydronium species with four‐fold H‐bond coordination.

title: Pre‐Refinement Prediction of Dopant Site Occupancy in M‐Type Hexaferrites via Hierarchical and Uncertainty‐Aware Machine‐Learning
authors:
Dan Liu, 
Jianyu Ren, 
Ruoshui Liu, 
Yinong Yin, 
Jianfeng Xi, 
Xin Ming, 
Jiazheng Hao, 
Tongyun Zhao, 
Fengxia Hu, 
Baogen Shen
abstract:
Refined data are extracted from CIF files to construct a hierarchical machine‐learning framework integrating sublattice classification, Fe‐site occupancy prediction, and reliability assessment. External validation yields 96% accuracy for sublattice classification and a macro mean absolute error of 0.0584 for Fe‐site prediction. This study provides a basis for initial occupancy hypotheses and refinement prioritization in M‐type hexaferrites.








ABSTRACT
Dopant site occupancy bridges chemical composition, local crystal structure, and macroscopic functional responses in M‐type hexaferrites. However, reliable occupancy hypotheses are difficult to establish before structural refinement. Here, we develop a pre‐refinement machine‐learning framework using 494 dopant‐level records extracted from refined structures. This workflow combines Ba/Sr‐vs.‐Fe sublattice classification, fractional occupancy prediction over five inequivalent Fe sites, and reliability‐aware assessment. The CatBoost classifier achieves 96% accuracy on external validation for sublattice assignment. For Fe‐sublattice dopants, homogeneous occupancy‐model screening and heterogeneous cooperative occupancy‐model screening yield a macro mean absolute error as low as 0.0584, while preserving dominant‐site identification and occupancy ranking. The results show that dopant site occupancy is jointly controlled by dopant chemistry, target‐dopant amount, and co‐doping environment rather than a universal site‐preference rule.
