A comment on phylogenetic tests of the haplodiploidy hypothesis for eusociality
Si-scRNA-seq: Enabling ambient-stable single-cell transcriptomics through spatially confined biosilicification
authors: Liang ZhouTing RuanYing HeGuangting XieJingyu QiXiaobao CaoC. Jeffrey BrinkerYa LiuWei Zhuahttps://ror.org/0530pts50Guangdong Engineering Research Center of Low-Carbon Synthetic Biotechnology, State Key Laboratory of Pulp and Paper Engineering, School of Biology and Biological Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou 510006, People’s Republic of Chinabhttps://ror.org/02drdmm93National Cancer Center/National Clinical Research Center for Cancer/Cancer Hospital & Shenzhen Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences and Peking Union Medical College, Shenzhen 518116, People’s Republic of Chinachttps://ror.org/03ybmxt82Guangzhou National Laboratory, Guangzhou 510005, People’s Republic of Chinadhttps://ror.org/05fs6jp91Center for Micro-Engineered Materials and the Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, The University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM 87131ehttps://ror.org/0530pts50Institute of Emergent Elastomers, School of Materials Science and Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou 510640, Guangdong, People’s Republic of China
abstract:
Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is constrained by rapid RNA degradation during sample storage, necessitating cold-chain logistics. Here we present spatially confined biosilicification (SCB), wherein RNA is encapsulated within a nanoscopic layer of amorphous silicon dioxide, as a highly effective methodology enabling ambient-temperature preservation of single-cell transcriptomes. By judiciously incorporating a silicification inhibitor, SCB achieves spatiotemporal control over both intra- and extracellular silica deposition, preventing excessive crosslinking and cell aggregation while preserving RNA biointegrity and accessibility. scRNA-seq performed with biosilicified cells (Si-scRNA-seq) maintained high transcriptomic fidelity with fresh samples (R
                     2 
                    = 0.95 after 7 d) extending RNA half-life to 54.8 d at 25 °C, a 685-fold improvement compared to unprotected samples. Furthermore, Si-scRNA-seq confers robust resistance against oxidative and UV degradation. Compatible with mainstream platforms at ~0.1 RMB per sample, Si-scRNA-seq successfully resolves cellular heterogeneity in clinical lung, liver, and ovarian cancer specimens after extended room-temperature storage. Si-scRNA-seq provides a scalable and cold-chain–free solution for single-cell transcriptomics in research and clinical settings.

abstract:
The first draft diploid genome assembly (HuRef) of an individual in 2007 was a milestone in genomics. Here, we report HuRef2.0, a revision of HuRef assembled using only Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT) Simplex-reads and the hifiasm assembler. Results are close in continuity to the telomere-to-telomere (T2T) assemblies but were assembled from standard DNA samples without using multiple sequencing and mapping technologies, including ultra-long-reads and/or proximity-ligation. Three ONT flowcells (~103× coverage) from fresh blood DNA produced an assembly comprising 26 contigs, with gapless assembly of 23 chromosomes (Chr). Two gaps on ChrY were locally assembled to yield the final T2T-assembly, HuRef2.0, with base accuracy >Q60.34 and 2,393 phase blocks with an NG50 value of 2.36 Mb. Assembly from a single ONT flowcell (~35× coverage) consistently produced an assembly more contiguous than GRCh38.p14, providing a foundation for further optimization and scaling. Assembly quality was assessed by direct chromosome-level alignments to a reference genome, variant calling, and annotation of gene-rich regions at Chr22q11, the extended
                     MHC 
                    locus, and at several difficult to assemble regions, including the
                     rRNA 
                    gene clusters, the subtelomeric region on Chr4q35, ChrY, and the centromeres. More accurate but shorter Pacific Biosciences HiFi-reads produced less contiguous assemblies than from equivalent coverage of error-corrected ONT reads, indicating the importance of read-length. We compared HuRef2.0 to an assembly of a low-passage EBV-transformed lymphoblastoid cell line derived from the same donor. At least at a 400 kb resolution, we did not observe notable structural differences in the two assemblies.

title: Contactless continuous guidance of matter in its main states using curved elongated Bessel-like acoustic fields
abstract: Acoustic manipulation uses sound waves to exert force on matter, enabling contactless movement, trapping, and the structuring of particles in bulk media. It offers a contamination-free approach for handling matter in applications spanning across chemistry, biology, and advanced manufacturing. However, state-of-the-art techniques, including acoustic holograms or phased arrays of transducers (PATs) are limited to transporting individual particles or small clusters one by one, and are not suitable for dispersed matter such as gases or aerosols. Here, we introduce a method for guiding a continuous flow of matter along reconfigurable three-dimensional trajectories using elongated Bessel-like acoustic fields (EBAFs). These fields generate converging radial acoustic forces along a programmable path, forming stable mid-air conduits that continuously transport matter. Compared to existing methods such as near-field acoustic levitation, acoustofluidic separation, particle manipulation with vortex and Airy beams, the proposed method offers enhanced versatility, scalability, and real-time control of transport trajectories in mid-air without requiring physical guiding structures. We developed methods to generate EBAFs with PATs tailored to different particle sizes and material properties, and experimentally demonstrated guidance of solids, liquids, aerosols, and gases along programmable trajectories. This technique enables containerless laboratory operations, precise and contamination-free reagent or energy delivery, and integration into advanced additive manufacturing processes that require controlled distribution of matter in different states to target zones.

title: Local growth laws determine global shape of molluscan shells
authors: Huan LiuKaushik Bhattacharyaahttps://ror.org/05dxps055Division of Engineering and Applied Science, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125
abstract: Molluscan shells come in various shapes and sizes. Despite this diversity, each species produces a shell with a characteristic shape that is independent of environmental conditions. We seek to understand this robust complexity. We are guided by two principles in the spirit of D’Arcy Thompson. First, the growth is governed by the repeated and continuous application of a fixed growth law, even as the shell evolves in overall shape, without any complex biological machinery to monitor and control the growth. Second, the growth law depends solely on local geometry at the shell’s growing edge. The first principle naturally leads to the mathematical statement that the shape of the shell is generated by the action of a Lie group on a protoconch. The second naturally leads to a particular representation of the Lie group. We use this representation to show that the shapes of nearly all known molluscan shells can be described by essentially three parameters: a scalar (scaling), a vector (orientation), and a curve (edge of the protoconch). We relate these parameters to the phylogenetic tree. In addition to the morphogenetic insight, our results potentially point to a alternative growth-based approach to engineering complex structures.

title: Capillary physics links HIV capsid geometry to nuclear pore translocation
authors: Alexander W. BrownSami C. Al-IzziJack L. ParkerSophie HertelDavid A. JacquesHalim KusumaatmajaRichard G. Morrisahttps://ror.org/01v29qb04Department of Physics, Durham University, Durham DH1 3LE, United Kingdombhttps://ror.org/03r8z3t63Department of Applied Mathematics, School of Mathematics and Statistics, University of New South Wales, Sydney, NSW 2052, Australiachttps://ror.org/03r8z3t63School of Physics, University of New South Wales, Sydney, NSW 2052, Australiadhttps://ror.org/03r8z3t63Australian Research Council Centre of Excellence for the Mathematical Analysis of Cellular Systems, University of New South Wales Node, Sydney, NSW 2052, Australiaehttps://ror.org/04qtj9h94Department of Biotechnology and Biomedicine, DTU Bioengineering, Danmarks Tekniske Universitet, Kgs. abstract: The protective capsid encasing the genetic material of HIV can traverse the nuclear pore complex (NPC) intact, despite being far larger than conventional passive cargo. This is attributed to the properties of the capsid surface, which promote partitioning into cohesive assemblies of the disordered proteins that form the NPC’s permeability barrier: phenylalanine-glycine nucleoporins (FG-Nups). The implication, at the mesoscale, is that capsid–NPC interactions are characterized by the interfacial physics of wetting and capillarity. To capture this, we develop a minimal theory that reduces to an interplay between capsid geometry, effective cytoplasmic and nucleoplasmic contact angles, and a ratio of interfacial tensions. By combining analytical calculations, sharp- and diffuse-interface numerics, we make several predictions: A geometry-dependent trade-off between penetration depth and the wetting transition; asymmetric capillary forces that generate torques and lead to metastable “stalled” states that are tilted; a topological classification of the possible mechanisms underlying the largest energetic barrier; and spontaneous symmetry breaking of displaced FG-Nups. These behaviors connect capsid shape and orientation to the topology and symmetry of FG-Nup displacement, and to the molecular compositions on each side of the pore. They are consistent with published cryoelectron tomography orientations, which provide an initial estimate of the cytoplasmic contact angle. Crucially, our results identify a capillary advantage for the HIV capsid’s characteristic broken-symmetry geometry.

authors: Silvia H. BarcellosLeandro S. CarvalhoKenneth M. LangaSneha NimmagaddaPatrick Turleyahttps://ror.org/01y2jtd41La Follette School of Public Affairs, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI 53706bhttps://ror.org/01y2jtd41Department of Population Health Sciences, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI 53726chttps://ror.org/03taz7m60Center for Economic and Social Research, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA 90089dhttps://ror.org/03taz7m60Department of Economics, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA 90089ehttps://ror.org/00jmfr291Department of Internal Medicine, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109fhttps://ror.org/00jmfr291Survey Research Center, Survey Research Center, Institute for Social Research, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48106
abstract: There is little causal evidence on factors that can protect individuals against Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) risk. We study the causal effect of education on ADRD, exploiting a regression discontinuity generated by a compulsory schooling reform. ADRD was ascertained based on medical history, hospital records, and death registries, addressing concerns about selective sample attrition. We find that education reduces incidence of ADRD. Using molecular genetic data, we show that the reform weakened the relationship between genetics and ADRD incidence, implying genetic risk of dementia is not immutable and can be modified by social policy.

title: Integrating ecology with genetics to explain gene reuse during repeated evolution
abstract: The role of determinism and chance in the evolutionary history of life is often analyzed through the lens of the repeatability of evolution. Although it is now clear that evolution often repeats itself, we are only beginning to understand why this varies in degree. For example, the probability of gene reuse during repeated bouts of adaptation often declines with time since divergence, but the causes of this pattern remain unclear. Here, we explore two core hypotheses for time-dependent variation in the repeatability of gene reuse during adaptation. Specifically, gene reuse depends on the extent to which lineages have 1) similar genomes such that they have similar genetic architectures, mutations, and mutational effects (i.e., a fairly well-appreciated “shared genetics” hypothesis), and 2) similar ecologies such that they have similar environments and patterns of natural selection (i.e., a mostly unexplored “shared ecology” hypothesis). The latter hypothesis emphasizes ecology’s role in gene reuse and has received little explicit attention. In particular, testing the shared ecology hypothesis requires moving beyond a simple dichotomous characterization of ecology to embracing ecological divergence as a multivariate and continuous phenomenon. Although such tests are only beginning to emerge, they already illustrate how integration of ecological factors can help explain variation in gene reuse. Here, we advocate a framework that integrates the influence of both genetic and ecological factors in the repeatability of evolution and can be applied to a range of organisms to better understand the role of determinism and chance in biological diversification.

abstract: Nature Ecology & Evolution, Published online: 23 October 2026;  doi:10.1038/s41559-026-03192-1  Modelling larval dispersal pathways reveals that protected deep-sea areas lack sufficient connectivity to replenish one another. The addition of strategically placed protected corridors linking the existing areas would protect current larval dispersal pathways and improve biodiversity conservation capacity in abyssal ecosystems that face mining threats.

title: Dispersal corridors enhance modelled near-bed larval connectivity across deep-sea protected area networks
abstract:
Abstract 
                   The Clarion–Clipperton Zone (CCZ) is the focal region for imminent deep-sea nodule mining, with over 1.1 million square kilometres already under exploration licence. Although the International Seabed Authority has designated Areas of Particular Environmental Interest (APEIs) to protect regional biodiversity from mining impacts, there has been no formal assessment of whether this network functions as a coherent connected system. Here we use Lagrangian dispersal modelling and network analysis to provide a region-wide assessment of modelled larval connectivity across the CCZ and show that simulated larval exchange among APEIs is extremely limited. Under physically driven near-bed dispersal and reasonable pelagic larval dispersal times of 19–69 days, fewer than 0.02% of particles reach another APEI, with inter-APEI gaps exceeding modelled dispersal capacity. CCZ-wide dispersal is structured into four semi-isolated connectivity communities, and under mining disturbance when self-supply is removed from Areas of Mining Interest, unprotected non-mining areas emerge as the dominant modelled source of replenishment. Strategic corridor additions increase inter-APEI dispersal 406-fold and nearly doubles modelled replenishment from protected areas under disturbance, providing a reproducible, connectivity-informed evidence base for conservation design ahead of commercial mining.

Metabolically robust ratiometric autoluminescent reporters
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Self-sustained luminescence enables non-invasive monitoring of molecular events at the whole-organism level, but its intensity depends on both gene expression and cellular metabolism, limiting quantitative interpretation. Here we present an approach that disentangles the contributions of gene expression and metabolism. By co-expressing an engineered reference luciferase variant that uses the same substrate but emits light at a different wavelength and monitoring the colour ratio, we substantially reduced signal variability, enabling quantitative physiological imaging despite changes in metabolic activity.

title: A kleptomyiophilous orchid exploits milichiid flies through mimicry of common pentatomoid bugs with high levels of toxicity
abstract: Liu et al. report that the orchid Bulbophyllum claviforme (eastern ecotype) deceives a milichiid fly pollinator by mimicking injured pentatomoid bugs—a prey item flies steal from predators. Surprisingly, the orchid mimics common yet highly toxic bugs, which suggests that floral mimicry likely evolved through an abundance-dependent process, the magnet species effect.

abstract: Hasegawa et al. show that a class of bile salt hydrolases (BSHs) harbored by Bacteroidales species promote elimination of vancomycin-resistant enterococcus (VRE) in the presence of Lachnospiraceae bai+ bacteria. In the gut, bacteria producing this subclass of BSH eliminate and displace VRE through deoxycholic acid (DCA) production.

title: Perforin triggers iron-induced mitochondrial damage to drive ferroptosis and anti-tumor immunity
abstract: Perforin is best known for delivering granzymes into tumor cells, but this study shows it has a second, independent killing function: it drives iron uptake and mitochondrial iron overload that trigger ferroptosis. This granzyme-independent pathway links cytotoxic immunity to iron metabolism, predicts patient response to checkpoint blockade, and points to iron supplementation as a possible lever for boosting anti-tumor immunity.

title: Taurine lowers inflammaging by regulating the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages
abstract: Taurine levels increase with age in mice and humans. Boosting taurine levels even further in aged mice increases health span and dampens inflammation through its regulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome.

title: Cell-type dependence of effects from transcranial electric brain stimulation
abstract:
There is an urgent need for better treatment options for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, depression, and epilepsy. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) is a non-invasive, safe, inexpensive, and promising method that could address some of this unmet need. The therapeutic value of tES has been well demonstrated, but the effect is highly variable. To enable tES to reach its full potential requires a better understanding of how tES modulates neural activity so that tES treatments can be tailored to specific neurological conditions and individual patients. The neural response to tES is, however, highly complex, and the parameter space involved in optimizing tES treatments is daunting. This has made it difficult to obtain general insights into how tES modulates neural activity, and a central challenge lies in the cell-type-specific and frequency-dependent nature of these responses. In this study, we investigated cell-type-specific neuronal responses to tES over a broad frequency range, using a large database of biophysically detailed neuron models. We found that pyramidal cells respond strongly to low-frequency tES, but their responses drop sharply with frequency. In contrast, inhibitory neurons show a smaller reduction and, on average, become more responsive than pyramidal cells above
                     
                       
                         
                         
                           
                             ~ 
                             60 
                           
                         
                       
                     
                    Hz. By leveraging a reciprocity theorem we demonstrated that the effect of tES on a given cell-type is proportional to the frequency-dependent current-dipole moment that determines the EEG-signal contribution of this cell-type. We further identified the dendritic asymmetry as key in determining tES responses across the frequency spectrum. Counterintuitively, we also found that while total cell length increases tES sensitivity at low frequencies, it can have the opposite effect at high frequencies. Furthermore, we derived an analytical formula for idealized neuron models which can approximately predict the tES sensitivity of different cell types at any given frequency. By characterizing the role of morphology and stimulation frequency in determining tES responses of single cells, this is an important step towards a better understanding of tES at the fundamental level. These results also provide an efficient and accurate method for characterizing and comparing the tES responses of different neural populations across the frequency spectrum, which facilitates optimizing tES for cell-type specific targeting.

title: The evolutionary accessibility of cultural fitness landscapes
abstract:
by Laurel Fogarty, Rebecca B. Hoyle 

Many human cultural and technological traits have a complex and peculiar structure. They are often characterized by multiple closely interacting parts that can form modules, and change as a result of innovation, collaboration, and social learning. A full understanding of the ways in which such cultural traits evolve requires a model that accounts for the close epistatic interaction of the constituent parts, and for the uniquely cultural processes that act on them. Here, we generalize the concept of ‘adaptive landscapes’, where populations search a landscape for optimal combinations of components. This generalization accounts for epistatic interactions, and includes processes such as modularization, communication, and collaboration, that are not features of genetic systems but may be quite common features of cultural systems. We show that modularization in combination with collaborative communication of search results is more successful, but sometimes more costly, than searching a full adaptive landscape. However, in many of the circumstances under which technology evolves, a full search of many thousands of possible modules may not be feasible since time, financial, energetic, and environmental constraints are likely to be strong. Under these conditions, our models suggest that there is a critical value for the number of modules to search below which the global optimum is more likely to be reached by searching the full landscape. The value of this threshold depends on the complexity of the technology. Overall, we suggest that analysis of cultural fitness landscapes is likely to be a fruitful avenue for research into technological change especially when combined with elements of human learning and interaction known to be important features of cultural evolution.

title: scDIG: an R Shiny application for interactive density-based gating of single-cell proteomic and transcriptomic data
abstract:
Background
                      Delineating biologically meaningful cell populations within single-cell embedding spaces requires methods that balance expert guidance with reproducibility. Current approaches range from subjective manual selection to fully automated algorithms that may obscure rare but biologically significant populations. 
                  
                     Results
                      We present scDIG, a Shiny-based tool that integrates bimodal index-driven feature selection, feature-weighted kernel density estimation, and interactive contour-based gating to define cell populations directly within two-dimensional projections of scRNA-seq and CITE-seq data. Applied to CITE-seq PBMC data from subjects in the Cardiovascular Assessment Virginia (CAVA) cohort, scDIG resolved transcriptionally distinct CD4⁺ T cell subpopulations within continuous embeddings not readily captured by conventional clustering and identified  GZMB -enriched cytotoxic lymphocyte subsets from RNA expression data. Sensitivity analysis confirmed that defined gates correspond to coherent cell populations in high-dimensional feature space. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                       s cDIG provides a robust, reproducible framework for density-based gating of single-cell data, bridging the interpretability of manual expert gating with the rigor of algorithmic population definition. The app is freely available for non-commercial use at  https://au-cbgm-shiny.augusta.edu/gating , with source code at  https://gitlab.com/pbombina/scdig .

title: A kinematic interpretation of spatial expression gradients from single-snapshot spatial transcriptomics
abstract:
Background
                      Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression across tissue position, but temporal or mechanistic interpretation of a spatial gradient requires an explicit model. We derive a kinematic interpretation for tissues with a stationary position-conditioned expression field and positive mean cell displacement along an anatomical axis. Under these assumptions, a gene’s gradient sign equals its net-production sign. The measured statistic remains a spatial gradient, and without an independent velocity estimate the framework does not recover absolute rates. 
                  
                     Results
                      We evaluate the framework on a human liver atlas with 16 standard-Visium sections, three matched Visium HD sections and companion single-nucleus RNA-seq; the primary cross-donor analysis uses eight live-donor sections. Gradient direction is reproducible: mean cross-donor correlation is 0.87 on a strict 66-gene panel and 0.67 on a broad 15,192-gene panel. On prespecified top-quartile subsets, cross-platform sign agreement is 14/14 genes for M2 and 13/14 for M6 ( n  = 14 per donor); cross-pipeline agreement is 76%. Four diagnostics and a geometric argument show that the gene-gene coupling matrix is not stably identifiable or interpretable as a regulatory Jacobian from one sampled trajectory. In graded steatosis across four donors,  GLUL ,  LYZ  and  ORM1  show consistent spatial-gradient responses to lipid, but wild-cluster calibration finds cluster-robust significance anticonservative; we report directional observations, not significant discoveries. On the mouse crypt-villus axis, all 15 canonical markers recover their expected directions on an anatomy-derived coordinate. 
                  
                     Conclusion
                      The framework provides a reproducible, splicing-free estimator of spatial expression gradients applicable to imaging-based platforms. Under explicit steady-state and positive-flow assumptions, gradient direction has a kinematic interpretation as net-production direction; cross-sectional data establish gradient reproducibility, not time-resolved dynamics. Separating the observable from its conditional interpretation, and diagnosing the coupling matrix’s identification failure, defines both the method and its inferential boundary.

title: PELICAN: a new bacteriophage genome annotation tool
abstract:
Background
                      Bacteriophages, or simply phages, are viruses that infect bacteria. They can serve as antibacterial agents, particularly against important bacterial pathogens. Accurate gene identification in phage genomes is essential for research and therapeutic applications. Detecting genes linked to lytic or lysogenic lifestyles, toxins, or bacterial fitness helps guide phage selection. 
                  
                     Results
                      We present PELICAN, a command-line tool for bacteriophage genome annotation. The PELICAN pipeline has four stages: (i) integration of multi-tool predictions; (ii) probabilistic and machine learning-based evaluation of non-consensus genes; (iii) resolution of overlapping predictions; and (iv) codon bias check of overlapped positions to produce a final annotation. For validation, we used reference phage genome annotations validated by transcriptomics and compared the results to those of other phage genome annotation tools. PELICAN had the best recall, but a higher false positive rate than some of the other tools. We present evidence that most of these false positives may be in fact true positives. Our evidence is primarily based on protein folding scores of the putative proteins coded in the predicted coding regions. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      PELICAN is a novel tool for bacteriophage genome annotation that provides improved gene recall and competitive F1 values compared to an existing similar tool.

title: Alignment of RNA secondary structures with arbitrary pseudoknots using structural sequences
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Background 
                     Comparison of RNA secondary structures is fundamental for RNA classification, motif analysis, and evolutionary studies. While efficient methods exist for pseudoknot-free structures, the comparison of RNA secondary structures with arbitrary pseudoknots remains computationally challenging. The aim of this study is to introduce a novel sequence-based representation and an associated alignment distance for efficiently comparing RNA secondary structures with arbitrary pseudoknots. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     We introduce a novel representation of RNA secondary structures with arbitrary pseudoknots based on integer sequences, called structural sequences. On this representation, we define the SERNA distance, an extension of the classical edit distance with structural correctness constraints, and prove that it is a metric. We present SERNAlign, an open-source tool that computes the SERNA distance using dynamic programming with quadratic time complexity. To evaluate the proposed distance, we conduct two complementary experiments within a clustering-based evaluation framework: classification of experimentally validated pseudoknot motifs, which directly targets the design goal of SERNA, and phylogenetic clustering of ribosomal RNAs as a robustness check against existing structural distances. Across both tasks, SERNA demonstrates competitive clustering performance with respect to state-of-the-art comparison methods, while providing improved discrimination in complex motif settings and significantly lower computational cost compared to structure-based approaches.

title: The AI debate is missing half the system
abstract: Last month, leading executives of artificial intelligence (AI) companies warned the United Nations Security Council about the risks of losing human control over this rapidly advancing technology. Their recommendations focused heavily on safeguards, evaluation, and governance of AI models and systems, largely overlooking the risks that arise from the interactions of AI with people and institutions. AI safety needs to be addressed at the level of the human–AI system, not the AI model alone.

Noncoding transcription controls the developmental dynamics of long-range gene regulation
abstract:
The genomic regions regulating gene expression are often themselves transcribed into a variety of noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs). However, the regulatory roles of this noncoding transcription remain largely unknown. By using live imaging, we reveal that the sequential transcription of ncRNAs emanating from distinct regulatory elements underlies gene activation in
                     Drosophila 
                    embryos. Single-allele covisualization uncovers that optimal gene activation is achieved by only moderate levels of enhancer activity. Disrupting enhancer-associated ncRNAs causes precocious gene activation, providing evidence that ncRNAs control the timing of gene expression in development. We further show that enhancer transcription can regulate long-range interactions within complex regulatory landscapes. We propose that ncRNAs locally modulate regulatory element activity in cis to shape genome organization and orchestrate the temporal control of gene expression in development.

title: Sequential diagnosis with language models
abstract:
We explored the capabilities of frontier language models in sequential diagnosis, a diagnostic paradigm that captures the iterative nature of clinical reasoning. Given a brief clinical presentation, clinicians selectively acquired information to reach a diagnosis, enabling assessment of diagnostic accuracy and workup cost. We developed an interactive benchmark and an artificial intelligence (AI) system that simulates a panel of physicians, continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests. Using this benchmark, the system achieved 83.2% accuracy on
                     New England Journal of Medicine 
                    clinicopathological conference cases and 80.3% on MIMIC-IV-ED emergency department admissions, outperforming generalist physicians (36.1 and 46.8%, respectively). Although these findings were obtained in a controlled benchmark setting, they highlight the promise of language models for supporting more accurate, lower-cost diagnoses.

title: The Virtual Biotech: A multi-agent AI framework for therapeutic discovery and development
abstract: Drug development requires evidence integration across biological scales and modalities, but relevant tools are fragmented. We introduce the Virtual Biotech, an organization of artificial intelligence (AI) agents modeled on a drug-development company, with agentic divisions spanning target discovery, safety assessment, modality selection, and clinical development. We demonstrate its utility at three drug-development decision points. First, more than 37,000 agents annotated outcomes from 55,984 trials and found that drugs targeting cell type–specific genes were 48% more likely to reach market with 32% fewer adverse events. Second, it integrated multimodal evidence to propose a therapeutic strategy in lung cancer. Third, it analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial and inferred potential mechanisms of failure. These results demonstrate that human-guided multi-agent systems can conduct transparent, multiscale analyses to inform therapeutic-development decisions.

title: Natural product biosynthesis by guanidine prenyltransferases in plants and bacteria
abstract:
Guanidine exists almost exclusively as a resonance-stabilized cation, making its direct enzymatic functionalization challenging. We identified the cyanobacterial enzyme NosH, which catalyzes direct prenyl transfer to free guanidine. Structural and mechanistic analyses revealed guanidine activation by a two-aspartate clamp coupled to prenyl-donor binding through a distinct catalytic architecture. Guided by these features, we identified a large family of guanidine prenyltransferases across bacteria and plants. Plant enzymes produced guanidine alkaloids such as galegine in vitro and heterologous expression of a plant ortholog in
                     Nicotiana benthamiana 
                    produced galegine in planta, providing a direct enzymatic link to plant-specialized metabolism.

title: Decoupled self-assembled monolayer and perovskite deposition for efficient flexible solar modules
abstract:
The power conversion efficiency (PCE) and stability of flexible perovskite solar modules (PSMs) are less than those of their rigid devices because surface hydroxyls desorption on flexible substrates, which disrupts self-assembled monolayer (SAM) anchoring and perovskite crystallization. We developed a decoupled SAM-perovskite codeposition strategy that accelerates SAM anchoring by reducing the SAM-perovskite interaction and ameliorates perovskite crystallization. The certified PCE with phenethylammonium iodide as the passivation molecule was 20.2% on PSMs with device areas of 750 cm
                     2 
                    . With 1,3-diaminopropane dihydroiodide as the passivator, the PCE of 22.0% for a device area of 14.55 cm
                     2 
                    decreased by 8% after 1044 hours under maximum power point tracking at 85°C and 65% relative humidity. The devices pass all sequences of an international commercialization assessment standard for flexible portable PSMs.

title: Visualizing symmetry-broken Chern insulators and their quantum melting
abstract: In the presence of a magnetic field, electronic states of moiré quantum materials develop a Hofstadter spectrum that provides a distinctive setting for studying the interplay between band topology and strong electron-electron interaction. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we studied Hofstadter’s states in bilayer graphene aligned with hexagonal boron nitride and directly visualized the formation of interaction-driven symmetry breaking Chern insulators. Our measurements revealed the formation of phases that double, triple, or quadruple the moiré unit cell at fractional filling of the Hofstadter bands as well as states with complex intra–unit cell wave functions. We visualized two distinct quantum phenomena in different Chern states, including quantum melting driven by the appearance and proliferation of topological defects and a quantum transition co-occurring with phase competition and separation.

title: Imaging electron-hole asymmetry in the quantum melting of generalized Wigner crystals
abstract: Two-dimensional moiré materials provide a versatile platform to explore phase transitions in strongly correlated systems. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we imaged the density-driven melting of generalized Wigner crystals (GWCs) and Mott insulators (MIs) in electron-doped, near-60°–twisted molybdenum diselenide bilayers featuring a triangular moiré superlattice. We observed notable electron-hole asymmetry in GWC melting: Hole-doped GWCs yielded interaction-driven disordered states, whereas electron-doped GWCs melted into delocalized liquid-like states. This asymmetry arose from the broken particle-hole symmetry of the moiré superlattice, which produced electron and hole Fermi pockets with different momentum geometries upon GWC condensation. MI states melted without such asymmetry, consistent with the absence of a symmetry-breaking density modulation. This work provides direct visualization of the emergent phases that appear as GWCs undergo quantum melting transitions.

title: Dynamic functionality–enabled fast and selective transport in nanochannels
abstract: Nanochannels capable of fast and selective mass transport are central to applications in energy, resources, biomedicine, and the environment. However, extreme nanoscale confinement, often coupled with rigid channel environments, imposes substantial frictional and adhesive barriers, causing sluggish transport and constrained selectivity. We identified nanochannel dynamics as a key to addressing these challenges by harnessing the intrinsic mobility (e.g., self-rotation) of confined functionalities to enhance molecular transport. Through a combination of experiments and simulations, we demonstrated that such dynamics reshape transport by promoting kinetic energy transfer and enabling more efficient molecular relays, thereby improving separation performance beyond current benchmarks. Our findings highlight the role of nanochannel dynamics in regulating mass transport under confinement and provide a framework for designing advanced nanochannel systems.

title: Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain
Safeguarding global terrestrial vertebrate species from future sea level rise
abstract: Sea level rise (SLR) threatens terrestrial biodiversity, yet its spatiotemporal and species-specific impacts remain unclear. Integrating relative SLR projections across five shared socioeconomic pathways (SSPs) with area of habitat (AOH) maps for 34,120 terrestrial vertebrate species, we project that species exposed to SLR will increase from up to 13,680 in 2050 to 15,324 by 2100, including 57 to 63% of birds, 47 to 52% of mammals, 28 to 36% of reptiles, and 20 to 24% of amphibians. In Southeast Asia, inland inundation areas support high richness. Under SSP5-8.5, species facing >10% habitat inundation surge from 18 in 2050 to 109 by 2100, with reptiles and already threatened species overrepresented. Safeguarding SLR refugia—the noninundated habitats for exposed species—is critical, yet more than 96% lie outside protected areas, which means that early international action is required.

title: Late Holocene reexpansion of the Laurentide Ice Sheet
abstract: During interglaciations, the Laurentide Ice Sheet (LIS), which is the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, retreats to Arctic Canada, where it achieves a minimum configuration. The reexpansion of the LIS following this minimum marks the start of the next glaciation. Here, we show that the last remaining remnant of the most recent LIS, Barnes Ice Cap (Baffin Island, Canada), achieved its minimum interglacial dimensions after ~3.6 thousand years ago, before reexpanding ~2000 years ago, marking the onset of the next glaciation. The new LIS reached maximum dimensions in ~1960 CE, after which anthropogenic summer warming resulted in a negative mass balance, ice margin recession, and the termination of the next glaciation. The demise of the next glaciation, despite the ongoing decline in summer insolation, illustrates the influence of anomalous greenhouse gas forcing on climate.

title: Intron retention regulates STAT2 function and associates with immunotherapy response in lung cancer
abstract:
Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors has revolutionized cancer therapy and enabled considerable therapeutic advances for treating various diseases, including lung cancer. However, the molecular determinants of variable patient outcomes remain unclear. Using long-read RNA sequencing, we mapped the landscape of alternative RNA splicing in human primary lung adenocarcinomas. We identified more than 149,000 full-length messenger RNA (mRNA) isoforms, more than half of which were unannotated and many that occurred in immune-related genes, particularly within the type I interferon response pathway. We functionally characterized retained introns in the
                     STAT2 
                    gene that produced altered protein isoforms that regulated immune signaling and interferon responses and correlated with patient survival after anti–programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy. These findings position alternative splicing as a regulator of tumor immune responses and reveal intron retention in
                     STAT2 
                    as an interferon regulatory axis that correlates with PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor response.

title: BAK and BAX form a multiprotein complex to drive mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death
abstract:
The apoptotic regulators BAX and BAK, once activated, form homo-oligomers to trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP), activating the apoptosome and caspases. Activation of BAX-BAK without apoptosome activation triggers sustained efflux of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and caspase-independent cell death. However, the molecular basis of mtDNA efflux remains unclear. We purified a macromolecular complex comprising BAK, BAX, activator BH3-only molecules, voltage-dependent anion channels 1 and 2 (VDAC1 and VDAC2), and prohibitins that released mtDNA from mitoplasts. BAX-BAK activation resulted in VDAC closure, mitochondrial calcium influx, and mtDNA efflux. Loss of VDAC1, VDAC2, or prohibitins prevented BAX-BAK activation–induced mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death without affecting MOMP or mitochondrial inner membrane herniation. These findings support differential regulation of cytochrome
                     c 
                    and mtDNA efflux by distinct BAX-BAK complexes.

title: Wireless electrocatalytic closed-loop system for drug-free management of diabesity
abstract: Lifestyle-related type 2 diabetes and associated obesity (diabesity) affect >2.5 billion people worldwide and impose nearly $3 trillion in annual health care costs. We developed an implantable, wirelessly powered electrocatalytic closed-loop health optimization (ECHO) device containing platinum-decorated gold nanoclusters embedded in graphite felt that enabled selective, electrically tunable oxidation of blood glucose to renally cleared gluconate. In type 2 diabetic mice, wireless, low-power activation (0.75 volts, 10 milliamperes) restored glucose homeostasis within 1 hour, shifted metabolism from glucose to lipid utilization, reduced body weight and triglycerides, and increased circulating free fatty acids and ketone bodies without detectable hypoglycemia or adverse physiological, inflammatory, or behavioral effects during 6 weeks of treatment. Coupling this ECHO device to a commercial continuous glucose monitoring system enabled autonomous, smartphone-controlled, drug-free closed-loop management of experimental diabesity.

title: Electronic bound states in the continuum in a two-dimensional metal
abstract:
Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are quantum states that remain localized despite lying within a continuum of extended, delocalized states. Whereas optical BICs have been realized in photonic systems, achieving electronic bound states embedded in a metallic background remains an ongoing challenge. In this study, we used scanning tunneling microscopy to identify two defect-induced electronic states that remain localized within the metallic continuum of Pd
                     5 
                    AlI
                     2 
                    , a two-dimensional van der Waals metal. Our calculations suggest that electron-hopping interference on the decorated checkerboard lattice of Pd
                     5 
                    AlI
                     2 
                    gives rise to a (quasi) flat band built from spatially localized eigenstates that are orthogonal to the dispersive continuum. Atomic defects within this frustrated lattice shift the associated flat-band localized states into the metallic continuum, forming robust, symmetry-protected BICs.

title: Thermodynamic origin of the phonon Hall effect in a honeycomb antiferromagnet
abstract:
The underlying mechanism of the thermal Hall effect generated by phonons in a variety of insulators is yet to be identified. In this work, we report on a sizable thermal Hall conductivity in nickel phosphorus trisulfide (NiPS
                     3 
                    ), a van der Waals stack of honeycomb layers with a zigzag antiferromagnetic order. The longitudinal (κ
                     
                       aa 
                     
                    ) and the transverse (κ
                     
                       ab 
                     
                    ) thermal conductivities peak at the same temperature, and the thermal Hall angle, at this peak, respects a previously identified bound. The amplitude of κ
                     
                       ab 
                     
                    is extremely sensitive to the amplitude of magnetization along the
                     b 
                    axis but is not correlated with the phonon mean free path, which points to an intrinsic origin.

title:
Genome architecture modulates
                     35S 
                    and
                     5S rDNA 
                    homogenization in Asteraceae
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   Concerted evolution is the model by which multicopy gene families are homogenized across genomes, with ribosomal DNA (rDNA) as its textbook example. However, the extent and efficiency of this process may vary depending on genomic factors. The plant family Asteraceae provides a natural comparative system to address the evolutionary dynamics of rDNA, as it is uniquely characterized by the coexistence of two contrasting genomic arrangements: a separate (S‐type) and a linked (L‐type) organization of 5S and 35S rRNA genes. Here we analyzed rDNA arrangements in 71 representative Asteraceae species (50 S‐type and 21 L‐type) and, using WGS data and repeatome analyses, we have reconstructed full rDNA units and quantified the intragenomic variability across coding (genic) and non‐coding (spacer) regions. No intermediate (coexisting L‐type+S‐type) genotypes were found. Our results reveal contrasting patterns of 5S rDNA variation depending on its genomic context. S‐type species exhibit high levels of 5S polymorphism in both genic and spacer regions, while L‐type species show near‐complete sequence homogeneity, consistent with variation in homogenization efficiency and selective constraints related to copy number and chromosomal position of 5S rRNA genes. In contrast, 35S rDNA shows a low polymorphism level overall. The findings support a context‐dependent view of concerted evolution across rDNA and highlight the influence of genome architecture on rDNA evolution. In particular, the contrasting behavior of 5S (highly conserved when linked but highly variable when separate) emerges as a key example of how structural genomic context shapes the evolution of even the most conserved housekeeping genes.

title:
Gap‐Free
                     Cannabis sativa 
                    Assemblies Reveal Post‐Polyploid Genome Remodelling and Refine the Evolution of Cannabinoid Synthase Genes
authors:
Jiangjiang Zhang, 
Chuchu Qin, 
Zhao Li, 
Lining Zhao, 
Ashok Biswas, 
Touming Liu, 
Mingbao Luan, 
Lin Li, 
Defang Li, 
Jianbin Yan
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   
                    Despite the therapeutic importance of cannabinoids, the scarcity of gap‐free
                     Cannabis 
                    genomes has limited the dissection of the genetic and genomic basis of cannabinoid biosynthesis and genome evolution. Here, we generated two haplotype‐phased, gap‐free, gold‐standard assemblies and used them to investigate post‐polyploid genome remodelling and refine the evolutionary history of cannabinoid synthase genes. Analyses of these gap‐free assemblies recovered a
                     γ 
                    whole‐genome triplication (WGT) signal shared with core eudicots and provided no evidence for additional lineage‐specific whole‐genome duplication (WGD) in
                     Cannabis 
                    . The extant
                     Cannabis 
                    genome reflects long‐term retention and divergence of a subset of
                     γ 
                    ‐derived duplicates, together with subsequent non‐WGD‐derived gene duplications and repeat‐associated remodelling that contributed substantially to present‐day genome diversification. Furthermore, phylogenomic, structural and syntenic evidence indicate that a precursor duplication predating the
                     Cannabis 
                    –
                     Humulus 
                    split gave rise to two lineages retained in
                     Cannabis 
                    on chromosomes 7 and 2. In
                     Cannabis 
                    , the chromosome 7 lineage subsequently expanded and diversified into the functional cannabinoid synthase genes, whereas
                     Humulus retained 
                    only the lineage resembling the
                     Cannabis 
                    chromosome 2 copy. This asymmetric retention and diversification provide new insights into the origin and specialization of cannabinoid biosynthesis in
                     Cannabis 
                    . Together, these results provide a high‐quality genomic framework for understanding the history of polyploidy, the evolution of the cannabinoid synthase gene and genome diversification in
                     Cannabis 
                    .

title: Microbial volatile humulene orchestrates plant–microbe alliance to establish disease‐suppressive rhizosphere
authors:
Yishuo Huang, 
Fengling Zhang, 
Jinlong Zhang, 
Weiqi Zhang, 
Ningqi Wang, 
Xiaofang Wang, 
Zhong Wei, 
Gaofei Jiang, 
Waseem Raza
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         
                          Microbial volatile organic compounds (mVOCs) suppress growth and virulence traits of soil‐borne pathogens, yet their ecological roles in disease suppression remain unclear. Here, we show that the sesquiterpene humulene from
                           Streptomyces 
                          acts as a multifunctional regulator that suppresses bacterial wilt through coordinated inhibition of
                           Ralstonia solanacearum 
                          , plant metabolic reprogramming, and rhizosphere microbiome modulation.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          We combined
                           in vitro 
                          pathogen assays, pot experiments, microbiota transplantation, rhizosphere 16S rRNA profiling, root‐exudate metabolomics, and plant and pathogen transcriptomics to investigate the direct and microbiome‐mediated effects of humulene.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          Humulene reduced disease severity and pathogen abundance via a microbiome‐dependent mechanism. Microbiota transplantation confirmed that the humulene‐conditioned microbiome retains transferable disease‐suppressiveness. Humulene also selectively enriched antagonistic
                           Streptomyces 
                          , not by direct growth promotion, but by reprogramming tomato root exudation to produce lipid‐derived petroselinic acid, which promoted
                           Streptomyces 
                          growth, humulene production, and pathogen suppression. Root transcriptomics further revealed activation of lipid metabolic pathways involving alternative fatty acid desaturation and oxylipin signaling.
                         
                       
                       
                         Together, humulene functions as an ecological signal that integrates pathogen suppression, host lipid metabolism, and microbiome assembly to establish a disease‐suppressive rhizosphere, enabling microbiome‐informed control of bacterial wilt.

title: Two roads to a full ear: How maize domestication shaped form and function
abstract: Early farmers turned bushy teosinte into maize by two genetic routes: one route reshaped the plant's architecture, and a newly identified route changed its physiology, sending more sugar and nitrogen to the ear. Both increased the share of the plant that becomes grain, and both can guide future crop improvement.

title: An edible invitation: Recruiting beneficial fungi through what they eat
abstract: Orchid seeds cannot germinate without help from fungi. This commentary features a recent study showing that  Cremastra appendiculata  seeds release two small compounds that attract a helpful fungus and also serve as food for it. This suggests that plants may recruit fungal partners before contact by offering edible chemical cues to nearby fungi.

title: Conserved DNA methylation architectures are associated with transcriptional robustness and regulatory plasticity in the woody perennial tea plant
abstract:
Abstract 
                   DNA methylation is an important mechanism in plant development and environmental adaptation, yet how distinct methylation features contribute to transcriptional stability and regulatory flexibility in long-lived woody plants remains poorly understood. Here, we integrated DNA methylomes, transcriptomes, and chromatin accessibility profiles from two Camellia sinensis varieties to examine the regulatory characteristics and conservation of two specific methylation architectures: gene body methylation (gbM) and DNA methylation valleys (DMVs). We found that gbM genes showed distinctive gene structures, broad and relatively stable expression, and highly conserved methylation states between orthologs. gbM-gbM orthologs also showed evidence of stronger selective constraint in a sequence-length-dependent manner, consistent with a close relationship between gbM and stable transcription of housekeeping genes. In contrast, DMVs were highly hypomethylated regions associated with TE depletion and pronounced TF footprint signals, both of which were closely linked with methylation level, while DMV-associated genes were enriched for developmental and stress-responsive functions. Genome synteny analyses further revealed substantial conservation of DMV patterns and TF footprint profiles between tea varieties, indicating broad conservation of DMV-associated regulatory features across divergent genetic backgrounds. Together, these findings reveal two complementary epigenetic architectures in a woody perennial plant, with gbM preferentially associated with transcriptional robustness and DMVs with regulatory features linked to development and environmental responses.

title: The MfMYB1–MfWRKY51/MfLBD1 regulatory switch modulates anthocyanin biosynthesis under low temperatures
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Seasonal leaf coloration, driven by anthocyanin dynamics, is a crucial adaptive response to thermal environments, yet the underlying transcriptional mechanisms remain largely elusive. Here, we utilized the ornamental crabapple Malus ‘Fengwu’, which exhibits a striking red-to-green transition upon warming, to unravel the thermo-responsive regulatory network. Low temperature maintains red pigmentation and high antioxidant capacity, whereas warming leads to a rapid decline in anthocyanin content. We identified MfWRKY51 and MfLBD1 as crucial transcriptional repressors of anthocyanin biosynthesis, exhibiting elevated expression in green leaves and downregulation under low-temperature conditions. Genetic and biochemical analyses demonstrated that MfWRKY51 and MfLBD1 inhibit anthocyanin accumulation and reduce antioxidant capacity, whereas silencing either gene enhances anthocyanin accumulation and antioxidant capacity. Mechanistically, MfWRKY51 directly binds to the promoters of anthocyanin structural genes (MfDFR, MfANS, and MfUFGT), while MfLBD1 binds to the MfDFR promoter, collectively repressing their transcription. Furthermore, MfMYB1, strongly induced by low temperature and jasmonate (JA), acts as a central positive regulator that directly binds to the promoters of MfWRKY51 and MfLBD1 to repress their transcription. Reciprocally, MfWRKY51 directly suppresses MfMYB1 transcription, forming a mutual-repression feedback loop that functions as a temperature-sensitive switch. This regulatory module is functionally conserved between ornamental crabapple and cultivated apple, where low temperature promotes anthocyanin accumulation by repressing MdWRKY51 and MdLBD1 orthologues. Collectively, our findings reveal a conserved transcriptional network integrating temperature and JA signals to fine-tune anthocyanin metabolism, providing mechanistic insights into plant seasonal adaptation.

title:
Time–Space-Resolved Fluorescence Spectroscopy in
                     Chlamydomonas 
                    Cells under Light-Harvesting Regulation
abstract:
Abstract 
                   We report here a technical advancement that enables time-resolved fluorescence spectroscopy in spatially resolved domains of a living cell at low temperatures. The technique is based on a combination of a self-developed cryo-confocal microscope and a streak camera. An instrumental response time of 24 ps was achieved. This technique was applied to reveal the light-harvesting dynamics in local domains within single Chlamydomonas reinhardtii cells. Organisms performing oxygenic photosynthesis have evolved a regulation mechanism, called state transitions (ST), that maintains the excitation balance between PSI and PSII. Cells were induced either to state1, where LHCII is primarily bound to PSII, or state2, where a fraction of LHCII has moved and is bound to PSI. The observation was made at 80 K, where PSI and PSII show clearly separated fluorescence emission bands. We separately analyzed fluorescence rise dynamics in the wavelength regions of 685–693 nm assigned to PSII and 705–724 nm assigned to PSI in both the PSI-rich and PSII-rich domains. The observed rising fluorescence dynamics reflect the excitation energy flow from the antenna to the core parts of these PSs. The time constant of the fluorescence rise of the PSII emission was slower in the PSII-rich than in the PSI-rich domain in both state1 and state2, whereas that of the PSI emission was slower for the PSI-rich than for the PSII-rich domain in state2. Based on these results, we concluded that the intracellular inhomogeneity in the PSII/PSI fluorescence ratio comes partially from the heterogeneity of the antenna sizes of the PSs.

title: MnWRKY22 Mediates Tissue-Specific Resveratrol Biosynthesis through Coordinated Regulation of the Stilbene Synthase Gene Cluster in Mulberry
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Resveratrol, a pharmaceutically significant stilbenoid accumulates in mulberry roots. To elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying this tissue-specific biosynthesis, we systematically analyzed the stilbene synthase (STS) gene family in mulberry. Our investigation revealed that nine out of ten MnSTS genes form tandem repeats in a single genomic cluster. Co-expression clustering and phylogenetic analysis implied that these genes undergo purifying selection, resulting in highly consistent co-expression patterns across tissues, with particularly specific high expression in roots and calli. Subsequent weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) identified the transcription factor (TF) MnWRKY22 as a key regulatory candidate. Functional validation confirmed that MnWRKY22 is specifically expressed in roots and calli and directly binds to W-box elements in all MnSTS promoters, thereby activating their transcription. Suppression of MnWRKY22 expression significantly reduced both MnSTS transcript levels and resveratrol accumulation, while its overexpression enhanced MnSTS expression and resveratrol production. Notably, overexpression of MnWRKY22 in leaves ectopically activated otherwise silent MnSTSs, enabling de novo resveratrol synthesis. This study reveals the coordinated evolutionary characteristics of the MnSTS gene family and establishes MnWRKY22 as a unified regulator of tissue-specific resveratrol accumulation in mulberry. These findings provide a foundation for enhancing resveratrol production through metabolic engineering approaches.

title:
Salicylic Acid-Induced MdTGA9-MdERF138-
                     MdHCT 
                    Module Is Associated with Lignin Deposition and Improved Anthracnose Resistance in Autotetraploid Apple
abstract:
Summary 
                   Apple anthracnose, caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, severely threatens global apple production. Autotetraploid ‘Hanfu’ apples show stronger anthracnose resistance than diploids, but the underlying molecular mechanism remains unclear. This study identified a novel salicylic acid (SA)-regulated lignin biosynthesis signaling pathway that is closely associated with the enhanced resistance in autotetraploid ‘Hanfu’ apples. Autotetraploid apples accumulated higher endogenous SA levels, and the SA-responsive transcription factor MdTGA9 was markedly induced by both SA treatment and C. gloeosporioides infection. Mechanistically, MdTGA9 acts as a nuclear transcriptional activator to directly bind to the MdERF138 promoter and activate its expression. MdERF138 then transactivates the lignin biosynthetic gene MdHCT, thereby promoting lignin accumulation. Functional verification showed that MdTGA9 overexpression in apple calli, fruits and leaves significantly enhanced anthracnose resistance, and MdERF138 and MdHCT were confirmed as positive regulators of this resistance. Collectively, this study reveals a previously uncharacterized MdTGA9-MdERF138-MdHCT regulatory cascade that integrates SA signaling and lignin-based physical defense, which accounts for the enhanced disease resistance of autotetraploid apple. These findings provide valuable gene resources and a new molecular mechanism for disease-resistance breeding in apple.

title: HYPK-ing up COP1 to put the brakes on photomorphogenesis
Photosynthesis-derived carbon gates cell cycle activation to enable hormone-autonomous shoot regeneration
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Shoot regeneration is a powerful model for cell fate reprogramming but how it occurs in nature remains poorly understood because studies in Arabidopsis thaliana conventionally rely on in vitro assays supplemented with exogenous hormones and sugars. Here, we established the Hormone-autonomY Direct Regeneration Assay (HYDRA) in which removal of the shoot apical meristem (SAM) initiates shoot regeneration from the cotyledon-hypocotyl boundary without hormone or sugar supplementation. We identify photosynthesis-derived carbon and the boundary domain as two separable but convergent requirements for shoot regeneration in HYDRA. Following SAM removal, carbon availability increases in the boundary domain where it activates cell-cycle progression via the RETINOBLASTOMA-RELATED1 (RBR1) pathway. Carbon deprivation blocks regeneration despite induction of shoot meristem genes, indicating proliferative activation is limiting. Pre-existing shoot-competent boundary cells give rise to regenerated shoots upon cell-cycle activation, while their perturbation impairs regeneration despite sufficient carbon. Carbon therefore gates the proliferative activation of these cells, enabling functional shoot meristem formation. Additionally, exogenous carbon supply overcomes the requirement for SAM removal to induce shoot formation, indicating that carbon availability also acts as an initiation cue. Together, this study reveals an inherent capacity for hormone-autonomous shoot regeneration and identifies photosynthesis-derived carbon as a central regulator of this process.

title:
Mediator CKM and MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 reinforce auxin responsiveness to sustain
                     MUTE 
                    expression during stomatal lineage differentiation
abstract:
Abstract 
                   MUTE functions as a pivotal transcription factor that governs the transition from self-renewal to differentiation in meristemoids during stomatal development. This transition requires MUTE expression to reach a critical threshold, yet the mechanisms that maintain its expression homeostasis remain unclear. Here, we show that the Mediator CDK8 kinase module (CKM) acts as a transcriptional coactivator of the MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 complex to regulate meristemoid fate. Specifically, CKM cooperates with MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 to promote the transcription of the auxin-responsive genes, such as SAUR52 and SAUR53, thereby enhancing local auxin response in meristemoids. AUXIN RESPONSE FACTORs (ARFs), including ARF6, ARF7, and ARF19, then bind to MUTE promoter and contribute to its transcription, establishing a positive feedback loop. Disruption of CKM or MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 components reduces SAUR52/53 expression and auxin responses, leading to decreased MUTE transcription, excessive meristemoid self-renewal divisions and arrested differentiation. These defects can be partially rescued by exogenous auxin application or by overexpression of SAUR53 in the mutants. Together, our results uncover a self-reinforcing transcriptional-auxin circuit in which CKM-assisted MUTE-ICE1/SCRM2 amplifies auxin response, and auxin reciprocally sustains MUTE expression. This feedback mechanism ensures that MUTE reaches the threshold required to terminate meristemoid self-renewal and initiate differentiation, revealing how transcriptional regulation and hormone signaling are integrated to control stem cell-like behaviors during tissue patterning.

title: Quantum-boosted deep generative learning unveils the energy-landscape of single cell omics
Highly textured crystalline films enabled by supercooling for short-channel vertical organic field-effect transistors exhibiting high on/off ratios
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Vertical organic field-effect transistors (VOFETs), where the channel length is determined by the thickness of the semiconductor, show great potential for future electronic devices. However, fabricating high-performance VOFETs with channel lengths of just a few tens of nanometers remains challenging, because ultrathin active layer is prone to leakage currents and electrical shorting. Here, a supercooling-assisted crystallization strategy is proposed to fabricate highly textured ultrathin C8-BTBT crystalline films for short-channel VOFETs. Compared with conventional slow-crystallization methods, this strategy stabilizes the preferred molecular orientation during crystallization, yielding highly ordered crystalline films with improved molecular tilt and enhanced vertical charge transport. By integrating these films with a self-assembled graphene source electrode, VOFETs with channel lengths as short as 25 nm were successfully fabricated. The optimized devices with a 50 nm-thick semiconductor layer exhibited an on/off ratio close to 109 and a current density of 137.15 mA cm⁻2. Furthermore, the excellent film uniformity enabled consistent device arrays with a density of 2500 units cm⁻2, providing a feasible route toward high-density, solution-processed small-molecule organic integrated circuits.

title: TERS-ABNet: deep learning for single-molecule reconstruction with atomic precision from TERS mapping
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Determining the chemical structure of a single molecule on a surface from spectroscopic data constitutes a challenging high-dimensional inverse problem. While tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS) enables chemically specific imaging of single molecules with sub-nanometer spatial resolution, reconstructing complete molecular structures from TERS maps remains difficult due to ambiguous vibrational signatures and heavy reliance on expert interpretation. Here, we introduce TERS-ABNet, a deep-learning framework that reformulates single-molecule structure determination as an image-to-graph inference task. Leveraging a two-track architecture, the model simultaneously predicts probabilistic maps for predefined atom and bond/group classes, enabling the direct construction of explicit atom-bond graphs without dependence on conventional vibrational-mode assignment. Trained on simulated datasets, TERS-ABNet achieves ~94% accuracy in atom-type classification (mean coordinate error: ~0.23 Å), enabling reliable recovery of molecular connectivity and full reconstruction of single-molecule structures from TERS maps. The framework generalizes across diverse spatial resolutions and structural complexities through transfer learning, and successfully retrieves partial atom- and bond-resolved features of a single porphyrin molecule from experimental TERS data. This work establishes a generalizable deep-learning paradigm for inferring explicit atom-bond graph representations from high-dimensional spectroscopic imaging data, offering a transformative pathway towards automated molecular structure determination in nanoscale characterization.

title: China’s greenhouse gas budget 2025
Phase-change thermal energy storage: Materials, thermophysics and emerging applications
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Phase change materials (PCMs) can reversibly store and release considerable thermal energy through nearly isothermal and isometric phase state transitions, thus have attracted broad attention in energy decarbonization, passive thermal management, and emerging fields such as medicine and intelligent robots. However, critical challenges at material, device, and system levels remain to be addressed. These include the development of pure or composite PCMs with superior thermophysical properties, the design of effective latent heat storage devices, and the optimization of system integration. This review provides a comprehensive overview of phase change thermal storage, beginning with the mechanisms underlying the regulation of PCMs’ thermophysical properties. We summarize recent advances in the physical and chemical modification of PCMs by molecular engineering, multi-component doping, and rational design of composite microstructure and morphology to improve thermodynamic and heat-transfer performance. We then highlight advanced latent heat storage device design using passive and active strategies for increasing both energy and power density, and outline PCM-integrated systems across multifunctional applications including energy harvesting and storage, thermal management, medical treatment, intelligent machine, and catalysis. Finally, we discuss future research directions towards next-generation PCMs, high-performance devices and intelligent system integration.

title: Blinks are strategically coupled with head movements in unconstrained natural gaze behavior
authors: Alexander GoettkerMary Hayhoeahttps://ror.org/033eqas34Department of Psychology, Justus Liebig University Giessen, Giessen 35396, GermanybDepartment of Psychology, Centre for Mind, Brain and Behaviour, Universities of Marburg, Giessen and Darmstadt, Germanychttps://ror.org/00hj54h04Center for Perceptual Systems, University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX 78712
abstract: Blinks are a ubiquitous yet largely unnoticed aspect of human vision, despite causing frequent interruptions of visual input that can amount to up to 10% of waking time. By leveraging a large dataset of unconstrained gaze behavior during two natural tasks, we found a behavioral strategy to limit the impact of blinks: blinks were strategically coupled with head movements, which minimizes information loss due to unreliable visual input during head movements. Specifically, blink probability increased with higher head velocities and showed strong temporal modulation relative to head movement onset: Blink probability was reduced before head movement initiation and then peaked during the head movement. The strength of this coupling was tailored to the individual needs of participants, with participants with higher baseline blink rates showing stronger synchronization. This indicates that blinks are a part of an individually coordinated strategy when orchestrating eye and head movements during unconstrained natural behavior.
