Instead, both groups seem to rely less on what is likely a (reduced) random-policy SR strategy in alcohol-related contexts – and instead more on model-free control. Results suggest that the use of an adaptive, resource-efficient decision-making strategy is selectively downregulated in substance-related contexts. This study highlights the importance of considering contextual modulation and nuanced decision strategies in understanding habitual and goal-directed behavior in mental health conditions such as addiction.

title: Spatio-temporal machine learning for multi-horizon prediction of bluetongue outbreaks
abstract:
Reliable early warning of infectious disease outbreaks remains a major challenge for surveillance systems, particularly for vector-borne pathogens whose transmission depends on interactions among hosts, vectors, and climate-sensitive environmental conditions. Data-driven forecasting offers a promising approach for predicting outbreak risk using surveillance and environmental data. This study develops a logit-weighted ensemble (LWE), a machine-learning framework that predicts outbreak occurrence 1–6 months ahead at the administrative unit–month scale using routinely available outbreak notifications and gridded climate data. Bluetongue virus (BTV), an arbovirus of ruminants transmitted by
                     Culicoides 
                    biting midges, provides a well-characterised system in which transmission is strongly shaped by climate, making it a useful system for applying and testing this approach. The framework is evaluated using surveillance data collected between 2005 and 2024 from France, Greece, and Italy, selected for their long-running and high-quality outbreak surveillance records. Across all three countries, the LWE achieved the strongest and most stable predictive performance under a recall-focused evaluation that prioritises correctly identifying outbreak months. It outperformed or matched 14 benchmark models, with differences becoming more pronounced at longer lead times (month +3 onward), when predictions are more uncertain and outbreaks are relatively rare. Predictability varied across countries, with the highest performance in Greece, strong performance in France, and lower, more variable performance in Italy, reflecting differences in how consistently outbreaks occur and spread across regions. Overall, the results demonstrate that horizon-aware, climate-informed forecasting can reliably identify months and locations at elevated risk of outbreak occurrence up to six months in advance, supporting surveillance planning and preparedness across heterogeneous European settings. The ensemble framework provides a robust and portable strategy for outbreak prediction using routinely collected surveillance and environmental data.

title: SADRP: A structurally aware multi-modal framework for drug response prediction
abstract:
Motivation 
                     Predicting drug sensitivity across diverse cancer samples is a fundamental challenge in personalized therapy and drug discovery. This task requires comprehensive characterization of both drug and cancer cell line features. Current approaches often fail to fully capture the complex structural characteristics and interactions of drug compounds and struggle to integrate multi-omics features derived from the same sample, limiting their feature representation capacity. Consequently, there is a need for modeling frameworks that can jointly model molecular structural features and multi-modal cellular contexts in a unified manner. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     We present SADRP, a structurally aware multi-modal framework for drug response prediction, designed to model complex molecular structures and multi-omics data. For drug representation, SADRP incorporates Shortest Distance Path (SDP) encoding and edge encoding to capture both topological relationships and bond-type chemical semantics. For cell line profiling, a multi-view interactive encoder integrates gene expression and DNA methylation, capturing cross-omics synergistic complementarity. SADRP consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, while also identifying potential therapeutic candidates and biomarkers, providing mechanistic insights and supporting applications in drug discovery and personalized medicine.

title: Multiscale modeling reveals non-linear dynamics of AKT-mediated NO-ROS crosstalk in shear stress-induced endothelial phenotype
abstract: Endothelial dysfunction is a critical initiating event in atherosclerosis. The regulatory role of the AKT signaling pathway in the transition between injury and repair remains unclear. This study developed a multiscale model to elucidate how AKT signaling modulates endothelial repair under shear stress. The framework integrates hemodynamic stimuli, cellular behaviors, and nonlinear AKT/NO/ROS biochemical kinetics coupled with endothelial phenotypic transitions. Results demonstrate that endothelial dysfunction is driven by a spatial mismatch between NO production and ROS consumption rather than global deficiency. Phenotypic restoration is governed by the nonlinear interactions within the NO-ROS network. Systematic simulations identified a golden window, where Day 1 intervention and moderate AKT activation effectively restored endothelial cells and normalized redox status. Conversely, excessive activation caused supra-physiological over-suppression. These findings suggest that repair is determined by the tight coupling of redox homeostasis and immune dynamics, highlighting intervention timing and dosage as critical factors for precision vascular therapy.

title: Environmental volatility is associated with adaptive caution in visual search
abstract: Real-world distractors occur in environments whose states change at different rates. We asked whether such volatility alters initial overt oculomotor allocation, later target verification and response commitment, or both. Observers performed an additional-singleton search task with concurrent eye tracking while distractor presence followed high- or low-volatility sequences, with overall distractor prevalence held constant. Trial-pooled oculomotor capture was higher under high volatility, a pattern that appears to indicate altered filtering. Matching the same-location run position removed that difference, with no detectable difference in capture across volatility regimes at matched run position. The pooled capture effect was therefore consistent with a structural consequence of the volatility manipulation, which enriched high-volatility blocks with early-run positions where capture is intrinsically high. The volatility effect itself appeared on distractor-absent trials. Under high volatility, response times were longer, fixations more frequent, final-target dwell longer, and errors fewer, while target-acquisition latency itself was unchanged. Same-location repetition learning showed no detectable difference in slope across regimes. A hierarchical drift-diffusion model (DDM) and a complementary volatility Kalman-filter (VKF) comparison converged in showing that manual responses carried both boundary-related and drift-related structure. With distractor frequency held constant, the per-trial effect of volatility therefore emerged after the first saccade as an increase in response caution rather than in oculomotor capture. This pattern is consistent with precision-weighted adjustment to environmental uncertainty.

title: MineGraph facilitates plastid and mitochondrial graph pangenome analysis in plants
abstract: The rapid growth of genomic sequencing is driving the implementation of graph pangenomes in evolutionary studies, yet the computational costs and complex interpretations at higher taxonomic levels hinder their broad use. Here, we present an evolutionary graph pangenome (evograph) pipeline to streamline diversity analyses across species and families. Applying this framework to 709 Poales chloroplast genomes indicates that genomic diversity is driven primarily by species-specific variation. We resolve a 77.7 Kbp consensus genome and apply graph theory metrics to highlight distinct genus-level evolutionary signatures. Evographs provide a powerful, nuanced framework for resolving evolutionary complexity across high taxonomic levels.

title: BioSIFTR: functional inference from shallow shotgun sequencing using biome-specific genome catalogues benchmarked in gut microbiomes
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Shallow shotgun sequencing is an accurate microbiome profiling method, but its use for functions is limited. BioSIFTR extrapolates shallow shotgun read mapping to precalculated pangenome functions in 15 MGnify biome-specific catalogues, which span host-associated and environmental microbiomes. We benchmarked BioSIFTR on synthetic communities and on three gut microbiomes — red junglefowl, mouse, and human — using matched deep shotgun and 16S rRNA metabarcoding data, outperforming similar approaches. Further validation will require matched benchmark datasets and is a priority for future work. BioSIFTR is thus a practical method for functional inference from cost-effective shallow shotgun sequencing, currently validated in gut microbiomes.

title: HGACL-DRP: Heterogeneous graph attention dual-perturbation contrastive learning network for drug response prediction
abstract:
Background
                      The marked heterogeneity of cancer poses a substantial challenge to precision drug therapy, resulting in considerable variability in patient responses to identical treatments. Accurately predicting drug sensitivity thus represents an urgent and critical challenge in the field of pharmacology and personalized medicine. Existing methods have limitations in addressing the complexity of multi-modal biological data and heterogeneous graphs. Additionally, their heavy reliance on labeled data hinders model generalization. 
                  
                     Results
                      In this work, we propose the Heterogeneous Graph Attention Dual-Perturbation Contrastive Learning Network for Drug Response Prediction (HGACL-DRP). This framework constructs an optimized heterogeneous graph structure by integrating multi-omics features and implementing a robust neighbor filtering mechanism. HGACL-DRP innovatively introduces a Dual-Perturbation contrastive learning paradigm that incorporates both feature and structural perturbations specifically designed for drug response prediction, thereby enabling the self-supervised learning of more robust heterogeneous graph node embeddings. On two major public datasets, the Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) and the Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE), HGACL-DRP exhibits exceptional performance across multiple classification metrics, achieving a mean AUC of 95.48% on CCLE and 98.99% on GDSC. Compared to existing state-of-the-art drug response prediction algorithms, HGACL-DRP demonstrates statistically significant improvements in predictive accuracy. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      The innovative multi-view graph augmentation strategy and attention mechanism are designed to enhance personalized drug selection and facilitate novel drug discovery. HGACL-DRP is anticipated to address the challenges posed by drug response heterogeneity, thereby providing reliable support for clinical decision-making. 
                  
                     Clinical trial number
                      Not applicable.

title: Prompting alone is insufficient for large language model-based clinical variant classification
abstract:
Background
                      Accurate clinical genetic variant classification is becoming increasingly challenging as data volume and knowledge complexity increase. Large Language Models (LLMs) could potentially automate evidence retrieval and assist variant interpretation. 
                  
                     Aim
                      To systematically evaluate the capacity of general-purpose LLMs (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity) to support clinical genetic variant classification. 
                  
                     Methods
                      We analyzed 475 variants across 185 genes, with reference classifications established by expert variant scientists. Classification was performed by the four LLMs using a detailed structured prompting strategy and compared with a commercial non-LLM specialized platform. Performance was evaluated at the classification and criteria levels and stratified by various variant characteristics. 
                  
                     Results
                      Detailed prompting generally improved performance. Mean LLM classification concordance was 69.0% (70.2% precision and 68.2% recall), which was substantially lower than the 81.1% concordance (80.2% precision and 84.5% recall) achieved by the specialized commercial non-LLM platform tested. Concordance varied across variant types, with unadjusted mean concordance ranging from 87.2% for intronic variants to 56.0% for splice-region variants; adjusted associations were model-specific. At the criteria level, performance was highly criterion-specific: sensitivity exceeded 80% for BP7, PP3, PVS1, and PM2, but criterion-call precision and exact-strength agreement were substantially lower for several criteria. 
                  
                     Conclusions
                      General-purpose LLMs used through direct or structured prompting demonstrated substantial limitations in clinical genetic variant classification compared with a specialized interpretation platform. These findings indicate that the common conversational approach of asking an LLM to classify a variant, even with detailed instructions, is insufficient for autonomous clinical use.

title: ENflorA: a flexible tool for the bulk submission of next generation sequencing data to the European Nucleotide Archive
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Background 
                     With the advancement of sequencing technologies and increasing quality of assembly and annotation tools, the amount of biological sequence data produced by research grows rapidly. To keep this data accessible for potential re-analysis, it is typically stored in public online databases, such as the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA). However, the increase in data entails an increase in time needed for metadata curation and upload. We propose a tool to simplify and automatize the upload of experimental and metadata to public repositories. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     We developed ENflorA, a set of scripts by which sample, sequence read and (annotated) assembly data can be uploaded to ENA in a simple and standardized manner. Our software allows easy metadata entry via spreadsheets, is suitable for batch upload of data from different sources, and can be fully integrated in bioinformatic workflows. It is platform independent and can be run natively on High Performance Computers, integrates an lftp upload option for big files and a test upload option. 
                   
                   
                     Conclusions 
                     By easing the ENA submission process, ENflorA contributes to making high-throughput sequencing data findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable.

title: A new explainable AI pipeline for cancer cell segmentation and classification for microscopy images
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Background 
                     The development of novel therapeutic approaches to cancers requires significant time and labour, especially for uncommon cancers (e.g. of mesenchymal origin). In addition, these rare cancers typically receive less research attention but still need sufficient analysis. For example, a trustworthy analysis of tissue samples to identify cancer progression and cell response to candidate therapies is a task to develop certain treatments and drugs. Thus, this research work develops a new explainable Deep Learning pipeline for accurate, high-throughput and autonomous recognition of metastasising cells from large-scale fluorescence microscopy images, which can be used to evaluate cell response with low cost and high trustworthiness, and facilitate the therapeutic approaches development. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     The pipeline includes pre-trained and domain-generalised segmentation to identify single cells, training the latest self-supervised transformers: DINO-based models to provide normal or metastasising classification, and leveraging Explainable AI methods to produce biologically meaningful model explanations towards the trustworthiness of model predictions; this is crucial in future clinical applications. Compared to supervised learning-based models, DINO achieves the best predictability (over 97% F1-weighted score) when only training the classifier, and the most efficient downstream adaptation. Besides, all DINO-based models can classify successfully when finetuning the entire model (DINOv3 achieves the highest F1-weighted score with 98.35%). We have also used an additional cross-magnification test and a self- / weakly-supervised model comparison to discuss the generalisation ability and superiority of DINO-based models. Biologically accurate model explanations are produced via heatmaps and analysed through quantitative metrics and qualitative evaluation; the important cell regions in the model decision-making process align well with biological consensus. We also demonstrate that biologically meaningful cytoskeletal features can be detected and exploited by the developed pipeline for cancer cell classification, which facilitates the development of cytoskeleton-based diagnosis. 
                   
                   
                     Conclusion 
                     We develop a precise, efficient, and trustworthy pipeline that can facilitate the development of effective and bespoke cancer treatments via AI-assisted testing of the response of cancer cells to various treatments and drugs.

title: Elucidating and exploring specialised plant metabolism through a pangenomic and pantranscriptomic lens
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   Specialised metabolism is an important factor in how plants cope with biotic and, to a lesser extent, abiotic stress. Current approaches to identify and study the genes involved in such metabolic pathways mainly leverage genomic and transcriptomic datasets of plants, in order to improve our understanding of plant resilience. Even though modern sequencing techniques have provided access to high‐quality reference genome or transcriptome datasets, sequencing costs have for a long time forced a restriction to a selected reference accession. However, individual plants within a population often exhibit substantial differences in metabolic profiles, sometimes even leading to completely different chemotypes. This generated an urgent need to transition from single‐reference accessions to the wider diversity of plant populations or even beyond the species level. Thanks to decreasing costs and improved reliability of sequencing techniques, this is now possible through pangenomic or pantranscriptomic approaches. In this review, we provide an introduction into the current state of the fields of pangenomics and pantranscriptomics and highlight recent examples on how these approaches have been used to elucidate and investigate specialised metabolic pathways in plants. We also provide an overview of database resources that might be useful for researchers in the field. Lastly, we present a critical summary and discussion of limitations and trends that are important for future innovations. With these developments in mind, we anticipate that pangenomics and pantranscriptomics will play a crucial role in exploring and harnessing the diversity of plant specialised metabolism beyond single individuals.

title: Issue Information
Hierarchical Regulatory Module AcERF1–AcHAT5–AcERF10 Modulates Ethylene‐Dependent Starch Degradation in Postharvest Kiwifruit
authors:
Yupei Zhang, 
Jinyin Chen, 
Huaxuan Hu, 
Congcong Yang, 
Kangyuan Xie, 
Caining Yang, 
Wenbin Kai, 
Chuying Chen, 
Yingying Yang, 
Jiaoke Zeng, 
Ming Chen, 
Zengyu Gan
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   
                    The transcriptional regulatory network underlying ethylene‐governed starch‐to‐sugar conversion remains poorly understood. We elucidated the hierarchical regulatory cascade linking ethylene signalling to starch degradation in postharvest kiwifruit. Ethylene treatment accelerated fruit softening, starch degradation, and soluble sugar accumulation, whereas 1‐methylcyclopropene treatment produced opposite effects in kiwifruit. Weighted gene co‐expression network analysis identified 3 β‐amylase genes (
                     AcBAM3.1/3.3/3.5 
                    ) and 16 transcription factors (TFs) as highly correlated with starch‐to‐sugar conversion. AcERF10 was isolated as a direct transcriptional activator of
                     AcBAM3.1/3.3/3.5 
                    and the ethylene biosynthetic gene
                     AcACO1 
                    .
                     AcERF10 
                    overexpression promoted starch degradation and sugar accumulation; silencing this gene resulted in opposite phenotypes.
                     AcERF10 
                    was directly activated by AcERF1 and AcHAT5—TFs that are induced by ethylene. AcERF1 bound to and activated the promoter of
                     AcHAT5 
                    , while AcHAT5 bound to the
                     AcERF10 
                    promoter and interacted with AcERF10 to synergistically activate expression of
                     AcBAMs 
                    and
                     AcACO1 
                    , identifying a regulatory cascade of AcERF1‐AcHAT5‐AcERF10. Overexpression of either
                     AcERF1 
                    or
                     AcHAT5 
                    promoted downstream gene expression, accelerated starch degradation, and enhanced sugar accumulation, whereas silencing of either gene suppressed these processes. This study uncovers an ethylene‐triggered, multi‐layer transcriptional regulatory network that governs starch‐to‐sugar conversion during postharvest kiwifruit ripening, providing new mechanistic insights into ethylene‐regulated fruit quality development during postharvest storage.

title:
The Cytosolic Iron–Sulfur Cluster Assembly Targeting Complex Is Hijacked by
                     Magnaporthe 
                    Effector
                     AvrPi9 
                    to Suppress Rice Resistance
authors:
Huanbin Shi, 
Zhiquan Liu, 
Ying Zhang, 
Runjing Li, 
Zhizhen Fu, 
Ya Chen, 
Hui Wen, 
Liang Cai, 
Zhengting Chen, 
Jiehua Qiu, 
Yanjun Kou
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   
                    The cytosolic iron–sulfur (Fe‐S) cluster assembly (CIA) targeting complex mediates the maturation of cytosolic and nuclear Fe‐S proteins and governs core eukaryotic cellular processes. However, whether this complex contributes to plant disease resistance remains unclear. Here, we show that the
                     Magnaporthe oryzae 
                    avirulence effector AvrPi9 targets the host CIA targeting complex to suppress rice blast resistance. AvrPi9 physically interacts with and stabilizes OsAE7, a core subunit of the CIA targeting complex. Using biochemical and genetic approaches, we demonstrate that OsAE7 facilitates Fe‐S protein maturation, including the Fe‐S protein aconitase OsACO1, and negatively regulates blast resistance in cooperation with another CIA targeting complex subunit, OsCIA1, and the carrier protein OsNAR1 in rice. Furthermore, ectopic expression of
                     AvrPi9 
                    enhances the activity of the CIA complex and the maturation of OsACO1. Knockout of
                     OsACO1 
                    elevates ferrous iron levels, triggers a reactive oxygen species (ROS) burst, and activates pathogenesis‐related gene transcription, thereby strengthening rice resistance to blast. Our findings reveal a critical role of the CIA targeting complex in plant disease resistance and uncover a novel virulence strategy whereby AvrPi9 hijacks the host CIA pathway to dampen basal resistance and promote infection.

title:
From isotopologues to isotopomers: advances in mass spectrometry‐based positional
                     
                       13 
                      C
                     
                    analysis in plants
authors:
Valéria F. Lima, 
Jônatas G.S.B. Oliveira, 
Luisa Wittemeier, 
Joachim Kopka, 
Danilo M. Daloso
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                    Carbon fluxes throughout metabolic networks can be investigated experimentally through
                     13 
                    C‐isotope labelling experiments (
                     13 
                    C‐ILE) and
                     13 
                    C‐metabolic flux analysis (
                     13 
                    C‐MFA).
                     13 
                    C‐ILE involves the application of isotopically labelled substrates to a biological system to detect label distribution throughout the metabolic network, while
                     13 
                    C‐MFA is a computational approach that quantitatively estimates fluxes by fitting isotope‐labelling data to metabolic network models.
                     13 
                    C‐MFA can encompass more metabolic reactions and provide subcellular flux estimates that remain difficult to validate directly using current
                     13 
                    C‐ILE approaches. Overcoming major bottlenecks of
                     13 
                    C‐ILE is thus needed to improve and validate
                     13 
                    C‐MFA. Mass spectrometry (MS)‐based
                     13 
                    C‐ILE has been carried out mostly at isotopologue rather than isotopomer level. Isotopologues differ in their isotopic composition, while isotopomers have the same isotopic composition but at different positions within the molecule. Thus,
                     13 
                    C‐isotopomer approaches discriminate which atoms of a metabolite have received
                     13 
                    C, enabling better comprehension of the regulation of metabolic pathways. Here, we highlight the major challenges to improve MS‐based positional
                     13 
                    C analysis and discuss the advantages of this approach over MS‐based methods with low or no carbon‐positional resolution. We further demonstrate how positional
                     13 
                    C analysis has been used to estimate enzyme activity
                     in vivo 
                    and to study plant metabolism.

title:
Duplication and functional divergence of
                     
                       TCP4 
                     
                    genes in turnip
authors:
Cheng Li, 
Caspar C. C. Chater, 
Hefan Li, 
Jiaying Gao, 
Yuanwen Duan, 
Yongping Yang, 
Xudong Sun
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         
                          Gene duplication is widely recognized as a significant catalyst for plant adaptive evolution. The retained duplicated genes usually undergo functional divergence to govern plant growth and stress resistance. Turnip (
                           Brassica rapa 
                          var.
                           rapa 
                          ) shows a broad capacity for environmental adaptation. Here, we investigate how duplicated
                           TCP4 
                          genes modulate turnip growth and development.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          We identify three
                           TCP4 
                          paralogs,
                           BrrTCP4 
                          ,
                           BrrTCP4a 
                          and
                           BrrTCP4b 
                          in turnip, characterize their expression patterns and analyze sequence variation in their conserved domains. We further model their three‐dimensional structures and compare their protein–protein interactions and downstream regulatory networks.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          We show that
                           BrrTCP4 
                          ,
                           BrrTCP4a 
                          and
                           BrrTCP4b 
                          exhibit distinct expression profiles. A single mutation within the conserved TCP domain leads to differences in protein–protein interactions among BrrTCP4, BrrTCP4a and BrrTCP4b. Combined with DAP‐Seq, ChIP‐qPCR and luciferase assays, our results demonstrate that BrrTCP4 and BrrTCP4a activate
                           BrrCOs 
                          and
                           BrrFTs 
                          to regulate turnip flowering, while BrrTCP4b preferentially participates in the trehalose synthesis pathway by targeting
                           TPP 
                          and
                           TPS 
                          genes.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          Our research findings indicate the functional divergence of
                           BrrTCP4 
                          ,
                           BrrTCP4a 
                          and
                           BrrTCP4b 
                          to balance growth and stress responses in turnip, thereby advancing our understanding of how gene duplication drives functional specialization and contributes to plant evolutionary adaptation.

title: Leaf nutrient resorption across contrasting soil parent materials: it is not just about efficiency
authors:
Sushmita Dhakal, 
Kazi R. Mehnaz, 
Kristine Y. Crous, 
Catriona A. Macdonald, 
Ian J. Wright, 
David S. Ellsworth
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         In theory, nutrient resorption from leaves should be higher in sites with lower soil nutrients, increasing the retention and reuse of nutrients that are limited in supply. However, evidence for this relationship has remained inconsistent for decades, particularly where the percent of nutrient resorbed is concerned. Furthermore, plant resorption responses to soil phosphorus (P) concentration remain poorly understood. 
                       
                       
                         Leaf nitrogen (N) and P concentrations and resorption percentages (efficiencies) were measured for 68 Australian plant species sampled across four nutrient‐rich vs nutrient‐poor site‐pairs representing contrasting soil parent materials. 
                       
                       
                         
                          N and P concentrations in senesced leaves were significantly lower on nutrient‐poor than on nutrient‐richer sites, enabling greater internal conservation of these nutrients on nutrient‐poor sites. Resorption efficiencies averaged 45% for N and 69% for P and did not differ between contrasting soils. Though not sensitive to site, P resorption efficiency (P
                           RE 
                          ) was positively related to the proportion of labile P in leaves (
                           R 
                           2 
                           = 0.54).
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          We demonstrated for the first time that senesced leaf P concentrations and the corresponding P
                           RE 
                          are distinctly shaped by plant adaptation to soil nutrient scarcity, and internal labile P pools, respectively. The high P
                           RE 
                          of Australian species informs an upper bound for this process in global vegetation models.

title:
Elevated
                     
                      CO
                       2 
                     
                    drives nonlinear trait responses and reshapes growth‐virulence trade‐offs in a plant pathogen
authors:
Li‐Na Yang, 
Hao Liu, 
Meng Xie, 
Zhiguo Fang, 
Yangmei Wang, 
Jiasui Zhan
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         
                          Atmospheric CO
                           2 
                          is rising at unprecedented rates. While its physiological effects on plants are well‐documented, the direct evolutionary impact on plant pathogens remains unknown. We investigated how CO
                           2 
                          interacts with other abiotic factors to shape the evolutionary potential of pathogens.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          We combined controlled CO
                           2 
                          gradient experiments with quantitative genetics to assess the interactive effects of CO
                           2 
                          , temperature and geography on
                           Phytophthora infestans 
                          . We measured intrinsic growth rate and aggressiveness, the two key pathogen traits, across seven geographically distinct populations and partitioned their phenotypic variance into heritability and plasticity components.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          Both intrinsic growth rate and aggressiveness showed a shared quadratic response to CO
                           2 
                          , peaking
                           c. 
                          2000 ppm before declining. Elevated CO
                           2 
                          reduced phenotypic variance in aggressiveness under extreme concentrations. CO
                           2 
                          also reconfigured the life‐history correlation between growth and aggressiveness, shifting it from positive under ambient CO
                           2 
                          to negative near the optimum. Heritability exceeded plasticity for aggressiveness in most populations, indicating that virulence responds primarily through selection. Trait responses were modulated by local climate and geography, with the strongest CO
                           2 
                          ‐driven increases occurring under thermal and geographic extremes.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          Our results demonstrate that rising CO
                           2 
                          acts as a direct agent of selection, nonlinearly reshaping pathogen phenotypic architecture and life‐history strategies in a geographically heterogeneous manner.

title:
An
                     AGC 
                    kinase cascade regulates
                     ROP 
                    signaling for the correct timing of pollen germination
authors:
Tong Zhao, 
Andrea Lepper, 
Franziska Anzenberger, 
Sarah Brajkovic, 
Kim König, 
Hiromasa Shikata, 
Yao Xiao, 
Bernhard Küster, 
Claus Schwechheimer, 
Remko Offringa, 
Philipp Denninger
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         In flowering plants, the timing of pollen germination is crucial for successful fertilization and an important trait for seed and fruit crops. Environmental factors tightly regulate pollen germination, with germination‐suppressing conditions on the pollen‐producing anther and germination‐promoting conditions on the receiving stigma. 
                       
                       
                         
                          Using genetic, biochemical, and cell biological methods, we show that this environmental sensitivity of pollen germination in
                           Arabidopsis thaliana 
                          is regulated by a 3‐PHOSPHOINOSITIDE‐DEPENDENT KINASE 1 (PDK1)‐AGC1.5/AGC1.7 kinase cascade.
                         
                       
                       
                         We show that PDK1 hyperphosphorylates downstream AGC1.5/7 kinases to enhance their activity. Pollen‐specific phosphoproteomics identified multiple proteins involved in pollen growth whose phosphorylation is controlled by AGC1.5/7. Two germination‐promoting RHO OF PLANTS GUANINE NUCLEOTIDE EXCHANGE FACTORS (ROPGEFs) are phosphorylated by AGC1.5/7 at a novel site, reducing ROPGEF plasma membrane polarization. Loss of PDK1‐AGC kinase signaling resulted in precocious pollen germination on the anther, which was rescued by high AGC1.5 kinase activity. Conversely, AGC1.5/7 overexpression or a phosphomimic ROPGEF version inhibited precocious pollen germination. Distinct subcellular localization of PDK1 and AGC1 kinases upon pollen germination is likely to alleviate their inhibitory effect. 
                       
                       
                         Our data indicate that the correct timing of pollen germination requires the fine‐tuned activity of a PDK1‐AGC1 kinase cascade inhibiting ROPGEFs on the anther, preventing precocious pollen germination.

title:
MYB156 
                    promotes root sucker formation by repressing
                     
                       IDD14 
                     
                    and
                     
                       CKX1 
                     
                    to elevate cytokinin levels in
                     Populus
authors:
Hongying Pang, 
Biying Li, 
Yajuan Chen, 
Liping Ding, 
Wanwan Lyu, 
Xiaoqin Wang, 
Hongzhi Wang, 
Jianhua Wei, 
Lin Zheng
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         Root suckers enable clonal propagation of rooting‐recalcitrant poplars, conferring rejuvenated traits such as enhanced survival and accelerated growth. Despite widespread clonal propagation and ecological restoration, the essential genes controlling sucker development remain unidentified. 
                       
                       
                         
                          MYB156 is a positive regulator of root sucker formation in white poplar (
                           Populus davidiana 
                          ×
                           P. bolleana 
                          ).
                           MYB156 
                          is predominantly expressed in proliferation‐competent root cells, including vascular cambium and phellogen. Gain‐ and loss‐of‐function analyses demonstrated that
                           MYB156 
                          overexpression enhanced root suckering and secondary growth, whereas
                           myb156 
                          mutants were severely compromised in both. Meanwhile, cytokinin levels increased two‐ to fivefold in roots with
                           MYB156 
                          overexpression but were significantly reduced in
                           myb156 
                          mutant roots.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          MYB156 directly represses
                           IDD14 
                          and
                           CKX1 
                          , reducing cytokinin catabolism and alleviating
                           IDD14 
                          ‐mediated suppression of cytokinin accumulation;
                           IDD14 
                          RNAi lines similarly showed elevated cytokinin and enhanced suckering.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          Cytokinin response elements in the
                           MYB156 
                          promoter and MYB156 autoactivation establish a cytokinin‐MYB156 positive feedback loop amplifying cytokinin signaling in meristematic zones. Live imaging with the cytokinin response reporter
                           TCSn 
                          :
                           RFP 
                          demonstrated that suckering in
                           MYB156 
                          ‐overexpressing plants shifted from the phellogen to the vascular cambium. These findings establish a MYB156‐
                           CKX1 
                          /
                           IDD14 
                          ‐cytokinin module that creates a permissive context for suckering, providing a transcriptional blueprint for clonal propagation.

title:
B‐
                     BOX 
                     DOMAIN PROTEIN 
                    19 shapes tea quality by modulating the ratio of catechins and theanine and confers cold tolerance in tea plants
authors:
Lianghui Yi, 
Jie Yu, 
Fangdong Li, 
Qingji Hou, 
Didi Wu, 
Yanrui Zhang, 
Zhaoliang Zhang, 
Chuankui Song, 
Wei Tong, 
Enhua Xia
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         
                          Early spring cold spells threaten tea plant (
                           Camellia sinensis 
                          ) yield and disrupt the catechins‐to‐theanine ratio that determines the desirable balance of umami and astringency taste of tea. However, the molecular mechanism coordinating cold tolerance with this key quality trait remains unclear.
                         
                       
                       
                         Here, we identified a light‐responsive B‐BOX DOMAIN PROTEIN CsBBX19 as a core regulator simultaneously shaping tea quality and cold tolerance. 
                       
                       
                         
                          Results demonstrated that silencing
                           CsBBX19 
                          relieves the transcriptional repression of theanine‐biosynthetic genes (
                           CsTSI 
                          and
                           CsAlaDC 
                          ) to elevate theanine levels, yet weakens the activation of catechins‐biosynthetic genes (
                           CsANS1 
                          ,
                           CsANR1 
                          ,
                           CsLAR1 
                          , and
                           CsSCPL1 
                          /2/5) to reduce catechins content. The
                           CsBBX19 
                          ‐modulated theanine accumulation also enhanced the cold tolerance of tea plants by suppressing cell‐wall‐loosening EXPANSIN (
                           CsEXPA10/20/21 
                          ) and activating the
                           CsCBF3 
                          ‐mediated cold response pathway. Furthermore, the expression of
                           CsBBX19 
                          significantly reduced by light via a feedback loop involving CsHY5, which directly binds to the promoter of
                           CsBBX19 
                          to repress its transcription, while CsBBX19 conversely interacts with CsHY5 to reinforce its autoactivation, thereby fine‐tuning the catechins‐to‐theanine ratio and cold resilience in tea plants.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          Our findings underscore the central roles of
                           CsBBX19 
                          in light‐mediated cold response and tea quality formation, providing valuable targets for synchronously improving cold resilience and quality in tea plants.

title: Refining indel- and structural variant-trait associations with LAVrefiner
abstract:
Structural variants (SVs) are major sources of human genetic diversity. Despite advances in SV discovery, most single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-centric frameworks overlook sequence-level information and encode overlapping variants as independent features, potentially reducing power in association studies, biasing heritability estimation, and limiting prediction accuracy. Here, we present LAVrefiner, a scalable, sequence-aware method that decomposes overlapping sequence-resolved SVs and indels into nonoverlapping refined sequence components and generates genotype matrices compatible with standard SNP-based analyses. In tandem repeat (TR) regions, LAVrefiner further supports motif-aware allele comparison and repeat copy-number estimation. When applied to variants from the 1000 Genomes Project, LAVrefiner identifies 224,708 refined variants. Simulations show that LAVrefiner is fast and memory-efficient while maintaining robust genotype representations under TR-associated sequencing noise. In gene expression analyses, models combining LAVrefiner-derived copy-number estimates with refined variants yield the highest heritability estimates and prediction accuracy in short tandem repeat (STR) and variable number tandem repeat (VNTR) regions, outperforming models based on the original SV/indel representation and existing TR copy-number tools.
                     Cis 
                    -expression quantitative trait locus (
                     cis 
                    -eQTL) mapping further shows that refined variants can localize regulatory signals to specific sequence components, including an independent VNTR-derived signal at the TFRC locus. Together, LAVrefiner provides an efficient, context-aware strategy for integrating sequence-resolved SVs and indels into existing genetic analysis frameworks.

title: The Vizitig pangenome and pantranscriptome explorer
abstract: Vizitig is the first platform for real-time exploration and querying of DNA and RNA sequence de Bruijn graphs across many samples, unifying visualization, metadata, and flexible search. It constructs compacted colored de Bruijn graphs from raw sequencing reads and reference sequences, then provides an interactive web interface for graph exploration. It integrates raw and reference-based data, handles complex variation, and provides a human-readable feature-based (also referred to as metadata) query language with scalable graph loading. Its domain-specific query language supports composable searches combining sequences of arbitrary size, genomic features such as gene or exon identifiers, and experimental factors such as sample identifier or abundance thresholds. On-demand subgraph loading retrieves only regions of interest, enabling interactive exploration of large datasets in the graphical user interface without loading the entire graph into memory. We demonstrate Vizitig's capabilities through case studies in pantranscriptomics and pangenomics. In pantranscriptomics, we recover fusion transcript breakpoints on long and short reads. In pangenomics, we explore sequence variations across yeast, rice, nematode, and human pangenomes. Vizitig scales from small virus genomes to human-scale pangenomes (our largest experiments comprises up to 20 assembled human haplotypes, on a laptop). Vizitig enables fast, reproducible analysis in both pangenomics and pantranscriptomics while providing a deployable and user-friendly working environment.

title: Base composition reflects RNA polymerase II displacement
abstract: RNA Polymerase II (Pol II) transcribes all protein-coding and many nonprotein-coding genes in the genome. Pol II transcription termination is crucial for RNA maturation and, when disrupted, can lead to altered RNA processing and RNA export. Termination involves two intertwined processes: RNA cleavage and Pol II release from the DNA (displacement). Despite its importance, the exact mechanisms underlying Pol II displacement from the DNA remain poorly understood. Moreover, under certain cellular stress conditions, there is a partial failure of cleavage, leading to a shift of the position of displacement further downstream, a phenomenon known as readthrough transcription. We present a systematic analysis of Pol II termination across cell types and species and provide novel insights into the mechanism of displacement. Using a probabilistic mixture model to quantify Pol II dynamics across entire gene bodies from nascent RNA sequencing data, we find that genes fall into two classes defined by conserved base composition patterns near the displacement site. Both classes share a T-rich region upstream of displacement, and one class additionally carries a GC-rich region surrounding displacement. We find that GC-rich predisplacement regions have more accessible chromatin and higher levels of phospho-threonine 4 on the CTD of Pol II. Additionally, we find that displacement at genes with only the upstream T-rich pattern are more likely to be affected by perturbations that alter displacement, including heat shock, viral infection, kinase inhibition, and arsenic treatment. Thus, our work identifies two types of Pol II displacement regions, which are differentially affected by perturbations of cellular homeostasis.

title: Inter-individual gene expression variability implies stable regulation of brain-biased genes across organs in three ray-finned fishes
abstract: Phenotypic variation among individuals provides the raw material for evolution, and gene expression is a key mediator between genetic and phenotypic variation. As for phenotypes, the range of gene expression is limited and biased by evolutionary and developmental constraints. Observed expression variability due to biomolecular stochasticity and cell-to-cell heterogeneity has been well-studied in isogenic populations of unicellular organisms. However, for multicellular organisms with a diversity of cells and tissues sharing the same genetic background, the interplay between expression variability, gene and organ function, and gene regulation remains an open question. Here, we use highly multiplexed 3'-end bulk RNA sequencing to generate transcriptome profiles spanning at least nine organs in outbred individuals of three ray-finned fish species: zebrafish, Northern pike, and spotted gar. Per organ, we quantify individual-to-individual gene expression variability independent of mean expression level. Lowly variable genes are enriched in cellular housekeeping functions whereas highly variable genes are enriched in stimulus-response functions. Furthermore, highly variable genes evolve under weaker purifying selection at the protein-coding sequence, indicating that intra-species expression variability predicts inter-species protein sequence divergence. Genes that are broadly expressed across organs are both highly expressed and lowly variable, whereas organ-biased genes are typically highly variable within their top organ. Among organ-biased genes, patterns of expression variance are dependent on the top organ. Specifically, brain- and gonads-biased genes have lowly variable expression across different organs, suggesting stabilizing selection. These patterns suggest that gene regulatory mechanisms evolve under organ-specific selective pressures.

title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom (Re) and the degree of non-equilibrium (SK/ε). By applying Weaver’s well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.

title: Integrated soft robot capable of surviving extreme underwater shock loads
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Soft robots have been developed for underwater tasks owing to their compliant, damage-tolerant bodies, which foster an expectation that soft bodies are inherently robust in aquatic environments. However, most reported systems operate under moderate or quasi-static conditions, and overlook a critical vulnerability—when cavity-rich soft structures are subjected to underwater shocks, the embedded cavities collapse violently, triggering a phenomenon we term ‘soft-matter implosion’. This process generates internal pressures several times higher than the incident pressure and can severely damage onboard electronics. Using a simplified cavity-containing structure, we combine underwater impact experiments and finite element simulations to reveal the mechanism of soft-matter implosion and quantify the peak pressure under different parameters. These results inform a function-structure co-design framework that suppresses implosion while preserving overall flexibility. Guided by this framework, we built a rigid-casing-free, fully integrated manta‑ray‑inspired soft robot that survives single impacts up to 49.8 MPa and sequential impacts at 31.5 MPa, and resumes flapping locomotion after impact. This work establishes an impact‑resistant soft robot platform and provides a generalizable design strategy for durable, flexible machines operating in challenging underwater environments.

title:
Recent geographic dispersal and environmental adaptation of
                     indica 
                    rice
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Rice (Oryza sativa), one of the key domesticated cereal crops, is comprised of several subspecies or variety groups. A major variety group, O. sativa var. indica was domesticated in the Indian subcontinent ∼4500 years ago via introgression of domestication alleles from var. japonica and today represents the predominant rice that is grown worldwide, particularly in tropical and subtropical regions in Asia. Using genome data from 957 indica landraces, including 194 newly re-sequenced cultivars and 38 herbarium specimens collected over the last 167 years, we reconstruct how indica rice moved from the Indian subcontinent to other parts of Asia. Unlike japonica rice, indica rice seems to have dispersed relatively recently (within the last 2,000 years) to China, mainland and island Southeast (SE) Asia. Interestingly, we find that the island SE Asia indica rice landraces show gene flow with island SE Asian japonica landraces. We also find significant gene-environment associations of indica rice with local climatic and edaphic variables that may be associated with local adaptation, and possible cultural selection for grain quality traits, associated with indica dispersal.

title: Unilateral cross-feeding constrains adaptive evolution, even in the producer without direct fitness effects
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Cross-feeding interactions are pervasive in microbial communities and profoundly shape community structure, stability, and function. While previous studies have explored how cross-feeding affects evolvability, this work has predominantly focused on bidirectional mutualistic interactions in engineered auxotrophic systems where both partners reciprocally exchange essential metabolites. However, most metabolic interactions in natural microbial communities are unidirectional, with organisms feeding on the metabolic waste products of other species. Our study addresses this gap by examining how a unidirectional cross-feeding interaction affects the evolutionary dynamics of both the producer (Acinetobacter johnsonii) and consumer (Pseudomonas putida) over 800 generations of experimental evolution. We found that co-culture constrained adaptive evolution in both species. Co-cultures exhibited lower πN/πS ratios (0.75 for P. putida; 1.04 for A. johnsonii) than monocultures (1.44 and 2.02, respectively), indicating stronger purifying selection against nonsynonymous mutations in the community context. Lineage tracking through whole genome sequencing of populations and clones revealed greater lineage diversity and complexity in monocultures, with more mutations showing significant parallelism across replicate populations. Additionally, P. putida evolved increased dependence on its partner; co-culture-evolved P. putida grew significantly worse than its ancestor when A. johnsonii was removed. These findings indicate that ecological interactions can reshape fitness landscapes and constrain adaptive evolution even when fitness benefits are unidirectional, with implications for understanding microbial community stability and predicting evolutionary dynamics in complex communities.

title:
Early holobiont-level divergence and adaptation across seafloor geochemical contrasts in the deep-sea squat lobster
                     Shinkaia crosnieri
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Deep-sea hydrothermal vents and methane seeps host unique animal communities sustained by chemosynthetic symbioses, yet how biological diversification proceeds across these geochemically distinct and geographically fragmented habitats remains poorly understood. Previous studies have largely focused on either host genomic adaptation or symbiont diversity as drivers of isolation, leaving unresolved how environmental geochemistry and host-microbe associations jointly shape evolutionary trajectories in chemosynthetic ecosystems. Here, we addressed this gap by combining chromosome-level host genomics, population resequencing, and episymbiont metagenomics in the deep-sea chemosynthetic lobster Shinkaia crosnieri, a dominant species inhabiting both hydrothermal vents and methane seeps. Genomic innovations—including sensory trade-offs (vision loss versus chemosensory expansion), metabolic compensation for pigment loss, and positive selection on respiratory protein—underpin deep-sea colonization of S. crosnieri. Populations from the Okinawa Trough vent and the South China Sea seep exhibit pronounced genetic divergence, potentially driven by Pleistocene vicariance and reinforced by divergent selection across sulfur-enriched (vent) versus sulfur-depleted, methane-dominated (seep) environments. This selection target host genes involved in chemoreception and immunity, with coordinated signatures in both sequence evolution and structural variation. Crucially, holobiont-level adaptation is amplified by habitat-specific recruitment of episymbionts: sulfur-oxidizing Campylobacterales/Thiotrichales dominate vent-associated lobsters, while methanotrophic Methylococcales prevail at seep counterparts. These symbionts partition energy niches metabolically, with seep-associated communities enhancing biosynthesis of key cofactors (e.g., coenzyme Q, tetrahydrofolate). Host transporters for these nutrients are concurrently upregulated, demonstrating functional synergy. Our findings establish that diversification in extreme environments operates holobiont-wide, where geochemical gradients synergistically shape host genomic plasticity and symbiont metabolic specialization to drive early-stage divergence.

title: Correction for Liu et al., A spinoreticular pathway mediates nocifensive responses to noxious mechanical stimuli
abstract: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 43, October 2026.

title: Harry L. Swinney: Nonlinear science and chaos pioneer
authors: Daniel LathropMichael SchatzKatepalli Sreenivasanahttps://ror.org/047s2c258Department of Physics, University of Maryland, College Park, MD 20742bhttps://ror.org/01zkghx44Department of Physics, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA 30332chttps://ror.org/0190ak572Department of Physics, Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Tandon School of Engineering, New York University, New York, NY 10012
abstract: Harry Leonard Swinney passed away peacefully at his home in Austin, Texas, on July 13, 2026, at the age of 87. Harry was an exceptional experimental physicist, well-known for elegant studies of instabilities, nonlinear dynamics, chaos and pattern formation in a wide variety of fluid, chemical, and granular systems, work whose influence propagated into numerous scientific and engineering disciplines well beyond the particular problems that prompted it. The late Russell Donnelly of the University of Oregon used to say, “Harry is a prince”; Russ meant it, in the spirit of the tenth-century Persian poet Ferdowsi, as a compliment affirming the nobility, dignity, integrity, and grace with which Harry pursued his science and treated everyone he worked alongside.
