abstract: Editing  TaBADH1  alone or  TaBADH1  and  TaBADH2  via CRISPR/Cas9 produced fragrant wheat with up to 11.24-fold higher 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline than the wild type without yield penalty, revealing asymmetric functional redundancy between these two genes and providing elite germplasm for wheat quality improvement

title:
The VvmiPEP397-VvmiR397-
                     VvLAC14 
                    module regulates salt tolerance in grapevine
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Soil salinization poses a significant constraint to the sustainable development of the grape industry. Although miR397 is known to be involved in plant stress responses, its regulatory mechanism in grapevine salt tolerance remains unclear. In this study, we systematically deciphered the role of the VvmiPEP397-VvmiR397-VvLAC14 module in grapevine salt stress responses using transgenic approaches, transcriptome sequencing, and molecular biology techniques. Our results show that salt stress significantly induces VvMIR397 expression. We identified a functional small peptide, VvmiPEP397, from its primary transcript. Exogenous application of this peptide enhanced VvMIR397 expression and improved salt tolerance in grapevine calli and plants. Overexpression of VvmiR397 significantly enhanced salt tolerance in both grapevine and Arabidopsis, whereas silencing its expression increased sensitivity. Transcriptome analysis further identified the laccase gene VvLAC14 as a direct target of VvmiR397. VvmiR397 negatively regulates VvLAC14 expression through transcript cleavage, reducing lignin accumulation. Conversely, VvLAC14 overexpression increased lignin content and compromised salt tolerance, whereas knockdown of VvLAC14 had opposite effects. This study establishes, for the first time in grapevine, a complete regulatory pathway comprising a small peptide, a miRNA, and a target gene—VvmiPEP397-VvmiR397-VvLAC14—revealing a novel mechanism by which this module influences salt tolerance through the regulation of lignin metabolism. Our findings provide new targets and a theoretical foundation for salt-tolerant grapevine breeding.

title: ABA and Stomatal Biology: From Transcriptional and Biosynthesis to Multicellular Coordination Across Cell Types
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Abscisic acid (ABA) was first identified in plants over six decades ago and is now recognized as one of the central phytohormones in plants, regulating growth, development, and physiological adaptation to environmental changes. In this Centennial Update, we use two influential ABA-related articles published in Plant Physiology in the early 2000s and discuss complementary advances in stress-responsive transcription and ABA biosynthetic regulation. We extend the Update from ABA-relevant gene discovery to recent advances in multicellular coordination of stomatal control. Growing evidence supports the view that ABA-regulated stomatal movement and gas exchange are coordinated across multiple cell types, including guard cells, mesophyll cells, bundle sheath cells, and vascular tissues in roots and leaves. We also highlight emerging tools to dissect this ABA-mediated multicellular network by using emerging technologies in single-cell and spatial omics, plant optogenetics, and artificial intelligence (AI). These advances will shape ABA research from single cell models toward multicellular collaborative networks for understanding plant-environment interactions. Together, this article links the history of ABA research with emerging single-cell resolution datasets and AI-assisted computational approaches, proposing a framework for moving ABA biology from well-established guard-cell signaling models toward a broader understanding of multicellular ABA coordination.

title:
Transcription Factor TabZIP12 Orchestrates the ABA Signaling Pathway to Regulate Drought Tolerance in Wheat (
                     Triticum aestivum 
                    L.)
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Drought-induced osmotic stress severely compromises crop yield productivity and threatens global food security. This study reports TabZIP12, a wheat bZIP transcription factor, in regulating osmotic stress tolerance. Under drought and abscisic acid (ABA) treatment, TabZIP12 expression was significantly upregulated with a dose- and time-dependent manner. Y-2H, BiFC, Co-IP, and In vitro pull-down assays confirmed a physical interaction between TabZIP12 and the kinase TaSnRK2.6. This kinase further interacted with the phosphatase TaPP2C50, which in turn interacted with the ABA receptor TaPYL1. These interactions suggest the TabZIP12-involved constitution of a synergistic signaling module (TaPYL1–TaPP2C50–TaSnRK2.6–TabZIP12). Transgene analyses revealed the essential functions of the signaling module members. Of which, TaPYL1, TaSnRK2.6, and TabZIP12 positively while TaPP2C50 negatively regulated drought tolerance, due to their roles in modulating key physiological processes associated with stomatal movement, osmolyte biosynthesis, root morphology, ABA biosynthesis, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging. TabZIP12 possessed an ability in binding with the promoters of critical stress-responsive genes, namely SLAC1 gene TaSLAC1-4, P5CS gene TaP5CS1, PIN-FORMed gene TaPIN3, NCED gene TaNCED3, and APX gene TaAPX6 and activated their activation. Transgenic validation confirmed these genes in positively modulating drought adaptation. Notably, in a wheat variety panel sharing contrasting drought response, the transcripts of TabZIP12 and its target genes correlated significantly with plant dry matter and yield under drought conditions. Haplotype analysis identified TabZIP12-Hap1 as a favorable allele associated with enhanced drought tolerance. Our findings elucidate novel mechanisms underlying the bZIP-mediated drought response and provide valuable genetic resources for breeding drought-resistant wheat varieties.

title: Convergent evolution of an oxidative damage tolerance mechanism preserves replication fidelity in plant organellar DNA polymerases
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Plant mitochondria and chloroplasts are sources of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that trigger oxidative DNA lesions. Among these, 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine (8-oxodG) is particularly mutagenic because it exhibits ambiguous base pairing, as DNA polymerases efficiently incorporate adenine opposite 8-oxodG, leading to G·C→T·A transversions. Despite exposure to oxidative stress, plant organellar genomes exhibit some of the lowest nucleotide substitution rates in nature, implying that their DNA replication machinery may have evolved mechanisms to cope with oxidative lesions such as 8-oxodG. In family-A DNA polymerases, including yeast and animal mitochondrial DNA polymerases, the balance between faithful dCMP incorporation and mutagenic dAMP incorporation opposite 8-oxodG is governed by a bulky or positively charged residue. Surprisingly, although the equivalent position in the Arabidopsis thaliana organellar DNA polymerases AtPolIA and AtPolIB is occupied by glycine—a residue predicted to promote mutagenic dAMP incorporation—both enzymes nevertheless preferentially incorporate accurate dCMP opposite 8-oxodG. Our structure–function analyses demonstrate that AtPolI´s fidelity opposite 8-oxodG is conferred by a lysine located near the templating base, which generates steric and electrostatic constraints that favor the 8-oxodG(anti):dCTP pairing while disfavoring the mutagenic 8-oxodG(syn):dATP pair. This mechanism represents an example of convergent evolution, as the fidelity-determining lysine in plant organellar polymerases is in a different position than the analogous residues in yeast-animal mitochondrial polymerases but achieves the same function. Together, these findings suggest that plant organellar DNA polymerases have evolved specialized properties that promote accurate bypass of oxidative DNA lesions, which may contribute to the maintenance of the exceptionally low mutation rates observed in plant organellar genomes.

title:
Paradoxical energetics in the polar diatom
                     Fragilariopsis cylindrus 
                    exposed to extreme low light
abstract: Abstract It is generally considered that Arctic diatoms endure total darkness during polar winters by shifting to a hypometabolic state based on internal reserve mobilization. They can nonetheless rapidly initiate under-ice blooms at extreme low-light levels in early spring. The limits and mechanisms underlying this ability remain unknown. To explore the absolute minimum light required for photoautotrophic growth, we investigated the physiological and transcriptional state of the polar diatom  Fragilariopsis cylindrus  across a winter-to-spring light gradient. While cell division is arrested at 0.18 µmol photons m −2  s −1 , photosynthetic electron transport remains operational down to 0.1 µmol photons m −2  s −1 , which suggests an uncoupling between photosynthesis and biomass accumulation. Crucially, nondividing cells do not enter hypometabolism but instead maintain a functional photosynthetic metabolism without reserve consumption, redefining the lower limit of photoautotrophic life. While cells optimize photon capture efficiency between 3 and 15 µmol photons m −2  s −1  relative to 30 µmol photons m −2  s −1 , this strategy collapses below 1 µmol photons m −2  s −1 . In this dim-light regime, cells activate nonphotochemical quenching and a sustained xanthophyll cycle, which indicates a paradoxical requirement for energy dissipation. We propose that at these extremely low light levels, light absorption appears to exceed the minimum energy requirements for cell maintenance. To manage this active imbalance, cells dissipate excess energy as heat through active nonphotochemical quenching and possibly carbohydrate secretion, indicating a paradoxical requirement for energy dissipation despite extreme photon scarcity. This mechanism allows them to maintain a primed photosynthetic metabolism to facilitate rapid growth recovery upon the return of light after the winter solstice.

title: An investigation of the dual mechanism of uORF-mediated regulation of GGP1 expression and the effects on drought stress in cotton
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Upstream open reading frames (uORFs) are intrinsic regulatory elements that fine-tune gene expression at the translational level without altering genomic sequences or protein structures. Here, we targeted the conserved uORF that resides in the 5'-untranslated region (5'-UTR) of a GDP-galactose phosphorylase gene (GhGGP1) in cotton (Gossypium hirsutum). Regulation of GGP1 is a key control point of plant L-ascorbic acid biosynthesis. Using a dual-luciferase reporter system, we demonstrate that this uORF represses translation of the downstream GGP1 coding sequence in a feedback manner in response to elevated ascorbate, confirming previous findings in other species. Furthermore, CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of the uORFGhGGP1 generated homozygous uorfGhGGP1 mutants with unchanged transcript levels but markedly increased protein abundance and L-ascorbic acid accumulation. Under drought stress, these mutants exhibit reduced malondialdehyde levels, enhanced total antioxidant capacity, and improved drought tolerance. Mechanistically, we further show that under drought conditions, the transcription factor GhBBM directly binds to the uORF-containing cis-regulatory element, enhancing (GhGGP1) transcription and drought resistance. Together, our findings establish the uORFGhGGP1 as a dual-layer regulatory module that integrates transcriptional activation by GhBBM with translational control of the downstream protein encoding open reading frame, thereby fine-tuning drought stress responses in cotton.

MARDy 2.0: a platform for exploring and analysing antifungal resistance mutations
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     The rising incidence of antifungal drug resistance represents a major and growing threat to global public health and food security. Therefore, understanding the genetic and molecular mechanisms that underpin antifungal resistance is essential for both clinical management and agricultural disease control. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     We present MARDy 2.0, an updated platform replacing the original Mycology Antifungal Resistance Database. MARDy 2.0 provides an interactive platform for exploring antifungal resistance data from the community resource FungAMR, and protein structures from UniProtKB or predicted structures using AlphaFold. The platform provides enhanced tools for data exploration and analysis and is freely accessible via an interactive web interface that supports search filtering and downloads, BLAST-based sequence similarity searches, an experimental natural-language query interface for exploratory analysis, a mutation plot for visualizing mutations in a protein context, and structural predictions showing mutation locations. MARDy 2.0 provides a platform to facilitate research into antifungal resistance evolution, surveillance, and mitigation strategies. MARDy should be used and cited alongside the underlying resources it integrates, FungAMR. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     Accessible at https://mardy.net.

title: DNA-BFN: Bayesian flow networks for generative modeling of regulatory DNA sequences
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Designing regulatory DNA sequences is challenging due to their discrete nucleotide alphabet and complex higher-order dependencies underlying regulatory function. Many existing generative models, particularly diffusion-based approaches, learn by injecting stochastic noise into sequences and training denoising processes, which can distort discrete sequence structure and weaken biological constraints. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     Here, we introduce DNA Bayesian Flow Networks (DNA-BFN), a generative framework that models regulatory DNA sequences through iterative Bayesian updates of per-position nucleotide distributions. By directly modeling per-position categorical beliefs, DNA-BFN realizes a diffusion-like generative process without explicitly perturbing discrete nucleotide sequences, enabling fully differentiable training while preserving discrete sequence structure. Across eight regulatory sequence datasets spanning diverse species, scales, and sequence lengths, DNA-BFN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, faithfully preserves sequence feature statistics and regulatory patterns, enables few-shot sequence design, and achieves faster sampling efficiency. These results show that framing sequence generation as progressive uncertainty reduction in probability space provides an effective and generalizable approach for nucleotide sequence design. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     The software and its source code are publicly available at https://github.com/WangLabTHU/DNA-BFN. The dataset, source code and model weights are available in the Zenodo repository: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20177972.

title: FMCerNet: frequency-aware multi-label learning for fine-grained cervical cytology screening
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Automated cytology screening is essential for early cervical cancer prevention, where gigapixel whole-slide images (WSIs) are typically partitioned into tiles for tile-level feature extraction and subsequent WSI-level diagnosis aggregation. However, existing tile-level methods remain constrained by limited input sizes, which frequently obscures sparse and morphologically subtle abnormal cells. Furthermore, these methods commonly formulate tile-level representation learning as a coarse single-label classification task, thereby failing to capture the complex co-occurrence patterns and morphological heterogeneity of cervical cytological abnormalities. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     We propose the Frequency-Aware Multi-Label Learning Network (FMCerNet), a tile-level feature extractor equipped with a Large-Field Frequency-Enhanced ViT backbone and a Coarse-to-Fine multi-label classification head. The former incorporates a Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Transform module to efficiently extract frequency-domain features from large-scale tiles, whereas the latter enhances fine-grained tile representation decoding through hierarchical supervision. Experiments on both public and private datasets demonstrate that FMCerNet improves the accuracy of positive screening and fine-grained subtype classification while maintaining high inference speed. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     Code at https://github.com/imAzhou/FMCerNet and archived on Zenodo (doi: 10.5281/zenodo.22886105).

title: Scientists disrupt less but more persistently with career aging
authors: Nan DengLiying YangShlomo HavlinAn Zengahttps://ror.org/034t30j35National Science Library, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, Chinabhttps://ror.org/05qbk4x57Department of Information Resources Management, School of Economics and Management, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, Chinachttps://ror.org/03kgsv495Department of Physics, Bar-Ilan University, Ramat-Gan 5290002, Israeldhttps://ror.org/022k4wk35School of Systems Science, Beijing Normal University, Beijing 100875, China
abstract: Disruption describes the extent to which a scientific work overturns the prior knowledge on which it builds and leads to a new line of research. A scientist’s tendency to produce disruptive work has been found recently to decline over the career. However, the disruption index captures only how strongly a paper overturns prior work and ignores whether that disruption is later accepted or overturned by subsequent research. The persistent disruption (PD) framework adds this second perspective, identifying work that disrupts prior research and is then consolidated rather than displaced by later work. We examine how PD evolves over the career and find the opposite pattern: The probability of producing a persistent disruptive paper increases with career age. Senior scientists disrupt prior work less often compared to young, but once they do, the disruption tends to persist rather than being quickly superseded. Our results suggest that this reversal feature is due to the experience and we corroborate it across several dimensions of recognition. We also show that, at a fixed level of disruptiveness, the more senior the scientist is, it attracts more citations, social-media attention, and research grants. Nobel laureates also show delayed persistent disruptions. They exhibit high disruptive ability early in their careers, yet their prize-winning work appears years later. This lag further indicates that experience is needed to turn disruptive ability into the field’s most celebrated contributions.

title: Geography of groundwater use and depletion in internationally shared aquifers
authors: Marc F. MüllerKyle F. DavisJulie FaureDavide Danilo ChiarelliFengwei Hungahttps://ror.org/00pc48d59Department of Systems Analysis, Integrated Assessment and Modeling, Eawag-Swiss Federal Institute of Aquatic Science and Technology, Dübendorf 8600, Switzerland, bhttps://ror.org/03d8jqg89United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health (UNU-INWEH), Richmond Hill, ON L4B 3P4, Canadachttps://ror.org/01sbq1a82Data Science Institute, University of Delaware, Newark, DE 19713dhttps://ror.org/01sbq1a82Department of Plant and Soil Sciences, University of Delaware, Newark, DE 19713ehttps://ror.org/01sbq1a82Department of Geography and Spatial Sciences, University of Delaware, Newark, DE 19716fhttps://ror.org/01nffqt88Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Politecnico di Milano, Milan 20133, Italyghttps://ror.org/00mkhxb43Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering and Earth Sciences, University of Notre Dame, Notre Dame, IN 46556
abstract:
Transboundary aquifers (TBAs) underlie 35% of global groundwater-irrigated cropland, yet few are covered by formal cooperative arrangements. Whether this limited cooperation is consequential depends in part on where groundwater is used within shared aquifers, because pumping far from international borders may generate little cross-border impact. Combining
                     
                       
                         ∼ 
                       
                     
                    116,000 well observations with global irrigation data across all 426 known TBAs, we assess how groundwater use and depletion differ from comparable domestic systems and how they are distributed relative to international borders. While we find no evidence of greater average depletion in TBAs, depletion is more strongly concentrated toward international borders in shared aquifers and varies substantially across systems. Irrigation is also more intensive and concentrated toward borders in shared aquifers, although much of this pattern is attenuated after accounting for border rivers. Groundwater-supplied irrigation remains more border-proximate after accounting for these rivers. A dyad-level typology distinguishes shared systems according to where groundwater demand is concentrated, linking their potential for cross-border interaction to different management options. These findings suggest that transboundary groundwater governance should be organized around the geography of groundwater use and potential cross-border interactions rather than treating shared aquifers as uniform governance units.

title: Toward cooler cities by larger homogeneous functional clusters
authors: Xucai ZhangXiaobing WeiXiaoping LiuHonghong WeiYue ZhengHongkai GuYangzi CheYeran SunMing LuoWeilin LiaoHaosheng HuangKangning Huangahttps://ror.org/00cv9y106Department of Geography, Ghent University, Ghent 9000, Belgiumbhttps://ror.org/041kmwe10Medical Research Council Centre for Global Infectious Disease Analysis, Department of Infectious Disease, School of Public Health, Imperial College London, London W12 0BZ, United Kingdomchttps://ror.org/0064kty71Guangdong Key Laboratory for Urbanization and Geo-Simulation, School of Geography and Planning, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou 510275, Chinadhttps://ror.org/006teas31SILC Business School, Shanghai University, Shanghai 201800, Chinaehttps://ror.org/013meh722Department of Land Economy, University of Cambridge, Cambridge CB2 1RX, United Kingdomfhttps://ror.org/0419fj215State Key Laboratory of Remote Sensing and Digital Earth, Aerospace Information Research Institute, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100094, Chinaghttps://ror.org/05qbk4x57University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 101408, Chinahhttps://ror.org/02vpsdb40Division of Arts and Sciences, New York University Shanghai, Shanghai 200124, China
abstract: Urban heat island (UHI) intensifies heat-related risks and environmental degradation in cities worldwide, yet existing mitigation strategies have largely overlooked how the spatial scale of homogeneous functional building clusters influences local climate. This scale may matter because buildings with similar functions often share similar morphology, activity schedules, and anthropogenic heat-release patterns, allowing their spatial contiguity to shape ventilation and heat accumulation. Here, we introduce the Urban Homogeneous Scale (UHS)—an indicator that measures the spatial scale of contiguous, functionally similar building clusters—and analyze 233,844 observations across 101 global cities to assess its potential for mitigating surface UHI. We find that larger UHS is associated with lower surface UHI: every 100-meter increase in UHS corresponds to 4.5% decrease in daytime UHI. This daytime cooling effect is particularly more pronounced in inland, humid, and high-income regions. In low-income regions, larger building area and higher building volume more strongly weaken UHS cooling capacity than in wealthier regions, revealing a socioeconomic inequality in UHS’s mitigation benefits. Our findings identify the spatial scale of building clusters as a essential dimension of urban form associated with urban heat burden, and suggest that considering UHS alongside targeted controls on built environmental characteristics may inform future heat-mitigation planning.

title: Immense but not immutable: A sudden and sustained decline in deep-pelagic life in a large oceanic ecosystem
authors: Tracey T. SuttonRosanna J. MilliganApril B. CookKevin M. BoswellHeather Bracken-GrissomTamara FrankHeather JudkinsJon A. MooreIsabel C. RomeroMichael VecchioneMarta D’EliaMatthew W. JohnstonPedro A. PeresNina M. PruzinskyJohn A. QuinlanJoseph D. WarrenDaniel R. abstract:
The deep-pelagic habitat of the Gulf of Mexico comprises 90.4% of its volume and houses an exceptionally diverse deep-pelagic animal community that provides numerous ecosystem services, including carbon cycling and prey provisioning for oceanic predators. Here, we report sudden, severe, and persistent declines in the abundance of deep-pelagic fishes, crustaceans, and cephalopods that have persisted for over a decade. Over a 3.5-y period, animal abundances declined by 60 to 85%, taxon depending. Particularly hard-hit were ecologically foundational taxa such as euphausiids and lanternfishes. The magnitude of population-level decline that occurred during this 3.5-y period was greater than any observed over a 60-y period in the California Current system, the only comparable dataset, making this the fastest and most severe faunal decline reported for Earth’s largest ecosystem type. These declines were detected both via direct sampling and acoustic sensing, providing independent corroboration. Genomic analyses indicate reductions in genetic diversity among dominant taxa, both a corroboration and a consequence of the decline. Furthermore, resource managers report that these trends parallel those of managed or protected Gulf species that are dependent on deep-pelagic prey, including endangered species (e.g., beaked whales, Rice’s whale). No naturally occurring factors (e.g., temperature, oxygen, food supply) correlated with the observed declines, suggesting an anthropogenic proximate cause. That the declines began shortly after the
                     Deepwater Horizon 
                    oil spill points to that event as the most parsimonious explanation. These findings suggest that despite its immense size the deep-pelagic biome is vulnerable to human-induced disturbance and possesses limited resilience to facilitate recovery.

title: Calibration, accuracy, and domain variation across one million collective forecasts from prediction platforms

abstract:
Using approximately one million resolved contracts and questions across four collective forecasting platforms, twelve domains, and time horizons ranging from hours to years, we evaluate the calibration and accuracy of collective forecasts in real-world settings. We found that forecast probabilities were overall highly calibrated: events assigned a probability of

This broad pattern was evident across platforms and many domains, although fine-grained analyses revealed systematic tendencies toward over- or underestimation in highly consequential areas. While this does not mean that forecasting platforms provide certainty about individual events, our findings suggest that large-scale aggregation of judgments contains meaningful information about real-world uncertainty; when examined in aggregate, the predictions generated by the platforms provided informative estimates of event likelihood.

title: Understory diversity is positively associated with overstory carbon sequestration
authors: Yakun ZhangRui ZhangScott X. ChangHan Y. H. ChenAnthony R. TaylorMasumi HisanoChen ChenSai PengYa WangXin ChenJiasheng WuXinli ChenPeter B. ReichaState Key Laboratory for Development and Utilization of Forest Food Resources, Zhejiang Agriculture and Forestry University, Hangzhou 311300, ChinabKey Laboratory of Carbon Sequestration and Emission Reduction in Agriculture and Forestry of Zhejiang Province, College of Environmental and Resources Sciences, Zhejiang Agriculture and Forestry University, Hangzhou 311300, Chinachttps://ror.org/0160cpw27Department of Renewable Resources, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB T6G 2E3, Canadadhttps://ror.org/015d0jq83College of Grassland Science, Inner Mongolia Agricultural University, Hohhot 010011, Chinaehttps://ror.org/00jmfr291Institute for Global Change Biology, and School for Environment and Sustainability, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, MI 48109fhttps://ror.org/023p7mg82Faculty of Natural Resources Management, Lakehead University, Thunder Bay, ON P7B 5E1, Canadaghttps://ror.org/05nkf0n29Faculty of Forestry and Environmental Management, University of New Brunswick, Fredericton, NB E3B 5A3, Canadahhttps://ror.org/03t78wx29Graduate School of Advanced Science and Engineering, Hiroshima University, Hiroshima 739-8529, Japanihttps://ror.org/034t30j35Key Laboratory of Vegetation and Environmental Change, Institute of Botany, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100093, Chinajhttps://ror.org/04dqdxm60Appalachian Laboratory, University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science, Frostburg, MD 21532khttps://ror.org/017zqws13Department of Forest Resources, University of Minnesota, St. Paul, MN 55108lhttps://ror.org/03t52dk35Hawkesbury Institute for the Environment, Western Sydney University, Penrith, NSW 2753, Australia
abstract: Forests are a major terrestrial carbon sink, and higher overstory diversity is often associated with greater carbon accrual in trees and soils. Yet the contribution of the understory vegetation, the most species-rich forest stratum, to tree and soil carbon accumulation remains largely unknown. Here, we analyzed Canada’s National Forest Inventory database to explore whether understory diversity (richness and evenness of shrubs, herbs, and bryophytes) is associated with carbon accumulation in overstory trees and soils across environmental gradients of air temperature, climate moisture, and nitrogen deposition. We found that herb and bryophyte species richness were positively associated with decadal tree carbon accumulation, with the strongest effects at warmer, drier, and nitrogen-limited sites. In contrast, understory diversity showed no consistent association with soil carbon accumulation. On a decadal scale, increasing herb and bryophyte species richness from their minimum to median values corresponded to 15% and 6% increases in tree carbon accumulation, respectively. These results provide large-scale observational evidence that diversity in lower vegetation layers is positively associated with overstory carbon sequestration and reveal strong environmental modulation of these multistratal biodiversity–ecosystem functioning relationships. These findings suggest that species-rich herb and bryophyte communities should be considered in strategies for sustaining forest carbon sinks, especially under warmer, drier conditions and nutrient limitation.

                     HMGA2 
                    , and
                     CSF1 
                    as the likely neoplastic cells; these cells constitute the minority of the cells in the tumor. These cells express no synovial markers, confirming KPGCT as a distinct entity, separate from TGCT. The bulk of the tumor consists of
                     CSF1R 
                    -expressing macrophages and multinucleated giant cells (MNGCs), suggesting an important role for CSF1–CSF1R signaling. In addition, we find that the likely neoplastic cell population shows activation of the hippo signaling pathway, a possible central pathway in KPGCT tumorigenesis. The CSF1–CSF1R axis likely stimulates the migration and proliferation of macrophages, which form the majority of cells in the tumor, as well as their differentiation into MNGCs. These results provide a rationale for the use of CSF1R inhibitors, which have already shown efficacy in TGCT, as a therapy for KPGCT.

title:
Biotic response networks are an important organizer of the transcriptome in wild
                     Arabidopsis thaliana 
                    populations
authors: Ana Paula Leite MontalvãoKevin D. MurrayIlja BezrukovNatalie BetzLucas P. HenryPaloma DuranPatrick BoppertMartina KolbFabrice RouxJoy BergelsonDetlef WeigelWei Yuanahttps://ror.org/0243gzr89Department of Molecular Biology, Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen, Tübingen 72076, Germanybhttps://ror.org/0190ak572Department of Biology, New York University, New York, NY 10003chttps://ror.org/0190ak572Center for Genomics and Systems Biology, New York University, New York, NY 10003dhttps://ror.org/01ahyrz84Laboratoire des Interactions Plantes-Microrganismes, CNRS, Institut national de recherche pour l‘agriculture, l‘alimentation et l‘environnement, Université de Toulouse, Castanet Tolosan 31326, Franceehttps://ror.org/03a1kwz48Institute for Bioinformatics and Medical Informatics, University of Tübingen, Tübingen 72076, GermanyHaim AshkenazyTien-Hao ChangChoghag DemijirianRémi DuflosAlejandra Duque-JaramilloKatrin FritschiAndrew GlossAnette HabringKatharina KleinEric LadermanIrene LecciaRoxane LionHanna MärkleBaptiste MayjonadeTimothy C. MortonAnkita PandeyAlexandre PerratKamal RadharamananAngelique RatSonia SilvaManmeet SinghDaniel de SouzaHannah Whitehurst
abstract:
Extensive laboratory experimentation has revealed conserved molecular pathways controlling growth and stress responses in plants, yet how these programs operate in natural settings remains poorly understood. We have investigated the organization of the transcriptome in wild populations of
                     Arabidopsis thaliana 
                    by sampling plants across 60 natural sites in Europe and North America over two seasons. Transcriptomes varied extensively among individuals and were only weakly structured by geography or season. No groups of plants stood out due to clear biotic or abiotic stress signatures known from the laboratory. While only a small portion of transcriptome variance was explained by disease symptoms or environmental and phenotypic variables, infection-associated signals accounted for the largest share of the explainable fraction. Biotic-response networks identified in controlled laboratory conditions were well conserved in wild transcriptomes, while other networks, including abiotic-response networks were substantially reorganized in wild plants. Together, these results indicate that while certain transcriptional modules are easily reidentified when moving from the wild to controlled conditions, many regulatory relationships differ in these two contexts, highlighting how ecological complexity shapes transcriptome organization in natural populations.

title: mechanoLight: A genetically encoded fluorescent biosensor for visualizing 5-HT2AR mechanotransduction in live cells
authors: In-Yeop BaekHyunbin KimDuwan KwonHahnbeom ParkJihye Seongahttps://ror.org/01zqcg218Department of Converging Science and Technology, Kyung Hee University, Seoul 02447, Republic of Koreabhttps://ror.org/04h9pn542Department of Pharmacology, Seoul National University College of Medicine, Seoul 03080, Republic of Koreachttps://ror.org/04h9pn542Neuroscience Research Institute, Medical Research Institute, Seoul National University College of Medicine, Seoul 03080, Republic of Koreadhttps://ror.org/04h9pn542Department of Biomedical Sciences, Seoul National University College of Medicine, Seoul 03080, Republic of Koreaehttps://ror.org/04h9pn542Brain Korea 21 FOUR Biomedical Science Project, Seoul National University College of Medicine, Seoul 03080, Republic of KoreafBiomedical Research Division, Korea Institute of Science and Technology, Seoul 02792, Republic of Koreaghttps://ror.org/00cb3km46Seoul National University Bundang Hospital, Seongnam 13620, Republic of Korea
abstract:
G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs) are pivotal sensors of the mechanical environment, yet how they sense and transduce physical stimuli into biochemical signals within live cells remains largely elusive. Here we introduce mechanoLight, a genetically encoded red fluorescent biosensor designed to report the mechanical activation of the 5-hydroxytryptamine 2A receptor (5-HT2AR). By incorporating a circularly permuted mApple (cp-mApple) into the third intracellular loop of 5-HT2AR with the optimized linker (m-linker), mechanoLight selectively detects conformational changes of 5-HT2AR in response to fluid shear stress while exhibiting minimal sensitivity to 5-HT. In sharp contrast, psychLight2, the previously developed green 5-HT2AR biosensor, primarily detects ligand-induced 5-HT2AR activation, suggesting that mechanoLight and psychLight2 capture distinct conformational modes of 5-HT2AR activation. Integrated analysis of linker-swapping experiments, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the flexibility of the m-linker underlies the mechanosensitivity of mechanoLight. We further extend this strategy to other mechanosensitive GPCRs, enabling visualization of their mechanoreactivity in live cells. The mechanoLight signal reflects the mechanosensitivity of 5-HT2AR, as shear stress-induced 5-HT2AR activation triggers Gα
                     q 
                    -dependent signaling pathways, including phospholipase C (PLC) activation, intracellular Ca
                     2+ 
                    mobilization, and ERK phosphorylation. Mutational analysis further identifies N-terminal glycosylation and helix 8 as structural determinants of 5-HT2AR mechanotransduction. Together, our findings establish 5-HT2AR as a mechanotransducer and introduce mechanoLight as a powerful tool for deciphering the molecular principles of GPCR mechanotransduction in live cells.

title: Neuromodulatory control of cortical function: Cell-type-specific regulation of neuronal information transfer
authors: Nishant JoshiXuan YanNiccoló CalciniPayam SafaviAsli AkKoen KoleSven van der BurgTansu CelikelFleur Zeldenrustahttps://ror.org/016xsfp80Department of Neurophysics, Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour, Radboud University, Nijmegen, 6525 AJ, The Netherlandsbhttps://ror.org/00rbjv475Netherlands eScience Center, Amsterdam, Noord-Holland, 1098 XH, The NetherlandscGeorgia Tech-CNRS IRL 2958, https://ror.org/01zkghx44Georgia Institute of Technology-Europe, Metz 57070, Francedhttps://ror.org/01zkghx44Department of Psychology, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA 30332
abstract: Neuromodulatory systems such as dopamine and acetylcholine enable cortical circuits to rapidly shift between behavioral states, yet it remains unclear how receptor-specific signaling reshapes what single neurons compute. Here, we combined whole-cell recordings from excitatory and inhibitory neurons in layer 2/3 of mouse somatosensory cortex with information-theoretic analyses under frozen-noise stimulation. We quantified stimulus-to-spike information transfer and profiled each neuron across four functional domains: passive membrane biophysics, action potential dynamics, intrinsic adaptation currents, and input feature selectivity captured by spike-triggered averages. Activation of D1, D2, or M1 receptors revealed three main findings. First, neuromodulators altered fractional information and firing output in a cell-type- and receptor-specific manner, demonstrating selective regulation of encoding. Second, unsupervised clustering based on functional attribute sets showed that receptor activation reorganizes baseline functional grouping, consistent with a dynamic computational phenotype. Third, multiset correlation and factor analysis revealed that neuromodulation systematically reorganizes covariance among functional domains. In excitatory neurons, dopaminergic activation decreased coordination between input feature selectivity and other functional properties while strengthening coordination among response-based features such as spike dynamics and adaptation. Inhibitory neurons, by contrast, generally exhibited increased coordination across domains. In unison, these findings identify neuromodulation as a reconfiguration signal that reshapes not only individual cellular properties, but also the statistical architecture linking them across the recorded cohort, thereby revealing a higher-dimensional mode of single-neuron regulatory control in the cortex.

title: Leveraging existing grid infrastructure for rapid US renewable and storage deployment
authors: Emilia ChojkiewiczUmed PaliwalDuncan CallawayAmol PhadkeaEnergy and Resources Group, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720bGoldman School of Public Policy, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720
abstract: Rapid electricity demand growth, grid connection delays, and supply chain constraints create a serious risk of supply shortages and rising electricity costs in the next few years. This paper studies the strategy of adding colocated renewables and storage at existing power plants to take advantage of spare grid capacity. Using satellite imagery, we assess solar and wind potential near 3,890 U.S. fossil and renewable plants. By 2030, we find that existing fossil plants could host up to 597 GW of economically viable solar and wind without exceeding the existing interconnection capacity of each site. Existing renewable plants could host an additional 260 GW of firm capacity—comprising storage paired with added solar and wind capacity. These additions could accelerate clean energy deployment and enhance reliability and affordability, but realizing this potential is contingent upon regulatory reforms and coordinating the operational constraints of colocated resources.

title: Historical trends show more declining than increasing species among European pollinators
abstract: Anthropogenic global change presents a growing threat to insect pollinators. Yet, long-term, continental-scale assessments of their population trends remain limited. Here, we leveraged a curated database of over four million occurrence records, covering 88% of extant bee and hoverfly species in Europe, to assess persistence, richness, and occupancy trends over the past century. Species persistence at the European level was relatively high, with modern records available for 87% of bee and 89% of hoverfly species. Regional richness changes were modest, with declines in the Atlantic and Continental regions for both pollinator groups. Recent increases were observed in the Alpine region for bees, but species richness remained largely stable elsewhere. At the species level, however, a more concerning picture emerged: Most bee species and about half of hoverfly species declined in occupancy. Species traits explained little variation in these trends, although there was a weak tendency for cold-adapted bees to show steeper declines than warm-adapted ones. Genera showing some of the steepest declines include parasitic or dietary specialists, though neither of these traits significantly predicted occupancy trends. Overall, we highlight clear warning signs of species population declines, but with potential recovery opportunities if we take urgent actions to reverse those trends.

title: Modeling the global potential of smart farming innovations
authors: Shahrear RomanHadi HadiWyclife Agumba OluochDavid ZilbermanRobert FingerDavid Wuepperahttps://ror.org/041nas322Land Economics Group, Institute for Food and Resource Economics, University of Bonn, Bonn 53115, GermanybDepartment of Agricultural and Resource Economics, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, CA 94720chttps://ror.org/05a28rw58Agricultural Economics and Policy Group, Department of Management, Technology, and Economics, ETH Zürich, Zürich 33 8092, Switzerland
abstract: Smart farming innovations can improve agricultural productivity, resilience, and environmental sustainability, yet their real-world impact hinges on their diffusion dynamics, which in turn depend on their economic viability. We present here a global assessment of the profitability of smart farming innovation across croplands at a spatial resolution of ~5 km from the farmers’ and the societal perspectives. We cover application mapping for precision agriculture, automated application of inputs, autonomous weeding machines, GPS steering assistance systems, and autonomous irrigation systems. For this, we compiled a globally comprehensive dataset of smart farming innovation adoption locations (N = 4,422) based on a combination of a survey (N = 2,677) and a meta-analysis (N = 1,745) and combined them with remotely sensed and statistical data to train an ensemble of five geospatial machine learning models (generalized linear models, random forests, support vector machines, maximum entropy, and boosted regression trees), which show the global distribution of the different innovations’ profitability and its overlap with major environmental issues the innovations can help to mitigate. Simulations of future socioeconomic pathways combined with assumptions about future agri-environmental policies reveal that, especially in middle-income countries, the potential of smart farming will grow over time.

abstract:
Herein, we present three crystal structures of the most complex knotted protein to date, an
                     
                       
                         
                           8

                    knot with eight crossings, which belongs to a clasp knot family. The fold of this protein is also unique, and we call it the EIGHT fold (Extraordinarily Intricate Globular Helical Tangled fold). The
                     
                       
                         
                           8 
                           3 
                         
                       
                     
                    knot is found only in a certain group of bacteria, where it is strictly conserved, despite sequence identities as low as 10%. The
                     
                       
                         
                           8

It is possible that the EIGHT fold evolved from a single unknotted “half” that duplicated and formed a complex protein. Based on an in vitro study of three selected
                     
                       
                         
                           8

Unfolding kinetics of

                    knotted proteins reveal a complex, multiphase process spanning milliseconds to days. Six kinetic phases were resolved using stopped-flow fluorescence and far-ultraviolet absorbance circular dichroism spectroscopy, highlighting both rapid early events and slower rearrangements in secondary and tertiary structures. Finally, with a structure-based model, we showed that proteins with an
                     
                       
                         
                           8

                           4 
                           1 
                         
                       
                     
                    . Nevertheless, these proteins do not seem to fit with current folding theories known to date and require the development of a new approach.

The Diverse Epigenetic Epidemiology Partnership outlines priorities for building a more equitable global epigenomics research agenda and improving the relevance of epigenetic insights for global health.

abstract: Cryptic phytocytokines are embedded within large functional proteins. In some gene families, these peptide sequences differ markedly among members. How do they retain existing functions or acquire new ones as they evolve? A recent study by Gao et al. (2026) addresses this question in soybean, showing that precursor genes are interspersed with receptor-encoding genes within a genomic cluster. This arrangement may favor the co-inheritance of compatible ligand–receptor combinations as both families diversify.

title: Telomere-to-telomere genome assembly of the elite peanut cultivar Yuhua 15 identifies AhYABBY as a key regulator of pod and seed size
Plant genome evolution: From genomic variation to environmental adaptation
abstract: Short summary: Plant genome evolution is central to understanding environmental adaptation. This review surveys sequenced plant genomes, synthesizes how genomic variants are detected and how their evolutionary fates are determined. It further examines how major variant types drive adaptation and characterizes the genomic signatures of extremophiles. By integrating these multi-scale genomic insights, we provide a comprehensive framework for understanding plant adaptation that bridges microevolutionary mechanisms and macroevolutionary patterns, and discuss emerging trends and future directions.

title: A planet shaped by life
abstract: Our planet is different from others in the Solar System by virtue of carrying life and its surface layer being produced and shaped by living organisms. While the origins of fossils and sediments from the past are well characterised, some ongoing and more remote biomineralisation processes still need more research.

title: Functional roles of abyssal benthos in sustaining polymetallic nodule fields
abstract: Van Audenhaege et al. identify abyssal benthic species that actively clear sediment and uplift polymetallic nodules, reworking the entire seabed on yearly to decadal timescales. This process maintains hard substrata for colonization, supporting habitat heterogeneity and abyssal biodiversity. Their observations highlight the importance of overlooked processes in designing conservation strategies.

title: Electrical synapses mediate visual orientation behavior
abstract: Frighetto et al. reveal a neural circuit in the fly optic lobe that mediates saccadic orientation toward visual objects. Electrical synapses are a key feature of this visual pathway and are required for proper computation of visual signals and the resulting behavioral response.

title: Hunger recruits a parallel circuit encoding alcohol reward
abstract: Nuñez et al. identify a single octopaminergic neuron, VUMa3(mx), which is recruited into ethanol-seeking circuits in the mushroom body γ2 lobe when a fly is hungry. VUMa3(mx) activity increases with hunger and is maintained through positive octopaminergic autoreception to elicit an early shift from ethanol aversion to preference.

title: Gaia with a thousand faces
abstract: Florian Maderspacher explores the history, evolution and impact of the Gaia hypothesis — the notion that life and Earth act as a unit that self-regulates planetary conditions to ensure its persistence.

title: What the trees remember
abstract: Trees are often treated as the background to human history. They shade homes, line streets, mark property boundaries, and persist in landscapes as generations of people come and go. In When Trees Testify, plant biologist Dr. Beronda L. Montgomery brings trees out of the background and asks us to recognize them as witnesses. The trees in this phenomenal and deeply impactful book do not merely accompany American history: they preserve its knowledge, sustain its communities, and testify to its beauty, violence, survival, and contradictions.

title: Jiayang Li
abstract: Interview with Jiayang Li, who studies plant molecular genetics and crop breeding, particularly in rice, at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

title: Trace fossils
abstract: Mike Benton introduces ichnology, the study of fossilized traces left by animals and other organisms.

title: Chunking: What working memory gains and loses
abstract: Chunking compresses information into fewer meaningful units, reducing working memory demands. During chunking, neural representations in the prefrontal cortex exhibit reduced dimensionality and are biased toward chunk centers, suggesting lossy compression that improves overall retention while reducing precision within chunks.

title: Depression: Ketamine quiets an unruly habenula
abstract: Ketamine’s robust antidepressant effects often appear twenty-four hours after a single dose. A new study now provides evidence suggesting that this timepoint coincides with a quieting of habenula activation and reductions in aversive learning in healthy subjects.

title: Astrobiology
abstract: Sean McMahon introduces astrobiology, also known as exobiology — the interdisciplinary field studying the baselines, conditions and evidence for life beyond Earth.

title: The evolution of oxygen, temperature, and marine aerobic habitat for animals over the last billion years of Earth history
abstract: Kemi F. Ashing-Giwa and colleagues explore how oxygen and temperature have interacted over the last billion years to define marine aerobic habitat for animals.

title: Large animal restoration and carbon storage across climate-relevant timescales
abstract: Andrew Abraham and colleagues review the roles flagship megafauna play in Earth’s carbon cycle and identify six lessons for effectively incorporating large animal restoration as a long-term climate recovery strategy.

title: Tectonics, geomorphology and biodiversity
abstract: Loïc Pellissier and Sean Willett introduce ways in which geomorphic and tectonic processes shape the distribution and diversity of life.

title: Crop engineering: Plant genes tied to the weather
abstract: Coupling of a late blight disease resistance gene to a humidity-responsive cis-element in potato achieves resistance under high-humidity conditions that favor disease. This strategy sidesteps the yield penalties associated with constitutive resistance gene expression.

title: Plant evolution: How duckweeds became so small
abstract: Duckweeds are highly reduced flowering plants with a simplified body plan. A new study reveals that the duckweed frond retains ancestral organ identities despite compression and fusion. Together with previous evidence of root loss, these findings highlight distinct evolutionary routes to plant miniaturization.

title: Locomotor kinematics and head stabilization in rolling snakes
abstract: Kojima, Fukuyama et al. show that dwarf reedsnakes stabilize their heads while engaged in a highly unusual rolling behavior.

title: Ecosystem engineering, regime shifts and the rise of animals
abstract: Simon Darroch and colleagues review the rise of animal ecosystem engineering across the Ediacaran–Cambrian transition and its macroevolutionary impacts for origination and extinction of animals, as well as its importance for understanding the future of ecosystems.

title: Neuroimmune signaling: Dopamine release from fat tissue mediates pathogen avoidance
abstract: Animals must quickly learn to avoid food that makes them sick. A recent study in Drosophila melanogaster shows that ingesting pathogenic bacteria triggers dopamine release from fat cells that alters odor responses in the fly brain and switches feeding preference toward non-pathogenic food.

title: Navigation map has to be learned by migration-naïve Eurasian reed warblers
abstract: Utvenko et al. report that in the Eurasian reed warbler the first migration is guided primarily by an inherited compass programme, whereas a functional magnetic map develops through migratory experience.

title: Birds shape biogeochemistry and ecosystem function globally
abstract: Birds play essential roles in the transport and recycling of nutrients, with consequences for ecosystem function, structure, and global connectivity. In this review, Duvall and colleagues synthesize the contribution of birds to biogeochemical processes throughout Earth’s biosphere.

title: Deep microbial biosphere
abstract: In this primer, Beaver and Neufeld describe the deep microbial biosphere — the community of microbes living beneath the Earth’s surface in a vast ecosystem of terrestrial rocks, aquifers, marine sediments, and oceanic crust — and the important ways in which these organisms interact with the Earth’s geochemical cycles.

title: The deep-time history of soils and plants
abstract: In this essay, Strullu-Derrien and Rillig discuss the origins of soils and argue that, while modern ecology often centers on plants, soil ecosystems predate land plants by hundreds of millions of years. Embracing a vision of interdependent above- and below-ground systems is essential for preserving soil health and biodiversity.

title: Anthropogenic novel entities in the Earth system
abstract: The term ‘novel entities’ refers to anthropogenic substances and materials that have the potential to disrupt natural processes. In this primer, Zink et al. highlight the major types of novel entities, their global distribution, and ways in which they impact both human health and Earth’s many ecosystems.

title: Bioturbation
abstract: Jack Middelburg introduces bioturbation, the process by which animals and other organisms rework sediment and soils.

title: Structural basis of a SWI/SNF-associated transcription pre-initiation complex
A microbiome-bile acid axis mediates protection from chronic liver disease in females
abstract: isoUDCA, a female-enriched bile acid produced by a gut bacterial consortium favored by estrogen, promotes hepatic cholesterol handling and bile acid metabolism through SREBP2-STARD4-CYP7B1 signaling, thereby alleviating chronic liver injury.

title: The pyrin inflammasome senses OCTN2-mediated uptake of extracellular ʟ-carnitine from muscle injury or ingestion
abstract: ʟ-Carnitine is a nonproteinogenic amino acid highly abundant in myocytes, and both excess ingestion of myocytes and myocyte necrosis are associated with systemic inflammation. Here, we find that the pyrin inflammasome senses extracellular ʟ-carnitine through the high-affinity carnitine transporter OCTN2 (SLC22A5) and this leads to IL-1β-mediated inflammation. Our findings position OCTN2 as a potential target to reduce inflammation from exogenous or endogenous sources of extracellular ʟ-carnitine.

title: Nanoscale Buried Interface Control in Silicone Hydrogels Enables a Biointerface Engineering Platform
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   Engineering multifunctional biointerfaces requires quantitative understanding of how buried nanoscale coating architectures govern biological function, yet such relationships remain inaccessible because non‐destructive characterization of soft, curved interfaces is lacking. Here, we establish an integrated engineering–characterization–function platform that quantitatively resolves buried nanocoatings and directly correlates their architecture with interfacial performance. Using silicone hydrogel contact lenses as a representative biomedical substrate, robust semi‐interpenetrating polymer network (semi‐IPN) nanocoatings are fabricated and characterized by gas cluster ion beam X‐ray photoelectron spectroscopy (GCIB‐XPS), time‐of‐flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (ToF‐SIMS), and a newly developed atomic force microscopy (AFM) modulus‐based algorithm. This multimodal framework non‐destructively maps vertical chemical gradients, nanometer‐scale layer thicknesses, and interfacial mechanical distributions with sub‐100 nm precision, enabling quantitative visualization of conformal buried nanocoatings. The resulting structure–function relationships guide the rational engineering of poly(2‐hydroxyethyl methacrylate) (poly(HEMA)) interfaces with homogeneous surface coverage (∼89%), enhanced wettability, markedly reduced protein adsorption and cellular fouling, while fully preserving oxygen permeability, optical transparency, UV protection, and mechanical integrity. The platform further enables incorporation of functional monomers for light‐triggered therapeutic release without compromising device performance. Beyond contact lenses, this work provides a generalizable strategy for quantitatively engineering and predicting multifunctional nanocoatings across diverse biomedical interfaces.

 Electroforming-free, self-rectifying switching with polarity-dependent threshold modulation is realized in selector-only memory through Cu-ion migration in a bilayer stacked dual functional materials. The cover visualizes diffusive Cu-ion migration and transient filament dynamics in a bilayer selector-only memory, together with a three-SR-SOM full-adder architecture demonstrating compact logic-in-memory operation. abstract:
Visualizing Hidden Periodontal Pathogen Activity  
 Hidden within the periodontal pocket,  Porphyromonas gingivalis , a major periodontal pathogen, secretes Arg-specific gingipain. This protease cleaves peptides immobilized on CaCO 3  microspheres to release a chromogenic dye, transforming an invisible bacterial activity into a visible color signal for on-site detection. Multi-Condition Single-Cell Data  
 The yin-yang (Taiji) symbol at the heart of this cover visual encapsulates the dual mission of CAPER: to carefully remove unwanted technical variation while faithfully preserving true biological signals. The blue and orange cellular populations denote two contrasting conditions, such as stimulated versus control or disease versus healthy, and the diversity of cell shapes illustrates CAPER's capacity to retain condition-specific, cell-population-level heterogeneity. This balance is essential for enabling robust downstream discovery in multi-condition single-cell transcriptomics studies. More details can be found in the Research Article by Ye Li, Shiquan Sun, and co-workers (DOI:  10.1002/advs.76186 ).
