title:
Enteric ChAT‐Expressing Neurons Mediate the Protective Effect of
                     Lactobacillus plantarum 
                    in Inflammatory Bowel Disease
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   
                    The gut microbiota plays a crucial role in inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), yet how specific microbial components influence disease progression remains incompletely understood. Our study reveals that decreased abundance of
                     Lactobacillus 
                    species correlates with ulcerative colitis severity in patients. Among tested strains,
                     L. plantarum 
                    A736, isolated from traditional fermented foods, demonstrated protective effects in ameliorating dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)‐induced colitis in a mouse model. Strikingly, multi‐omics analysis revealed that
                     L. plantarum 
                    A736 uniquely enhances choline acetyltransferase‐expressing (ChAT
                     + 
                    ) neurons in the enteric nervous system and elevates acetylcholine (ACh) levels. Further analysis identified that
                     L. plantarum 
                    A736 metabolizes tryptophan to produce indole‐3‐lactic acid (ILA), and supplementation with ILA significantly mimics this strain's anti‐inflammatory effects by restoring ChAT
                     + 
                    neurons and cholinergic signaling. Crucially, selective ablation of colonic ChAT
                     + 
                    neurons abolished the protective effect of both
                     L. plantarum 
                    A736 and ILA, establishing their essential role in mediating these effects. These findings demonstrate that microbial metabolites can modulate enteric neuronal circuits to regulate gut immunity. The identified ILA‐ChAT
                     + 
                    neuron axis represents a novel neuro‐immune pathway that could be targeted for IBD treatment.

title: Additive Manufacturing of High‐Performance Polymers for Extreme Environments
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   Additive manufacturing (AM) of high‐performance polymers (HPPs) has gained significant research interest due to its potential for applications in extreme environments, including aerospace, automotive, marine, and defense sectors. Components in these applications are often subjected to prolonged exposure to high temperatures, high mechanical loads, and chemically aggressive environments. HPPs are well‐suited to such demanding conditions because of their high mechanical properties, thermal stability, flame resistance, and chemical durability. However, the inherent molecular and structural characteristics that provide these properties also pose notable challenges during AM of HPPs. In particular, the effective processing and fabrication of HPPs using AM techniques are limited by their rigid molecular structure, high melting temperatures and viscosities, and complex crystallization behavior. This review focuses on the processing and utilization of HPPs using commercially available AM techniques. Particular emphasis is placed on the relationships among polymer chemistry, rheology, thermal history, crystallinity, process‐induced defects, and mechanical performance. Recent applications of additively manufactured HPPs are critically evaluated. The review also compares qualification requirements, environmental durability, and technology readiness with those of conventionally manufactured components. Finally, unresolved challenges and future research priorities are identified to enable reliable, scalable, and certification‐ready additively manufactured HPP components for extreme‐service environments.

title:
Artificial Grain Boundaries Created by Freestanding Membrane Transfer Reveal Angle‐Dependent Ferroelectric Switching and Leakage in BaTiO
                     3
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   Grain boundaries (GBs) strongly influence polycrystalline ferroelectrics, but their discrete effects are difficult to isolate because of nanoscale heterogeneity. Here, we use freestanding membrane transfer to fabricate artificial  GBs with controlled, experimentally accessible in‐plane misorientation angles (). Macroscopic electrical measurements show higher coercive voltage and leakage current at the GB region than in the coherent grain region. Piezoresponse force microscopy directly reveals domain‐wall pinning at the boundary, which impedes lateral domain propagation and increases the effective switching barrier. Conductive atomic force microscopy further identifies the GB as a localized high‐conductance pathway, with leakage increasing strongly with,  in agreement with a Read–Shockley‐inspired model. Temperature‐dependent steady‐state DC measurements yield an activation energy of approximately 0.032 eV at the GB, an order of magnitude lower than in the grain interior. Comparison of Schottky and Poole–Frenkel analyses indicates that transport is more consistent with defect‐assisted, Schottky‐like thermally activated emission than with bulk Poole–Frenkel conduction. These results establish a tunable artificial‐GB platform that directly correlates misorientation angle with domain‐wall pinning, coercive voltage, and localized leakage, providing a pathway for grain‐boundary engineering in ferroelectric thin films.

title: Distinct extracellular architectures shape mechanical persistence in GPVI and CLEC-2 receptor assemblies
abstract: Glycoprotein VI (GPVI) and C-type lectin-like receptor 2 (CLEC-2) are platelet-activating receptors whose extracellular organization contributes to receptor association and signaling during thrombus formation, yet how alternative receptor architectures influence mechanical persistence remains unclear. We used molecular dynamics to compare a GPVI dimer based on 2GI7, a domain-swapped GPVI assembly derived from 7NMU, and a crystallographic CLEC-2 contact using the same pulling protocol and constant-force conditions. During the first 5 nm of imposed separation, reconstructed GPVI required less force and mechanical work than CLEC-2 and domain-swapped GPVI. Under constant-force loading from 400 to 600 pN, reconstructed GPVI also reached the same extension endpoint markedly earlier than the domain-swapped assembly, with passage times differing by more than an order of magnitude under several conditions. Extended pulling to approximately 10 nm produced complete loss of interreceptor heavy-atom contacts in reconstructed GPVI while local peptide and disulfide connectivity remained intact. In contrast, the domain-swapped preparation retained resistance over a larger part of the separation pathway and showed substantially greater mechanical persistence. These results show that alternative extracellular arrangements of the same receptor are not mechanically equivalent and that uncertainty in GPVI architecture can translate into large differences in force transmission and persistence under load. Such architecture-dependent persistence may influence the stability of extracellular receptor associations during thrombus formation and thereby affect the mechanical lifetime of receptor clusters under load.

title: The influence of cell morphology on the dynamics and stability of model bacterial communities
abstract: Understanding how structures arise in microbial communities remains an outstanding challenge in bacterial ecology. When replicating within dense and confined environments, bacterial populations may collectively self-organize as a result of mechanical interactions. We previously observed that model dual-populations of bacteria, colonizing open-ended microchannels, either quickly fixate to a single population or segregate into long-lived, coexisting populations. This latter quasi-stability results from the alignment of bacteria into lanes, forcing cells to grow toward the open ends of the channel, with inter-lane invasion events driving the boundary dynamics between populations. Here we apply agent-based (AB) simulations to explore the boundary dynamics between dual-bacterial populations of varying morphology and division rate. We find that the simulated boundary dynamics are well-described by a simple drift-diffusion model, which enables us to estimate the mean time to fixation within competitive scenarios where the fixation time is difficult to access by AB simulations. Coccus-like cells display a competitive advantage over bacillus cells as they can more effectively invade and ultimately fixate, while coexisting populations of bacillus cells are “effectively” stable. And while faster-dividing cells should have a selective advantage, their morphology determines if this advantage drives fixation or acts as a defensive strategy to maintain their population. These findings highlight the critical role that cell morphology and mechanics play in shaping bacterial communities.

title: Interpretable neural networks prioritize cancer driver genes from genome-wide dependency landscapes
abstract: Identifying cancer driver genes and their therapeutic impact remains a core challenge in computational cancer biology. We introduce xNNDriver and xAEDriver, two interpretable neural network frameworks that connect cancer mutations with genome-wide DepMap gene dependencies, pathway activity, and drug-response patterns. xNNDriver is a supervised pathway-guided model that evaluates whether a gene’s mutation status is encoded in the genome-wide dependency landscape; we interpret model fitness as a driver potential score, which quantifies the strength of this mutation-dependency signal and prioritizes genes with broad functional footprints. Across 3,008 candidate genes, xNNDriver recovers major established drivers and highlights literature-supported candidates, while pathway analyses reveal biologically coherent programs related to metabolism, growth factor signaling, and immune regulation. To capture combinatorial functional states, xAEDriver uses an unsupervised autoencoder to learn Driver Variant Representations (DVRs), latent binary features guided by the frequency distribution of known driver mutations. DVRs capture cell-line-specific dependency patterns and expression patterns and are associated with drug sensitivity and pathway activity. Together, these interpretable deep learning models demonstrate that gene dependency landscapes encode rich, interpretable signals of oncogenic function and provide a hypothesis-generating framework for prioritizing drivers, pathways, and therapeutic vulnerabilities for further experimental validation.

title: Natural killer cell receptor signaling and activation depend on cell cycle stages
abstract:
Natural Killer (NK) cells are lymphocytes of the innate immunity and provide key protection against infection and cancer. NK cells express a wide array of inhibitory and activating receptors on the cell surface including the activating receptor NKG2D. Receptor signaling in NK cells leads to rapid post-translational modification (e.g., phosphorylation) of sub-cellular signaling proteins within minutes of receptor stimulation that ultimately give rise to diverse effector functions including cell proliferation. Recent single-cell mass cytometry (i.e., CyTOF) experiments in macrophages showed variations of abundances of phosphorylated signaling proteins across cell cycle stages indicating a dependence of cell signaling kinetics on an order of magnitude slower kinetics (~ several hours) of cell cycle transitions. We investigated cell cycle dependence of NKG2D signaling kinetics in NK cells using longitudinal CyTOF measurements up to 256 minutes post stimulation performed on IL-2-treated NKG2D-stimulated primary human CD56
                     dim 
                    NK cells. The CyTOF experiments revealed cell stage specific kinetics of signaling proteins such as pVav1, pErk, and pS6, with the degranulation marker CD107a showing its largest upregulation specifically in the combined G2 and M (G2 - M) stage. We developed stochastic minimal computational models coupling signaling and cell cycle processes to investigate the effect of cell cycle transitions on NK cell receptor induced signaling kinetics. These models suggest that the observed cell stage specific NK cell receptor signaling kinetics arise due to active modulation of the receptor signaling kinetics by cell cycle progression. The framework can be extended to study the interplay between receptor signaling and cell cycle progression in other cell types.

title: DipSkmer: Reference-free population genomics with diploid genome skims
abstract:
Ecologists and conservation biologists rely on genetic diversity as a key essential biodiversity variable (EBV) used to track population health and dynamics, and utilize the population-scaled mutation parameter
                     
                       
                         
                         
                           
                             θ 
                           
                         
                       
                     
                    as a key metric of diversity. While whole-genome-sequencing (wgs) is increasingly affordable, it will be considerable time before the full diversity of life is represented by high-quality assembled genomes; even then, constant monitoring will still require repeated sampling across time and space. In contrast, genome skimming (low-coverage, short-read wgs) is highly cost-effective but challenging to analyze because the coverage is too low for assembly and reliable error correction. Mature methods, such as Mash, exist for estimating pairwise genomic distances based on the Jaccard similarity of
                     k 
                    -mer sets computed using sketching techniques. Some, such as Skmer, additionally model the impacts of low coverage. These methods have been successfully applied to assembly-free species identification and phylogenetics; however, their use in population genetics has been limited. Among other limitations, these methods implicitly treat genomes as haploid, and heterozygosity confounds estimates of genomic distance for diploid organisms. In this paper, we address this problem through several technical advances. First, we use coalescent theory to mathematically derive how the Jaccard index between the k-mer sets of two diploid samples changes with
                     
                       
                         
                         
                           
                             θ 
                           
                         
                       
                     
                    under a neutral Kingman’s coalescent model. Next, we model the impact of coverage and sequencing error to derive an estimate of
                     
                       
                         
                         
                           
                             θ 
                           
                         
                       
                     
                    from the Jaccard index, in addition to several auxiliary variables, which we also estimate from the genome skims. The resulting method, DipSkmer, enables more accurate estimates of coverage, sequencing error, and
                     
                       
                         
                         
                           
                             θ 
                           
                         
                       
                     
                    for diploid samples. Analyses of both simulated and empirical datasets show that for diploids and low distances (e.g., < 2%), DipSkmer’s estimate outperforms existing alignment-free methods such as Mash and Skmer, and closely approximates ANGSD, a reference and alignment-based tool.

title: Forecasting of infectious disease epidemics in sexual networks using attenuated renewal processes
abstract: Forecasting emerging infectious disease outbreaks is particularly challenging for sexual networks of men who have sex with men (MSM), where transmission can be shaped by heterogeneous and overdispersed contact structures, mixing assortativity, and both one-time and recurrent partnerships. Using stochastic epidemic simulations on synthetic MSM networks and empirical mpox case data from major cities, we systematically evaluated five classes of short-term forecasting models, from random walk approaches to semi-mechanistic attenuated renewal processes. Model performance was assessed using the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). Across both simulated and empirical epidemics in heterogeneous networks, renewal models attenuated by a reverse-sigmoid curve, to account for early depletion of highly-connected nodes, consistently outperformed alternatives, achieving more balanced and reliable forecasts. Our findings suggest a practical approach for robust forecasting in highly overdispersed networks, where distinguishing network effects from other factors remains challenging and usually requires additional data.

title: Going around phase defects: Addressing a fundamental flaw of phase singularity detection
abstract:
Phase mapping is a widespread method for identifying rotational electrical activity sustaining cardiac arrhythmias. However, conventional implementations assume that the cardiac phase map is continuous, leading to ill-defined phase indices in regions affected by functional conduction block, fibrosis, or anatomical boundaries. These regions of discontinuous or undefined phase, termed phase defects, lead to both false positive and false negative detections of rotational drivers. This work introduces an improved phase mapping implementation termed
                     extended phase mapping 
                    that explicitly detects and accounts for phase defects, enabling robust calculation of the phase index around them. Extended phase mapping is applied to (1) simulated excitation patterns using the Fenton–Karma model, (2) experimental optical mapping data of rat ventricular fibrillation, and (3) a clinical CARTO activation map of atrial tachycardia. Across all datasets, the extended approach eliminates erroneous detections and resolves previously missed rotations. Our results demonstrate that proper treatment of phase defects yields a unified and physiologically consistent characterization of all rotational drivers including near-complete and anatomical reentries. Therefore, we propose that explicitly accounting for phase defects, rather than tracking singular points alone, gives a more complete and consistent characterization of rotational dynamics in cardiac tissue.

MaMPK3 
                    ‐2 Phosphorylating and Stabilizing Transcriptional Repressor
                     MaAS1 
                    by Counteracting
                     MaRNF4 
                    ‐Mediated Ubiquitination During Banana Fruit Ripening
authors:
Ting‐Ting Luo, 
Ying‐Ying Yang, 
Hai‐Ke Tan, 
Wen Song, 
Wei Wei, 
Wei Shan, 
Jian‐Fei Kuang, 
Jian‐Ye Chen, 
Wang‐Jin Lu
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   
                    The ripening of fleshy fruits is strongly regulated by a complex interplay between transcriptional regulation and post‐translational modifications (PTMs). However, the specific PTM regulatory networks involved in fruit ripening remain poorly understood. In this study, we identify MaAS1, an R2R3‐type MYB transcription factor, as a key negative regulator of banana fruit ripening. MaAS1 directly binds to the promoters of the ripening‐associated genes
                     MaACS1 
                    ,
                     MaPME23 
                    and
                     MaEXPA15 
                    and represses their transcription. The mitogen‐activated protein kinase MaMPK3‐2 phosphorylates MaAS1 at three specific sites (Ser61, Thr92 and Ser120), thereby enhancing its transcriptional repressor activity and protein stability and ultimately suppressing fruit ripening. In contrast, the ethylene‐induced E3 ubiquitin ligase MaRNF4 mediates the ubiquitination and degradation of MaAS1, thereby promoting ripening. Notably, phosphorylation by MaMPK3‐2 antagonises MaRNF4‐mediated ubiquitination, maintaining MaAS1 levels and regulating ripening progression. Collectively, these findings reveal a regulatory module involving MaMPK3‐2, MaAS1 and MaRNF4, ultimately highlighting the intricate interplay between phosphorylation and ubiquitination in controlling fruit ripening, offering critical insights into the integrated regulatory network interconnecting transcription and PTMs during fruit ripening.

title:
PnMYB4a 
                    , a
                     R2R3 
                    transcription factor, modulates coumarin biosynthesis during melanization in the culms of
                     Phyllostachys nigra
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         
                          Culm colour is one of the primary traits determining the ornamental value of bamboos. The black pigment shown to accumulate in
                           Phyllostachys nigra 
                          was previously characterized as melanin, but the underlying regulatory mechanism for its deposition remains elusive.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          Herein, metabolomics data show that coumarins serve as precursor substrates for melanization in
                           P. nigra 
                          , and RNA‐seq and weighted gene correlation network analysis (WGCNA) revealed that the transcription factor PnMYB4a is integral to coumarin biosynthesis.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          Overexpression of
                           PnMYB4a 
                          promotes coumarin production in both
                           Oryza sativa 
                          and
                           Arabidopsis thaliana 
                          .
                           Pn4CL4‐2 
                          , a biosynthetic gene involved in coumarin biosynthesis, was identified as a direct target gene of PnMYB4a. Additionally, PnWRKY8 and PnWRKY72‐2 were found to interact with PnMYB4a both
                           in vivo 
                          and
                           in vitro 
                          . Both PnWRKY8 and PnWRKY72‐2 positively promoted coumarin accumulation in transgenic rice, but they repressed the expression of
                           Pn4CL4‐2 
                          by directly binding to W‐box elements within its promoter. Interestingly, PnMYB4a was found to alleviate the inhibitory effect on
                           Pn4CL4‐2 
                          by forming complexes with both PnWRKY8 and PnWRKY72‐2.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          Collectively, these findings revealed a PnMYB4a‐PnWRKY8/PnWRKY72‐2 regulatory module involved in the coumarin biosynthetic pathway in
                           P. nigra 
                          and provide new insights into the mechanisms of melanization and coloration in bamboo species.

title:
Metabolic convergence on
                     TOR 
                    signaling in the chestnut blight fungus and its regulation by host plant signals
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         
                          Transcriptomic analysis of the chestnut blight fungus
                           Cryphonectria parasitica 
                          identified 22 core genes regulated by Cryphonectria hypovirus 1 (CHV1) infection and sectorization. Twelve genes with common phenocopies were analyzed: all mutants displayed restricted colonial growth, intense pigmentation, hyperbranched terminal hyphae with swollen globose cells, and reduced conidiation. Although gene‐specific mutant phenotypes existed, responses to most stressors were similar to those of the wild‐type.
                         
                       
                       
                         Mutant growth was highly sensitive to nutrient conditions, and growth restriction was notably alleviated by supplementation with 1.0 M sorbitol, nutrient‐deficient media, or skim milk. All mutants showed hallmarks consistent with reduced target of rapamycin (TOR) signaling. Trehalose accumulation, a canonical fungal response to TOR inhibition, was observed in mutants via transcriptional upregulation of core trehalose biosynthetic genes, resulting in altered hyphal osmolarity and common mutant cell phenotypes. 
                       
                       
                         Plant signals overrode the mutants' phenotypes, strongly promoting their growth and differentiation. Although a severely retarded growth defect was observed in mutants, mutants' virulence remained intact, which can be ascribed to the host‐plant signals. 
                       
                       
                         Cryphonectria hypovirus 1 (CHV1)‐infected mutants exhibited greater growth restriction, accompanied by genotype‐specific CHV1 titers. Despite gene‐specific variation, common phenocopies indicate that diverse metabolic pathways converge on the TOR pathway in the fungal response to host‐plant and CHV1 infection.

title:
S 
                    ‑glutathionylation of MaWRKY44 orchestrates a MaZFP139‐MaWRKY44‐MaGSTU07 cascade to enhance banana cold tolerance
authors:
Shuqin Lin, 
Wen Song, 
Shaoting Liao, 
Haike Tan, 
Jianji Qi, 
Danling Cai, 
Wei Wei, 
Wei Shan, 
Jianfei Kuang, 
Jianye Chen, 
Wangjin Lu
abstract:
In banana, at low temperatures (7°C), the transcription factor MaZFP139 activates  MaWRKY44  expression. MaWRKY44 binds to the W-box sites in the promoter of the glutathione S-transferase gene  MaGSTU07  to enhance reactive oxygen species scavenging. S-glutathionylation protects MaWRKY44 from oxidation-induced degradation, reinforcing antioxidant defenses and limiting peel browning in bananas.

  
 ABSTRACT 
 Chilling injury caused by low temperatures severely reduces the postharvest quality and marketability of banana fruit. Although glutathione  S ‑transferase (GST)-mediated reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging constitutes a core antioxidant defense against cold oxidative stress, the transcriptional and post‑translational mechanisms governing this process remain largely elusive. Here, we discovered that  S ‑glutathionylation of the WRKY transcription factor MaWRKY44 functions as a previously unknown redox switch that orchestrates a hierarchical transcriptional cascade to enhance cold tolerance. LC‑MS/MS identified Cys45 and Cys199 as conserved  S ‑glutathionylation sites of MaWRKY44. Biochemical and molecular analyses revealed a biphasic redox switch: Mild ROS triggers reversible glutathionylation to stabilize MaWRKY44 and enhance its DNA‑binding capacity, whereas sustained oxidative stress drives irreversible cysteine over‑oxidation that abolishes its transcriptional function. Mechanistically, we identified a C2H2 zinc finger transcription factor, MaZFP139, as a direct upstream activator of MaWRKY44, which in turn specifically binds to the W‑box motifs of the  MaGSTU07  promoter to drive its transcription. Transient gain‑ and loss‑of‑function assays in banana, together with stable heterologous transformation in tomato, demonstrated that the MaZFP139-MaWRKY44-MaGSTU07 cascade positively mitigates cold‑triggered ROS accumulation and peel browning. Collectively, our findings uncover a multilayer transcriptional‑redox module governing fruit cold tolerance, and provide potential molecular targets for improving postharvest cold storage performance in tropical fruits.

title: Identity-by-descent captures shared environmental factors at biobank scale
abstract: Genealogical ties leave traces beyond shared genetic material: relatives tend to share environmental exposures and cultural practices that persist across generations. Here, using genomic and electronic health record data from 13,143 individuals in the Biorepository and Integrative Genomics, we apply a hierarchical community detection algorithm that groups individuals into four major communities and 17 subcommunities based on the proportion of their genome shared identity-by-descent (IBD). This approach captures a fine-scale demographic structure beyond traditional ancestry classifications. By integrating neighborhood-level geographic data with census-derived environmental metrics, we reveal unequal exposure to environmental stressors between subcommunities, which correlates with differential rates of health conditions, including elevated respiratory condition prevalence in subcommunities under greater pollution burden. Through an interventional mediation analysis we find that a substantial part of the excess subcommunity-level risk remains unexplained by measured environmental factors alone, consistent with a contribution of unmeasured shared exposures captured by IBD-based grouping. Subcommunity-level disparities persist in sensitivity analyses adjusting for self-reported race, indicating that IBD-based clustering captures health-relevant information beyond demographic categories commonly used as proxies for social determinants of health. We implement an open-source dashboard for interactive exploration of IBD-defined communities, disease prevalence, and environmental exposures. Together, we demonstrate that IBD-based clustering jointly captures genetic and environmental determinants of health, offering a scalable framework for precision health and population genetics that translates biobank data into actionable insights.

title: Parental genome reprogramming drives allelic convergence while preserving parent-of-origin memory during human early embryonic development
abstract: Human sperm and oocytes carry highly distinct DNA methylation landscapes, yet parental DNA methylation ultimately converges to a largely equivalent state, raising the question of when and how the allelic DNA methylome is reprogrammed toward convergence. Here, we present an integrated allelic analysis of DNA methylation and transcriptome dynamics throughout human pre- to peri-implantation development, a stage that lays the foundation for future development. We find that oocyte-specific hypermethylated regions retain maternal-biased DNA methylation asymmetry throughout early development, whereas paternal hypermethylation at sperm-specific regions is erased after fertilization and re-established during peri-implantation. Whole-genome parental DNA methylation levels converge across all lineages at embryonic days 8 to 12, prior to gastrulation, although the timing of this equilibrium differs among genomic elements. Notably, a subset of transposable elements, including SVAs and LTR12 elements, remains persistently maternally hypermethylated. Finally, we identify parent-of-origin-biased genes involved in early human embryonic development and find that these genes are enriched for dosage-sensitive genes. We further show that epiblast-specific parental expression bias is associated with genes implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders. These findings highlight the developmental and clinical relevance of allele-specific DNA methylation and transcription regulation during the earliest stages of human development.

title: Reconstruction of contact signals from repeated elements with Hicberg
abstract: Throughout evolution, genomes have acquired various repetitive elements, such as transposons, ribosomal DNA, duplicated genes, and tandem repeats. These sequences pose significant challenges to current high-throughput sequencing pipelines, which generate short reads that cannot be unambiguously mapped to reference genomes. We present an innovative algorithm, Hicberg, designed to leverage reads typically discarded by standard pipelines. Hicberg employs statistical inference coupled with probability distribution computation to accurately infer missing 3D contacts of repetitive elements within a genome from paired omic data, such as Hi-C data. Our results demonstrate that Hicberg provides new insights into the potential impact of repetitive elements on the spatial organization of genomes. Notably, we observed the positioning of molecular motors that create chromosomal loops associated with certain transposons in yeast. These findings underscore the importance of an integrative approach to better understand genomic complexity and pave the way for deeper explorations of repeated elements.

title: The divergent 3D genome landscapes of aging and neurodegenerative mouse models
abstract:
Chromatin structure is essential for gene regulation and genome stability, as neurons must preserve their 3D genome organization throughout life. This structure gradually deteriorates with aging and is further disrupted in neurodegenerative diseases. To investigate whether aging and neurodegeneration share early chromatin changes or diverge, we perform Hi-C on cortical neurons from adult, aged, and brain-specific
                     SIRT6 
                    -knockout (S6-KO) mice and compare them to the previously published Hi-C data sets from a CK-p25 Alzheimer's disease model stratified by γH2AX levels. All models show early features such as weakened interactions between chromosomes in expanded nuclei, A- to B-compartment shifts, and loss of architectural loops. However, aged neurons retain TAD prominence, short-range interactions, and enhancer–promoter loops, whereas pathological models showed reduced TAD prominence, shorter loops, and disorganized A–B mixing. These changes correlate with increased DNA damage. Our findings suggest that aging represents a “primed” state, in which chromatin regulation begins to erode, but further stressors like DNA damage are associated with progression toward neurodegenerative breakdown.

title: A tail of 2 proteins: the cytoplasmic tail of Cf receptor-like proteins modulates effector-triggered activation of cell death
abstract: Plant immune receptor proteins detect molecular signatures of pathogen infection to activate defense responses. Most receptor proteins belong to one of two groups: receptors at the cell surface survey the apoplast, while nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) receptors detect molecules which have been secreted by a pathogen and translocated into the host cell. Cell surface receptors share an extracellular, ligand-binding, “sensor” domain and a transmembrane domain. They can be further subdivided into receptor-like kinases (RLKs or RKs), which contain an intracellular kinase domain, and receptor-like proteins (RLPs or RPs), which lack a kinase domain and instead typically have a short intracellular C-terminal tail ( Fig. 1a ).

title: Conserved DEAD-box RNA helicases regulate RNA silencing and plant immunity and are targeted by a powdery mildew effector
abstract: Abstract RNA silencing is a conserved defense mechanism that protects plants against viruses, bacteria, fungi, and oomycetes. Although diverse pathogens have evolved effectors that suppress host RNA silencing, whether powdery mildew fungi exploit this strategy and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unknown. Here, we identify CSEP0004, a secreted effector from the barley powdery mildew fungus  Blumeria hordei , as an RNA silencing suppressor that promotes fungal virulence. CSEP0004 physically interacts with the evolutionarily conserved DEAD-box RNA helicases  Hordeum vulgare  RNA helicase 37 ( Hv RH37) and  Hv RH52. Genetic analyses demonstrate that  Hv RH37 and  Hv RH52 positively regulate chitin-triggered reactive oxygen species production, resistance to  B. hordei , and small RNA accumulation in barley, while their  Arabidopsis  homologs  At RH11/37/52 perform conserved functions in small RNA accumulation. Mechanistically,  Hv RH37 and  Hv RH52 are associated with  Hv AGO1, a core component of the RNA-induced silencing complex, and function as biochemically active RNA helicases capable of binding and unwinding double-stranded RNA. CSEP0004 disrupts the  Hv RH37/52–AGO1 association and inhibits  Hv RH37/52 helicase activity in a dose-dependent manner. Together, our findings uncover a previously unrecognized mechanism by which a fungal effector suppresses host RNA silencing through targeting conserved DDX3-like DEAD-box RNA helicases, establishing these helicases as key regulators of RNAi-mediated immunity and identifying RNA helicase-dependent RNA remodeling as a critical regulatory node exploited by fungal pathogens.

title: LMBD2 interacts with components of the ECH/YIP complex and contributes to post-Golgi trafficking in Arabidopsis
abstract: Abstract The plant cell wall, composed primarily of polysaccharides, is essential for normal plant growth and development. Many of these polysaccharides are synthesized within and subsequently secreted via the endomembrane system. Mutations in genes including  MURUS3  ( MUR3 ),  YPT / RAB GTPase - interacting protein 4 homologs  ( YIP4a/YIP4b ), and  ECHIDNA  ( ECH ) result in dwarf plants, which is believed to be a consequence of impaired cell wall polysaccharide secretion. Here, we identify a LMBR1 (Limb Development Membrane Protein 1)-like membrane protein (LMBD2) and find that loss of LMBD2 suppresses the secretion and growth defects in the  mur3 ,  yip4a yip4b , and  ech  mutants. LMBD2 localizes to the  trans -Golgi apparatus and  trans -Golgi network/early endosome, where it interacts with YIP4b and orchestrates  trans -Golgi network/early endosome-mediated trafficking. Furthermore, LMBD2 can competitively attenuate the interaction of YIP4b and ECH. Our findings establish LMBD2 as a component of endomembrane trafficking homeostasis in plant cells and offer new insights into endomembrane dynamics and their influence on plant development.

title:
Navigating deep learning-based
                     ab initio

Representation-aware conformal prediction for reliable uncertainty quantification in drug-target affinity
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Quantifying predictive uncertainty is essential for computational drug discovery to reduce experimental costs and false positives. However, most drug-target affinity (DTA) models focus on improving prediction accuracy without reliable uncertainty estimates. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     We propose representation-aware conformal prediction (RCP)-DTA, a representation-aware conformal prediction framework that constructs adaptive prediction intervals based on feature similarity. By constructing local calibration sets, our approach generates sample-specific prediction intervals that achieve empirical coverage close to the nominal confidence level. To improve representation quality, RCP-DTA employs a cross-modal architecture that integrates pretrained sequence representations and structural information. Binding site context is incorporated via virtual pocket feedback to enhance residue representations, followed by gated fusion for adaptive integration of sequence and structural modalities. Evaluations across multiple DTA benchmark datasets demonstrate that RCP-DTA achieves competitive affinity prediction performance while providing reliable uncertainty quantification. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     Code and data are available at: https://github.com/Lee515628/RCP-DTA

title: Letters and biological process: linguistic structure encodes hierarchical depth in the gene ontology
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     We asked whether the natural language used to name Gene Ontology (GO) Biological Process terms encodes hierarchical position in the GO directed acyclic graph. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     Semantic representations of term names, combined with Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection visualization and k-means clustering (k=20) recovered biologically coherent semantic groups whose depth distributions differed strongly (Kruskal–Wallis H=5244; p<10−300; η2=.217). Term-name length increased with depth (Pearson r = .34, Spearman ρ=0.37; slope =3.2 letters per level), and this positive scaling held under shortest-, longest-, and average-path depth definitions. Vocabulary entropy followed a bell-shaped diversification–specialization curve with an intermediate-depth peak (maximal at depth 4) that lies outside a Monte Carlo null envelope across most depths, and null-model tests supported a genuine linguistic–hierarchical association. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     The go_lingdepth Python package, regenerated result tables, and figure-generation scripts are available at https://github.com/Sadiya-ISU/Letters-and-Biological-Process and archived on Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21501473).

title: Efficient and scalable Python implementation of ANCOM-BC and ANCOM-BC2 for omics differential abundance testing
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Summary 
                     Analysis of Compositions of Microbiomes with Bias Correction (ANCOM-BC) and its successor ANCOM-BC2 are critical algorithms for differential abundance analysis. Designed for handling compositional data, they feature the ability to estimate the unknown sampling fractions and correct the bias induced by their differences. While the original R package implementing the two methods is robust for standard dataset sizes, the increasing magnitude of modern multiomics studies presents computational challenges, often resulting in a runtime bottleneck for high-dimensional data. Here, we present native Python implementations of both ANCOM-BC and ANCOM-BC2 in the scikit-bio package, significantly accelerating the workflow and enabling their application to large-scale datasets. By leveraging vectorization with NumPy and numerical optimization in SciPy, we enhanced the efficiency of both methods without compromising their statistical accuracy. The benchmarking results revealed a dramatic increase in performance in both simulated and real datasets. We demonstrated that our Python implementations generated test results matching the original R code, while achieving 380- and 147-fold faster runtimes and 97.4% and 96.2% lower memory consumption on the largest tested dataset, respectively. The Python implementations allow for the analysis of datasets that are significantly larger than previously possible, and enable applications to alternative omics data types and complex statistical models that vary greatly by the number of samples, features, and covariates. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and Implementation 
                     https://github.com/scikit-bio/scikit-bio

title: CryoTriplane: triplane-based neural radiance field representation for high-resolution cryo-EM 3D homogeneous reconstruction
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Determining the three-dimensional (3D) structure of proteins is a cornerstone of structural biology, providing essential insights into their underlying biological mechanisms and functional roles. Cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) single-particle analysis allows researchers to investigate biomolecules at near-atomic resolutions, unraveling the structure of biomolecular complexes. However, reconstructing high-fidelity 3D volumes from extremely noisy projections, particularly under the interference of structural heterogeneity, remains a challenging task. Traditional Fourier-domain methods often suffer from frequency-dependent signal attenuation and uneven information distribution. While recent deep-learning-based frameworks attempt to predict high-frequency components directly in frequency space, they are highly susceptible to noise and often introduce artifacts. State-of-the-art (SOTA) real-space method circumvents Fourier-domain defects, yet remains constrained by the inherent spectral bias of multi-layer perceptrons, as fixed positional encoding fails to sufficiently capture intricate high-frequency details. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     We propose cryoTriplane, a real-space 3D homogeneous reconstruction network that utilizes a hybrid spatial representation to adaptively capture fine structural details. By combining fixed positional encoding for noise-robust structural initialization with structure-aware positional encoding for high-frequency refinement, our method achieves 3D reconstructions that are simultaneously globally consistent and locally fine-grained. Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative evaluations across five simulated and four real-world datasets demonstrate that cryoTriplane significantly outperforms existing methods in resolving fine structural features. Furthermore, validation through downstream atomic modeling underscores cryoTriplane’s ability to recover high-quality density maps. Specifically, our method achieves sequence coverage improvements of 4.6% and 5.5% on the EMPIAR-10005 and EMPIAR-10492 datasets over the SOTA approach, respectively. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     Our code is available at https://github.com/chengyr1999/CryoTriplane. The real datasets used in this study are publicly available from EMPIAR.

title: Inverse probability weighting-based mediation analysis for microbiome data
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Mediation analysis is an important tool for elucidating causal mechanisms in biomedical research and has recently gained increasing attention in microbiome studies. Motivated by a microbiome study of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) patients, we investigate whether the effect of induction chemotherapy (IC) intensity on infection status is mediated through gut microbial taxa. This problem poses substantial methodological challenges due to the high dimensionality, zero inflation, and dependence of microbial mediators, as well as the presence of an exposure-induced mediator–outcome confounder, antibiotic use. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     To address these challenges, we propose a novel nonparametric identification formula for the interventional indirect effect, a causal mediation estimand that remains identifiable in the presence of exposure-induced mediator–outcome confounding. Building on this identification result, we develop an inverse probability-weighting estimator and construct standard normal bootstrap confidence intervals for inference. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed method achieves accurate effect estimation and maintains appropriate type I error rates and power in finite samples. Application to the AML microbiome study provides evidence of a statistically significant interventional indirect effect of IC intensity on infection risk through alterations in the gut microbiome. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     The R code for the simulation studies is available at https://github.com/YX-ZHANG-1/CausalMediationMicrobiome and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21960802

title: Seumetry: a versatile and comprehensive R toolkit to accelerate high-dimensional flow and mass cytometry data analysis
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Recent progress in flow and mass cytometry technologies enables the simultaneous measurement of over 50 parameters for an individual cell. The resulting increase in data volume and complexity present challenges for conventional analysis methods, which are based on manual gating, are time-consuming and fail to capture unknown or minor cell populations. Advances in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) technologies have prompted the development of computational analysis tools designed to process and analyze high-dimensional biological data. Building on these advances, we here present Seumetry, a framework that combines flow and mass cytometry data-specific analysis methods with the capabilities of Seurat, a powerful tool for the analysis of scRNAseq data. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     Seumetry offers methods for advanced quality control, data visualizations, and differential population abundance and protein expression analysis. We tested Seumetry on an in-house generated complex dataset of immune cells from different layers of human intestines, demonstrating that Seumetry accurately identifies distinct immune cell populations. Furthermore, benchmarking against public datasets showed that Seumetry aligns with manual-gated results, further validating its use for high-dimensional flow and mass cytometry data. In summary, Seumetry provides a new scalable framework for the comprehensive analysis of high-dimensional cytometry data with seamless integration into commonly used scRNAseq analysis tools, enabling in-depth analysis methods to facilitate biological interpretations. 
                   
                   
                     Availability 
                     Seumetry code is available open source under an MIT license and the current version can be viewed and used via Github: https://github.com/imsb-uke/Seumetry; and archived on Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21216681. Flow cytometry data generated for this manuscript is available via Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.11935872.

title: In This Issue
The companion website
Near-infrared photochromic miniprotein enables photoacoustic molecular imaging of acute inflammation and intracellular antigens
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Using near-infrared photoswitchable photochromic genetically encoded probes, differential photoacoustic tomography (PAT) enables deep-tissue imaging with high resolution and sensitivity; however, current bacteriophytochrome-based probes are bulky multidomain proteins exceeding 55 kDa, which constrains their use for designing PAT molecular reporters. Here we engineer rsmiRFPnano, a compact cyanobacteriochrome-derived photoswitchable PAT probe. With a molecular weight below 19 kDa, rsmiRFPnano efficiently incorporates biliverdin, exhibits high extinction coefficients in both photochromic states and demonstrates robust performance in live cells. We established rsmiRFPnano-based reporters for NF-κB and AP-1 pathways, which display low basal activity and strong activation-dependent responses. These reporters effectively visualized acute inflammation using noninvasive PAT in vivo, further validated through cellular-level spatial omics mapping. We then created photoswitchable nanobody probes, rsNIR-Fbs, stabilized upon antigen binding and rapidly degraded otherwise, enabling selective photoacoustic immuno-imaging of intracellular antigens in vivo. Together, these results establish rsmiRFPnano as an ultracompact and versatile platform for molecular PAT.

abstract: Short Summary: This study demonstrates that circadian clock proteins PRR5, PRR7, and PRR9 function in auxin-enhanced ABA responses during seed germination. These PRR proteins interact and synergize with ARF10/ARF16 to stimulate ABI5 transcription and its enrichment at downstream target promoters, while coordinately enhancing the ABA-induced accumulation of ABI5. These findings reveal a molecular mechanism linking the circadian clock, auxin, and ABA pathways.

title: The unexpected case of strigolactones in rice acclimation to drought
Marked for protection: ac4C guides mRNAs into stress granules during heat stress
abstract: Rising global temperatures and increasingly frequent heat events pose a major threat to crop productivity and food security. Heat stress disrupts plant physiological and metabolic processes, compromising growth, development, and ultimately yield (Lesk et al. 2021). Understanding the molecular mechanisms that allow plants to withstand elevated temperatures is therefore increasingly important for improving crop resilience. Post-transcriptional regulation provides plants with a rapid means of reshaping gene expression during stress.

title: Dual-mode dynamics in hippocampal populations enable rapid and precise spatial coding
abstract: Ren et al. show that hippocampal spatial maps emerge through a dual-mode cellular architecture. Crucially, offline network dynamics prospectively organize both a stable neural backbone for immediate spatial coding and experience-dependent cells that progressively refine the map.

title: The chytrid fungus threatens the last epidemiologically naive Neotropical montane amphibian biodiversity hotspot
abstract: Plewnia et al. identify the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta as a major epidemiologically naive refuge from the amphibian chytrid fungus. Environmental modeling and infection trials reveal high vulnerability to invasion, thus highlighting the urgent need for biosecurity to protect this exceptionally diverse and endemic amphibian community.

title: A high-dimensional population code in the bat motor cortex during natural dexterous flight
abstract: Bats use their hand-like wings to reproduce natural flights with wingbeat-level precision. Rather than mainly tracking the wingbeat cycle, the wing motor cortex generates sparse, distinct population states with little shared variance across wingbeats, resulting in a high-dimensional code distinct from that typically observed in constrained tasks.

title: Mechanisms of transcription control by distal enhancers from single-gene nanoscopy
abstract: High-resolution real-time imaging of enhancer-promoter communication reveals how the two genomic loci are actively brought together through cohesin-mediated loop extrusion and how E-P interactions are temporally coordinated with transcriptional bursts. Unexpectedly, components of the RNA Pol II general machinery form nanoscale clusters at distal enhancers, and embedding the promoter into such clusters boosts GTF activities and triggers burst initiation.

title: PTPRS mediates invasion of tetanus neurotoxin into the central nervous system
abstract: Tetanus neurotoxin enters the central nervous system through motor neurons. This study identifies PTPRS as the long-sought retrograde transport receptor that directs toxin trafficking in motor neurons into the spinal cord, uncovering a host pathway that can be targeted for post-exposure treatment and for drug delivery into the central nervous system.

title: Rare k-mers reveal centromere haplogroups underlying human diversity and cancer translocations
abstract: By defining centromere haplogroups from rare k-mer variation, Shiraishi et al. uncover extensive hidden diversity and link centromere structure to human evolution and disease-associated genomic instability.

title: A Clinical Study of Decellularized Tissue Engineering Hyaline Cartilage Graft (dLhCG) for Articular Cartilage Repair
abstract:
ABSTRACT 
                   Current clinical approaches for knee cartilage repair are often limited by hypertrophy and fibrosis in the regenerated tissues. A decellularized tissue‐engineered hyaline cartilage graft (dLhCG), composed of a type II collagen‐based extracellular matrix, has been developed to overcome this limitation. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated the ability of dLhCG to achieve hyaline cartilage repair and maintain a stable hyaline phenotype. In this prospective, first‐in‐human, exploratory clinical study (ChiCTR2400094194, ChiCTR2500100526, and ChiCTR2500105847), dLhCG was implanted to treat full‐thickness knee articular cartilage defects (Outerbridge grade III/IV) in 17 patients. Stable graft integration with the surrounding native tissue was observed up to 18 months postoperatively. Significant improvements were noted in clinical outcome scores and MOCART scores. MRI T2 mapping evaluated as the ratio of repair‐tissue echo time to adjacent healthy cartilage, yielded values approaching 1, suggesting hyaline‐like biochemical and structural characteristics. No serious clinical adverse events were reported; asymptomatic imaging abnormalities, including bone marrow edema, were noted in some cases. These findings provide preliminary evidence of the feasibility, short‐term safety, and encouraging outcomes of dLhCG for hyaline‐like cartilage repair, warranting further investigation in controlled clinical trials.

title: Sparse neuronal C4 elevation induces network-wide transcriptomic and lipid-droplet remodeling in the cortical microenvironment
abstract:
The complement component C4 regulates synaptic refinement and plasticity in the brain and has been implicated in multiple neurological and psychiatric disorders, with especially strong genetic evidence linking elevated
                     C4A 
                    expression to schizophrenia. However, it remains unclear whether localized C4 elevation in a small neuronal population is sufficient to reshape broader cortical gene-regulatory programs and cellular phenotypes. To address this question, we overexpressed mouse
                     C4 
                    in approximately 2% of prefrontal cortical neurons using in utero electroporation and performed bulk RNA sequencing on microdissected prefrontal cortex. Despite the sparse manipulation, C4-OE was associated with broad transcriptional remodeling across tissue composed predominantly of untransfected cells, including coordinated changes in cholesterol biosynthesis, axon- and synaptic-associated programs, vascular/ECM pathways, and immune- and stress-related responses. Comparison with a schizophrenia synaptic proteomic dataset identified limited global correspondence but selective gene- and pathway-level overlap in specific molecular programs. Reference-based projection of directional DEG signatures onto a cortical single-cell transcriptomic reference further identified cell-type-associated structure, including prominent astrocyte- and vascular-associated axes and distinct lipid/metabolic, vascular/endothelial–interferon-associated, and immune/stress correlation domains. Spatial validation with MFISH showed increased
                     Hmgcr 
                    expression in neighboring GFP-negative cells, while PLIN2 imaging revealed increased DAPI-associated/perinuclear lipid-droplet burden within the local C4-OE field. Together, these findings support a model in which sparse neuronal C4 elevation is associated with broader remodeling of the local cortical environment, including a non-cell-autonomous component involving neighboring-cell lipid-associated responses. These results expand the interpretation of C4 risk biology beyond synapse elimination alone and suggest that focal immune-gene dysregulation can engage lipid-homeostatic, stress-related, and cell-type-associated transcriptional programs relevant to cortical circuit vulnerability.

title: Identification of letters distorted by physiologically-inspired spatial scrambling
abstract:
In the geniculostriate pathway of the human visual system, neuronal projections carry signals from a particular retinal locus in parallel from one anatomical area to the next. Imprecision in the fidelity of these projections would place constraints on the ability of the system to perform tasks requiring positional information. We investigated the impact that “spatial scrambling” between stages would have on visual performance. We consider two stages in a simple canonical model of the early visual cortex where scrambling might occur: either the input to the first orientation-tuned mechanisms (analogous to V1 simple cells), or the output from those mechanisms. These are referred as “subcortical” (SCS) and “cortical scrambling” (CS). We developed a wavelet decomposition and resynthesis algorithm to mimic these effects, and measured human performance in letter identification affected by the two types of scrambling. Our results showed SCS and CS have distinguishable effects on both perceived noisiness of letters and letter identification threshold. Comparing human performance against a suite of pre-trained and custom convolutional neural networks (CNNs) that were trained on the scrambled stimuli, relative efficiency (calculated from the ratio of human:CNN thresholds) is higher for CS than SCS. However, in modelling human inefficiency by reducing the proportion of wavelets available to the CNNs, humans are
                     less 
                    efficient in CS than SCS. These differences in efficiencies show humans are better at processing orientation redundant stimuli (CS) than orientation noisy stimuli (SCS). We hypothesize this reflects differences in integration properties at the input and output stages of simple cells in the cortex.

title: Latent encoding of movement in primary visual cortex
abstract: Neurons in the primary visual cortex (V1) are classically thought to encode spatial features of visual stimuli through simple population codes: each neuron exhibits a preferred orientation and preferred spatial frequency, both of which remaining invariant to other aspects of the visual stimulus. Here, we show that this simple rule does not apply to the representation of major features of stimulus motion, including stimulus direction and temporal frequency (TF). We collected an extensive dataset of cat V1 responses to stimuli covarying in orientation, direction, spatial frequency, and TF to assess the extent of motion selectivity. We show that preferred TF is mostly uniform across the cortical surface. Yet, in over half of V1, the preferred direction is reversed with changing stimulus TF, revealing four distinct map motifs embedded in V1’s functional architecture. Similarly, despite the lack of spatial modulation for the preferred TF map and the lack of invariance for the preferred direction map, we found using convolutional neural networks that direction, TF and stimulus speed can be accurately decoded from V1 responses at all cortical locations. These findings suggest a latent encoding of information where subtle, spatially distributed modulations of V1 activity may convey fine information about stimulus motion, pointing to a novel primary sensory encoding mechanism despite complex co-variation of responses to multiple attributes across V1 neurons.

title: Understanding cell fate decisions with temporal attention
abstract: Understanding non-genetic determinants of cell fate is critical for developing and improving cancer therapies, as genetically identical cells can exhibit divergent outcomes under the same treatment conditions. In this work, we present a deep learning approach for cell fate prediction from raw long-term live-cell recordings of cancer cell populations under chemotherapeutic treatment. Our Transformer model is trained to predict cell fate directly from raw image sequences, without relying on predefined morphological or molecular features. Beyond classification, we introduce a comprehensive explainability framework for interpreting the temporal and morphological cues guiding the model’s predictions. We demonstrate that prediction of cell outcomes is possible based on the video only, our model achieves balanced accuracy of 0.94 and an F1-score of 0.93. Attention and masking experiments further indicate that the signal predictive of the cell fate is not uniquely located in the final frames of a cell trajectory, as reliable predictions are possible up to 8 h before the event. Our analysis reveals distinct temporal distribution of predictive information in the mitotic and apoptotic sequences, as well as the role of cell morphology and p53 signaling in determining cell outcomes. Together, these findings demonstrate that attention-based temporal models enable accurate cell fate prediction while providing biologically interpretable insights into non-genetic determinants of cellular decision-making.

title: Antimony 3: Extending human-readable model definitions for SBML Level 3 Core and Packages
abstract:
Antimony is a human-readable language for defining and sharing models developed by the systems biology community. It enables scientists to describe biochemical networks with a simple syntax, while supporting seamless conversion to and from the Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML) community standard. Since Antimony’s original release, both SBML and modeling practices have evolved significantly, creating a need to update Antimony to maintain its standards compliance and practical relevance. In this paper, we introduce Antimony 3, a comprehensive update that formalizes its cumulative improvements and extends its support for SBML Level 3 Core and Flux Balance Constraints (FBC), Distributions, Layout, and Render packages. Antimony 3 enables model specifications that combine kinetic reactions with flux balance analysis, represent uncertainty using probability distributions, add biological context through annotations, and define publication-ready visualizations, all within a unified plain-text format. Antimony 3 is delivered as a lightweight C/C++ library with a stable C API. It is available through official bindings for Python, Julia, and JavaScript/WebAssembly, as well as a cross-platform desktop GUI, which enables straightforward use across scripting environments, desktop applications, and browser-based tools. Antimony 3 is released as open-source software under the BSD 3-Clause License and is available at
                     https://github.com/sys-bio/antimony 
                    .

title: Surface proteomics reveals arginine metabolism as a vulnerability in high grade serous ovarian cancer
GraTools, a user-friendly tool for exploring and manipulating pangenome variation graphs
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Background 
                     Pangenome variation graphs (PVGs) are powerful tools for studying genomic variations in populations, as they represent genomic diversity through multiple genome alignments. However, current tools often lack integration and efficiency, and require format conversions to be used, which hinders their usability. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     Here, we introduce GraTools, a fast and user-friendly command-line tool for manipulating PVGs using the original GFA file, which is part of the GraSuite [1]. After a one-time graph import, GraTools enables the rapid extraction of subgraphs, retrieval of FASTA sequences, and the performance of comprehensive analyses, including the calculation of the core/dispensable genome ratio or the identification of group-specific segments. Importing the data results in conversion to standard formats (BAM/BED), enabling the reuse of well-optimised existing tools and allowing efficient storage and querying of large, complex PVG data structures. Scalability is ensured by a modular architecture that supports parallel processing and asynchronous I/O operations. GraTools supports coordinates defined on the primary reference and alternative genomes within the graph without re-import, and its outputs can be easily visualised or manipulated using external tools. Using an Asian rice pangenome graph comprising 13 accessions, we demonstrate GraTools' ability to easily extract subgraphs, compute depth statistics and identify subspecies-specific segments. Its intuitive command-line interface, real-time execution feedback, and detailed logging system make this tool suitable for a wide range of applications, from population genetics to breeding and genomic medicine, for biologists and bioinformaticians alike. 
                   
                   
                     Conclusions 
                     
                      Through its unified graph manipulation interface, GraTools offers an interesting alternative to existing tools for manipulating PVGs, facilitating rapid, efficient, and flexible downstream analyses. GraTools is available as an open-source tool (GNU GPLv3), and its documentation can be found at
                       https://gratools.readthedocs.io 
                      .

title: Grazing reshapes plant nitrogen use trade‐off between soil uptake and internal remobilization
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   
                    Perennial plants rely on two key ecological strategies to supply nitrogen (N) for photosynthetic tissue construction: root N remobilization (internal cycling) and soil N uptake. How plants trade‐off these strategies determines the economy of N use and is likely context‐dependent. Yet, it is rarely quantified
                     in situ 
                    across growth stages and under varying management, limiting the mechanistic understanding of how plants rebalance N‐use trade‐offs to adapt to grazing disturbance. To address this gap, we conducted an
                     in situ 
                    experiment using
                     15 
                    N isotope labelling techniques in a semiarid grassland to quantify the contributions of these two strategies at two plant growth stages under nil, summer or autumn grazing. We found that the plant relied more on soil N uptake (58%) during the regreen stage, but more on N remobilization (57%) during the rapid‐growth stage. Grazing, especially in autumn, significantly leaned N use trade‐off toward conservative N remobilization. The shift in plant N use strategies was driven primarily by plant growth demand and soil N supply, but not root N stock. Plant N use trade‐off leaned toward internal cycling when source traits were below or sink traits were above the thresholds, for example, soil N availability <9.0 mg kg
                     −1 
                    or shoot carbon content >41.88%. Our study highlights the importance of the N resource‐sink relations in mediating the trade‐off in plant N use strategies, buffering grazing stress to grassland plants. These findings provide a mechanistic basis for improving ecosystem N cycling modeling and adaptive grazing management.

title: Repeated genetic adaptation under demographic limits in kiwifruit
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   
                    Population genetic theory predicts that species with narrow geographic distributions experience stronger genetic drift, higher inbreeding, and greater mutational burden than their widespread relatives, yet how demographic history shapes the genomic basis of adaptation remains poorly understood. We hypothesized that (i) restricted‐range species exhibit reduced genetic diversity, elevated inbreeding, and greater mutation load owing to smaller long‐term effective population sizes; (ii) despite these demographic constraints, shared environmental pressures can still drive repeated adaptation; (iii) repeated adaptation may arise through ancestral standing genetic variation, adaptive introgression, or independent
                     de novo 
                    mutations. We tested these hypotheses using two kiwifruit species,
                     Actinidia hemsleyana 
                    (narrow‐ranged) and
                     Actinidia eriantha 
                    (widespread), which differ markedly in demographic history and range size but occupy overlapping environments in subtropical China. We show that demographic contraction and inbreeding have eroded genome‐wide diversity in the range‐restricted species, accompanied by a substantially higher load of deleterious mutations. Despite these contrasting demographic legacies, both species exhibit repeated genomic responses to shared climatic gradients, with adaptation targeting similar genes. Such repeated adaptation was driven primarily by ancestral standing variation, with smaller contributions from adaptive introgression and only limited evidence for independent
                     de novo 
                    mutations. These results reveal that demographic constraints shape genome‐wide diversity and mutation load but do not preclude repeated adaptation when shared genetic variation remains available.

title: Plasticity of metabolism in plants
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   The ability of plants to reprogram their metabolism in response to fluctuating environments, referred to as metabolic plasticity, is a key feature that enables sessile organisms to maintain growth, survival, and reproduction under changing conditions. As a mechanistic component of phenotypic plasticity, metabolic plasticity can buffer environmental perturbations and confer adaptive advantages. However, despite growing evidence for extensive metabolic remodeling under stress, the genetic and regulatory basis of this plasticity remains incompletely understood. Here, we review metabolic plasticity across major metabolic domains in plants, with emphasis on carbon, nitrogen, photorespiratory, and lipid metabolism, emphasizing how environmental cues and genetic regulation jointly shape metabolic responses. We conclude that, although metabolic plasticity is widespread in plants, its mechanistic and genetic basis remains incompletely understood; population‐scale studies and mathematical modeling offer promising avenues to resolve this gap and extend current insights from model systems to crops.

title:
A rapid and efficient
                     in planta 
                    assay for assessment of RNA editing factor performance
abstract:
SUMMARY 
                   
                    Land plant mitochondria and plastids are endosymbiotic organelles that possess their own, reduced genomes. Gene expression is largely regulated at the transcript level, predominantly by nuclear‐encoded proteins. Notably, up to thousands of cytidines in organellar RNAs are specifically edited to uridines, mostly restoring conserved genetic information. Key players in this process are nuclear‐encoded pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins, which bind target RNAs in a one‐PPR:one‐nucleotide manner, following a two‐amino‐acid‐based code. Cytidine deamination is catalyzed by intrinsic or trans
                     ‐ 
                    acting DYW domains. The modularity and programmability of PPR‐RNA interactions make PPR editing factors attractive candidates for the development of biotechnological tools. However, RNA target selection is not determined by the ‘PPR code’ alone, hampering the generation of highly effective and specific editors. Refining such tools requires efficient assays to dissect the determinants of editor‐RNA interaction. Here, we introduce a rapid assay to assess PPR editor specificity through transient expression in the cytosol of
                     Nicotiana benthamiana 
                    , which offers a large and diverse transcriptome that enables extensive off‐target editing. Profiling of these off‐targets provides comprehensive information on an editor's target selectivity. Compared with a previous setup in the model moss
                     Physcomitrium patens 
                    , which relies on stable transformation, the required experimental time is reduced from months to days. We demonstrate the power of the system by characterizing the off‐targets of the moss editor PpPPR56. The new assay allows rapid functional assessment of editing factor variants and removes a bottleneck in understanding editor‐RNA interactions, which is a prerequisite for the rational improvement of PPR‐based RNA editing tools.

title: Ten rules for robust taxonomy in ecological datasets
abstract:
Summary 
                   Accurate taxonomy, including species identification and naming, underpins ecological inference, yet taxonomic information in ecological datasets is often inconsistently recorded or weakly standardized. With the increasing integration of ecological datasets across taxa and regions, datasets with poor taxonomic practices can hinder data exchange and propagate errors. We propose 10 rules to improve the storage and management of taxonomic information in ecological datasets. These rules draw on our experiences in plant ecology and taxonomy, but the conclusions may be generalized to other organisms and disciplines. They emphasize aspects from species identification to the permanent storage of verifiable records (e.g. voucher specimens) and include taxonomic standardization, nomenclature, validation, and updating. We also address the treatment of morphotypes and incomplete identifications, the use of automated name‐matching tools, and (meta)data standards. Closer collaboration between ecologists and taxonomists is key to ensuring more robust datasets. The application of these rules consumes more time and resources, but they enhance data quality and interoperability, saving time during data integration and improving the reliability and scalability of ecological research.

title:
Excess endopolyploidy associated with cellular defects in neo‐autotetraploid
                     Arabidopsis arenosa 
                    is in part corrected by a naturally evolved allele of
                     CYCD3;2
abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         
                          Endopolyploidy (within‐organism polyploidy) is an often‐beneficial aspect of development. But polyploids, which have a higher baseline genome content, have been reported to have less endoreduplication than diploid relatives. Why has remained unclear; we explored this in
                           Arabidopsis arenosa. 
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          We measured endopolyploidy levels and phenotyped cellular traits, comparing diploids, neo‐autotetraploids, and established autotetraploids of
                           A. arenosa 
                          . We used a genetic approach to ask whether
                           CYCD3;2 
                          , a polyploidy regulator with evidence of selection in tetraploids, might be responsible for endopolyploidy‐related phenotypic differences between neo‐ and established polyploids, and whether there are associated costs.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                          Neo‐tetraploids had the most 16C and 32C cells, whereas established tetraploids have proportions of 16C and 32C cells comparable to diploids. Tetraploid plants homozygous for a novel allele of
                           CYCD3;2 
                          have reduced endopolyploidy compared to homozygotes for the diploid allele and, surprisingly, also show cellular defects seen in neo‐tetraploids. Suggesting this link is specific, we find that
                           A. thaliana cycd3;2 
                          mutants have not only increased endopolyploidy but also root hair defects like neo‐tetraploids.
                         
                       
                       
                         Our results suggest reverting endopolyploidy in polyploids to diploid‐like levels could be advantageous, and that one driver might be cellular defects that arise with excess high‐ploidy cells.

title:
Avirulence genes of
