abstract:
Summary 
                   
                     
                       
                         
                          We examined the frequency of and variation in eight avirulence (
                           AVR 
                          ) genes from 840
                           Magnaporthe oryzae 
                          field isolates collected from the Southern United States relative to rice resistance (
                           R 
                          ) genes deployed from 1959 to 2017. Little coding or noncoding variation was detected in
                           AVR‐Pi9 
                          ,
                           AVR‐Pib 
                          ,
                           ACE1 
                          and
                           AVR‐Pizt

                           R

                          In the United States,
                           AVR‐Pik 
                          , corresponding to rice
                           R 
                          gene
                           Pi‐k 
                          alleles deployed at varying levels since the late 1960s, was present in 37% of the isolates over six decades.
                           AVR‐Pita1 
                          , corresponding to
                           Pi‐ta 
                          deployed in the late 1990s, reached a low point in the 5‐yr period following
                           Pi‐ta

                          Our results suggest a fitness penalty for
                           M. oryzae 
                          isolates carrying nonfunctional AVR variants and provide concrete data on how changes in plant
                           R 
                          gene composition can impact pathogen populations. These findings will inform localized strategies for
                           R 
                          gene usage and durable control of blast disease.
                         
                       
                       
                         
                           AVR

title: TaANT11‐4A enhances grain yield by orchestrating photosynthesis and carbohydrate metabolism through direct transcriptional activation
authors:
Pengpeng Zhang, 
Jingjing Wen, 
Shan Gao, 
Jiajun Ma, 
Jiahui Jin, 
Xiaofei Ma, 
Wen‐Ting Liu, 
Juan Li, 
De‐Jun Han, 
Yue‐Qiang Zhang, 
Kun‐Ming Chen
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                    The AINTEGUMENTA (ANT) transcription factor family plays important roles in floral organogenesis and plant development; however, the mechanisms by which ANT proteins regulate yield remain unclear. Here, we conducted a genome‐wide search and identified 64
                     ANT 
                    genes in the wheat genome. Association analysis of yield‐related traits in 403 wheat accessions revealed that
                     ANT 
                    family genes were significantly associated with grain size and weight. Among these genes,
                     TaANT11‐4A 
                    showed a strong association with yield‐related traits. Three single‐nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) near
                     TaANT11‐4A 
                    modulated its expression and defined two haplotypes.
                     TaANT11‐4A 
                     
                       Hap2 
                     
                    was identified as an elite allele associated with increased grain size. Overexpression of
                     TaANT11‐4A 
                    significantly increased grain size and overall plant biomass, largely owing to higher photosynthetic rates and increased activities of key enzymes involved in photosynthesis and carbohydrate metabolism in the transgenic plants. Further analyses demonstrated that TaANT11‐4A directly binds to and activates
                     TaEGY2 
                    ,
                     TaAAE1 
                    , and
                     TaAAE2 
                    , which are involved in photosynthesis and carbohydrate metabolism. Consistent with these findings, knockout of
                     TaEGY2 
                    reduced grain size and yield, whereas overexpression of
                     TaEGY2 
                    or
                     TaAAE2 
                    increased these traits relative to the wild type (WT). Collectively, our results demonstrate that TaANT family proteins, particularly
                     TaANT11‐4A 
                    , are key regulators of wheat grain size and yield through the direct transcriptional activation of genes that coordinate photosynthesis and carbohydrate metabolism.

title:
Whole-genome duplication reshapes gene–miRNA regulatory networks underlying improved salt stress tolerance in
                     Medicago sativa
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Whole-genome duplication (WGD) is a recurrent feature of plant evolution and crop improvement, yet its direct contribution to abiotic stress tolerance remains difficult to disentangle from hybridization effects. Using full-sibling diploid (2x) and neotetraploid (4x) Medicago sativa genotypes generated through bilateral sexual polyploidization, we investigated how WGD alone reshapes physiological performance and gene–miRNA regulatory networks under salt stress. Neotetraploid plants displayed enhanced tolerance to salinity, maintaining higher chlorophyll content, stomatal conductance, and shoot integrity, alongside reduced visual damage compared with diploid siblings. Transcriptome profiling revealed that ploidy level, rather than salt treatment per se, was the dominant driver of gene expression variation. Indeed, WGD resulted in extensive and largely constitutive transcriptional reprogramming, with more than 2,000 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) distinguishing 4x from 2x plants under both control and saline conditions. By contrast, under salt stress, 705 DEGs specifically differentiated tetraploids from diploids and were enriched in receptor-like kinases, phosphorylation pathways, ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis, flavonoid biosynthesis, and WRKY- and MYB-centered regulatory modules. Co-expression network analysis identified salt-associated modules linking signaling and antioxidant pathways with stress-related physiological traits. Small RNA sequencing further showed that WGD reshapes post-transcriptional regulation, with limited salt-induced miRNA changes but the emergence of ploidy-dependent miRNA hubs, including miR2593e and a novel miRNA, targeting signaling and defense-related genes. We hypothesize that WGD establishes a stress-ready regulatory architecture in which coordinated transcriptional and post-transcriptional network rebalancing acts as a buffering system that improves alfalfa physiological performance under salinity, without strong induction of canonical salt-responsive genes.

title:
The transcription factor EIL1-MYB78 module negatively regulates cold tolerance in
                     Actinidia chinensis
abstract: Abstract Kiwifruit has become an important horticultural crop widely planted in temperate and subtropical regions. However, most commercially cultivated kiwifruit, particularly those of  Actinidia chinensis , are highly sensitive to cold stress. To overcome this industrial bottleneck, it is crucial to reveal the molecular mechanisms behind cold stress responses, ultimately providing new insights into the breeding of cold-tolerant kiwifruit varieties. Here, we found that EIL1 negatively regulates cold tolerance of  A. chinensis  by directly binding to the promoters of  CBF1  and  CBF2  to inhibit their expression. Besides, we found that EIL1 interacted and synergized with MYB78 to negatively regulate cold tolerance in  A. chinensis . Further evidence suggested that the interaction between EIL1 and MYB78 enhanced the transcriptional repression activity of both proteins on  CBF1  and  CBF2 . Therefore, we conclude that the EIL1-MYB78 module negatively regulates cold tolerance by directly inhibiting the expression of  CBF1  and  CBF2  genes in  A. chinensis .

title: PUCHI controls MYB94 and MYB96 to form the root cap cuticle of developing lateral roots
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Lateral root organogenesis underlies root branching and plays a key role in plant root system architecture. While the transcriptional and hormonal control of lateral root development has been extensively studied over the past decades, an increasing number of studies highlight the importance of specific metabolic pathways contributing to the lateral root regulatory network. The AP2/ERF transcription factor PUCHI has recently been shown to orchestrate the induction of very-long-chain fatty acid biosynthesis in developing lateral root primordia. In parallel, a root cap cuticle, reminiscent of the very-long-chain fatty acid–rich cuticle covering the emerging primary root, was shown to cover developing lateral root primordia and facilitate their emergence. Here, we demonstrate that PUCHI plays an essential role in lateral root cap cuticle formation. We identified the transcription factors MYB94 and MYB96 as key intermediates in this PUCHI-dependent, cuticle regulatory network. Similar to PUCHI, MYB94 and MYB96 induce the expression of a set of very-long-chain fatty acid- and cutin–related genes in lateral root primordia. The loss of function of either PUCHI or that of MYB94 and MYB96 compromises lateral root cuticle deposition, delays lateral root emergence, and alters the expression pattern of lateral root meristematic genes. These results shed light on a PUCHI- and MYB94 and MYB96-dependent regulatory network controlling the lateral root cap cuticle formation and influencing lateral root primordium development and emergence.

title: Global hotspots and trends of ecological water scarcity in river basins
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Healthy freshwater ecosystems are crucial for sustainable development, yet they face growing threats from unsustainable water use. However, current water scarcity metrics focus almost exclusively on human demand, overlooking whether sufficient water remains to sustain ecosystems. We address this gap by presenting the first evaluation of ecological water scarcity (EWS) across 1,182 river basins, introducing a novel indicator that recognizes ecosystems as legitimate water users to those of humans. Our findings reveal that in the 2000s, 412 basins (35% globally; 17% annual, 18% seasonal) experienced EWS, with affected areas expanding by 10 million km² since the 1950s. Human intervention intensified EWS in 13% of basins and caused 53% of seasonal and 60% of annual EWS cases. By the 2050s, affected basins range from 392 under RCP2.6–SSP1 to 416 under RCP8.5–SSP5, with persistent hotspots in regions of intensive water use. These findings show that climate mitigation can reduce future EWS risk, but environmental flow protection, water-use efficiency, water recycling, ecologically informed infrastructure operation and ecosystem restoration are also needed to safeguard freshwater ecosystems.

title: Air-gap engineering enabled ultrafast 9-bit ferroelectric semi-gate transistor array for high-efficiency image denoising
abstract:
Abstract 
                   The insufficient lateral electric field gradient limits the programming/erasing speed of conventional semi-floating gate transistors, while charge leakage leads to poor data retention and compromised operating characteristics. Here we design a ferroelectric semi-gate (FSG) transistor featuring a triangular air gap adjacent to the drain region. The device exhibits an as-programmed on–off ratio exceeding 107, remaining above 105 after 11 weeks, and a memory window of approximately 6 V. The localized lateral electric field accelerates program and erase operations to 60 ns and 75 ns, respectively. The spontaneous polarization field of the ferroelectric HfZrO layer strengthens charge retention in the HfO2 charge-trapping layer, enabling robust nonvolatile memory performance with a retention time exceeding 106 s. This synergistic integration of air-gap engineering and ferroelectric polarization yields an optimal trade-off between speed, retention and multilevel operation. By exploiting its superior multilevel capability with 9-bit distinguishable current states, we realize Ising-model-based image denoising using a 32 × 32 transistor array. These FSG transistors show promising potential for high-speed, low-power random-access memory applications.

PDEformer-2: a versatile foundation model for two-dimensional partial differential equations
abstract:
Abstract 
                   Partial differential equations (PDEs) are fundamental to modeling physical systems. Traditional PDE solvers are often computationally expensive. Neural operators require independent training for different PDEs, and tend to be data-greedy when adapted to new scenarios. To this end, we introduce PDEformer-2, a versatile foundation model for solving diverse two-dimensional PDEs. The model receives the PDE form as input through a flexible computational graph representation and outputs solutions that can be queried at any spatio-temporal point. Pretrained on a 40 TB dataset spanning varied equation types, domains, boundary conditions, variable counts, and time dependence, PDEformer-2 enables instant zero-shot predictions for familiar PDEs and adapts faster to unseen ones than specialized baselines, achieving lower errors with limited samples. It also facilitates efficient inverse problem solving, successfully recovering unknown PDE parameters, including scalar coefficients and fields, in experiments.

title: Evolution and metabolite signaling of fumarases (class I and II): origin, function, and subcellular targeting
abstract:
Abstract 
                   This study explores the evolutionary origins of class I and II fumarases across the tree of life, focusing on the prevalence and phylogenetic patterns of their enzymes. Using a dataset of ∼21,000 complete proteomes and MMseqs2 easy-search against known fumarase sequences, we identified representative sequences for each class and constructed phylogenetic trees. 
                   Class I fumarases are found primarily in bacteria and in several eukaryotic groups, including Protozoa, SAR, and algae, with absence in fungi and archaea and low presence in plants and animals. Their patchy distribution and absence in archaea suggest horizontal gene transfer from bacteria to eukaryotes. Class II fumarases are ubiquitously distributed across bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes. Phylogenetic and genetic analyzes suggest a closer relationship between eukaryotic class II fumarases and bacterial homologs (particularly Alphaproteobacteria) compared to archaea. These results support the hypothesis that class II fumarase originated early on in bacteria and was then inherited by vertical gene transfer by eukaryotes. 
                   Analysis of protein sequences and structures for both classes demonstrates high evolutionary conservation, consistent with their essential catalytic function. Fumarases, TCA cycle enzymes, have been implicated in DNA damage response in numerous organisms, in all domains of life. These enzymes have also been shown to be dual targeted to mitochondria and the cytosol/nucleus in eukaryotes. We have examined how these two functions are linked to the evolution of fumarases and concluded that the extramitochondrial functions and subcellular localization of fumarases were determined much later in evolution. We conclude that metabolic signaling and its specific metabolites may provide the driving force for the fumarases' dual function, dual targeting, and interaction with different entities in the cell.

title: Polypharmacological target-aware molecule generation
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Designing compounds capable of modulating multiple target proteins simultaneously (i.e. polypharmacology) is critical for treating complex diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative disorders. However, AI-driven multitarget drug design remains severely hindered by the scarcity of multitarget 3D structural data and the inefficiency of traditional “generate-then-filter” pipelines. There is a pressing need for scalable methods that can satisfy diverse binding constraints across multiple proteins without relying on scarce structural priors. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     To overcome these bottlenecks, we reformulate multitarget drug design as a sequence-based generation task and introduce PolyTamGen, an end-to-end autoregressive framework. We first curate a large-scale ligand-centric bioactivity dataset from ChEMBL and BindingDB, comprising 1.6 million unique ligands and 4.9 million bioactivity entries. PolyTamGen encodes target protein sets using ESM3, compresses these high-dimensional features into compact tokens via an attention module, and feeds them into a sequence-based compound generator to produce the final multitarget ligands. We further apply Direct Preference Optimization to improve docking-based affinity proxies and drug-likeness. Extensive experiments on dual- and triple-target benchmarks demonstrate that PolyTamGen improves joint success rates over representative baselines while maintaining high chemical validity and diversity. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     The code is available at https://github.com/bjzgcai/PolyTamGen. The processed data, model checkpoints, and benchmark results are available at Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20594128.

title: Joint enzyme–reaction retrieval and catalytic optima prediction via multimodal fusion
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Enzyme–reaction retrieval prioritizes candidate biocatalysts for experimental follow-up, where recommendations should indicate catalytic compatibility and suitable pH and temperature conditions. Existing retrieval models optimize matching scores, whereas catalytic optima predictors are typically enzyme-level regressors because condition annotations are sparse. This separation leaves ranked pairs unevaluated for condition suitability and optima predictions without reaction context. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     We present GERO, a multimodal fusion framework integrating enzyme sequence semantics, sequence-derived pocket geometry, and molecular reaction representations through feature-gated fusion for condition-aware retrieval and catalytic optima estimation. We define the tolerance-restricted hit rate (Hit@k-TR), which requires both correct top-k retrieval and condition predictions within predefined tolerances. Across enzyme- and reaction-similarity splits, GERO improves Hit@k-TR over two-stage baselines under the primary tolerances. Benchmark examples and an iodinin biosynthesis case study illustrate candidate ranking and assay-condition estimation for experimental prioritization. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     Source code is available at https://github.com/ykxhs/GERO.

title: CMGL: confidence-guided multi-omics graph learning for cancer subtype classification
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Multi-omics integration can improve cancer subtyping, but modality informativeness and noise vary across cancer types and patients. Most graph methods for multi-omics data learn modality contributions within the downstream classification objective, leaving predictive reliability for each patient implicit. As a result, uninformative modalities can weaken the fused representation, while unreliable omics can introduce noisy patient relationships into graph propagation. To address these two problems, we propose confidence-guided multi-omics graph learning (CMGL), which produces a separate reliability estimate before fusion and uses consensus patient neighborhoods for graph classification. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     CMGL estimates modality confidence for each patient through evidential deep learning, fixes these values during fusion across omics, and performs classification on an independently specified consistency graph. On four MLOmics cancer-subtype tasks and the 32-class pan-cancer task, CMGL consistently improves over the strongest baseline, surpassing it by 4.03% in average accuracy on the four single-cancer tasks. Its representations recover the PAM50 intrinsic subtypes of breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA), and the model trained on BRCA transfers without fine tuning to kidney renal clear cell carcinoma, stratifying patients into prognostically distinct groups. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     The code is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21921069.

title: FAMUS: a few-shot learning framework for large-scale protein annotation
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Gene function prediction is pivotal in genomic and metagenomic data analysis. Current annotation tools typically rely on the most similar sequence from the referencedatabase and struggle to robustly set meaningful hit thresholds, causing a major challenge for reliable annotation. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     Here, we present Functional Annotation Method Using Supervised contrastive learning (FAMUS). FAMUS compares query sequences to a full array of profile Hidden Markov Models, encoding each sequence’s complete similarity profile, rather than only its top-scoring hit, into a condensed vector space that minimizes the distance between proteins from the same family. Unannotated sequences are incorporated as negative examples during training, enabling robust detection of proteins that fall outside the reference database without requiring user-defined thresholds. FAMUS outperformed KEGG’s native KofamScan for KEGG Orthology annotation and InterPro’s InterProScan for PANTHER family annotation, especially on realistic, sparsely annotated data. We used this approach to build four protein annotation models spanning the KEGG Orthology, InterPro, OrthoDB, and EggNOG databases. FAMUS is a comprehensive, modular framework that supports both pre-defined and user-specific databases. It can be readily integrated into genomic and metagenomic analysis pipelines for accurate, large-scale functional annotation. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     All four models are available as a conda package and via our web server at https://app.famus.bursteinlab.org/, and source code is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/burstein-lab/famus/ as well as a source code snapshot at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23132542.

title: smiMAD: adaptive multi-view graph learning for paired spatial omics integration
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Paired spatial omics technologies measure transcriptomic profiles together with epigenomic or proteomic profiles while preserving tissue context. Integration remains challenging because modalities differ in feature distributions, sparsity, and spatial dependencies. Existing methods may not fully model complementary graph views or adapt spatial constraints, limiting preservation of spatial organization and modality-specific information. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     We present smiMAD for paired spatial omics integration. smiMAD models spatial-neighborhood and molecular-feature graphs through graph-view-specific and common-information branches. An adaptive gate integrates graph-view and modality information, while an alignment–decorrelation objective promotes common-information embedding consistency and reduces branch redundancy. A dynamic spatial-consistency strategy progressively relaxes spatial constraints during training. Across 17 simulated and 15 real RNA–ATAC (assay for transposase-accessible chromatin) and RNA–protein datasets, smiMAD achieved competitive clustering accuracy, spatial coherence, and multimodal integration performance. Molecular marker patterns provided support for the inferred spatial regions. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     The source code is available at https://github.com/fdu-wangfeilab/smiMAD, with the version used in this study archived at https://zenodo.org/records/22931624. Data are available at https://zenodo.org/records/17207079.

title: CAD-score-LT: versatile contact area-based comparison of macromolecular structures, interfaces, and binding sites
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Comparison of macromolecular structural models requires similarity measures that remain informative for complexes, interfaces, and binding sites. Widely used scores emphasize global superposition or distance deviations and are not designed primarily for direct assessment of contact patterns. A fast and flexible contact-area-based alternative is therefore highly relevant. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     We present CAD-score-LT, a high-performance implementation of the Contact Area Difference score (CAD-score) for superposition-free comparison of macromolecular structures. CAD-score-LT evaluates tessellation-derived contact, binding-site, and solvent-accessible surface areas at atom, residue, and chain levels, and supports selective scoring of substructures, interfaces, and binding regions. The software also provides sequence-guided preprocessing, chain remapping, symmetry-adjusted ligand scoring, local scores output, and clustering. Benchmarking against previous CAD-score implementations on CASP16 oligomer model pairs showed near-identical scores but more than one order of magnitude lower running times, with speedups reaching up to 100-fold for whole-structure scoring and 200-fold for inter-chain interface scoring. Case studies in supplementary material demonstrate utility for large-scale model clustering, analysis of protein–nucleic acid interfaces, and evaluation of protein–ligand docking models. 
                   
                   
                     Availability and implementation 
                     A repository with the CAD-score-LT software and the reproducible benchmarking and example workflows is available at https://github.com/kliment-olechnovic/cadscore-lt-supplementary-info and archived at Zenodo https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21983528. The latest CAD-score-LT software is openly available under MIT license as a standalone C++ application at https://www.voronota.com/expansion_lt_cadscore/, and as a Python library at https://pypi.org/project/cadscorelt/.

title: Dynamic graph prior-guided latent adaptation for generalizable single-cell perturbation response prediction
abstract:
Abstract 
                   
                     Motivation 
                     Predicting transcriptional responses to drug perturbations in unseen cellular contexts is a central challenge in single-cell perturbation modeling. This challenge creates a need for models that combine flexible state transitions with structured biological prior knowledge. Existing data-driven models often struggle to generalize across unseen cell types, while many prior-based models rely on static biological graphs without explicitly conditioning prior influence on perturbation-specific target support. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     We propose DGP-LA, a dynamic graph-prior latent adaptation framework that refines biological priors and injects them as gated latent corrections within a cell-state-conditioned transition model. DGP-LA couples a transition backbone with perturbation-conditioned sparse graph refinement. It propagates gene-aligned target support over the refined graph and selectively injects the resulting topology-aware signal into the hidden representation. On Tahoe and NeurIPS, DGP-LA improves Pearson Delta relative to State by 8.7% and 35.8% for generalization across unseen cell types. In zero-shot drug perturbation response prediction on unseen cell types, it improves Pearson Delta relative to CRISP by 79.1% and 67.6%. The model also improves DE-gene recovery, response discrimination, and Hallmark pathway recovery, supporting adaptive latent integration of biological priors for more generalizable and biologically interpretable perturbation modeling. 
                   
                   
                     Availability 
                     DGP-LA’s source code and reproducibility materials are available at https://github.com/bieyl/DGP-LA and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22155398.

Interfacial microenvironments enable abiotic ribonucleoside formation in micro- and nanoscale compartments
abstract:
The abiotic emergence of ribonucleosides remains a central challenge in origin-of-life research because ribonucleosides form inefficiently and are often unstable under prebiotically plausible conditions. Here we show that interfacial microenvironments within aqueous micro- and nanoscale compartments containing D-ribose, phosphoric acid, and nucleobases promote ribonucleoside formation by creating reaction-permissive physicochemical conditions independent of the specific compartment type. Across a diverse range of compartmentalized systems, including gas–oil–water micro/nanobubbles, gas–water micro/nanobubbles, microscale lipid-bilayer vesicles, and oil–water emulsion systems, ribonucleosides form abiotically in the absence of enzymatic catalysis. Under selected interfacial conditions, multiple ribonucleosides, including cytidine, are generated without added catalysts. Comparison among these systems reveals that interfacial architecture and coupled physicochemical properties strongly influence both reaction efficiency and product stability. CO
                     2 
                    -based micro/nanobubbles support sustained cytidine accumulation, highlighting the importance of coupled gas–liquid and liquid–liquid interfaces. Ribonucleoside synthesis also depends on compartment size, whereas variations in oil content within micro/nanobubbles selectively modulate inosine formation, underscoring the sensitivity of nucleoside chemistry to interfacial properties. These findings identify interfacial microenvironments within micro- and nanoscale compartments as a general physical framework for ribonucleoside emergence and suggest that ubiquitous compartmentalized interfaces on early Earth could have provided robust settings for prebiotic ribonucleoside chemistry.

title: Cell identity competes with surface tension to determine stromal organization in tumor spheroids beyond the CAF shell paradigm
abstract: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are often found forming a peripheral stromal barrier around tumors. Here, this paradigm is challenged using microfabricated 3D cancer–CAF spheroid models combined with quantitative magnetic force tensiometry. A surface tension atlas is established for eight cancer cell lines, three CAF populations, and heterotypic tumor–CAF assemblies, spanning nearly two orders of magnitude. Surface tension is first shown to govern spheroid morphology and modulate drug response. Besides, CAFs consistently occupy the highest end of the surface tension hierarchy, predicting core rather than peripheral localization and directly challenging the shell paradigm. Yet confocal imaging reveals not only central accumulation but also complete CAF-tumor mixing, including in spheroids where cancer cells exhibit surface tensions nearly two orders of magnitude lower than CAFs. Surface tension alone therefore fails to predict CAF organization. Instead, the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) state of cancer cells emerges as a major determinant: epithelial-like tumors promote CAF core accumulation, whereas mesenchymal-like states favor persistent mixing. Peripheral CAF localization emerges only under restricted conditions combining high tumor cohesion and sequential stromal recruitment. Together, these results identify surface tension, EMT state, and assembly chronology as joint determinants of tumor–stroma architecture, revealing a context-dependent organization landscape rather than a universal CAF shell.

title:
Correction for Zamorano-Dominguez et al., Systemic

Discovery and characterization of miranthins, “Trojan horse” antibiotic modulators of bacterial composition in the oral microbiome
abstract:
Bacteria of the human microbiota encode an abundance of natural products that likely mediate bacterial competition, local colonization patterns, and human health and disease. However, very few of these compounds have been identified and characterized to date. During our investigation of
                     Streptococcus 
                     mitis 
                    , an important early colonizer of the oral cavity, we identified and structurally characterized a family of peptide natural products, termed miranthins herein, that contain an unusual macrocycle formed by an Asp-Cys β-carbon thioether crosslink. We determined that the most abundantly secreted miranthin is a “Trojan horse” antibiotic that enters sensitive cells via the Ami oligopeptide transporter, is hydrolyzed and activated by aminopeptidase N, and subsequently inhibits ribosomal translation to curb the growth of streptococcal competitors. The miranthins are narrow-spectrum antibiotics that could enable
                     S. mitis 
                    to modulate community dynamics in the oral cavity, highlighting the importance of peptide natural products in interspecies competition in the microbiome.

title: Thermodynamic origin of atmospheric new particle formation: Theory for stable nucleating pairs
abstract:

title:
Nonclassical growth to mesoporous quasi-single crystal CeO
                     2 
                    superstructures with a well-defined surface
abstract:
Single-crystal materials are essential for fundamental catalysis studies and advanced technologies; however, synthesizing single crystals that simultaneously integrate mesoporosity, tunable size, and well-defined surfaces remains challenging. Here, we report a wet-chemical, template-free strategy to synthesize mesoporous quasi-single-crystal CeO
                     2 
                    superparticles (SPs). Operando wide- and small-angle X-ray scattering combined with theoretical modeling reveal a nonclassical growth mechanism driven by the oriented attachment of nanocluster building blocks. This process yields high-surface-area quasi-single crystals that preferentially expose energetically favorable (111) facets on both the external surfaces and internal pore walls, thereby enhancing the stabilization of active sites when used as heterogeneous catalyst supports. Using this approach, we demonstrate broad applicability by synthesizing highly dispersed precious metal–loaded CeO
                     2 
                    (M/CeO
                     2 
                    , M = Pd, Pt, Rh, or Ir) and metal-doped CeO
                     2 
                    (Cu–CeO
                     2 
                    ) SPs. Moreover, Pd/CeO
                     2 
                    SPs exhibit effective stabilization of Pd clusters in CO
                     2 
                    hydrogenation to methanol, delivering a high methanol selectivity of 85% and markedly improved durability compared with conventional supports.

title: Integrating cooperative breeding with reciprocity and culture extends Hamilton’s rule to humans
abstract: We study how kinship and reciprocity shape giving and child care support in societies with limited access to markets. Extending Hamilton’s rule to incorporate reciprocity, we test it using behavioral data from dictator games and surveys in remote matrilocal and patrilocal villages of northeast India (N = 406 parents of young children). We replicate with data from urban Manila neighborhoods (N = 301) and the Solomon Islands (N = 624). Consistent with predictions, transfers to recipients increase with genetic relatedness to the donor and even more with relatedness to the donor’s child—a hallmark of reciprocity anchored in shared genetic investment. Nonanonymous conditions amplify giving, especially to nonkin. Cultural norms shape cooperation, but do not trump genetic relatedness. These results underscore the role of affinal ties and reciprocal exchange in sustaining cooperation, and suggest a mechanism through which cooperative breeding could contribute to the emergence of generalized reciprocity and human sociality.

title:
Structural insights into the coupling mechanism of vectorial CO
                     2 
                    uptake by DAB1
abstract:
CO
                     2 
                    transporters enable bacterial CO
                     2 
                    -concentrating mechanisms by catalyzing directional hydration of CO
                     2 
                    , yet the basis of this vectorial carbonic anhydrase (CA) activity remains an open question. We used cryoelectron microscopy to determine the structure of the DAB1 complex from
                     Thermocrinis albus 
                    to 2.29 Å, revealing a heterotrimer in which a deeply buried β-CA active site in DabA is structurally coupled to the proton-translocating subunit DabB. Two conformational states define distinct solvent channels for substrate entry and product exit. A suppressor screen identifies mutations that disrupt coupling while retaining CA activity, underlying the importance of conserved residues that link proton translocation to active-site remodeling. These results support a model in which proton-driven conformational changes regulate substrate access to the active site, enabling vectorial CO
                     2 
                    hydration.

title: Phylogenomics confirms Palaeoptera monophyly and illuminates the origin of winged insects
abstract: The origin and early radiation of winged insects (Pterygota) represent one of the most transformative events in terrestrial evolution, yet phylogenetic relationships among their basalmost lineages (Ephemeroptera, Odonata and Neoptera) continue to be a central debate within insect systematics. Here, we present the most taxonomically comprehensive phylogenomic analysis to date, leveraging genomic and transcriptomic data from 101 species, including 16 sequenced ephemeropteran genomes. Employing 1,367 universal single-copy orthologs across two supermatrices, we used concatenation- and coalescent-based frameworks under homogeneous and heterogeneous, and multispecies coalescent models. Our analyses support Palaeoptera monophyly. Although coalescent-based methods initially suggested a Chiastomyaria (Ephemeroptera + Neoptera) topology, subsequent signal dissection and topology tests confirm that the preponderance of genomic signal favors a monophyletic Palaeoptera. Furthermore, we identify incomplete lineage sorting and gene tree estimation error as the primary drivers of previous topological conflicts. Our molecular dating results point to an Early Devonian origin of crown-Pterygota, whereas crown-Palaeoptera first emerged in the Late Devonian. By reconciling molecular evidence with morphological synapomorphies, such as wing-base sclerite homologies, this study provides a coherent framework for the early evolution of winged insects, supports a single origin of wings, and identifies the neopteran wing-folding mechanism as a singular evolutionary innovation.

title: A multiscale framework for heme crystallization inhibition: From single-molecule step-capping to parasite suppression
abstract:
Heme crystallization is central to malaria parasites’ survival during the erythrocytic stage of the disease, yet how clinically relevant antimalarial drugs modulate this process at the molecular level remains unclear. Here we employ stage-resolved parasite assays and multiscale in vitro approaches to explore the interactions between lumefantrine (LF), one of the popular components of current combination therapies, and hematin crystallization. Pulse LF suppresses
                     Plasmodium falciparum 
                    during both ring and trophozoite stages. Under biomimetic conditions, LF markedly reduces β-hematin crystal growth rates. High-resolution atomic force microscopy reveals that individual LF molecules bind directly to crystal steps, physically constraining step motion through a previously unreported step-capping mechanism. This localized inhibition propagates to the mesoscale, producing step broadening, reduced interstep spacing, and causing surface kinetic roughening. In contrast to its strong inhibition of crystal growth, LF enhances hematin nucleation by promoting the formation of mesoscopic hematin-rich clusters, as detected by a combination of scattering and microscopy techniques. Attachment of the nucleated crystallites to larger crystal surfaces initiates a nonclassical inhibition sequence by straining the crystal interface, which further impedes step growth.

title: Improved assessment of Alaskan Arctic coastal wave exposure accounting for landfast ice
abstract: Simulations of the ocean wave climate are critical for assessment of coastal processes and hazards in observation sparse regions such as the Arctic. While the multidecade wind and ice datasets necessary for driving long-term wave simulations have proven reliable for such efforts, the presence of landfast ice along shorelines at scales not represented by these data has been a persistent uncertainty impeding accurate analysis of impacts to Arctic coasts. Here, we explore this uncertainty by producing a historical high-resolution wave simulation and combining simulation outputs with landfast ice data for the Alaskan Arctic. The resulting dataset yields an improved assessment of coastal waves and identifies stark contrasts in the seasonal wave exposure of the Chukchi and Beaufort regions. Notably, analysis shows that absent supplemented landfast ice, coastal ice cover is broadly underestimated by 10 to 25 d, resulting in wave energy being overestimated by 5 to 10% in shallow depths nearshore. Notably, these figures can reach up to 70 d of underestimation for ice cover and 48% overestimation of wave energy in certain locations. The persistent overestimation and potential for extreme positive biases in coastal wave assessment highlight the need for representation of landfast ice in Arctic coastal analysis efforts and our analysis reveals the spatial and temporal biases for related research.

title: Double periodicity of the AnkyrinG-associated complex in the axon initial segment
abstract:
The axon initial segment (AIS), situated within the first 20 to 60 µm of the axon, is essential for action potential generation and maintenance of axonal identity [M. N. Rasband,
                     Nat. Rev. Neurosci. 
                     11 
                    , 552–562 (2010)]. Its structure relies on the beta (β)-IV-spectrin/AnkyrinG (AnkG) scaffold arranged periodically underneath the plasma membrane, harboring diverse membrane proteins [K. Xu, G. Zhong, X. Zhuang,
                     Science 
                     339 
                    , 452–456 (2013); K. L. Hedstrom, Y. Ogawa, M. N. Rasband,
                     J. Cell Biol. 
                     183 
                    , 635–640 (2008)]. Although a ~190-nm cytoskeletal periodic organization is well established, the precise stoichiometry and spatial arrangement of AIS proteins within the ~190-nm spatial period remain rudimentary, mostly for lack of sufficient spatial resolution and labeling efficiency. Here, using expansion microscopy and cryoelectron tomography, which overcome these technical limitations, we present data on the organization of the AnkG-associated complex within the ~190-nm spatial period. We demonstrate that exactly two AnkG molecules are situated within each period and with their C termini separated by ~80 nm. By contrast, the AnkG-associated cell-adhesion protein neurofascin-186 appears in clusters of varying sizes that are consistent with the periodic organization of AnkG pairs, yet suggesting a more complex molecular arrangement between the two molecules. Altogether, our approach provides insights into AIS molecular organization and protein stoichiometry.

title: Coordinated transformations of the labyrinth and occiput during the dinosaur–bird transition
abstract: Evolutionary shape changes of the vertebrate semicircular canals (SCCs) are often ascribed to evolutionary transitions in locomotion, including the origin of flight during the dinosaur–bird transition. However, the potential for transformations of braincase architecture to influence SCC shape independent of sensory-functional adaptation has generally been overlooked. We evaluate the influence of both factors using a large dataset of 146 living and recently extinct crown birds, including taxa representing ~24 independent evolutionary losses of flight, together with Mesozoic stem avialans, nonavialan dinosaurs, and pterosaurs. Among crown birds, evolutionary changes in locomotor capabilities, including the total loss of flight, have only weak effects on SCC shape, contrasting with large effects from changes in braincase geometry. Notably, rotation of the occiput toward a ventral orientation is associated with important changes to SCC shape that match those observed during the dinosaur–bird transition. This suggests that evolutionary transformations of SCC shape during the Mesozoic origin of avian flight resulted from evolutionary changes in the orientation of the craniocervical joint, and not from tuning of SCC sensory function. These findings illuminate the importance of integrated morphological changes to the head-neck system during bird origins and challenge the long-standing assumption that SCC morphology enables confident inferences of the locomotor capabilities of extinct vertebrates.

title: Direct physical contacts with epithelial cells regulate leukocyte actin dynamics to facilitate intraepithelial motility in vivo
abstract: Efficient immune cell migration requires physical interactions with surrounding tissues. While tissue matrix mechanics influence leukocyte motility, it is unknown how leukocytes exert pushing and pulling forces to traverse cell-dense epithelial tissues in vivo. Here, we leverage the optical transparency of larval zebrafish to identify how physical interactions with epithelial cells regulate mechanisms of neutrophil force generation to navigate cell-dense tissues. Confining forces from epithelial cells induce a mechanosensitive central actin network, mediated by Cdc42 and Wiskott–Aldrich Syndrome Protein, which exerts expansile forces on surrounding cells to dilate a path for migration. In concert, direct cell-to-cell (leukocyte–epithelial) contacts mediated by integrin ɑE recognition of epithelial cadherin generate traction forces to enable forward motility. Together, our findings identify how physical interactions with the surrounding cellular environment regulate leukocyte motility through epithelial tissue in vivo.

title: A Kv4.2-mGluR5 complex drives enhanced depotentiation in a mouse model of improved cognitive flexibility
abstract:
Memory updating promotes cognitive flexibility by enabling suppression of outdated information to optimize behavioral strategies in response to a changing environment. While some circuits involved have been identified, the synaptic mechanisms underlying this process remain uncertain. Here, using a recently developed Kv4.2 knock-in mouse model (Kv4.2TA), we identify a metaplasticity in the hippocampus that accompanies an improvement in cognitive flexibility. Mutation of a C-terminal phosphorylation site (T607) in the alpha subunit of the voltage-gated K
                     + 
                    channel protein Kv4.2 drives boosted depotentiation of spike timing-dependent long-term synaptic potentiation mediated by mGluR5 receptors, putative constituents of Kv4.2 macromolecular complexes. We found that mGluR5 receptors are required for the improved cognitive flexibility observed in Kv4.2TA mice. These findings reveal a synaptic correlate associated with memory updating in cognitive flexibility and spotlight the Kv4.2-mGluR5 complex as a therapeutic target for disorders characterized by impairments in cognitive flexibility.

title: A water-pinning hot spot drives templated tau aggregation
abstract:
Tau assembles into fibrillar aggregates that are pathological hallmarks of a group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively called tauopathies. Templated aggregation of naïve tau to seeding-competent fibrils that proceed from cell to cell is a key driver of prion-like progression of tauopathies. This study tests the hypothesis that tau, an intrinsically disordered protein, achieves in-register stacking to form seed-competent fibrils by a pinning action of tau to each other and/or the seed surface via a single dominant hotspot to avoid mismatch in tau stacking to fibrils. Structured solvation water has been proposed to be a signature of such hot spots at both the tau fibril-end surface and soluble tau monomers. Although jR2R3-P301L tau exhibits a heterogeneous hydration landscape in its intrinsically disordered state, with enhanced water structuring near the P301L mutation site, it is unclear whether a localized hotspot exists at the fibril end surface and surface water facilitates the initial contacts in templated aggregation. Using rapid
                     1 
                    H-
                     15 
                    N SOFAST-HMQC NMR to track seed-induced aggregation of jR2R3-P301L in real time, complemented by molecular dynamics simulation of fibril surface hydration, we identify a residue-specific pinning hotspot that is prone to dewetting followed by sequential folding and incorporation of the remaining segment in a two-step dock-and-lock process. Site-specific spin labeling further demonstrates that blocking this pinning hotspot disrupts templated aggregation, leading to shorter fibrils. The identification of a dominant pinning site will facilitate the rational design of binders to effectively disrupt fibril extension or serve as diagnostic or therapeutic strategies.

title: Heterochronicity shapes brain network formation
abstract: Brain network formation unfolds on a nonuniform developmental timetable, with different cortical regions generating connections at different developmental phases. Generative network models (GNMs) aim to uncover the principles underpinning the organization of connectomes by creating synthetic networks according to simple computational rules. These models capture the connectome’s topology, operationalized here as the cumulative distributions of network metrics (e.g., modularity, small-worldness, rich-club structure). However, GNMs typically ignore the differential timing of connectivity formation, and by omitting this temporal programme they often misplace topological features in physical space. Here, we add a heterochronous growth term to GNMs and use a model fitness function that weighs topology and topography equally. Topography refers to the spatial embedding of the network—the actual anatomical positions of the axonal tracts. With these advances, we can generate synthetic networks that more faithfully reproduce the spatial layout of diffusion-MRI connectomes from two independent adult cohorts. Compared with classical, temporally agnostic models, heterochronous simulations improve model fit, accurately locate cortical hubs and modules across individuals, and converge on a single caudal-to-rostral gradient of brain maturation. Overall, integrating heterochronicity makes GNMs more faithful to brain development, and allows for better identification of individual differences in network formation.

title: P-body-mediated RNA decay controls neural crest EMT
abstract:
Neural crest cells, a multipotent vertebrate stem cell population, undergo a tightly regulated epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) to delaminate from the neural tube and initiate migration. Neural crest EMT is controlled by a transient pulse of
                     Draxin 
                    , which acts as a molecular rheostat of canonical Wnt signaling, and is then rapidly downregulated by unknown mechanisms. To address this, here we use in vivo reporter assays and live RNA imaging to show that
                     Draxin 
                    mRNA is rapidly degraded posttranscriptionally via its 3′ untranslated region. We found that
                     Draxin 
                    transcripts are targeted to cytoplasmic processing bodies (P-bodies), which are membrane-less sites of RNA processing and decay. Disruption of P-bodies by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated depletion of the RNA helicase DDX6 prevented posttranscriptional downregulation of
                     Draxin 
                    and impaired neural crest EMT in vivo. These findings parallel observations in human patients carrying
                     DDX6 
                    mutations, who exhibit defects in P-body assembly and craniofacial abnormalities associated with neural crest dysfunction. Together, our results identify P-bodies as regulators of
                     Draxin 
                    mRNA decay and reveal a spatially organized mechanism of RNA turnover that controls neural crest EMT during vertebrate development.

title: Astrocytic facilitation of somatic NMDARs underpins hippocampal E-S potentiation
abstract: EPSP–spike (E-S) potentiation is a form of plasticity defined by a persistent increase in neuronal spike output for a given synaptic input, reflecting enhanced E-S coupling independent of synaptic strength. However, its cellular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we show that brief induction of E-S potentiation triggers a sustained calcium activity increase in astrocytes adjacent to the hippocampal CA1 pyramidal layer. Mechanistically, E-S potentiation critically requires GluN2B-containing N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) localized to the neuronal soma. Sustained astrocytic activity promotes E-S potentiation through vesicular release of D-serine, which enhances tonic activation of somatic NMDARs, suppresses A-type potassium currents, and produces a lasting increase in neuronal excitability. Functionally, this astrocyte-dependent E-S potentiation lowers the threshold for subsequent long-term potentiation, conferring a metaplastic influence on hippocampal circuits. These findings identify an astrocyte-neuron signaling mechanism that drives intrinsic plasticity and establish somatic NMDARs as a key site of astrocytic regulation of hippocampal output.

title: Imaging and recording of synaptic zinc in the brain by covalent chemistry–based semisynthetic biosensors
abstract:
Labile zinc ions (Zn
                     2+ 
                    ) are stored in glutamatergic vesicles at specific excitatory synapses in the central nervous system and released into synaptic clefts in an activity-dependent manner. However, the precise roles of synaptic Zn
                     2+ 
                    remain unclear due to a lack of tools capable of analyzing Zn
                     2+ 
                    with synapse-level spatial resolution in vivo. Here, we developed neuroreceptor-based semisynthetic biosensors that function as integrating dosimeters, recording synaptic Zn
                     2+ 
                    by covalent chemistry in the living mouse brain. Using a chemical knock-in strategy, we introduced activity-based Zn
                     2+ 
                    probes with distinct affinities into endogenous α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazole-propionic acid or γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptors. These in-brain-constructed Zn
                     2+ 
                    sensors enabled region-specific mapping of Zn
                     2+ 
                    in synaptic clefts in the living mouse brain. Imaging-based analyses revealed differences in apparent Zn
                     2+ 
                    levels at excitatory and inhibitory synapses across hippocampal regions during kainate-induced seizures, providing insights into the physiological and pathological functions of synaptic Zn
                     2+ 
                    .

title: Antiferromagnetism and tightly bound Cooper pairs induced by kinetic frustration
abstract:
Antiferromagnetism and superconductivity are often viewed as competing orders in correlated electron systems. Here, we demonstrate that kinetic frustration in hole motion facilitates their coexistence within the square-lattice repulsive Hubbard model. Combining exact analytical solutions on tailored geometries with large-scale numerical simulations, we reveal a robust pairing mechanism: Holes on opposite sublattices behave as if they carry opposite effective charges due to spin singlet formation from kinetic frustration. This emergent property suppresses phase separation and fosters a coherent
                     
                       
                         d 
                       
                     
                    -wave superconducting channel embedded within a long-range antiferromagnetic background. Our findings establish a minimal yet broadly applicable framework for stabilizing strong-coupling superconductivity in doped Mott insulators.

title: Multiyear dual-isotope fingerprinting at South Asian receptor sites constrains carbon monoxide sources and enhanced oxidation
abstract:
Carbon monoxide (CO) is an indirect short-lived climate forcer with uncertainties both in sources and its role in atmospheric oxidation. Based on nine winter-long dual-isotope campaigns at two South Asian receptor sites intercepting the continental outflow, we quantified CO source contributions and emission–sink dynamics. Combustion accounts for 68 to 74% of South Asia regional CO (including 34 to 37% from biomass burning) with secondary atmospheric oxidation contributing 26 to 32% (dominated by oxidation of nonmethane volatile organic compounds (NMVOCs) at 21 to 26%, with methane oxidation contributing 5.5 to 6.4%). These isotope-observational constraints suggest a twice higher role for atmospheric oxidation than in model estimates. Spatially, the absolute contributions of both primary and secondary CO decrease from the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the northern Indian Ocean, while the relative contribution of oxidation-derived CO increases, indicating enhanced secondary CO production near source regions. Observation-model comparison suggests that transport from the continental areas dominates CO over adjacent oceanic regions, with minor local production. During the COVID-19 emission perturbation, combustion-derived CO fell sharply in absolute terms, NMVOC-derived CO rose, and CH
                     4 
                    -derived CO remained stable, providing an observational constraint on the sensitivity of atmospheric oxidation to emission changes. Our results reveal a significant contribution of CO from atmospheric oxidation in South Asia, calling for a reassessment of regional emission–oxidation coupling in models and of mitigation strategies.

title: Nutrient legacies from elephant megacarcasses create coldspots of biodiversity and hotspots of ecosystem processes
authors: Courtney G. ReedNathan P. LemoineMichelle L. BudnyVincent C. ClarkeJohan T. du ToitRyan HelcoskiHelga KnoetzeJane M. LucasJoshua P. SchimelIzak P. J. SmitTercia StrydomAimee G. TallianDave I. ThompsonDeron E.
